title: The Kalvatar Archipelago
subtitle: A world between salt and stars
summary: On Argentus, a vast archipelago stretches south from Assios to the polar ice. Most of it lies beyond the Council’s charts.

sections.title: An ocean of islands
paragraphs: The last census counted more than 5,800 islands. Nobody knows the true number. Islands rise, islands drown, and some appear only at the King Tide.
The Council of the Charted Isles governs about one island in six. Beyond its reach lie independent communities, wild water, old powers, and stories that have never reached Goldwind.

sections.title: A shared language, many worlds
paragraphs: The Island tongue carries trade between peoples who keep their own languages, customs, and histories. A voyage from the far Frontier to the ice takes five or six months without misadventure. News is often months old by the time it arrives.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: How many islands?
How much is governed? The rest, most of the map, is uncharted: frontier, wild water, and rumor.
Everyone speaks the Island tongue for trade; most people also speak the tongue of their own people or region.

Your ancestors, or your neighbors' ancestors, came here as refugees. About 190 years ago, the great houses of Assios lost their war against the Korvan Imperium and fled south across the sea in a slow, desperate Exodus: the Landing. Everything the Council is, it built from that defeat. The Imperium still rules half of Assios, still fights the long Thousand-Year War against the Baronies and the Free Cities, and still looks south.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A whaler swears he counted an island off the southern lanes that was there on the way out and gone on the way home. The Chartwrights have filed it anyway.” (heard among the Chartwrights)

facts: More than 5,800 islands; the true number is unknown

epigraph.quote: Five thousand eight hundred islands, they say. Ask a chartwright and she'll tell you the number is wrong, and that it was wrong yesterday too.
epigraph.by: A Goldwind ferryman to a passenger

title: Northern Frontier
subtitle: Hold or drown.
summary: The cold northern gateway: iron, fog, hospitality, and the strait that separates the islands from Assios.

sections.title: The northern door
paragraphs: The Frontier stands between the archipelago and the mainland’s long war. Its ports are built around hard weather, hard work, and the duty of keeping a door open for the people behind you.

sections.title: Ports and customs
paragraphs: Ironfort is where the Charter was signed. Bastion is the seat of House Faust and its tourneys. Greyhaven lives with the Murk, a fog thick enough that ships find one another by bells. Stormreach keeps the storm-watch.
A stranger at a Frontier door is given a bowl before a question. Hospitality here is a law of survival, not a matter of good manners.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Northern Frontier is the door of the archipelago, and everyone who lives here knows it. Every great house in Kalvatar has, somewhere in its family, an ancestor who landed in the Frontier fog and decided to stay. That history gives the region its pride and its patience. The people here measure a person by what they can do in a crisis, and they expect the rest of the archipelago to remember who holds the gate.

The Frontier is not rich in the way the Heartland is rich. It sells strength instead of luxury: horses, iron, salt, timber, and the labor of its garrisons. Its wealth comes mostly from the Gate-Tithe, the tenth part of every Anchor's worth of goods that passes through the gate between Kalvatar and Assios, and from the knowledge that the Frontier stands between the islands and the Korvan Imperium. Both things make the Frontier's loyalty to the Council conditional and its suspicion of the Heartland almost constant.

The region's sociability is a matter of the hearth and the harbor rather than the salon. Hospitality is given without fuss: a hot bowl, a place by the fire, and no questions until morning. Turning a stranger out into the cold is the one unforgivable thing, and the old fog-towns have hanged men for it.

sections.title: Geography
paragraphs: The Frontier is a scatter of islands and headlands along the cold northern waters, with the strait to Assios on its north edge. The coastline is cut into deep inlets, sea-stacks, and shoals, and the fog comes in off the water for days at a time, especially in the Murk, the autumn fog season that the Storm-Watch was made to answer.

The main islands fall into three groups. The Ironfort Reach holds the capital-port and its satellite harbors, with the broadest and safest anchorage in the north. The Bastion Holds are a chain of fortress islands along the eastern sea-road, linked by causeways and bridges that the Faust engineers built and rebuilt over four generations. The Stormreach Coil is the strait that the Vanris house controls, where the currents pull hard between the islands and the wind comes around the headlands with a shriek that sailors learn to hear before they see the weather.

Inland, the Northreach moors rise in gorse and heather toward the high Tarvan country. The land is poor for crops but excellent for horses and sheep, and it is the homeland of the horned Tarvan clans, who keep their own ways and their own moots on the open heath. The Saltreach pans lie on the flat western coast, where the sea is let in through sluices and left to dry in the wind, and where the Hallorn salt-houses have grown rich enough to buy a Council seat's worth of influence in a bad year.

sections.title: Life and Society
paragraphs: The Frontier is a melting-pot of arrivals, soldiers, sailors, traders, and refugees off the Crown Route, shaped by hard weather into a practical and unsentimental people. The working day begins with a harbor bell. The dress is heavy and functional: wool, leather, oiled cloth, and iron, in greys, browns, and naval blue, because Ironfort woad is the cheapest dye in the north and salt-stains and soot do not show on it. Fur-lined hoods come from the Northreach pelts, and the house-colors appear as tabards, sashes, and cloak-clasps.

Salt fish and black bread, root-and-barley stew, smoked meats, hard cheese, and Ironfort black ale carry a household through the Murk. The street meal is the picket, a smoked-herring stick sold from the quayside barrows. The sea-burial is the Frontier's most solemn rite. The dead are given to the water with their name spoken once and not again, and their kin-knit sweater, a family pattern worked into every garment, tells the sea and the harbor who they were.

The region's common games reflect its work. The Haul is the dockers' rope-pulling contest that settles disputes between crews, and the Gatehold board game is a Frontier pastime of walls, garrisons, and sieges. The Frontier's youth prove themselves at the great martial tourneys of Bastion, and the Storm-Watch lights every harbor-lamp in the north before the Murk comes in.

The house-courts hear the serious cases, the Faust iron law and the Holst customs-codes govern the trade, and punishment runs to fines, the lash, labor, exile, or the rope. Exile in the Frontier is a slower sentence, since the sea does not forgive a man who has no harbor to go back to.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Gate-Tithe is cheating us in both directions. It keeps the gold in Ironfort and sends the paper to Goldwind.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“The Widow's Teeth are singing a new tune. The old women say a boat will be lost in the Gap before the Murk is over.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“Johann Faust has been seen in a Greyhaven tavern with a man who wears the Last Psalm's badge. Nobody knows which side he means to take.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“Mortimer Vanris will sell the Stormguard to the Heartland before the year is out. His brother has already written to the Council about it.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)

epigraph.quote: We don't ask what you are. We ask if you'll stand on the wall when the fog comes in.

title: Central Heartland
subtitle: Coin remembers.
summary: The rich, temperate center of charted Kalvatar: Council chambers, observatories, guilds, porcelain, and power.

sections.title: The charted center
paragraphs: Goldwind is the capital, home to the Council, the University, and the Reckoners’ Hall. Beyond it, Sunhold is the largest island and a proud rival, while Highspire watches the stars and Everfall glows beneath its volcano.

sections.title: A region of obligations
paragraphs: Wealth travels here through contracts, favors, and names that matter. The Heartland’s political life is inseparable from its guilds and houses, and debts have a way of outliving the people who first incurred them.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Heartland is the controlled core of the archipelago, the prosperous and temperate middle where the Council sits, the University teaches, and the great houses compete for every seat that matters. It is cosmopolitan in a way the Frontier is not. Scholars, courtiers, bankers, master-artisans, and the servants of a hundred competing interests all live here, and all of them learned young that a smile and a blade are the same tool held at different angles. The Heartland is the most civilized region in the islands and the most dangerous to underestimate.

The Council's five seats are filled from the Heartland, and the Congress and the Reckoners' Hall decide who can borrow, build, and buy. The region holds the great banks, the University's Arcane Registry, the Concord's grandest temple, and the castle-heights of House Vol Kaern, whose shadow falls across the Council it does not yet rule. Every ambitious family in the archipelago has a cousin who wants a seat in Goldwind, and every seat in Goldwind is a debt waiting to be called.

The Heartland's politics are braided through its social life. The social season, with its balls and matches, is a parliament by other means. University convocations are as political as they are academic. The Concord blessings of sun and tide, the Merrin Games in the harbors, and the noble weddings of the Veldane web are all occasions for a seat to be promised or a debt to be remembered. "A smile in Goldwind has two faces," the saying goes, and it is the first thing a visitor learns.

sections.title: Geography
paragraphs: The Heartland is a cluster of islands near the middle of the charted sea, with the rich farmlands of the western slopes, the bright terraces of Sunhold, the fens of the Goldwind gulf, and the eastern coast of Silverport and Easthold facing the open water. The land is temperate, with mild winters and warm summers, and the Heartland's winds are famous. The gulf of Goldwind has the steadiest sailing-breeze in the archipelago, which is why Eamos built his town there, and why the kites of the Heartland's great kite-duels fly on glass-dusted lines above the harbor on summer afternoons.

The Goldwind Gulf is the region's heart. The harbor, the banking quarter, the University, and the Council Hall stand on ascending rings above it, and the Vol Kaern heights crown the whole city. The Sunhold Terraces climb the western hills in step-cut tea-gardens of brightleaf and vines. Highspire is a spire-island of the Starborn house, its towers reaching above the cloud, with the Singing Cliffs along its shore. Aurelion lies on the northern coast in the smoke of its forges. Everfall is a volcanic isle in the east, its craters and glass-fields above the sleeping Savage Lord KakanKal and the Darlath mines. Silverport and Easthold face the open sea on the east, and Westwatch holds the stone and coal of the western heights. Pearl Groove is a shallow lagoon of pearl-clans, the source of the reefpurple that colors the robes of the Council and the high clergy.

sections.title: Life and Society
paragraphs: The Heartland's people are urbane, political, and fond of display. Dress is status made visible: silks, brocades, and fine wools, with house-colors and sigils worn with care and the ever-shifting fashions of Goldwind set by the Congress's tailors. Reefpurple is reserved by custom for Council seats and high clergy; the dyes of the south pay Holst's customs-codes on the way in and are worn as a claim on the wearer's means. University folk wear the copper rings of their licensed spell-rank. The working folk of the Heartland wear oat-and-blue.

Food is the cuisine of plenty. Spiced dishes and delicate sauces, Silverport's incense-spiced fare, fine wines from the Sunhold hills, the goldcask spirit kellum aged in wine-casks, and the bitter ceremonial cacao of the south all find their way to the Heartland's tables. The Heartland's hot drink is the pale brightleaf cup with citrus, and the coffee-houses fight the terrace-growers over it with the fervor of a feud. The Windborne Cake, a sweet loaf of the Goldwind bakers, is sold on the harbor wall at dawn, and the Windborne Choir sings from the wall as the bakers' shutters open.

The region's pastimes are the card game Council, which is played in every salon and taught to the children of the houses, and the kite-duels of the summer afternoons. The Turning, the sunset promenade along the Goldwind harbor wall, is the city's great social stage. On a summer evening, everyone who matters walks the wall, and everyone who wants to matter walks it too.

The Heartland's sayings are courtly and double-edged. The Council's law, the Concord's moral weight, the houses' own courts, and the Holst customs-codes overlap, and the Arcane Registry is enforced with particular zeal. Wealth and standing bend outcomes, and everyone pretends otherwise, which is itself a kind of law.

sections.title: The southern pool fashion
paragraphs: Some nobles and wealthy households have begun importing Jewelfins from Jakupur. Indoor pools built around a single spectacular fish are becoming a fashionable display of wealth, with separate pools needed for a larger collection.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Mortimer Vanris will sell the Stormguard to the Heartland before the year is out. His brother has already written to the Council about it.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“Tana Sukuun has sold a Dreadmaw to the Heartland. The buyer is a Vol Kaern agent, and the saurian is named after the Vol Kaern tower.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“Dio Emberheart has been seen walking in the Sunhold gardens. The people who saw him say he was not quite the same man who walked there last year.” (heard in the Central Heartland)
“Kastan Vol Kaern is buying Bastion's debts through the Zane house. He will own the Frontier's gate before the Council knows he has begun.” (heard in the Central Heartland)

epigraph.quote: In Goldwind every debt is remembered, every favor is counted, and every smile has a ledger behind it.
epigraph.by: A Heartland factor, explaining the city to a cousin

title: Southern Wilds
subtitle: The jungle keeps its own.
summary: The largest region is a mosaic of jungles, river peoples, Confederacies, colonists, and freed communities.

sections.title: Many peoples, two laws
paragraphs: Native chant-keepers and colonial courts disagree over land, authority, and whose account of the past will stand. The south is home to many distinct peoples and Confederacies, not a single culture.

sections.title: Where the rivers lead
paragraphs: Jakupur is the saurian city-state of the White Flame. Southhaven is a colonial port of coffee and southleaf. Golgarma holds Orka ruins, while the Bonewilds are a country of immense, sun-bleached bones.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Southern Wilds are the largest region in the archipelago and the least governed. They are a mosaic, not a country: proud native tribes and Confederacies, colonists and freed thralls, saurian-tamers, rebels, pirates, and merchants, all living under the same heat and the same pressure. The south is the richest and most varied culture in Kalvatar, and its people will tell you so, often and with a laugh. Where the Heartland is one cosmopolitan blend, the south is a constellation of distinct cultures sharing one land. That is its glory, and it is the lever its exploiters use against it.

Two laws fight across the Wilds. The native law of the chant-keepers, the war-codes, and the restorative judgment that seeks to mend the tribe is one. The colonial law of the Council, the Charterhouse Company's indenture contracts, and the tyrant-houses' brutal order is the other. Which law reaches a person depends entirely on who they are. The gap between the two is where the rebels of the south are born, and where the saurian racing, the slaver rings, and the Crimson Legion find their recruits.

The Council's writ is thinnest here. The Armada's Emerald Wrath patrols the rivers in gunboats, the Charterhouse Company sells the southern salt and the indentures, and the great houses send their stewards to Southhaven to count the coffee. The Wilds run themselves, and the outside powers have learned to bargain with them rather than rule them.

sections.title: Geography
paragraphs: The Southern Wilds are a warm, wet, and wide country of jungle, river, and mountain. The land runs from the great western landmass, with its forests and river-basins, to a long crescent of islands curving east and half-enclosing a central inner sea.

The western landmass is the largest land in the archipelago and the heart of the native world. Its rivers, the Nine Mouths and the Laughing Flood among them, carry the water of the deep green to the sea. The Anvil Reach is a cold cordillera rising from the jungle's heart, where the trees thin into stone and snow, the one place in the warm south where winter lives year-round. The Cathedral Green is a forest of titan trees whose root-vaults form natural naves, and the Bonewilds are a white plain of half-buried titan bones under the southern sun. The inner sea is warm and shallow, bounded by the islands, and its shores hold Jakupur, Southhaven, and the old Orka stairs.

Along the southwestern edge of the landmass, the jungle grows thick and soundless toward the Sealed Waters, and the Council's maps stop at Zal'Kareth. Beyond that line, the sailors say, the coast goes wrong. The jungle to the south and east is the Wilds' oldest country, and it is the one the Verdant Pact defends with its lives.

sections.title: Life and Society
paragraphs: The Wilds share a vocabulary of dress across all their peoples: a warm palette of reds, oranges, golds, and earth-tones against black; light, flowing, body-baring garments; abundant gold at neck, arm, and ear; head-coverings against the sun; and body-art that records lineage and deed. Within that language the peoples diverge sharply. The dry-isles and desert peoples wear the most theatrical version of the southern line, with crimson fringed sashes, teal and white turbans, and gold past restraint. The southern courts dress in black shot with gold, with broad pectoral collars and the diamond mark at the brow of the old houses. The deep-jungle tribes wear feather and fur, black-and-white geometric patterns, bone and turquoise, and face-paint in white and ochre. The island folk keep a cleaner, classical line of white and sea-green. The rootless, the pirates and sellswords who belong to no people, wear a hard, layered cut of all of it, and carry the rare and costly firearm where they can afford one.

Food is generous and communal. Saurian meat is at the center of the southern table, from the Bellowback roasts to the Cluckmaw eggs. Jungle fruit, river fish, peppers, and bright spices fill the rest. Strong sweet coffee from Southhaven's hills is the morning cup, and the bitter ceremonial cacao, the Cacau Amargo, is kept for the rites. The southern drink is tsoka, a sour-sweet fermented root-beer that is passed around in a single gourd, and to refuse the gourd is an insult. Mammal-dairy is a luxury, since the saurians lay eggs and give no milk.

The region's festivals are loud and bright. The Green Waking is the great festival of the jungle's renewal. The Night of the Ancestors honors the dead, and the chant-keepers recite the lineages until dawn. The Laughing Water is Malim's river-festival of races, music, and fish-offerings at the foot of Malim's Stair. The Sunspine Run, the great saurian racing meet of Jakupur, is a festival in its own right. Threaded among them are the tribute-rites to the Savage Lords, where joy and fear share a drumbeat.

The pastimes of the south are the ringstone, a hip-ball game played through a high stone ring that settles village quarrels, and Swiftcrest racing at the Sunspine Run. The still-heat midday stop is a custom that every southern town observes: the markets close, the shutters drop, and the whole town sleeps through the hottest hours. The Tidecall on the southern beaches is played with the same cork buoy and the same tide-timed ending as on the Frontier, and the southern teams have never lost a Charter Match to a northern side.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Sissix-the-Comet has lost a heat for the first time in two seasons. The jockey who beat her has a Vossreth brand on his wrist and no memory of the race.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“A Scarlet Mother's priest was seen in Southhaven buying the Fennick factors' coffee in bulk. Nobody says what he wants with so much of it.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“The Vorthani First Ascent has taken in a guest who will not carry a stone. The monks say she is not a guest.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“Tana Sukuun has sold a Dreadmaw to the Heartland. The buyer is a Vol Kaern agent, and the saurian is named after the Vol Kaern tower.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

epigraph.quote: The jungle doesn't care what your Charter says. Ask the jungle.
epigraph.by: A river guide of the Nine Mouths

title: Icy Expanse
subtitle: The ice forgives nothing.
summary: The frozen far south: whalers, sealers, Frost Elves, the Long Night, and the uncompromising obligations of hold-law.

sections.title: Life at the edge
paragraphs: Frosthold is an honest whaling town. Varan Port, called Fairweather, is the islands’ largest black market. Kaldmark is the seat of its house; Crystalhaven stands among blue ice, and Snowvah is the last named settlement.

sections.title: Food, fire, and the law
paragraphs: On the ice, refusing warmth and food to a traveler is murder and is punished as murder. Hold-law, blood-feud, and exile bind communities where the distance between one shelter and the next can be fatal.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Icy Expanse is the frozen continent at the far south of the charted sea, and the last place where the Council's writ can be felt before it freezes. The people who live here are few and tough as old leather: whalers, ice-fishers, hunters, smugglers, and the Frost Elves who share the dark with them. They are a superstitious people, and with reason. They live beside Vukharr's hunger, and a people who live that close to a hunger learn to take omens seriously. In that cold, exile is a slower sentence of death.

The Expanse produces the things the rest of the archipelago cannot do without. Whale-oil burns in every lamp in Goldwind. Ambergris fixes every perfume in the Heartland. The furs line the Frontier's hoods, and the icebrand, freeze-distilled and smoked, is the south's favorite spirit at the start of the Long Night. In return, the Expanse imports timber and grain, which the ice cannot grow, and iron, which the ice cannot make. It is a poor land that sells its bones to the rest of the world, and it has learned to trade them hard.

The Expanse is also the country of the Fairweather Combine. House Kaldmark fights the Combine on the border and cannot win, and the Combine's ships come and go under the Council's own noses with the blessing of the corrupt Varan Lodge. The Frozen Vow, the Armada's Eighth Fleet, is stretched thin across the coast, half-bought and unbroken. The Vow does not thaw.

sections.title: Geography
paragraphs: The Expanse is a country of ice and sea. Its northern coast is ringed with fjords, glacial rivers, and whaling bays, and its interior is an ice-plateau cut by canyons that the wind carves into strange shapes. The sea-ice closes the bays from autumn to spring, and the Rime Ways open beneath it, a network of channels that the dwarves and the smugglers both use. The sun sets for weeks at a time in the Long Night, and the aurora lights the sky in green and white bands for most of the dark.

The coast holds the towns. Frosthold stands on a rocky peninsula above the bay of the whale-fleets, with its great fortress-walls and its oil-houses. Kaldmark is a fortified hold in the hills beyond Frosthold, watching the border with the Combine. Varan Port lies in a sheltered harbor on the eastern shore, behind a line of wrecks that the Combine's salvagers have never fully cleared. Crystalhaven is a wrecking-town on the blue-ice coast, where the False Lights hang their lanterns. The interior is empty except for the Frost Elves' warbands, the Auroral Vault's canyons, and the Whalefall Gardens, a shallow bay where the leviathan-falls seed gardens of pale life. Snowvah, at the northern edge of the settled ice, is the last town before the quarantined waters.

sections.title: Life and Society
paragraphs: The people of the Expanse dress in heavy furs and hides, layered deep. Sealskin and whale-leather, thick wool, and hoods and wraps are worn in whites, greys, and browns, and the ornament is carved bone and ivory: amulets and charms worn against the cold and against the things in the ice. The Frost Elves wear the same furs and bone, black-braided and inked in stark knotwork, with an animal-skull trophy at the hip and a great axe in hand. A warband paints its faces as Vukharr's skull before a raid, and the paint is the warning every coastal town knows to fear.

Food is meat and fat. Whale, seal, ice-fish, and blubber are preserved, dried, and fermented against the Long Night. A guest is given fat and fire without question, because turning someone out into the cold is murder, and the Expanse has never tolerated that murder with any patience. Hard spirits warm the blood, and the icebrand is the spirit of choice, freeze-distilled and smoked over whale-oil lamps.

The Expanse's festivals are grim and joyous in turn. The Long Night is the famine-watch, when the deep Expanse fears Vukharr is moving and the lamps are kept lit in every hall. The Return of the Sun is the joy of the first daylight, and the whalers' feasts follow every great kill. The Ghostlight Vigil is kept on the night of the strongest aurora over the Auroral Vault, when the people of the coast go out onto the ice to see the lights pool below the canyon rim, and the Frost Elves do not raid beneath it.

The Long Tell is the storytelling-contest of the winter halls, where every teller must tell a story that is true for the listeners, and the listeners decide whether the story is true. The lamp never goes out in a Frost hall. The seam between two sheets of ice is the measure of a family's standing, and a family with a wide seam is pitied and envied in equal measure.

The Brine Brotherhood's whaling councils rule the coast. At Varan Port, justice is coin, knife, and the Lodge's corrupt ledger. Among the independent folk, blood-feud and exile keep the peace, and a feud can last three generations.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Frost Elves have stopped raiding the Auroral Vault. The Frost Elves say Vukharr is dreaming of something new.” (heard in the Icy Expanse)

“Mira has been seen at Crystalhaven with Granny Skerrow's grandson. A smuggler's heir is never seen with a wrecker's grandson unless one of them means to take the other's chair.” (heard in the Icy Expanse)
“The black circle in the sky is spreading. A whale-fleet that sailed too far last year came back with the sky over its masts gone black.” (heard in the Icy Expanse)

epigraph.quote: You share your fire with a stranger because next winter you'll be the stranger.

title: The Coral Kingdoms
subtitle: Be kind to the water.
summary: Beneath the trade lanes lie courts with their own sovereigns, customs, and claims upon the drowned.

sections.title: The realms beneath
paragraphs: Merfolk and many other sea peoples keep courts below the dry world. Shore communities maintain sea-pacts with them, and the presence of a coral family in a port is a reminder that the deep is paying attention.

sections.title: A visitor’s courtesy
paragraphs: Greet the sea-folk in song. Any song will do; effort counts. Gifts of sound, such as bells and music boxes, are prized. Bare cold iron is an insult.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Coral Kingdoms are the realm of the sea-peoples, and they are older than the Firstborn. The courts that live in them are not a single state but a set of realms divided by depth, temperament, and history. Like the Fae, the sea-peoples are divided between two natures: the Sunlit Courts, the bright sea, which are beautiful, warm, and, more often than not, kind; and the Sunken Courts, the dark sea, which are ancient, alien, predatory, and patient. The surface has learned, over centuries, that the sea-folk keep their word, and that the surface had better keep its own.

The Coral Kingdoms are not hostile to the surface as a whole. They trade with it through the Tidecallers, who have brokered the sea-pacts over generations, and they have guided ships, rescued sailors, and sold wonders to the Heartland's collectors. The Sunlit mermaids are the surface's friends, and Emri, the celebrated Hunter, is their most famous face. But the pacts are a fence as well as a friendship. With the dark courts, the pacts are simply a line that keeps the surface out of the deep, and everyone who keeps them knows exactly what the line is for.

The open sea is the other half of the region. It is the eighty-four percent of the world that the Council does not control and the Chartwrights do not chart. Its reefs, its becalmed circles, its drowned colonnades, and its Krysta-veined coral reefs are the places where the lanes end and exploration begins. The King Tide belongs to the open sea, and the dark courts climb nearest the surface then.

sections.title: Geography
paragraphs: The sea around the archipelago is shallow and bright near the islands, deepening through the Twilight Reaches to the lightless trenches of Abyssara, the Black Below. The shallows are coral gardens in a thousand colors, the Pearl Shallows and Luminar Reef among them. The Twilight Reaches, or Corallion, are the contested middle, where the water goes black-green and the cities glow with their own cold light. The Sunken Thrones are the deep courts, crushing and ancient. Abyssara is the bottom of the bottom, where the trenches have never been broken and where the Savage Lord Thalgorath lairs.

The open sea is the water between the islands and beyond the lanes. It is warm in the south and cold in the north, and its currents carry the Burning Sea's heat through a band of warm water that no Charter ship has ever sailed without a loss. The Kraken's Maw is a passage between two reefs, where the great battle of 165 EC was fought. The Burning Sea is the warm and treacherous water that gave its name to the plague of 90 EC. Xathnatraz is a cursed isle of its own legend, a black rock far to the west.

sections.title: Life and Society
paragraphs: The surface's life in the Coral Kingdoms is the life of the pact-ports. The people of Pearl Groove dive for pearls and clean the murex beds for reefpurple, under the watch of the Belmaris house and the pearl-clans. The Pelagar house keeps the most secret of the pacts, and its island is the only surface house that deals directly with the Glass Gardens and the Whispering Current.

The sea-pacts are the surface's law in the water. A port gives the first catch of each season, the true names of its ships, and the burial rights over its drowned. A court gives safe water, storm-warnings, and the return of the drowned. Break the pact and the harbor's luck drowns with it. The pacts are sung on the surface, every year, at the first catch, and the sailors who sing them best are the ones the Tidecallers bless first.

Memory-pearls are the courts' gift of remembrance, and a person who holds one can relive a moment of the dead. The Whispering Current carries every word spoken over water, and its keepers trade in those words. The Grey Fathoms keep the drowned and ransom them back to their families, for a price in pearl and song. The Red Choir sings when blood is in the water, and its hymns are the most beautiful and the most terrible sounds in the sea. The Old Shells, the leviathan sage-turtles, answer three questions a generation, and no one has yet been able to predict which three.
The sayings of the coast are short and wise.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Emri has been seen swimming past the Drowned Colonnade with a bundle of silver on her back. Nobody has asked her what she is carrying.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)
“The Red Choir has started singing on a quiet night, when there is no blood in the water. The Tidecallers say the song is coming up the Starfall Reef.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)
“Pelagar has been buying the Starfall coral in bulk. The Glass Gardens have stopped trading with Pelagar in return.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)
“The Old Shells answered a question last month that no one had asked. The answer was the name of a ship, and the ship has not been seen since.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)

epigraph.quote: Sing when you come, bring a bell, and never put bare iron in their water. Then you'll live to tell me about it.
epigraph.by: A pearl diver of Pearl Groove

title: Ironfort
subtitle: Where the Charter began
summary: Landing site, first Council seat, and home of the Hunters’ founding house.

sections.title: The beginning of the count
paragraphs: In 1 EC, the refugee houses signed the Charter at Ironfort. The city became the first seat of the Council, and its place in the archipelago’s history is still felt in the northern gate.

sections.title: The Crucible
paragraphs: The Hunters’ founding house, the Crucible, is in Ironfort. Its mint strikes the iron endorsement coins used by candidates seeking a place in the annual Trials of Ascension. Goods passing through the Frontier also meet the Gate-Tithe: a Tide in every Anchor.

sections.title: Arriving
paragraphs: Ships come down the Crown Route out of the fog to find a great iron chain across the harbor mouth, raised and lowered by the Gate's garrison, and behind it a stone port of steep streets and fish drying on racks. Everything that sails between the islands and Assios stops here first, and pays.

sections.title: Who rules
paragraphs: House Ostrel collects the Gate-Tithe for the Council: a tenth of everything that passes to or from Assios, gathered by the Tithe-Mistress with a clerk's care and a garrison behind her. Ostrel also runs the scale-tables, where an imperial korvan changes for ten Tides instead of the eleven it weighs, and keeps the difference.

sections.title: What happens here
paragraphs: Ironfort was the Council's first seat, and the Charter was signed here in 1 EC. It is still the Hunters' founding house: the Crucible strikes the year's 300 irons to a new die, and every spring the queue of hopeful candidates stretches down the Hunter's Walk. The rest of the year the city salts fish, brews black ale, and watches the north.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Ironfort is the capital of the Frontier in everything but the name, and the first seat of the Council of the Charted Isles before the Council moved to Goldwind. The Tithe-Mistress of the Ostrel bond collects the gateway tax with a clerk's care and a garrison's weight behind it. Ironfort's streets carry the black ale, the woad, and the bell-codes of a port that has never forgotten where it came from.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Gate-Tithe is cheating us in both directions. It keeps the gold in Ironfort and sends the paper to Goldwind.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“The spark ferrets at Ironfort customs won't go near one particular noble's luggage. They don't spark. They hide.” (an Ironfort customs clerk)

epigraph.quote: Everything that comes south pays the Gate. Everything that goes north pays it twice.

illustration.alt: Ironfort’s garrison raises the harbor chain in fog and sleet while a merchantman waits outside the granite gate.
illustration.caption: The chain rises before the afternoon is dark.

title: Goldwind
subtitle: The city where the islands argue
summary: The capital of the charted isles, with some 92,000 souls and more than one kind of power.

sections.title: A city of five seats
paragraphs: Founded around 30 EC by Archmage Eamos on a gulf of excellent winds, Goldwind became the Council’s seat around 50–55 EC. It houses the University, the Arcane Registry, and the Reckoners’ Hall.

sections.title: Coin and consequence
paragraphs: The Goldspire Exchange holds the Spire Floor, where the Twelve Flags call commodity prices on Coinsday. The city’s laws make casting of the Third Circle or higher without a Writ a serious offense. In Goldwind, a copper ring can matter as much as a fine coat.

sections.title: Arriving
paragraphs: Ships come in on the steady gulf wind that gave the city its name. The first thing a newcomer sees is the city climbing in rings from the harbor: wharves and warehouses at the water, the banking quarter above them, the University of Kalvatar's copper-ringed spires and the Council's white halls higher still, and the castle-heights of House Vol Kaern over everything. Every street corner speaks three languages.

sections.title: Who rules
paragraphs: The Council of the Charted Isles sits in its five-seat chamber, and its rivalries are the city's weather. Day to day, the Lord Mayor's offices and the city watch keep order, the Concord lends the law its moral weight, and House Holst's customs-codes run the harbor.
Inside the walls the Arcane Registry is enforced strictly. Casting without rings in the capital is a serious matter, and justice, even-handed in principle, leans quietly toward standing.

sections.title: What people do here
paragraphs: They trade, borrow, argue, and study. The Great Heartland Bazaar sells food and goods from every corner of the islands. The Naval Recruitment Quarters sign on every would-be Hand of the Armada. The University's two great schools, the Goldwind Academy and the Sylariel Institute of Arcane Studies, fill the upper rings with students. On Coinsday the Twelve Flags call the prices of everything on the Spire Floor.

sections.title: Weather and water
paragraphs: Goldwind has a mild sea climate: warm summers, cool winters, moderate rain, and the breeze that never quite stops. Fish, turtles, and dolphins crowd the bay, whales breach offshore on their migrations, and old forests stand on the hills behind the city.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: It rises in rings from the great harbor. The wharves, the warehouses, and the clamor of the docks are at the bottom. The University of Kalvatar is the archipelago's oldest and largest school of the arcane, and its archives hold more of the old charts than the Chartwrights' own. The Reckoners' Hall is the marble seat of First Reckoner Maera Blackstrand, where the Mercantile Congress's debts are kept. The Grand Temple of the Concord rises over the city's heart, its great sun-and-tide window catching the morning. The Goldwind Harbor is the busiest market in the islands. The Cistern Door, a dwarven wall under the oldest cistern, is the city's favorite ghost story: they say its mortar was worked from the far side.

sections.title: Vellune’s window
paragraphs: On the rising streets above the harbor promenade, Vellune: Finery & Enchantments keeps one outfit in its shaded window and a fitting book full of appointments. Its owner, Amarise Vellune, is also one of the city’s newly chosen Arbiters; Tessa Bellfold manages the shop while she serves.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Gate-Tithe is cheating us in both directions. It keeps the gold in Ironfort and sends the paper to Goldwind.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“The dry road. The roads Below run island to island, and a smuggler who knew them could walk a cargo from Black Harbor to Goldwind without paying a single harbor due.” (common talk)

epigraph.quote: Three languages on every corner, and every one of them is selling something.
epigraph.by: A sailor on his first day in Goldwind

illustration.alt: Merchants unfold cloth on a market stair above Goldwind’s gulf, beneath the University’s copper-ringed spires.
illustration.caption: Morning trade climbs the rings of Goldwind.

title: Hunter’s Citadel
subtitle: The Hunters’ headquarters in Goldwind
summary: A hall, a lodge and a fortress climb the cliffs of Goldwind beside a single roaring cataract.

sections.title: The Hall at the foot of the falls
paragraphs: The cataract is loud enough to drown out a conversation on the approach to Hunters’ Hall. The Hall stands beside the plunge pool, where the climb begins. From its steps, you can follow the road with your eyes as it doubles back across the cliff.

sections.title: The Lodge and training grounds
paragraphs: The road climbs to the Hunters’ Lodge on the middle terrace. Hunters stay here, close to the training barracks and their practice yard. From the yard, the sea is visible beyond the cliff. The road goes on past the Lodge, climbing toward the top of the falls.

sections.title: The Platinum Hunters’ precinct
paragraphs: The highest level belongs to the Platinum Hunters. Their precinct sits above the lip of the cataract. From below, its walls are the last part of the Citadel you see before the rock gives way to sky.

facts: Hall, Lodge and training grounds, Platinum Hunters’ precinct
source: Goldwind city notes and the creator’s description of the Citadel

illustration.alt: The three terraces of the Hunters’ headquarters rise beside a cataract above the Goldwind coast.
illustration.caption: The climb from Hunters’ Hall to the precinct of the Platinum Hunters.

title: Highspire
subtitle: The sky has its own archives
summary: Observatories, House Starborn, and the cliffside eyries of the Aethyn.

sections.title: Above the harbor
paragraphs: Highspire’s heights belong to astronomers, star-rolls, and the winged Aethyn. House Starborn shares their patient attention to the heavens.

sections.title: The Singing Cliffs
paragraphs: Wind-bored crags near Highspire sound in chords as the weather turns. Harbor-masters listen to their changing pitch for tomorrow’s conditions, while the eyries rise above them.

sections.title: Arriving
paragraphs: Highspire is reached by a long climb. The harbor sits low, and the tower-city rises on its cliff above the cloud-line, so that on many mornings the town is in sunshine while the harbor below is lost in fog. Aethyn glide between the towers and the Singing Cliffs.

sections.title: What happens here
paragraphs: Star-charts and lenses. The Starborn observatories are the best in the islands, and navigators pay dearly for their charts. The harbor-masters read tomorrow's weather by the chord the cliffs sound when the wind turns.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Aethyn winged folk nest in the Singing Cliffs above the town, and the Aethyn astronomers share their watch with the Starborn in an uneasy partnership that both sides describe differently.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Sailors' songs count the great dragons of the world as nine. A Highspire star-reader once counted ten, and the University took her charts away.” (a Highspire lens-grinder)
“Highspire's astronomers keep one star on their charts that crosses the sky the wrong way.” (a Starborn page)

epigraph.quote: Down at the harbor it's fog. Up here, it's tomorrow.

illustration.alt: Astronomers work inside a Highspire observatory as an Aethyn glides past the sea-stacks beneath Valtaire and Ciel.
illustration.caption: Two moons, and another night of measurements.

title: Everfall
subtitle: Black sand, banked fire
summary: A volcanic island of forges and ember-lit nights, watched over by the people who keep the fire-vigil.

sections.title: The fire beneath
paragraphs: Everfall is associated with House Emberheart, the Cindren, and the Darlath mines. KakanKal, the Emperor of Flames, is said to sleep in the magma beneath the island.

sections.title: Glass and vigilance
paragraphs: The Glass Forest is a hillside of obsidian trees left by an ancient eruption. The islanders call it the Emperor’s first breath and listen when it chimes during earthquakes. Cindren and Vorthani keep a fire-vigil above the sleeping depths.

sections.title: Who rules
paragraphs: House Emberheart holds the isle. The Cindren work its forges and glass-fields, and the Ash Wardens watch the craters for any sign that KakanKal, the Emperor of Flames, is waking.
Inside the volcano's flank lie the halls of Emberdelf (Fulkhald), one of the two old dwarven holds that never fell to the Orka.

sections.title: What happens here
paragraphs: Krysta and fire. The Darlath mines cut through Krysta-rich rock that feeds the Heartland's refineries, and the mining houses and the Ash Wardens have never forgiven each other. Since the diggers broke into the Ember Roads in 172 EC, the lava tubes under the island lead down into the Below.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Everfall is a volcanic isle in the east of the Heartland, above the sleeping Savage Lord KakanKal, the Emperor of Flames. The Ash Wardens, a grim order of Cindren and others, watch the craters for signs of the Emperor waking, and oppose Rankar's mining in the deep rock with a fury the mining houses do not forgive.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A deep hum comes up through the floor of the Darlath mines at night, and the Cindren who work near it go dim.” (an Everfall glassworker)
“One crate of Darlath stone in twelve leaves Everfall marked 'broken' and is never seen at the refinery.” (an Everfall carter)
“The Cindren of Everfall say the Glass Forest chimed thirteen times last Graveday, and it has only ever chimed in twelves.” (an Ash Warden)

epigraph.quote: Count the chimes. If the Glass Forest rings more than the Wardens can count, you run.
epigraph.by: An Everfall mother to her children

illustration.alt: Two Cindren smiths work by forge light as ash falls on Everfall and the volcano colors the night cloud red.
illustration.caption: The street sleeps; the banked fires do not.

title: Jakupur
subtitle: The city of the White Flame
summary: A saurian city-state whose riders and sacred traditions belong to the native south.

sections.title: A city with its own standing
paragraphs: Jakupur is known for the Order of the White Flame. It belongs to a southern world of distinct cities, Confederacies, and peoples whose histories reach beyond the Council’s settlement of the islands.

sections.title: The southern mounts
paragraphs: Saurians are part of the south’s life and transport. Sukuun of Jakupur, one of the Twelve Flags, trades in them. An imported auroc is a costly novelty here, carrying a very different kind of prestige from a native saurian mount.

sections.title: Arriving
paragraphs: Jakupur rises in stone terraces from a bend of the inner sea, loud with saurians: swordtooths in the stable-yards, loambacks hauling stone up the ramps, altisaurs carrying whole platforms of passengers above the crowd. Ships put in at Mumit Port.

sections.title: Who rules
paragraphs: The Order of the White Flame governs as regent under Magus Thislum Blackhogen. Jakupur is the only independent power in the Wilds that the Council does not claim, and it uses Council coin by choice, not by law, and reserves the right to stop.

sections.title: What happens here
paragraphs: Saurians. Nearly every domesticated saurian in the archipelago was bred here, and a beast sold under Tana Sukuun's mark costs double. The Sunspine Run is the city's cathedral of speed, and the betting on it never sleeps.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The city's mastery of the saurian arts is generations deep, and Jakupur is the source of nearly every domesticated saurian in the archipelago. The Sukuun stables, run by the greatest tamer alive, Tana Sukuun, sell their beasts at double the price of any other bloodline, and a saurian sold under the Sukuun mark is a status that the Heartland's richest houses fight over.
Mumit Port and the people of Jakupur.
It governs in the name of a sovereign that the city's founding compact names and the magi do not.

The city's harbor is loud, crowded, and never closed, and ships from every corner of the islands unload at its stone quays. Sailors and merchants strike their deals at Kansha Marul and Omaktu Kinga, the two great houses of the waterfront.
The inn every traveler finds first, and the one most of them never leave for another. Its keeper, Old Daun, is the friendliest man in the south, and he hears every story twice.

The White Flame's watch, under Captain Armus Kalassos, with Lieutenant Yelessa Sokhar and Corporal Fenlit at his side. Its rot is Captain Dariok Mulsen, and the whole city whispers about whom he really works for.
Its patron is Meldius Daltrossos: rich, connected, courted by half the city, and never seen without his two bodyguards, Jodrik and Zhak.
Mercenaries under the charismatic Zulkarun, hired for every kind of work in the city and known for finishing it.

The merchant Damyel Dor'Valiath of Karazun trades rare goods out of his low, fast ship, which makes port sooner than any wind allows. The hunter Therrek Kraghammer has been trying to sign aboard for a year.
A dark elf who keeps quiet rooms above the harbor. Most of Jakupur had never seen a drow before him, and the city talks about him a great deal more than he talks about himself.

sections.title: Jewels beneath the roof
paragraphs: Wealthy Jakupur households keep Jewelfins in private indoor pools, one fish to a pool. Collectors with several build separate pools for them. The animals are magnificent and extremely aggressive; clandestine Jewelfin fights draw a lucrative underground betting trade.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Tana Sukuun has sold a Dreadmaw to the Heartland. The buyer is a Vol Kaern agent, and the saurian is named after the Vol Kaern tower.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“The dark elf at the Rusty Blade paid for his rooms with a coin nobody could name. Old Daun has nailed it over the bar.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

epigraph.quote: A northerner on a swordtooth? Bless him. Get the bucket.
epigraph.by: A stable-hand of the Sukuun yards

illustration.alt: Jakupur’s busy market avenue winds between tropical stone terraces as riders lead feathered saurians through the city.
illustration.caption: Riders and traders share the streets of Jakupur after rain.

title: Varan Port
subtitle: Fairweather, if you believe it
summary: The largest black market in the islands, at a port whose nickname promises more than its weather.

sections.title: At the cold edge of trade
paragraphs: Varan Port is called Fairweather, though the weather never is. Goods, rumors, and people pass through a harbor famous throughout the archipelago for its black market.

sections.title: A long way south
paragraphs: A fair passage from Southhaven to Varan takes seven or eight weeks. The journey onward to the far ice adds another three or four. Convoys, weather, and the King Tide can make those figures optimistic.

sections.title: Arriving
paragraphs: Ships thread a line of old wrecks into a sheltered harbor of warehouses and crooked wharves. Nobody asks your name. Everybody asks your price.

sections.title: Who rules
paragraphs: The Fairweather Combine, and at its head Mother Kess: polite, matronly, and terrifying. She brokers the ransoms, settles the disputes, and owns everyone's debts.

sections.title: What happens here
paragraphs: Dark glass is the only coin that truly matters here. Smuggled freight moves at twice the honest rate, ransoms are settled at Mother Kess's table, and the Quiet Auction holds its sales in the back rooms. The Hunters' Varan Lodge looks the other way, for a fee.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Varan Port is the great black market of the far south, a town of warehouses and wharves behind a line of wrecks in a sheltered eastern harbor. She rules over three chairs. Marcus holds the vice trade and the trafficking. Mira holds the smuggling, and she is either the heir or the usurper, depending on whom you ask. Elendor holds the slave trade, and he is a high elf of a family that has never been seen without a white glove. The muscle is Admiral-Retired Gerrit Haskell and his fifteen ships. The Varan Lodge of the Hunters is corrupt, and its Lodgemaster takes Haskell's coin. The Quiet Auction, the black-pearl invitation of the Sea, is held in Varan's back rooms.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Pale moons. New Tides ring dull, say the scale-men of Fairweather, and they have started weighing them. The Mint says nothing.” (common talk)

epigraph.quote: Everything has a price here, dear. That's what makes it fair.
epigraph.by: Mother Kess, to a new arrival

illustration.alt: Fur-clad traders pass crates along Varan Port’s crooked wharf in blue twilight and blowing snow.
illustration.caption: Fairweather has another name for this weather.

title: The Gilded Shallows
subtitle: Gold beneath the water
summary: A lagoon whose Krysta-dusted sands turn the water gold at dusk.

sections.title: A wonder of the islands
paragraphs: The Shallows are pilgrimage water and honeymoon water. Their evening glow comes from Krysta in the sand. Swimming during the King Tide is forbidden, and the ban is enforced.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: Come at dusk, when the low sun catches the Krysta-dust in the sand and the whole lagoon turns gold for the length of a prayer. Pilgrims wade in to the knee; newlyweds row out to the middle. Nobody swims it on the Three Nights.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Gilded Shallows are glowing at night now, even when the tide is low. The Concord says it is a blessing. The Registry says it is a fire.” (heard in the Central Heartland)

epigraph.quote: Row out at dusk, kiss when the water turns gold, and you'll never quarrel about money. It's a lie, but a lovely one.

illustration.alt: Pilgrims wade in the Gilded Shallows at sunset while newlyweds row over Krysta-dusted golden sands.
illustration.caption: At dusk, the shallows turn gold for the length of a prayer.

title: The Singing Cliffs
subtitle: Tomorrow, heard in the wind
summary: Highspire’s wind-bored crags sound in chords before a change of weather.

sections.title: A wonder of the islands
paragraphs: Aethyn eyries crown the Singing Cliffs. Harbor-masters read the changing weather in their pitch, making the cliffside music part of the port’s practical life as well as its wonder.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: Stand on Highspire's harbor wall when the wind turns. The cliffs above sound a chord, low and slow for fair weather, rising and thinning before a storm. Children learn the chords before their letters, and a Highspire sailor will hum you tomorrow's weather if you ask.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Their pitch rises before a storm, and the harbor-masters take the chord as the day's forecast. The Aethyn nest on the crags' ledges, and their eyries are the only places the winged folk will talk about the Starborn.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Singing Cliffs sounded a chord last spring that no harbor-master had ever heard. The weather that followed was perfectly ordinary, which worried them more.” (heard in Highspire)

epigraph.quote: Low and slow, fair and fine. High and thin, bring the boats in.

illustration.alt: A winged Aethyn listens to the wind through the Singing Cliffs above Highspire’s harbor.
illustration.caption: Highspire reads the weather in the stone’s song.

title: The Glass Forest
subtitle: The Emperor of Flames’ first breath
summary: An obsidian forest on Everfall, left by an ancient eruption.

sections.title: A wonder of the islands
paragraphs: The hillside’s black glass trees are said to be the first breath of the Emperor of Flames. Earthquakes set them chiming. On Everfall, listening is often a form of vigilance.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: The obsidian trees stand black on the hillside above Everfall, edged sharp enough to cut a careless hand. Visitors go with an Ash Warden or not at all. When the ground trembles, the whole forest rings like struck bells, and the Wardens stop to count.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Forest chimes in the earthquakes that the Ember Roads bring up from below, and the Ash Wardens read the chimes as a count of the Emperor's breaths.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Cindren of Everfall say the Glass Forest chimed thirteen times last Graveday, and it has only ever chimed in twelves.” (an Ash Warden)

epigraph.quote: Every chime is one of the Emperor's breaths. We count them so we know when he's dreaming.

illustration.alt: An Ash Warden guides travelers among sharp obsidian trees above Everfall.
illustration.caption: The Glass Forest rings when the ground trembles.

title: The Cathedral Green
subtitle: A forest built like a sanctuary
summary: Titan trees open into root-vaults like naves, and the Liriath plant their dead beneath them. Every grave grows its own tree.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: A grove of titan trees whose roots arch into vaults like the naves of a temple. The canopy lets the light down in pale shafts, colored by the leaves it passes through, so that the floor of the Green looks like the inside of a window.
The Liriath plant their dead here, and each grave grows its own tree. To them it is a return to the living grove, and the place carries its memory in roots and seasons.

sections.title: Who lives there
paragraphs: The Liriath keep the Green, and the short-lived Florians bloom and fade in its clearings. Around the grove live tribes of the deep green who have been its neighbors for as long as either can remember: growers, canopy-walkers, and lantern-makers who bring their own dead to the edge and ask leave.
The light in the Green is kind. Visitors who come for a funeral often stay for the rest of their lives, and the villages at its edge are full of people who meant to leave in the morning.

sections.title: Walking the naves
list: **In silence.** Speech is for the edge of the grove.
**Never in a crowd.** A few at a time, with a Liriath or with leave.
**Never at night.**
**Take nothing.** Not a leaf, not a seed. A Liriath can lay a hand on a trunk and tell you who rests below, and whose leaf that was.

sections.title: If you come from here
list: You speak quietly, and you notice how loud everyone else is.
You know someone planted in the Green, and you know which tree.
You can walk a canopy road and read the weather from the light.
You left a place people travel a lifetime to stay in, and you get asked why.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Cathedral Green's trees have started to grow new graves. The Liriath say it is their own dead, but no one of their kind has died in the Green in forty years.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“Sit under the oldest tree long enough and it will tell you a name. It’s never one you know. Yet.” (a lantern-maker of the grove’s edge)

facts: walk the naves in silence, never in a crowd, never at night
light like stained glass, and people who came for a funeral and stayed

epigraph.quote: We do not bury our dead. We plant them, and the grove remembers what we forget.

illustration.alt: An ancient tree-like Liriath stands among immense roots in the sunlit Cathedral Green.
illustration.caption: The living grove remembers its dead.

title: The Auroral Vault
subtitle: Where the lights lie below
summary: An ice canyon where the aurora seems to pool beneath the rim like liquid light. The Frost Elves will not raid beneath it.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: The canyon lies deep in the ice and is reached only in the Long Night. From the rim, the green and white bands of the aurora seem to pour down the walls and collect at the bottom in a silent lake of color.
The Frost Elves call it Vukharr’s dreaming. Even in a country governed by hard necessity, some places keep their own prohibitions.

sections.title: Who lives there
paragraphs: Nobody lives in the canyon. Along its approaches camp the people of the deep ice: Frost Elf warbands, seal-hunters, sled-drivers, and the small tribes that follow the herds across the floes and take their names from the fox, the owl, and the light.
Under the lights, every one of them keeps the peace. Enemies share a fire on the rim and go back to being enemies a day’s travel away.

sections.title: The Ghostlight Vigil
paragraphs: On the night of the strongest aurora the people of the coast go out onto the ice to watch the lights pool below the rim. The whalers say that a person who walks the canyon floor on the Ghostlight night will see their own name written in the light, and will hear it spoken once more before they die.

sections.title: If you come from here
list: The dark does not frighten you, and neither does the cold. Waste does.
You have shared a fire with someone who would have killed you anywhere else.
You know sled-dogs, sea-ice, and how long a body lasts in the water.
You have stood on the rim. Whether you went down is your own business.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Frost Elves have stopped raiding the Auroral Vault. The Frost Elves say Vukharr is dreaming of something new.” (heard in the Icy Expanse)
“Some nights the lights flicker in a pattern. Three long, two short, over and over, like somebody’s lamp.” (a Snowvah seal-hunter)

facts: only in the Long Night, when the aurora burns
the Ghostlight Vigil, on the night of the strongest aurora
no Frost Elf raids beneath the lights

epigraph.quote: That is where the White Hunger dreams. We do not raid under a dreaming god.

illustration.alt: Travelers watch green auroral light pool in a vast ice canyon during the Long Night.
illustration.caption: From the rim, the aurora seems to pour into the Vault.

title: The Starfall Reef
subtitle: Stars beneath the hull
summary: Krysta-veined coral shines through the water in the territory of the Glass Gardens.

sections.title: A wonder of the islands
paragraphs: The reef belongs to the Glass Gardens. Its light is a wonder to travelers, but poaching it breaks a sea-pact. Beauty does not make something unclaimed.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: Seen from a hull at night, the reef shines up through the water like a second sky. The Glass Gardens let boats drift over it: no anchors, no nets, no hands in the water. Coral taken from it goes dark before it is dry.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Its coral is the Starfall coral prized by the Heartland's glassmakers, and its light fades when it is taken from the sea.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Red Choir has started singing on a quiet night, when there is no blood in the water. The Tidecallers say the song is coming up the Starfall Reef.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)

epigraph.quote: Take one piece and it goes dark in your hand. The reef only shines for the sea.

illustration.alt: A guardian swims beside luminous living coral beneath a drifting boat in Glass Gardens territory.
illustration.caption: No anchor, net, or hand in the water.

title: The Aethyn
subtitle: The winged watchers
summary: Cliff-folk and astronomers of Highspire whose ability to fly follows the pull of the two moons.

sections.title: The tide in a month
paragraphs: Aethyn flight waxes and wanes with Valtaire and Ciel. Under their full pull it is strong; when both moons are dark, flight becomes heavy and nearly grounded. The calendars and star-rolls of their eyries are correspondingly precise.

sections.title: High places
paragraphs: Highspire and the sea-stacks are their homes. Alongside House Starborn they keep astronomical records, favor measured speech, and regard needless haste as a lowland habit.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Layered flight-silks and fitted jackets free the wings. Weighted tail-sashes balance the glide; moon-tables and star-lines line the garments. The finest formal decoration faces downward, where it can be seen in flight.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Sirin, Kaelis, Orren, Thyssa, Ilessa, and Maro. An eyrie replaces a surname: Sirin of the Ninth Eyrie.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Aethyn are the archipelago's astronomers: keepers of the great star-rolls beside House Starborn, patient, precise, and happiest above everyone else. They are gliders and soarers, not tireless flappers. Give one a cliff, a thermal, or a tower to leap from and they own the sky; pin one to the floor of a valley and they are very nearly earthbound. Their whole month has a tide in it, because their strength rises and falls with Valtaire and Ciel.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about a century and a half; an Aethyn of a hundred is in the prime of a long, unhurried life.
Look: great feathered wings in colors as varied as an auroc's plumage, sharp far-seeing eyes, and an air of listening to something high up that no one else can hear.
Homeland: the crags of the Northern Frontier, the stone needles of the central isles, and above all Highspire, where the stars are close.
Faith: the Breath That Wanders above all, with Tramica (the wandering moon) and Skaia (stars and dreams).
Temperament: lofty in both senses. Distant, unhurried, and inclined to the long view, which the earthbound find either wise or maddening.
Dress: close-cut flight-silks that leave the wings free, weighted tail-sashes for balance, and star-lines embroidered into the linings. Formal dress is read from below.

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: You walkers see the stars as a ceiling. We see them as a road.
epigraph.by: An Aethyn chart-keeper of the Ninth Eyrie

illustration.alt: An adult male and female Aethyn with large feathered wings, fitted star-embroidered flight-silks, charts and astronomical instruments beneath the two moons.
illustration.caption: Star-keepers above the sea-stacks of Highspire.

gallery.alt: Astronomers work inside a Highspire observatory as an Aethyn glides past the sea-stacks beneath Valtaire and Ciel.
gallery.caption: Two moons, and another night of measurements.
gallery.label: A night at Highspire

title: The Cindren
subtitle: The ember-touched
summary: Forge-folk whose feelings glow beneath coal-dark skin.

sections.title: The heart made visible
paragraphs: Coal-dark skin is crossed by cooled-lava lines. Anger, affection, fear, and grief shine beneath it in different colors. Hiding emotion is difficult; blunt honesty and steadiness carry particular weight.

sections.title: Forge and fire-vigil
paragraphs: Many Cindren work House Emberheart’s forges or serve the Ash Wardens on Everfall’s volcanic slopes. Beside the Vorthani, they maintain a fire-vigil above the sleeping Emperor of Flames.

sections.title: Dress
paragraphs: Ash-grey wraps and fire-leathers leave the throat and forearms visible so the glow can speak. Feast dress uses cinder-silk and smoked-glass beads. Completely covering the glow is a funeral custom.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Brakk, Solen, Emra, Kessik, Darah, and Ilsk; hearth-surnames include Kilnborn, Ashvale, Slagmoor, and Embermere.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Cindren carry the Fire Beneath in more than name. Their skin runs from ash-grey to deep charcoal, seamed with lines that kindle when they feel: anger, love, fear, and grief each glow in their own color, so a Cindren's heart is always slightly public. It has made them a blunt, honest, steady people with no talent for lying and great contempt for those who have it.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about as long as humans, a little longer among the old forge-masters.
Faith: the Hunger That Warms, revered with wary intimacy: fire feeds, and fire devours.
Temperament: steady, plain-spoken, and trusting of anyone who doesn't lie to them. They prize calm for a practical reason: an angry Cindren is visible across a room.
Dress: ash-grey wraps and fire-leathers cut open at forearm and throat, where the glow speaks. Covering the glow entirely is what Cindren do at funerals.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A deep hum comes up through the floor of the Darlath mines at night, and the Cindren who work near it go dim.” (an Everfall glassworker)
“The Cindren of Everfall say the Glass Forest chimed thirteen times last Graveday, and it has only ever chimed in twelves.” (an Ash Warden)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: You can lie with your mouth. We can't lie with our skin, so we stopped bothering with the mouth.

illustration.alt: An adult female and male Cindren artisan with coal-dark skin and glowing ember seams, practical forge clothing and tools above a volcanic harbor.
illustration.caption: Ember-lit craft at an Everfall forge.

gallery.alt: Two Cindren smiths work by forge light as ash falls on Everfall and the volcano colors the night cloud red.
gallery.caption: The street sleeps; the banked fires do not.
gallery.label: The forge street of Everfall

title: The Galven
subtitle: The storm-blooded
summary: Blue-skinned storm-folk marked by living lightning, most at home when the deck pitches beneath them.

sections.title: A people of living lightning
paragraphs: Galven skin ranges from pale sky-blue through slate to near-black storm-grey. Branching light-marks brighten toward white as feeling rises. Silver, white, or pale-blue hair drifts with static. Their ears are human in shape; luminous eyes and lightning marks give their faces a storm-born cast. They have no wings.

sections.title: Ship-clans and weather-witches
paragraphs: Scattered ship-clans and storm-belt holds organize around captains and weather-lineages. Weather-witches preserve storm-songs and read the sky. The season’s first great storm draws gatherings wherever it is expected.

sections.title: The skin that cannot lie
paragraphs: Anger, fear, and courtship can all announce themselves in a flare of marks. A rare still-water Galven can keep that light quiet under real pressure. Elders’ markings branch deeply with a lifetime of storms.

sections.title: The Living Lightning
paragraphs: Their own god is Eirhal, the Living Lightning; above Eirhal is the Breath That Wanders, and beside it the thunderbird Badron, their beast-god. Taking a ship through a real blow is a rite of passage; deepest oaths are sworn in lightning.

sections.title: Dress and names
paragraphs: Sea-gear leaves the forearms bare; brass chains and wind-chimes answer the wind. Names pair a short given name with a birth-storm: Skai Ninth-Squall, Tuvel Longstorm, or Ossa Dawnsquall. Those born in calm take the name of the first storm they survive.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Their ears are shaped like a human's. They feel weather in the body, and they are loudest, quickest, and most alive when the sky goes black and the deck pitches under them.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Lifespan: about as long as humans; the Galven say they burn too bright for longer.
Ship-clans and storm-belt holds wherever the storms run fiercest, Stormreach above all.

Faith: Eirhal, the Living Lightning, beneath the Breath That Wanders, with the thunderbird Badron as their beast-god. Their faith is practiced more than prayed: they greet the first storm of each season and sail into weather that others flee.
Temperament: loud, free, and reckless to everyone else; simply free to themselves. A Galven becalmed on a flat, hot day is a twitchy and miserable creature.
Dress: oil-cloth and rope-leather cut to bare the forearms, where the lightning shows. Covering the marks is considered lying.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Galven crew sailed into a storm off Stormreach and came back with every mark on their arms burning white, laughing.” (heard at the Stormreach yards)

facts: Blue skin and luminous branching marks
source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Calm water is for people who have never been alive.
epigraph.by: A Galven helmswoman, steering into a gale

illustration.alt: An adult male and female Galven brace on a sailing ship in a storm, with blue skin, silver hair and glowing branching lightning marks.
illustration.caption: Two storm-blooded sailors at home in the squall.

title: The Liriath
subtitle: The long memory of the green
summary: Tree-tall plant-folk whose bodies, moods, and communities follow the turning of the seasons.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: Liriath are living trees and green growth. Bark, roots, moss, trailing vines, and branches form their bodies; faces emerge from knots, hollows, and fissures. Their blood is sap. Oak-like elders and willow-like figures show the range of their tree-kin.

sections.title: Seasons in the blood
paragraphs: Warmth brings bloom and vigor. Cold and drought draw them inward; a deep winter can root a Liriath into dormancy. Age is counted in seasons weathered, and the oldest stand as living monuments.

sections.title: The ancestor-groves
paragraphs: Liriath plant their dead. A life’s final rooting becomes a tree among the ancestors, making a grove simultaneously family, library, and resting-place. The oldest hold thousands of years of memory.

sections.title: The wound of the south
paragraphs: Clearing an ancestor-grove destroys living family and history. Some Liriath bargain and teach; others defend their ground with thorn, poison, and patient wrath. Many support the Verdant Pact.

sections.title: Faith and adornment
paragraphs: The Green Fire and the Spring Court shape their rites. The Green Waking celebrates renewal. Adornment is grown: shaped bark, trained moss, and seasonal flowers, with reed sashes for carrying. White flowers mark mourning; red mark courtship.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Sylsa, Fenroe, Ilyth, Ossare, Thal, and Miren. A name may be kept for a season or a century.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Liriath are walking green life, quickened (the chant-keepers say) by the Green Fire with the Spring Court's wild overflow in their sap. In this age they are the jungle the colonists are felling, and they feel the colonial wound in the body.

sections.title: Life and lore
paragraphs: Bloom-kin live about a century; tree-kin can stand for many centuries, and the eldest are half-tree and reckoned living monuments.
The seasons: Liriath bloom in the warm months and draw inward in the cold. In a deep enough winter they go dormant, which is why they are all but unknown on the ice.
Temperament: the patience of growing things. Slow to anger, slow to trust, and implacable once either has taken root.

sections.title: Optional: a grove-blessed Florian
paragraphs: Florians are the Liriath's tiny, wholly floral cousins, who live a single day and know nothing of time. They are a wonder of the world, not a player species. If a player and the GM want one anyway, the story has to answer one question first: a grove's deep blessing, or some magic, has stretched this Florian's bloom.
Rules: use the Liriath traits with bloom-kin. A Florian is far smaller than most Small creatures (knee-high at most), but for the rules it is Small.
The Florian has no sense of past or future. They have Advantage on saving throws to avoid or end the Frightened condition.
The GM decides how long the blessing lasts, and what it would take to keep it. That question is the character's arc.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Cathedral Green's trees have started to grow new graves. The Liriath say it is their own dead, but no one of their kind has died in the Green in forty years.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: I have been patient for three hundred years. I can be patient with you.

illustration.alt: Two Liriath shaped as a broad oak and a graceful willow, with branching crowns, root feet, moss and faces formed from knots and bark hollows.
illustration.caption: Oak and willow, two living forms of the forest.

title: The Florians
subtitle: A whole life, from dawn to dusk
summary: Small, wholly floral cousins of the Liriath who live a single day.

sections.title: A flower’s whole life
paragraphs: Florians are palm-high to knee-high, entirely floral, with petals and no wood. A typical life opens at dawn and ends at dusk. Rare blessed individuals last two or three days.

sections.title: The present is complete
paragraphs: A Florian arrives already itself and has no concept of time. Sunrise, noon, and evening hold a whole life, without a lost yesterday or a feared tomorrow. The Liriath cherish them as bright, brief joys of the green.

sections.title: The bloom shapes the person
paragraphs: Trumpet-flowers are bold; night-bloomers quieter; star-petalled kinds giddy and fey. A two-day Florian is an ancient elder to its own people.

sections.title: Day-names
paragraphs: Morning-of-Rain, Third-Bell, and Last-Gold name one bright life. Their place in the islands is as fleeting neighbors and friends of the groves.

sections.title: A whole life in a day
paragraphs: A Florian does not know its life is short, because it has no idea of time at all. It is born already itself, complete and joyful: a childhood at sunrise, a prime at noon, a contented old age in the gold of evening. The rare Florians who live two or three days are, to their own folk, ancient elders who have seen a whole other dawn.

sections.title: Every bloom its own key
paragraphs: A Florian is shaped by its flower. The bright trumpet-blooms are bold and laughing, the night-bloomers quiet and tender, the tiny star-petalled ones giddy and fey.

sections.title: Faith
paragraphs: Florians keep Yarrowen's day-feast, and Aoifel, the Archfey of the First Bloom, is their other patron.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Florian in the Cathedral Green has seen four dawns, and the Liriath have stopped speaking above a whisper near her.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

source: Bible Lite · §3; The Peoples of Kalvatar

epigraph.quote: Good morning! Isn't it the best day there has ever been?
epigraph.by: A Florian, every morning of its life

illustration.alt: A masculine blue-flowered Florian and a feminine orange-flowered Florian stand on a dew-covered leaf, with another tiny violet bloom-person behind them.
illustration.caption: A whole life unfolding in the first light.

title: The Vorthani
subtitle: Four hands. Four vows.
summary: Four-armed giant-kin of the mountain monasteries, known for discipline, patient craft, and work brought to completion.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: Vorthani stand eight to ten feet tall, with four arms. Their skin comes in the greys, duns, and bronzes of mountain rock, and in soft pastel lilac, rose, or pale yellow. Pale geometric birth-lines cross the skin, with earned blackwork recording vows. The upper arms lend power; the lower pair favor precision. Horns form individual crowns, and touching them is deeply rude.

Vorthani women are celebrated for statuesque beauty, often compared to images of goddesses. Muscular strength and a feminine bearing sit together; some have pastel-lilac skin and slender, elegantly rising horns.

sections.title: The Fourfold Way
