A night in a private room at a decent inn
Deck passage from Goldwind to Southhaven
1 Anchor (a harbor-made one costs a tenth)
A good sword, good armor, or a rare firearm
A monster contract for a Gold
50 Anchors: five years of a laborer's pay

title: Sayings You'll Hear
subtitle: The islands have a word for it.
summary: Hold or drown. Coin remembers. The jungle keeps its own. The ice forgives nothing. Be kind to the water.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: "Hold or drown." The Frontier.
"Coin remembers." The Heartland.
"A smile in Goldwind has two faces." The Heartland.
"The jungle keeps its own." The south.
"Paper burns, skin remembers." The south.
"The ice forgives nothing." The ice.
"Be kind to the water." Everywhere.
"The tide calls it." It's settled.
"Playing last water." The desperate end of anything.
"Tie your knot." Get your affairs in order.
"By the Three Nights!" and "By Ors!"
"Drown me."
"Tide's with you." Good luck.
"Someone kept the fire on that one." Quiet, unthanked work.
"The sill provides."
"We still have salt between us." This isn't over.
"Still carrying iron." A rookie holding an iron who has not yet sat the Trials.
"The chant remembers what the page forgets."
"Salt and kin!" answered by "Fair tide home!" The toast.

title: The Talk of 175 EC
subtitle: What the ports are saying.
summary: The King Tide is due in 177, the Charterhouse has won the salt monopoly, and the Legion is pushing north.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The headlines:
The King Tide is due in 177. Coastal land is quietly changing hands.
The Charterhouse Company won the southern salt monopoly. Two ports rioted; the brass-collars "restored order."
Crimson Legion raids are pushing north of Golgarma. The Emerald Wrath has asked for another squadron; the Council is "reviewing."
A new island has surfaced off the southern lanes. Three claims are filed, and the first survey crew is a week overdue.
Returned Crown pamphlets, calling to invite the Imperium back "on honorable terms," keep appearing in Ironfort. Nobody has found the printers.
Names on everyone's lips:
The Last Smile, pirate queen of the Free Tide.
Harrow Mane, the reaver-lord too brutal even for her.
The Crimson Legion and the Scarlet Mother.
The Midnight Patron of Karn Sorroch.
The Registrar, hunting unlicensed casters in Goldwind's fog.
Mother Kess of Varan Port.
The Returned Crown and the Tollmen, in the north.
The Southern Rebels, the Reclaimers, and the Chainbreakers, in the south.

title: Assios and the Wider World
subtitle: A region of the charted sea
summary: North across the strait lies Assios and the Korvan Imperium. West lies Khard Muur, and cursed Xathnatraz. Most of the world is only rumor.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Assios lies north of the Frontier across the strait, and only its southern coast is in view from the Ironfort quay on a clear day.

It is the seat of the Korvan Imperium under Emperor Theomar Vol Sunessi and his Inquisition: the militant creed of human inheritance, which roots out heresy, polices magic, and burns what it cannot convert.

The Imperium is the empire the Exodus fled. It still fights the Thousand-Year War against the Alliance of Baronies and the Free Cities, and it presses Kalvatar with coin and cult rather than open fleets.
Refugees and spies wash south constantly. Steel, wine, and books come through the gate; Free City firearms are carried south by smugglers; registered Krysta goes north.
The archipelago's dragonborn came from Assios, as refugees, exiles, and traders of the long war.
Khard Muur is a wild continent beyond the western ocean, of ruined kingdoms and unsettled wilds. Off its southwest coast lies Xathnatraz.
The wider world holds other continents, known to the archipelago only by rumor and the occasional wreck.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Nobody has ever painted the Imperium's Grand Inquisitor. The Frontier spies who claim to have seen him won't say what he looked like.” (an Ironfort customs clerk)
“Sailors back from Khard Muur say Valengrad crowned King Rune last year. They crowned him the year before too, and he was buried in between.” (a sailor back from the west)

facts: the Baronies and the Free Cities

title: The Wrong Coast
subtitle: Plague waters. Closed horizon.
summary: The quarantined waters of the far south, closed since 148 EC. The Council calls them plague waters. Sailors tell of grey ships and the Hum.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Sealed Waters of the far south, where the Wilds fray into the ice, have been closed by Council order since 148 EC as "plague waters."
Southern sailors call them the Wrong Coast.
They tell stories of grey ships with no names that sail without lanterns.
They tell of the Hum, a note under hearing that you feel in the hull on calm nights. Never hum along.
Southern custom: carry a silver Tide in your boot when you sail south, and lay a silver Tide on the tongue of the dead.
Compasses behave there, the stars behave, the sea behaves, and that, the sailors say, is what is wrong with it: it behaves as if it is holding its breath.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Wrong Coast. The quarantined waters of the far south are "plague waters," the Council says. Southern sailors tell stories of grey ships with no names that sail without lanterns, and of the Hum: a note under hearing that you feel in the hull on calm nights. Never hum along.” (common talk)

title: Aurelion
subtitle: Smoke you can see from Goldwind
summary: Aurelion is the forge-city of the north coast, and the seat of the Sunforge house.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Aurelion’s smoke is visible from Goldwind on a clear day, and its metalwork, firearms, and goldsmithery fill the Congress's warehouses. The Sunforge house is the master-smith house of the Heartland, fabulously wealthy and deeply tied to the Congress. Its forges, the Sunforge works, are the only place in the Heartland where a firearm can be made to proof standard, and the Aurelion smiths guard the secret of that proof as closely as the Council guards its seats.

title: Bastion
subtitle: The gate of the north
summary: Bastion is the seat of House Faust, the gate-fortress of the north.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Bastion stands on a fortified island at the mouth of the eastern sea-road, with a curtain wall that has held off every fleet that tested it. The Faust garrison is the largest standing force in the archipelago outside the Armada, and the house's remount farms supply horses to half the Frontier. The Bastion tourneys in the summer are the great martial spectacle of the north, and the winners carry the Faust sigil home with them as a mark of standing. Johann Faust, the captain of the Jubilant and a celebrated Hunter, is the house's most famous son, and his divided loyalty between blood and oath is the house's most discussed private trouble.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Kastan Vol Kaern is buying Bastion's debts through the Zane house. He will own the Frontier's gate before the Council knows he has begun.” (heard in the Central Heartland)

title: Black Harbor
subtitle: Where the fog pays no duty
summary: Black Harbor is the smugglers' capital of the Frontier, a warren of wharves and sea-caves in the fog below Greyhaven.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Black Harbor is the home of the Fogrunners, who carry untaxed cargo through the Murk by bell-codes so exact they can thread the Widow's Teeth blind. Its leader, Wenna Hollis, the Bellmistress, has never been caught, because no officer of the Gate-Tithe has ever been able to hear what she is saying. The Gullet, a tide-cave that leads down into the Below, opens at the harbor's north end, and the Fogrunners use it when the Council's patrols are thickest on the surface.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The dry road. The roads Below run island to island, and a smuggler who knew them could walk a cargo from Black Harbor to Goldwind without paying a single harbor due.” (common talk)

illustration.alt: Sailors unload a boat on the fog-bound wharves of Black Harbor beneath Greyhaven.
illustration.caption: Fog and bell-codes shelter the Frontier’s untaxed trade.

title: Briarcrown
subtitle: Quiet, prosperous, and watchful
summary: Briarcrown is the seat of House Silverthorn, a fortified town on a hill above the eastern shore.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Briarcrown is quiet, prosperous, and watchful, with a reputation for discretion that is nearly a crime in itself. Its houses have high walls and silent gardens, and the Silverthorn spies keep a register of every visitor to the Heartland's shadow markets. The house's rivalry with House Alastor is cold and deep. Neither trusts the other, and both trade in secrets for a living.

title: Crystalhaven
subtitle: A town built from other people’s ships
summary: Crystalhaven is a wrecking-town on the blue-ice coast.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Crystalhaven’s harbor is a half-moon of frozen water, and its streets are lined with the hulls of ships that came in with a light in their eyes and never went out. The False Lights are the town's wreckers, who hang false lanterns on the cliffs to lure ships onto the ice, and then strip the wreck. Granny Ylva Skerrow is the wreckers' matriarch, a tiny woman with a voice like a foghorn and a memory for every ship she has ever lured. Southern captains say "not every kind coast is kind" when they pass the blue-ice cliffs, and they make the sign of the Answering Light as they sail on.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Mira has been seen at Crystalhaven with Granny Skerrow's grandson. A smuggler's heir is never seen with a wrecker's grandson unless one of them means to take the other's chair.” (heard in the Icy Expanse)

title: Duskmire Haven
subtitle: Stilts, reeds, and very good false coin
summary: Duskmire Haven is a misty fen near Goldwind, a town of stilt-houses and reed-boats where the Registry's writ grows thin.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Duskmire Haven is the home of the Mint-in-the-Mire, the coiners whose drowned Anchors are so good that the Council's mint has twice bought them back by mistake. The master engraver is Ottar Glimm, a gnome of terrible genius and worse temper. The Knot, the market below Duskmire kept by goblins, opens in the fen's deepest reed-beds, and the goblins permit no names, no blades, and no light brighter than a candle.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Goldspire's heir was seen at a pawnbroker's on the Duskmire road, in a borrowed cloak.” (a Duskmire pawnbroker's boy)

title: Easthold, Westwatch, and Pearl Groove
subtitle: Three working towns of the Heartland
summary: Easthold is the fishing port of the east coast, with its fleets, herb-gardens, and seafood markets.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Westwatch is the mining town of the western heights, its quarries and coal-pits supplying the Heartland's stone and fuel. Pearl Groove is a shallow lagoon of pearl-clans, where the divers work the beds under the watchful eyes of the Belmaris house and its bell-mistress. The pearls and the murex-dyed reefpurple are the region's most exclusive exports, and the Coral Kingdoms' sound-trade passes through the Groove on the way to the Congress.

title: Elyria
subtitle: The white towers of the deathless
summary: Elyria is the elven hold of House Caelvaron, the only major seat ruled by the deathless.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Elyria’s towers are white and pale green, set among ancient trees on the eastern hills. The Caelvaron rulers rotate on the Hundred-Year Cycle, and the Elyria court is the most patient and least hurried in the Heartland. The elves of Elyria remember grudges older than the Charter, and the court keeps records that the Council would give much to read.

title: Frosthold
subtitle: Ice-stone, whale-bone, and oil
summary: Frosthold is the capital of the whaling coast and the strongest seat of the Brine Brotherhood, the fishers and whalers who keep the Expanse alive.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The fortress-walls are built of ice-stone and whale-bone, and the oil-houses along the bay burn the whale-fat that every lamp in the Heartland burns. The Brennvar house holds the oil-houses, and its Lamp-Mistress, Astri, rules the bay with a fairness that the Brotherhood respects and the Combine resents. The Tidecallers of the Concord keep a small temple on the harbor wall, and their sea-blessing is the first thing every whaling fleet receives before it goes out. Frosthold is the last place in the Expanse where a stranger can buy a warm room for a silver Tide.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Goldwind's lamps burn cleaner since Frosthold changed its oil. The lamplighters say the smoke smells faintly of coins.” (a Goldwind lamplighter)

title: Golgarma
subtitle: The city the Orka left
summary: A city of Orka ruins, vast monuments of stone that loom over the jungle like the bones of a dead god. The Crimson Legion holds it now.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: Golgarma’s avenues are wide enough for an army, and its monuments stand taller than the trees that have grown up between them. The ruins are still beautiful. A visitor who walks the great avenues at dusk can feel the Orka’s pride in the stone.
At the heart of the city the Orka cut a great stair down to the deeps. It is called Golgarma’s Throat, and it leads to the undercity of Nadhûr.

sections.title: Who holds it
paragraphs: The Crimson Legion holds the ruins and flies its banners from the stair, which it took this year. Its raids push north of Golgarma each season. The Emerald Wrath has asked for a second squadron to hold the river-ports against them, and the Council is reviewing the request.

sections.title: Who lived in its shadow
paragraphs: The tribes of the ruins lived among the outer monuments for generations: stone-readers, vine-cutters, and guides who knew which doors were safe. Orc clans count the city as an ancestor’s house and kept its outer shrines. Most of them are on the road north now, or hiding in the jungle within sight of home.
Digging crews still slip in for what the Orka left behind. Fewer come out than used to.

sections.title: If you come from here
list: You grew up playing on carved stone older than any kingdom, and nothing built since impresses you.
You know which doors your people never opened, and you were never told why.
The Legion took your home, and you know people who did not get out.
You can read a little of the old carving, or at least which way it points.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Legion didn’t fight its way down the Throat. Something opened it for them from below.” (a refugee stone-reader)
“There are lights in the high windows at night, in the quarter the Legion doesn’t camp in.” (an Emerald Wrath river pilot)

facts: Golgarma’s Throat, down to the undercity of Nadhûr
the Legion’s raids push north each season

illustration.alt: The Crimson Legion guards Golgarma’s great stone stair to Nadhûr amid colossal Orka ruins.
illustration.caption: The Legion holds the Throat.

epigraph.quote: My grandmother sold water on the great avenue. Now I sell it to the people running from there.
epigraph.by: a river-port trader north of Golgarma

title: Greyhaven
subtitle: Salt-fish and bells
summary: Greyhaven is a grey, hard port that lives inside the fog.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Greyhaven’s harbor is the richest salt-fish harbor in the Frontier, and its bells never stop during the Murk. The Stormweaver house, a Marchlord line of storm-sorcerers, keeps the Greyhaven lights burning through the fog, and the house's mages are paid by the Brine Brotherhood's fishing fleets to keep the fishing boats off the rocks. The Widow's Teeth lie just off the harbor mouth, and every Greyhaven child learns the bell-codes before they learn their letters, because a boat that cannot read the bells cannot find the harbor. The old quarter has a chapel on the cliff where the widows of the lost light lamps for the boats that have not come home.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Johann Faust has been seen in a Greyhaven tavern with a man who wears the Last Psalm's badge. Nobody knows which side he means to take.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)

title: Hollowkey
subtitle: The lagoon no chart admits to
summary: Hollowkey is a hidden lagoon in the uncharted south, the greatest of the Pirate Freeholds: a drift-market of lashed-together hulks where the Remnants of Blackheart, the Free Tide crews, and every outlaw captain in the south…

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Hollowkey is a hidden lagoon in the uncharted south, the greatest of the Pirate Freeholds: a drift-market of lashed-together hulks where the Remnants of Blackheart, the Free Tide crews, and every outlaw captain in the south trade, refit, and drink. Its rules are the Free Tide's rules. No Council flag flies there, no Council coin is accepted, and every deal is sealed by the sea. The Hollowkey harbor-master is a retired Armada Blade-Ensign who lost an arm to the Drowning Star, and who will tell anyone who buys him a tot exactly how the Star was fired.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Reinhardt Holst buys a drink for every old pirate in Hollowkey and asks each of them the same question: whose colors sank the Sea Seraph?” (a Hollowkey barkeep)

illustration.alt: A hidden southern pirate lagoon is filled with lashed-together hulls, wooden walkways, boats and market stalls.
illustration.caption: Trade and repairs carry on in Hollowkey’s floating market.

title: Kaldmark
subtitle: The black keep of the ice
summary: Kaldmark is the hold of House Kaldmark, the one true noble house of the Expanse.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Kaldmark is a fortified stronghold in the hills, with a black stone keep and a gate of whale-bone, and its banners carry the white bear-skull on a black field rimmed in ice-blue. The House holds a march of whaling-towns and ice against a frontier that kills the careless. Its Marchlord, Sten Kaldmark, governs with the hold's grim law, and he has learned exactly what his house's motto means. The Kaldmark icebrand stillhouses supply the house's warriors, and the house's blood-feud with the Varan Lodge is older than any living Kaldmark.

title: Karn Sorroch
subtitle: The Midnight Patron’s mines
summary: Karn Sorroch is the domain of Velemnos, the Midnight Patron, a dark and jungled land of infamous Krysta-mines worked by the unfree.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The town of Karn Sorroch is a fortified mining-camp on a river-bend, its gates kept by the thralls of the House of Vossreth, and its streets are lit by low-grade Krysta lamps whose stored workings glow blue within the stones. The Krysta comes out of the deep mines in carts under the Vossreth seal, and the mines are the richest source of dark glass in the south. No visitor is allowed to see the Patron, and most visitors who try do not come back out.

title: The Kraken's Maw
subtitle: Two reefs and a graveyard of fleets
summary: A passage between two reefs, where the great battle of 165 EC was fought.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The wrecks of the Armada and the Blackheart fleets lie on the reef's bottom, and divers say the wrecks still hum at dusk.

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

illustration.alt: Two adult salvagers row among weed-covered wooden wrecks in the Kraken's Maw in 175 EC, ten years after the battle, with the reefs fading into evening fog.
illustration.caption: Ten years on, the sea keeps its tally.

title: Northreach
subtitle: The horse country of the Frontier
summary: A country of gorse, heather, stud-farms, and long grey roads, where the finest horses in the islands are bred and the Tarvan clans come down to gather.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: Inland from the coast the moors rise in gorse and heather toward the high Tarvan country. The land is poor for crops and excellent for horses and sheep. Long grey roads join the stud-farms to the ports, and you can ride half a day on one without meeting a wall.
The Faust remounts breed here, and the Northreach studs produce the finest horses in the islands, which fetch twice their weight in Anchors in Goldwind.

sections.title: Who lives there
paragraphs: Stud-farming families who can recite a bloodline to the tenth dam. Trappers, whose towns supply the furs that line every Frontier hood. Loggers, whose camps cut the timber the Expanse cannot grow. And the Tarvan clans, who graze their own herds on the high moors.
A few herds of centaurs run the heath as well. The stud-farms hire them as horse-masters, and neither side is quite sure who works for whom.

sections.title: The Gathering
paragraphs: In the year when all the scattered Tarvan clans come down together, Northreach holds the Tarvan Gathering. It is a market, a moot, a festival, and a proving at once: horses are sold, feuds are settled, marriages are made, and champions fight for the honor of it.

sections.title: If you come from here
list: You could ride before you could read, and you judge people by how they treat a horse.
You know furs, timber, or bloodlines well enough to be cheated in none of them.
You are used to distance, weather, and neighbors a morning’s ride away.
You have been to a Gathering, and you still owe or are owed something from it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The best colt of the year always goes to a buyer nobody saw arrive. Paid in old coin, every time.” (a Northreach stud-groom)
“The centaurs won’t run the high moor past the standing-stones any more. They say the ground has a pulse.” (a Bastion ostler)

facts: the Northreach studs, the Faust remounts, furs, and timber
the Tarvan Gathering: market, moot, festival, and proving at once
stud-farmers, trappers, loggers, and the Tarvan clans

epigraph.quote: A Northreach horse will carry you anywhere. A Northreach dealer will take you about as far.

title: Saltreach
subtitle: The salt of the whole north
summary: Saltreach is a flat coast of pans, sluices, and salt-sheds, held by the Hallorn trading house, whose Lord-Mistress holds the Frontier's salt monopoly.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The salt-workers are the most organized labor in the north, and they have struck four times in living memory. The pans are the source of the salt that the Charterhouse Company buys to hold its southern monopoly, and the trade between the Hallorn sheds and the Company's agents in Southhaven is one of the most profitable and least discussed secrets of the Frontier.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A hush owl went quiet at a wedding in Saltreach last Storm Water, and the groom has not been seen since.” (a Frontier tavern)

title: Silverport
subtitle: Silk, incense, and pale stone
summary: Silverport is the eastern silk-port, a city of pale stone and fragrant gardens.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Silverport’s silk-farms and incense-houses supply the Heartland's silk, perfume, and fine oils. The Perfumers of Silverport are at open war with the Pocchin families, who refuse to join the guild, undersell everyone, and steal recipes for sport. The Saffrane house holds the silk trade. The city's markets sell the finest perfumes in the islands, and the rarest of them contain ambergris from Frosthold.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Tobbin pride say Saffrane's famous Black Rose was theirs first, and that they still have the bill of sale.” (a Pocchin, loudly)

title: Snowvah
subtitle: The last warm meal before the silence
summary: Snowvah is the northernmost settled town of the Expanse, a cluster of stone houses on a black-rock promontory above the ice.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Snowvah is the last place where a stranger can buy a warm meal before the silent country begins. The Snowvah folk are hard, quiet, and proud. They keep a watch on the sky beyond the last posts, and they do not talk about what they see there.

title: Southhaven
subtitle: The counting-house of the Wilds
summary: Southhaven is the colonial port of the southern coast and the commercial heart of the Wilds.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Southhaven’s harbor is lined with the warehouses of the great plantation houses, and its hills grow the coffee, southleaf, cane-sugar, and cotton that every Heartland salon consumes. The Charterhouse Company keeps its southern offices here, and its writ-men, the brass-collars, patrol the warehouse streets. The plantations are divided between the fair estates of House Greymoor and the unfree estates of House Vossreth, and the southern boycott is simple: "Greymoor coffee or none." The Blackleaf Runners smuggle southleaf in and indentured workers out through the river-ports. The Southhaven markets are the best place in the south to learn anything about anyone, and the worst place to be seen learning it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Scarlet Mother's priest was seen in Southhaven buying the Fennick factors' coffee in bulk. Nobody says what he wants with so much of it.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“Damyel's ship made Mumit from Southhaven in five days, against the wind. The fastest Justicar in the Emerald Wrath needs two weeks.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“Every tide anemone in Southhaven closed at noon on the same day last year, out of turn, for exactly as long as it takes to say a prayer.” (a Southhaven harbor-widow)

title: Stormreach
subtitle: Where the north builds its ships
summary: Stormreach is the seat of House Vanris and the largest shipbuilding yard in the north.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Stormguard Hold is a fortress on a rock above the strait, and the house's yards build the best storm-hulls in the islands and charge a premium for them. The Ninth Fleet, the Standing Storm, keeps its base here, and the Galven crews of the great Juggernaut storm-runners sleep in the lower wards. The town is named for the weather and lives by it. Its spring water fizzes naturally from the rock, and the Galven call it stormwater, shaking it into their kellum and swearing that lightning tastes the same. Mortimer Vanris holds the seat, and his brother Rodrick and the spymaster Cassandra Dosslas hold the house together around him.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Stormwater from the Stormreach spring tastes of the sea where it used to taste of rock.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“Fishers off Stormreach netted a brass hatch the size of a door, with a wheel on it.” (a Stormreach fishwife)

title: Sunhold
subtitle: Terraces, white walls, and brightleaf
summary: Sunhold is the brightest city in the Heartland, a town of terraces and white walls above the western coast.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Sunhold’s hills grow the brightleaf that the Terrace Guild presses into leaf-bricks, and its vines produce the Sunhold wines that the Goldwind banks judge by taste. The Sunhold Accord, signed on Veriden 6th, is a treaty of the Concord and the Council that the town hosts every year. The Terrace Guild feuds with the coffee-houses of Goldwind as a matter of identity, and the feud is the subject of a hundred songs.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Dio Emberheart has been seen walking in the Sunhold gardens. The people who saw him say he was not quite the same man who walked there last year.” (heard in the Central Heartland)
“The Sunhold terraces grow a brightleaf that the Registry buys every leaf of, and nobody has ever been allowed to taste it.” (a Terrace Guild picker)

title: Xathnatraz
subtitle: The isle nobody goes looking for
summary: A cursed black isle off the southwest coast of Khard Muur, where the dark of the old Eon was sealed. Ships that go looking come back with fewer people, or not at all.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Xathnatraz is a black isle off the southwest coast of Khard Muur, the wild continent beyond the western ocean.
Every child learns that long ago a sunless Eon of Darkness swallowed the world, and that its dark was sealed inside Xathnatraz.
Its lost kingdom of Alcyor fell long ago. Only the last bastion, Valengrad, still holds, under King Rune Vermillion.
No ship has landed there in living memory without the crew falling to a fever that burns in the blood.
"Don't sail west," the sailors say. Ships that go looking for it come back with fewer people, or not at all.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Don't sail west. Out past the edge of the charts lies cursed Xathnatraz, the isle where the dark of the old Eon was sealed. Ships that go looking for it come back with fewer people, or not at all.” (common talk)
“Sailors back from Khard Muur say Valengrad crowned King Rune last year. They crowned him the year before too, and he was buried in between.” (a sailor back from the west)

facts: off the southwest coast of Khard Muur

title: Zal'Kareth
subtitle: The last Council town
summary: Zal'Kareth is the last Council town on the southwestern edge of the Wilds, a fortified river-port beyond which the Council's maps go blank.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Zal'Kareth is the home of the Ninth Shovel, the grave-robbers and ruin-looters who feed the Quiet Auction with Orka relics and native sacred things. The Ninth Shovel is at war with the Reclaimers, the Sacred Flame, and anyone else who stands in the way of the next treasure. The town's walls are high, and its guard is paid well to look away from what comes up the river at night.

title: The Cistern Door
subtitle: The wall that is warm to the touch
summary: A dwarven wall under Goldwind's oldest cistern, whose mortar was worked from the far side.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Any visitor who lays a hand on the wall feels a faint warmth, and the dwarves of the Goldwind holds say the warmth is the debt being paid, one load at a time.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Cistern Door. At the bottom of Goldwind's oldest cistern is a dwarven wall, and someone has been working its mortar from the other side.” (common talk)

title: The Giant's Table
subtitle: The stone on the Giant’s shoulder
summary: A flat stone platform on the high Tarvan moor, set on the shoulder of the Sleeping Giant, the land-spirit that lies beneath the Northreach heath.

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: The high moor is gorse, heather, peat, and weather. The Giant’s Table stands on its highest shoulder: a flat platform of grey stone, ringed at a distance by standing-stones older than the clans.
The Tarvan say the Sleeping Giant lies beneath the heath and that the Table rests on its shoulder. A Tarvan who sits on the Table at dusk hears the Giant breathe.

sections.title: Who lives there
paragraphs: The horned Tarvan clans graze moorhorn and horses across the high country, keep their own ways, and hold their own moots on the open heath. Their dead are laid beneath the standing-stones, and graze, the clans say, in the Endless Pasture just beyond them.
Other moor-folk live among them: shepherds, peat-cutters, and trappers, who take the clans’ customs if not their horns.

sections.title: The First Grass
paragraphs: On the first morning of spring every clan in reach walks its herds once around the Table before they are let onto the new grass. Ulmach the Herd-Father is said to tread the stones ahead of them. Nobody leads a beast across the Table itself, and nobody sits on it in daylight.

sections.title: If you come from here
list: You can sleep in rain, find a path in fog, and tell whose cairn you are passing.
You count combat an honest art and a moot the right place to settle most things.
You have sat the Table at dusk, once, as every child of the moor does.
Flat country with no stones in it feels unfinished to you.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Tarvan on the Giant's Table heard the Sleeping Giant turn over in its sleep. She went home and sold every horse she had.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“The old stones stand a little taller than they did. The clans measure them every spring and tell the garrisons nothing.” (a Northreach trapper)

facts: the Sleeping Giant, and Ulmach the Herd-Father
the First Grass: the herds are walked around the Table on the first morning of spring
the Tarvan clans of the high moor

epigraph.quote: Sit quiet. Feel that? That’s not the wind.
epigraph.by: a Tarvan herder, to a child on the Table at dusk

title: The Knot
subtitle: The market under the reeds
summary: A market below Duskmire, reached through the reed-beds and kept by goblins.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Knot is the only trading place in the Below that the surface folk use by choice. Its rules are short: no names, no blades, and no light brighter than a candle.

illustration.alt: A goblin merchant bargains with visitors by candlelight in The Knot under Duskmire.
illustration.caption: No names, no blades, no light brighter than a candle.

title: The Maw-Pit
subtitle: Jakupur’s arena
summary: An arena cut into the rock of Jakupur's southern hill, where saurians fight one another and the condemned.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Maw-Pit is not a wonder of nature, but it is a wonder of the south, and visitors who have seen the Maw-Pit's sand after a fight never tell the same story twice.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Maw-Pit is holding a fight this month that does not have a condemned man in it. It has a child.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

illustration.alt: Handlers lead a giant feathered saurian into the rock-cut arena of Jakupur before a waiting crowd.
illustration.caption: The Maw-Pit fills before the contest begins.

title: The Rime Ways
subtitle: The roads under the ice
summary: A network of channels under the winter sea-ice, opened by the dwarves of the Expanse's deep holds and used by the smugglers when the ice is too thick for ships.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Rime Ways connect the Expanse to the Below, and the dwarves say a tally-mark is cut at every turning, and that the marks go down further than any man has dived.

illustration.alt: A dwarven guide points to tally marks inside the ice channels of the Rime Ways beside a skiff.
illustration.caption: At every turning, another tally in the ice.

title: The Serpent's Coil
subtitle: The reef that founded a house
summary: A ring of reefs in the Stormreach strait, shaped like a serpent coiled about a tower.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Vanris house took its founding from the sea serpent that led Valdar Vanris to the fortress-site, and the Coil is the serpent's body in stone. Captains who run the Coil in a storm say the reef moves at the King Tide, and the house has never been able to prove otherwise, or to prove it wrong.

title: The Sun's Grave
subtitle: Named on every old chart, explained on none
summary: A patch of open sea south of the Goldwind gulf that the oldest charts name and no chart explains.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Fishermen say the water there is warm in winter and that nets come up with gold leaf caught in them. Nobody fishes it twice.

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

title: The Veil of Shadows
subtitle: The curtain rises again.
summary: A shadow-theater in Goldwind's old quarter, halfway up the city's rings, where a single play has run every night for about a hundred and forty years without a dark night.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The actors perform behind a great veil of white silk. Goldwind's nobility never miss a season.

illustration.alt: An audience watches performers cast silhouettes behind a great white silk veil in a Goldwind theater.
illustration.caption: The same play fills the Veil of Shadows each night.

title: Abyssara, the Black Below
subtitle: The deepest court
summary: Abyssara is the trench beneath the trenches, where the dark has never been broken.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Abyssara is the lair of Thalgorath, and of something vast and ancient that the sea-peoples call by a name they do not say near the water. Even the deep courts will not go there. Abyssara is the place they fear.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Abyssara: what falls into the southwestern trench does not come back; what comes back is changed.” (common talk)

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

title: The Glass Gardens
subtitle: The city of living reef
summary: The Glass Gardens are the fair merfolk's realm in the Sunlit shallows, a city of living reef-architecture where the coral grows in shapes the sea-folk choose.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Glass Gardens’ towers are clear, and its streets are lit by bioluminescent fish. The Glass Gardens are the sea's most welcoming court, and the sea-folk trade memory-pearls there to surface visitors who come to them with a kind word and a clean hand.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Pelagar has been buying the Starfall coral in bulk. The Glass Gardens have stopped trading with Pelagar in return.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

illustration.alt: Two merfolk with fin-frills extend both hands toward a memory pearl amid the coral arches of the fully submerged Glass Gardens.
illustration.caption: A memory pearl changes hands in the Sunlit shallows.

title: The Grey Fathoms
subtitle: The court that keeps the drowned
summary: The Grey Fathoms are the realm of the kept drowned, a deep court whose sea-folk gather the dead of the surface and keep them in silver-lit caves.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Grey Fathoms’ ransom is fair: a family that comes to the Grey Fathoms with a pearl and a song may take a drowned relative home for a day. The Fathoms refuse the dead of the Wrong Coast, and their keepers have never said why.

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

title: The Old Shells
subtitle: Three questions a generation
summary: The Old Shells are the realm of the leviathan sage-turtles, great ancient creatures whose shells are the size of islands.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Old Shells answer three questions a generation, to any who come to them with a gift of sound and a true question. The Old Shells surface at the Stillwater, and their answers have shaped the Armada's naval doctrine twice in living memory.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Old Shells answered a question last month that no one had asked. The answer was the name of a ship, and the ship has not been seen since.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)
“The Old Shells have surfaced at the Stillwater three times this year. They used to come up once in a generation.” (a Last Psalm Tidecaller)

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

illustration.alt: A sage-turtle as large as an island surfaces beside a tiny sailing boat at Stillwater.
illustration.caption: A gift of sound and a true question approach an Old Shell.

title: Pearl Groove and the Pelagar Isle
subtitle: Where the surface trades with the deep
summary: Pearl Groove is the surface's pearl-port, a shallow lagoon of pearl-clans on the Heartland's coast, under the watch of the Belmaris house and its bell-mistress Orlaine.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Pelagar isle lies on the Coral edge, a small island of pearl-houses and sea-gardens, where the Pelagar house keeps its pacts and its secrets. Both ports are the surface's gateway to the courts, and both are watched by every faction in the Heartland.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Someone is buying every reefpurple dye that comes through Pearl Groove. The Council cannot find the buyer, and the Pelagar house will not say.” (heard in the Central Heartland)
“Pelagar has been buying the Starfall coral in bulk. The Glass Gardens have stopped trading with Pelagar in return.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)
“A memory-pearl sold in Pearl Groove shows a woman's face on the Sunken Thrones. She is looking up, and she is smiling.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

title: The Red Choir
subtitle: Hymns for blood in the water
summary: The Red Choir is the sahuagin blood-faith, a deep and savage court whose hymns rise when blood is in the water.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Red Choir’s choirmaster is Thalgorath, the Tide-Tyrant, and its priests sing him up from the depths on the King Tide. The Red Choir does not trade with the surface, and the Pelagar house has never been able to make it an offer it would accept.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Red Choir has started singing on a quiet night, when there is no blood in the water. The Tidecallers say the song is coming up the Starfall Reef.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

title: The Sunken Thrones
subtitle: The courts nobody has seen
summary: The Sunken Thrones are the deep courts, a midnight abyss of ancient sovereigns whose politics do not map onto anything a land-mind can hold.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: What little is known of them comes thirdhand through the Pelagar house, and the Pelagar house does not share it, because some of it cannot be told without changing the teller.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A memory-pearl sold in Pearl Groove shows a woman's face on the Sunken Thrones. She is looking up, and she is smiling.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

title: The Whispering Current
subtitle: Every word spoken over water
summary: The Whispering Current is the twilight secret-traders' realm, a court of currents that carry every word spoken over water.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Whispering Current’s keepers buy and sell the secrets of the surface's harbors, and the Skein, the great Heartland information-broker, has a standing contract with them. Speak carelessly over water in a Current port and the Current will remember, and the words will be sold at the next full moon.

facts: The Sea and the Coral Kingdoms

title: The Charterhouse Company
subtitle: Brass collars and company towns
summary: A Council-chartered trading company that bypasses the guilds: monopolies, company towns, and enforcers called brass-collars.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Outside the guilds stands the Charterhouse Company, a Council-chartered trading company with monopolies, company towns, and enforcers the docks call brass-collars.
Governor: Imelda Roque, "the Lady of Writs."
Holdings: the southern salt monopoly (won in 175 EC; two ports rioted), the Verdayan jade concession, and indenture contracts in the south.
Its southern offices are in Southhaven.
Everyone knows it wants the thirteenth flag-socket on the Spire Floor very badly.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The center socket. The Spire Floor has a thirteenth flag-socket at its center that has never held a flag, and the Charterhouse Company wants it very badly.” (common talk)

facts: Imelda Roque, the Lady of Writs

title: The Reckoners' Hall
subtitle: The bank that holds the islands’ debts
summary: The Congress's bank, under First Reckoner Maera Blackstrand, who holds half the islands' debts.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Everyone knows the real power of the Mercantile Congress is its bank, the Reckoners' Hall, the marble hall in Goldwind under First Reckoner Maera Blackstrand, who holds half the islands' debts.
Credit: the Reckoners lend at 1 in 20 to the Five great houses, and as high as 1 in 5 to a tradesman.
Bottomry (a loan on a ship and its cargo) runs from 1 in 50 on the coast to 1 in 5 on the ice, and three times that in a King Tide year.
A reckoning, a letter of credit, costs 2 in 100.
The Still Days freeze every debt.
Three Coinsdays unpaid put a name in the Ledger.
Under salvage law, the Reckoners register claims on named wrecks, and they pay the Council's bounties on proof.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Theodora Nightshade: she has slipped in and out of the Reckoners' Hall.” (the docks, about the Most Wanted)

illustration.alt: Clerks weigh coins and tend ledgers while captains and merchants wait in the Reckoners’ Hall.
illustration.caption: Clerks weigh coins and tend ledgers while captains and merchants wait in the Reckoners’ Hall.

title: The Twelve Flags
subtitle: The families of the Spire Floor
summary: The great merchant families who hold the twelve flag-posts of the Spire Floor in Goldwind and call the Coinsday board-price.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Twelve Flags are the great merchant families. Each holds one of the twelve flag-posts on the Spire Floor, the trading hall of the Goldspire Exchange in Goldwind, where every Coinsday they call the board-price of coffee, salt, oil, grain, and the rest. A post takes a bond of 1,000 Orsals and twenty years on the floor, and it passes only by family.
Goldspire, who own the Exchange: Merchant Lord Horace, heir Celestine.
The Corvane Line, the great shipping house that carries the Council's post: Matthias, "the Old Crow."
Saffrane of Silverport, silk and perfume: Madame Ilsabet.
Vantrey, the licensed Krysta brokers: Lord-Broker Edmar.
Belmaris of Pearl Groove, bells and the sea-folk's sound-trade: Bell-Mistress Orlaine.
Ostrel of Ironfort, farmers of the Gate-Tithe: Tithe-Mistress Maren.
Hallorn of Saltreach, salt and herring: Aldric.
Fennick of Southhaven, coffee and sugar factors: Ondine, a half-elf.
The Oruma, a native river-clan of the Nine Mouths: Grandmother Veyani. They took House Darrowen's post when it fell in 171 EC.
Sukuun of Jakupur, saurians: Teoma, brother of the great tamer Tana.
Brennvar of Frosthold, whale-oil: Lamp-Mistress Astri.
The Tobbin pride, a Pocchin family, to everyone's continuing astonishment: Mother Tatta and Pobbo.
Bannermen are the sworn houses, flag-captains, and bought bannerets of each flag, bound by the Flag-Oath. A broken oath gets the flag struck.
The center socket. The Spire Floor has a thirteenth flag-socket at its center that has never held a flag.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Scarlet Mother's priest was seen in Southhaven buying the Fennick factors' coffee in bulk. Nobody says what he wants with so much of it.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

facts: the Spire Floor, Goldspire Exchange, Goldwind

title: The Great Hunter Crews
subtitle: The names on the Board
summary: The crews every islander can name, from the Crimson Tide to the Karnivool, and the rival crews of the Board.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Famous crews:
Crimson Tide: Captain Bramgard, who breached and sank the Gaze of Abyss at the Kraken's Maw, and his First Mate Albion Tempest.
Rolling Thunder: co-captains Uther and Gunther Banestorm.
Jubilant: Captain Johann Faust of House Faust.
The Last Word: Captain Khaz'Aimar Maa'iq.
Zephyr: Sandros Magnus.
Karnivool: a Hunters' ship and a traveling show at once, under captain and ringmaster Avalan Grant.
Retribution's Wrath: Reinhardt Holst, disinherited by House Holst; the youngest Gold, seventeenth in the Ranking.
Iron Swan: Titania, who struck through the pirate line again and again at the Maw.
The rival crews everyone has heard of:
The Gilded Wake: Capt. Odessa Braith's house-sponsored darlings, who arrive second and claim credit first.
The Saltborn Nine: Warden Rhona Cravoch's exactly nine cold professionals, all Tarvan steel.
The Second Sons: Capt. Lucan Alastor's disgraced nobles, reckless, lovable, and broke.
The Flensers: "Old Knife" Petra Sallow's badge-stripped poachers no decent Lodge will name.

title: The Iron
subtitle: The coin that opens the Trials
summary: Not a rank: the iron coin a candidate needs to sit the Trials of Ascension. Only 300 are struck each year.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: There is no Iron rank. To sit the yearly Trials of Ascension you need a Hunter's endorsement, which is usually an iron: an iron coin struck with the Hunters' shield.
Only 300 irons are struck each year.
Whoever presents an iron sits the Trials. Lose yours, and someone else uses it, and that is your problem.
A candidate carrying one is called an iron, and "still carrying iron" means a rookie who has not yet sat the Trials.
Hunters buy irons at the Crucible in Ironfort, up to two a year at 10 Orsals each, or earn them on important contracts. Some contracts pay in an iron, and a Hunter may ask for one as part of the fee.
Most candidates work under the Hunter who gave them their iron. It is only a duty if the iron was given on that condition; an iron given without strings binds nothing.
Every year's irons are struck to a new die, so last year's is worthless. You can sit the Trials as many times as you like, if you survive them, but each attempt needs a new iron.

The iron market is seasonal. The Crucible mints the year's irons one to two months after the Trials, so the market shuts for that window and reopens for the rest of the year, peaking as the next Trials approach. In the Undertow an iron fetches 150 to 300 Anchors in that last season.

facts: 10 Orsals, two a year at most

title: The Sigil
subtitle: The badge that knows its bearer
summary: A Hunter's rank badge, forged at the Goldwind Lodge. It is bearer-bound: anyone else who holds it suffers, worse the higher the rank.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Every Hunter's Sigil is made in one place: the Sigil-Forge of the Goldwind Lodge, by the Sigilwrights under the Master Sigilwright, one of the most prestigious titles in the guild.
The curse is forged in. A Sigil carried by anyone but its rightful bearer works on them, and the longer it is held, the worse it gets. None of it kills.
Bronze: a mild headache, and a numbness in the hand that spreads with time.
Silver: nausea and vomiting, fainting spells, and a slow drain of strength.
Gold: like a deadly poison taking hold: fever, weakness, and pain that build by the hour.
Rank protects. A Silver Hunter is immune to a Bronze Sigil, and a Gold Hunter to Silver and Bronze.
Branches. Every Hunter belongs to a branch, and the branch is worked into the Sigil:
Mage: arcane motifs, crystals, and glyphs.
Scout: feathers, arrows, and predators.
Diplomat: scrolls, olive branches, and symbols of union.
Warrior: shields, weapons, and bold lines.
Design by rank:
Bronze: a simple single piece of bronze, with the iron of the Hunter who vouched for it set into the back.
Silver: engraved, often inlaid with gems or fine detail.
Gold: ornate and made of several materials, showing the bearer's deeds. A Gold Sigil may carry two branches.
Platinum: enchanted platinum of a craft no one else can match.
Awakened Sigils. Rarely, a Sigil awakens: it becomes a sentient thing with a personality of its own and bonds with its bearer like a partner.

title: The Trials of Ascension
subtitle: The yearly proving
summary: The Hunters' yearly exam, held in the month of Ezra. Its last leg is the Vow, where the candidate's iron is set into a new Bronze Sigil.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Trials of Ascension are the Hunters' exam, held once a year, in Ezra, the month of Mast and Sail.
You need an iron to sit them.
Those who pass swear the Oath and are made Bronze.
A candidate who fails is encouraged to sit them again; a few are offered support roles instead: clerks, quartermasters, Lodge staff, and the hands that keep the Hunters' ships at sea.
Shedding iron. The last leg of the Trials is the Vow, where the candidate swears the Oath before the hall. The iron they carried is set into the back of their new Bronze Sigil while the hall watches.
Turn any Hunter's Sigil over and that year's die shows.
Every Bronze Sigil therefore carries the iron of the Hunter who vouched for it.
The iron is spent in the Sigil, so it cannot be sold, pawned, or presented again.

title: The Coats and Ranks of the Armada
subtitle: Earn a color. Learn the chain.
summary: A coat identifies a branch, a rank a place in command, and a shipboard post a job that must be done. Together they make the Armada legible.

sections.title: Earning your coat
paragraphs: Every recruit begins as a Grey Coat. Earning a color is the first rite, after which the sailor is sorted into a branch. The colors cut across the rank ladder; knowing that someone is a White Coat does not by itself tell you which ship or squadron they command.

Blue Coats belong to the Cerulean Vanguard, the fighting line led by Brigid Thane. They pass the Cerulean Trials and keep the creed “In Valor, We Stand.” White Coats belong to Serane Marr’s Ivory Command, the largely noble strategic and diplomatic branch, entered through the Ivory Investiture: “Wisdom Guides, Power Follows.”

Black Coats are the Ebon Blade, entered through its own rite and bound to no fleet. Their work includes espionage and infiltration; their creed is “Might Makes Right.” A Black Coat normally ranks below a White Coat, but a sanctioned mission permits an override of contrary orders.

sections.title: The work inside the rank
paragraphs: An Oathwarden keeps the crew to the Charter and its oath; a Sword-Warden is master-at-arms and senior marine. The Ship’s Tidecaller is the Concord chaplain who blesses the sailing. The Master of Thunder is chief gunner; the Chartmaster is a Chartwright-certified navigator.

The Rook is the chief lookout, living high in the top: the name carries both tower and crow. These posts tell a visitor whom to seek for a particular kind of knowledge or responsibility aboard. A ship needs all of them long before an admiral gives the order to fight.

facts: Cerulean Vanguard, Ivory Command, Ebon Blade

title: The Nine Fleets
subtitle: Nine names sailors know by heart
summary: A Fleetlord, a ship and a duty for each part of the sea: the Armada’s nine fleets form a map of what the islands ask their navy to protect.

sections.title: Reading the fleet roll
paragraphs: Each fleet has a number, a name, a Fleetlord and a ship from which that commander flies a flag. Its station or charge explains the rest. Some watch a particular approach; others follow a kind of work wherever it leads.

The First and Second are the Twin Irons. Kalivos Durant’s Iron Wall shields Goldwind and the Heartland, while Dastan Graylock’s Iron Blockade holds the northern strait against the Imperium. One protects the center; the other guards its northern approach.

sections.title: Duties that cross the map
paragraphs: The Last Psalm carries Tidecallers on every hull and deals with the sea-pacts and Coral Kingdoms. The Spearfall takes the offensive wherever the Council directs it. The Killing Tide responds to crisis, rescue, evacuation and dangers rising from the deep. The Far Watch explores and charts with the Chartwrights.

The last three commands give the regional chart its harder edges: gunboats in the Southern Wilds, a thin watch across the Icy Expanse, and heavy-weather operations out of Stormreach. “The Vow does not thaw” is the Eighth’s promise to itself.

sections.title: The ship beneath the flag
paragraphs: A flagship is the ship carrying a commander’s flag. Nine Executioners were built, but the fleet roll is not a list of nine such hulls. Brightsight keeps the Falkoner, the ship he captained at the Kraken’s Maw; Smiling Uha commands from the Seeker and flies no Executioner.
A Fleetlord takes the style Battle-Admiral when commanding a joint line. The title describes that combined command without erasing the fleets’ separate identities.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Damyel’s ship made Mumit from Southhaven in five days, against the wind. The fastest Justicar in the Emerald Wrath needs two weeks.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)

gallery.alt: Dastan Graylock keeps watch over the northern strait from a fog-bound harbor tower, with the Charter's Oath beyond the window.
gallery.caption: The strait stays closed.
gallery.label: Dastan Graylock

gallery.alt: Falken Brightsight listens to a sea-court envoy at the Falkoner's embarkation steps, receiving a mother-of-pearl token beside a sea-pact bell.
gallery.caption: The oath travels both ways.
gallery.label: Falken Brightsight

gallery.alt: Enara Torraflame steadies an adult evacuee boarding the Intervention at blue hour after a squall.
gallery.caption: One more aboard.
gallery.label: Enara Torraflame

gallery.alt: Skarrei Ninth-Squall steers the Stormcrown into heavy weather, her human-shaped ears, blue skin and branching light-marks visible above her bare forearms.
gallery.caption: Into the weather.
gallery.label: Skarrei Ninth-Squall

title: Ship Classes of the Armada
subtitle: Read the hull before the flag
summary: Courier, pursuer, river gunboat or fortress-breaker: an Armada ship’s class tells an islander what work has arrived offshore.

sections.title: Duties with teeth
paragraphs: The Armada names its classes for the work they carry into the world. A Harbinger is a courier cutter, and sailors say its arrival means news, rarely good. A Vindicator sloop gives chase. A Justicar gunboat can work a river where the great battle hulls have no business going.

Warden frigates are the backbone of the fleets. Juggernaut heavy frigates are storm-runners, crewed by Galven; Interdictor cruisers make the Iron Blockade’s fist. A ship’s importance follows the waters and duty it is built to serve.

sections.title: The great battle hulls
paragraphs: The Dreadnought is the ship of the line, said to fear nothing. The Enforcer is a bombard built to deliver the Council’s verdict to fortresses. Above them stand the Executioners: nine men-of-war ever built, including Conqueror, Charter’s Oath, Stormcrown and Deepward.

A Fleetlord’s flagship need not be an Executioner. Falken Brightsight keeps the Falkoner that carried him through the Kraken’s Maw, and the Far Watch flies none. A familiar hull and a commander’s history can remain bound together across a promotion.

sections.title: The cost of crystal
paragraphs: Krysta armament is rare and ruinously expensive. The pirate cannon called the Drowning Star has given the Admiralty a weapon to reckon with, but it has not made crystal guns ordinary equipment. Most of the fleet roll is still best understood through a ship’s intended duty.

title: House Alastor
subtitle: The Rose House
summary: The Rose House: the tiefling Archlords of the Five, beautiful, perfumed, terrifying, rich in contracts and favors, and bound by a pact older than the Landing that no one in the house will name.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Alastor is one of the Five, and the tiefling house: horned, pact-bound, and seated at the very summit of the peerage. That a house of such folk stands among the Five tells you how much raw power and how many held secrets the Rose House commands. The others must treat the Alastors as equals, whether they can stomach it or not. Its sigil is a black rose dripping a single drop of red, on rose-pink and deep crimson, and its motto is the most honest in the islands: *"All Power Has a Price."*

The Alastors rule their Dominion through landed power and occult leverage in equal measure, and they trade in favors, secrets, and bargains with teeth. Their house-god is Nethis, the Sealed Word, and every Alastor marriage is a contract witnessed before him. Alastor is the founder's name; the blood is the Tessarius line.

The house's pact is ancient and infernal, and no Alastor has ever discussed it with anyone outside the family. The common folk call their patron a daemon, as they call every fiend. The Rose House says that is a common mistake.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** In the Imperium, a tiefling is Bound: collared, owned, and without law. The Tessarius were tieflings of the continent who were never Bound, and nobody outside the family knows how. When the great houses fled south, the Tessarius came with them under their head, Alastor Tessarius, and the house has carried his name since.

**Rosemarch (about 4 EC).** The Landing's lords gave Alastor the island nobody else would take: a green isle in what would become the Goldwind gulf, said by the fishermen to be cursed, where nothing would grow but briar. Alastor took it. Within ten years Rosemarch was the most fertile island in the gulf, and the fishermen stopped saying it was cursed, at least where the house could hear them.

**The Rose House (about 30 to 55 EC).** When Archmage Eamos founded Goldwind across the water, the Alastors built the Rose House on Rosemarch's eastern shore, facing the city. When Vol Kaern built its castle on the bare rock above Goldwind, the two houses found themselves looking at each other across the gulf every morning, and they have never stopped.

**Among the Five (about 70 EC).** No house may join the Five unless another falls out of it. When Caelvaron's ruler went into the Faewild for her ten years, the Council's business did not wait for her, and by the time she came back the Rose House sat in Caelvaron's chair. Elyria has never forgiven it, and the Rose House has never apologized.

**The letter (105 EC).** During the Ascendant's War, Archmage Eldric Morvane wrote to the Rose House offering an alliance and very generous terms. Zephyros's grandmother refused him in writing, in a letter so precise that Morvane's own captains read it aloud at his trial as proof of what he had tried. The house had the letter returned to it after the trial, and it hangs framed in the Rose House's library.
**The Kraken's Maw (165 EC).** Twelve Knights of the Pale Rose fought with the Coalition. Nine came back, and the three who did not were brought home and buried under the rose-beds.

**The pink gardens (after the heir's birth).** When Hyacinth was born, her mother, Lady Xanthea, planted thousands of pink flowers around the estate, and the Rose House's gardens became a landmark of the Heartland. In spring, Goldwind's harbor can see Rosemarch turn pink.

**Today (175 EC).** Zephyros rules, Hyacinth is the heir and the talk of every drawing room, and the Rose House funds a great deal of the University's research and exploration. The salons say a marriage contract between the heir and House Vol Kaern is waiting for a signature.

sections.title: The Rose House and Rosemarch
list: **The Rose House** is a long, low palace of red stone and black glass on Rosemarch's eastern shore, with terraces running down to the water and a private harbor below them. The gardens are open to visitors on the paths, and nowhere else. The wards between the beds are not for show, and a guest who steps off a path is not hurt; they simply find themselves, a moment later, back at the gate, with no memory of the walk.

**Rosemarch** is a green, rolling island of rose-farms, vineyards, and orchards, with the town of Briarwick at its harbor. Its roses are grown for attar, and in summer the whole island smells of them. Fishermen still do not fish its western shore at night, and will not say why.
**The library** of the Rose House is said to hold more contracts than any archive in the islands except the Nethis temples, and to hold some of those too.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 60,000 Orsals a year and says, in private, that it would not like to be wrong about it.

**Rose surety.** The Rose House stands surety for contracts between other parties, for a fee of one in every fifty of the sum. A contract with Rose surety is never broken, because breaking it is worse than paying. Half the great merchant bargains of the Heartland carry the black rose at the bottom.

**Attar and scent.** Rosemarch's roses are pressed for attar, and the house's own scent, *Black Rose*, is made for it by the Saffrane perfumers of Silverport. A vial costs more than a laborer earns in a year, and the house gives far more of it away than it sells.

**Estates.** Rosemarch's farms, vineyards, and orchards, and lands across the central Heartland, many of them acquired through contracts whose other party later wished they had read them more carefully.
**Favors.** The Rose House is owed by half the peerage. The favors are never priced, never written in coin, and never forgotten.
The house spends heavily on the University, whose research and expeditions it funds, and on its gardens, its knights, and its library.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Twelve houses are sworn to the Rose House. By an old custom, each of them carries a flower in its arms, given by the house on the day it swore.
list: **House Saphrel**, Holder. The contract-scribes. A Saphrel drafts every Rose surety, and the family is said to be able to read a contract upside down from across a table.
**House Ombrenne**, Warden of the Rose-Farms. Keepers of Rosemarch's fields and the attar-presses, and the bannermen who raise most of the house's levy.
**House Corvesh**, Holder. Captains of the Rose Guard for five generations, tieflings like their lords, and as silent.
**House Asphodane**, Banneret. A family of physicians and embalmers, who tend the house's sick and its dead, and whose flower is the asphodel.
**The Knights of the Pale Rose**, an order and not a house, some forty knights strong, sworn to Alastor. To be challenged by a Pale Rose knight is to be offered a duel you are not meant to survive.
**Eight more**, Holders and Bannerets of Rosemarch and the central Heartland.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: The Rose House does not need a large army. Very few people want to be at war with it.
list: **The Rose Guard:** about 1,500 soldiers in crimson and black, who keep the Rose House, Rosemarch, and the house's estates. They are known for being well paid and for never discussing their employers.

**The Knights of the Pale Rose:** some forty knights, the finest duelists in the Heartland, sworn to the house and led by tradition by a knight who married into it. Ser Merrick, Hyacinth's father, is their most renowned.
**The house itself:** warlocks, enchanters, an alchemist, and a spymaster at the high table. No one has counted what they could do in a war, and no one wants to find out.
**The full muster:** about 5,500 with the bannermen's levies.

**At sea:** six warships in the Castellan's Register: the frigates *Thorn* (the flagship) and *Bloom*, three sloops, and a cutter, moored in the Rose House's private harbor. About twenty merchant hulls carry attar, wine, and the house's guests.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war, the house's warships answer the Armada. The Rose House has pointed out, more than once, that the Charter is a contract, and that it reads its contracts.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **The witnessed contract.** Every Alastor marriage is a contract witnessed before Nethis, and so is every adoption, partnership, and promise of service. The house does not use the word *promise*. It uses *terms*.

**The reading.** Before any contract is signed at the Rose House, it is read aloud in full, by a Saphrel, to everyone who will sign it. Guests have been known to ask for it to be read twice. The house approves.
**The gilded horns.** On the day an Alastor is seated as head, the tips of their horns are gilded. Zephyros's are gold to the second ring.
**The terms at ten.** At ten, every Alastor child begins to learn the terms of the pact from the family's tutor, Valthor. No one outside the family has ever heard what they are.
**The guest-book.** Every guest at the Rose House signs the guest-book, and is told, kindly, before signing, what signing it means. It means very little. The point is that they were told.
**Terms at the Moot.** The bargains struck at the Moot of Banners are signed under Rose surety in a small room off the Banner Hall, and the Saphrels work through the night of the last session.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: **Zephyros.** Zephyros Alastor is old, elegant, and very still, with gilded horns and a voice that never rises. He has been head of the house for longer than most of the Council has been alive. He is courteous to everyone, owes nothing to anyone, and has never been known to make a bargain he did not mean to keep. That last is the part that frightens people.

**Hyacinth.** The heir is an occult swordswoman whom the drawing rooms call the Pink Lady: coquettish, coldly calculating, a duelist of real skill, and an heir with an ambition that outruns even being one of the Five. *"They do not kneel for me... yet,"* she said once, at a party, and the salons have repeated it ever since, never to her face. She is Lady Xanthea's only child.
**The family.**

**Lady Xanthea,** Zephyros's daughter and the house's diplomatic face, renowned for her charm and grace, and the Alastor most of Goldwind actually likes. She is Hyacinth's mother, married to Ser Merrick by a Nethis-witnessed contract, and the one who planted the pink gardens.

**Ser Merrick,** a renowned Knight of the Pale Rose who married into the house, and Hyacinth's father. He is the only person at the high table without horns, and the salons say he knows exactly what the pact's price is.
**Valthor,** a warlock, Zephyros's loyal advisor, and the tutor who teaches the house's young the terms of the pact.
**Azrakel,** the spymaster and a master of subterfuge, who is said to keep a hidden shrine to Sruth, the god of sold secrets.
**Nemeia,** an alchemist with a taste for forbidden knowledge, and the house's link to the University's more discreet laboratories.
**Selena,** an enchantress who moves people where she wants them, and rarely needs magic to do it.
**Agari,** a tiefling servant-emissary, not of the blood, a necromancer, and Hyacinth's closest friend. She travels with two bodyguards, Beck and Grolsh, who say less than she does.

**An evening at the Rose House.** The barge crosses the gulf at dusk, and the gardens are lit from below so that the roses seem to float. A Saphrel meets each guest at the gate with the guest-book. The wine is Rosemarch's, the scent is *Black Rose*, and the conversation is better than anywhere in Goldwind, because everyone is trying very hard to be careful and nobody manages it. Across the water the castle-heights glow, and sometimes, on the same night, violet.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: House Silverthorn and the Rose House wage a cold war of secrets, and neither has ever won a round in public. Caelvaron and Faust distrust the pact. The Rose House opposes Vol Kaern, for reasons of its own, and the two houses face each other across the gulf every morning. It funds a great deal of the University's research and exploration. Veldane has married into it more than once, and every Veldane wedding has a Rose House table.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Rose House signs every contract twice: once in ink, and once in something that does not dry.” (a Goldwind scrivener)
“Lady Xanthea Alastor and Lady Lysandria Caelvaron dance together at every Veldane wedding, and at no other.” (a Veldane wedding-guest)
“Azrakel Alastor keeps a shrine in the Rose House to Sruth, who buys and sells the secrets the other gods are meant to hear.” (a Rose House chandler)
“The Alastors are not daemon-sworn. Whatever they made their bargain with does not want souls. It wants signatures.” (a University scholar, who later declined to repeat it)
“Black Rose was not invented at Silverport. Ask the Tobbins.” (a Pocchin perfume-seller)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A letter to be carried through the warded gardens, and a path that changes behind you.
A contract from the Rose House, generous in every line. Read all of it.
Nemeia Alastor is funding an expedition, and wants it to bring back something she will not name in writing.
A Pale Rose knight has challenged someone the party needs alive.
A merchant bargain with Rose surety is about to be broken, and someone has to tell the broker what that means.

facts: a black rose dripping a single drop of red, on rose-pink and deep crimson
Tessarius; Alastor is the founder's name
the isle of Rosemarch, inside the Goldwind gulf, facing the castle-heights across the water
Rose surety on contracts; Rosemarch attar and the house's scents; estates; favors, which are never priced
about 60,000 Orsals a year (the Reckoners' guess, made nervously)
about 1,500 (the Rose Guard), and some forty Knights of the Pale Rose
six (two frigates, three sloops, a cutter); flagship the Thorn
twelve Knights of the Pale Rose with their squires, and the largest purse of any house
the University, whose research it funds; House Veldane, by every wedding
House Silverthorn, a cold war of secrets; House Vol Kaern, for reasons of its own
aliases: a black rose dripping a single drop of red, on rose-pink and deep crimson

epigraph.quote: All power has a price. We simply read the contract.
epigraph.by: Zephyros Alastor, to a Council clerk

title: House Blackstrand
subtitle: The Ledger's Lord
summary: The Ledger's Lord: the banker-house of Goldwind, whose head is First Reckoner of the Reckoners' Hall, whose seal is on every Orsal, which holds the debts of half the peerage, and which needs no Council seat to rule the Congress.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Blackstrand is the banker-house, a Highlord by influence: its landed rank is the least of its power. Its sigil is a black band over a gold coin, on green and black, and its motto is *"All Accounts Come Due."* The sigil is cut above the doors of the Reckoners' Hall, and the Hall's ledger-mark is struck on the reverse of every Orsal in the islands.

It holds the debts of half the peerage and a good share of the Congress besides, and its head can ruin more lords with a ledger than most could with a fleet. Lady Maera Blackstrand is the First Reckoner, master of the Reckoners' Hall and the true power behind the Mercantile Congress. She sits on no Council seat and needs none. The Congress's representative says only what Blackstrand can afford to let him say.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Blackstrands were money-changers of the Free Cities, a family that weighed coin at a scale-table in Castia's harbor. During the Exodus they lent to the great houses for their passage, and the house's chronicle says that every one of those loans was repaid. The house's enemies say that is why the house is so rich.

**The Reckoners' Hall (about 30 EC).** When Goldwind was founded, a Blackstrand and four other banking families founded the Reckoners' Hall in its new banking quarter, as a guild to keep deposits and lend. A Blackstrand has been First Reckoner for most of the Hall's history.

**The warrant (about 55 EC).** When the Council moved to Goldwind and set up the Charter Mint, it asked the Hall to warrant its coin. Since then no Orsal has been struck without a Reckoner's seal, and every Orsal carries the Reckoners' ledger-mark and a struck serial number.

**The Plague (about 90 EC).** During the Plague of the Burning Sea, when trade stopped and half the merchant houses of the Heartland could not pay, the Hall did not call in their debts. It bought them. When trade came back, Blackstrand owned the paper of most of the Congress.

**Today (175 EC).** Lady Maera is First Reckoner. The Hall has counting-houses in nine cities and none in Varan Port, where Fairweather keeps its own books. Three Coinsdays unpaid still puts a name in the Ledger, and a name in the Ledger is still known to every banker in the islands by the following Coinsday.

sections.title: The banking quarter
paragraphs: The house's seat is Goldwind's banking quarter, on the ring above the wharves.
list: **The Reckoners' Hall**, a square building of dark stone with no windows on the ground floor and the black band and coin over the door. Its great room has a hundred counting-desks and is as quiet as a temple.
**The vaults**, under the Hall, cut into the rock, warded by the house's own casters and by locks that, the salons note, are not Silverthorn's.
**Blackstrand House**, behind the Hall, the family's home: narrow, tall, and furnished with the gifts of grateful debtors.
**The counting-houses** in Ironfort, Bastion, Stormreach, Goldwind, Silverport, Aurelion, Southhaven, Frosthold, and Jakupur, the last by treaty and with ill grace.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The house's land brings in about 6,000 Orsals a year. Nobody counts the rest, because the rest is the Hall's, and the Hall does not publish. The family holds the largest share in it.
list: **Deposits.** The vault fee is one Anchor in every hundred, a year.
**Loans.** One in twenty a year for the Council or one of the Five, one in twelve for a great house, one in eight for a merchant, and up to one in five for a tradesman.
**Reckonings.** Sealed letters of credit payable at any counting-house, for two in every hundred.
**Bottomry.** Sea-loans on ships and cargoes, forgiven if the ship is lost, which makes the Hall the islands' insurer.
**Wreck and salvage.** The Hall registers every claim, for a tenth.
**The warrant.** The Hall's fee for sealing the Council's Orsals.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Three houses are sworn to Blackstrand, and they are the fewest of any great house, because Blackstrand does not need bannermen. It has debtors.
**House Thrane**, Holder. Reckoners for four generations, and the house's chief counters in the Hall.
**House Tessick**, Banneret. Keepers of the Ledger, the register of debts unpaid, who send its pages to every counting-house each Coinsday.
**House Ullard**, Banneret. Captains of the Counting Guard.
Half the bannerets House Quillane has minted are in some merchant house's books, and most of those merchant houses are in Blackstrand's.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Blackstrand keeps no army and no fleet, and the islands' lords fear it more than most houses that do.
list: **The Counting Guard:** about 250 guards who keep the Hall, the vaults, and the counting-houses. They have never had to fight a battle, only a great many very short arguments.
**The full muster:** about 600 with the bannermen's levies, which the house has never called.

**At sea:** no warships in the Castellan's Register, and no merchant hulls of its own. The Hall holds bottomry on hundreds of ships, which means that a large part of the islands' merchant fleet is, in a sense, Blackstrand's until it comes home.
**The real strength:** a letter from the Hall. A lord whose debt is called cannot pay his soldiers, and a lord who cannot pay his soldiers has none.
**The Charter Call** does not touch it. The house has noted that the Charter Call needs to be paid for, and that the Council borrows at one in twenty.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **Coinsday.** The Hall settles accounts on Coinsday, the fourth day of every Cycle, and the family eats a plain supper that night, whatever its guests are served.

**The third Coinsday.** Three Coinsdays unpaid puts a name in the Ledger. The house sends one polite letter on the first and one on the second. On the third it sends nothing, because it no longer needs to.
**The serial number.** Every Blackstrand child is given an Orsal at birth with a serial number noted in the family book. Maera's is still in her purse.
**No gifts refused.** The house accepts every gift from a debtor, and enters it on the credit side of the debtor's account, which the debtor is told.
**The quiet room.** The Hall's great room is kept silent. A raised voice there is fined one Tide, and the fine is entered.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
list: **Lady Maera.** Maera Blackstrand is a small, neat, white-haired woman with a soft voice and a perfect memory for figures. She attends very few parties and is discussed at all of them. The salons say she can tell you what any lord in the room owes, to the Tide, without looking it up, and they are almost right: she does not need to be in the room.
**Sabin.** Sabin Blackstrand is known in the maritime trade as Hera Seaworth, a figure of her own on the docks, and the family does not explain why Maera's niece uses another name at sea.

**At the Hall.** A lord comes to the Hall to borrow. He is shown to a quiet room, given good wine, and asked no questions about what the money is for. He signs.
