epigraph.quote: Everything up here outlasts you, except us.
epigraph.by: a Kaldmark huscarl, to a Heartland envoy

title: House Pelagar
subtitle: The Deep Trade
summary: The Deep Trade: the pearl-house of the Coral edge, grown rich on what comes up from the water, keeper of sea-pacts no other house honors, and the noble house the silent courts below are most willing to hear.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Pelagar is the pearl-and-deep-sea-trade house, one of the ten Highlords, grown rich on what comes up from the water. Its sigil is a pearl in an open shell, on sea-green and silver, and its motto is *"What the Tide Brings."*

It is the noble house that deals most directly, and most secretly, with the sea-peoples of the Coral Kingdoms. Pelagar keeps sea-pacts no other house honors, and knows more about the silent courts below than the Council would be comfortable learning. Its partner in the deep trade is House Belmaris, which casts the bells the courts buy. The two houses need each other and compete for every pearl.
There are whispers about how a land-house came to be so welcome in the deep.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Pelagars were not lords on the continent. Ilsa Pelagar, the founder, was a pearl-diver who came south with the Exodus, a widow with two children and nothing else.

**Ilsa (9 EC).** Ilsa drowned off the Heartland's eastern coast in 9 EC, diving for pearls to feed her children. The sea gave her back. The house's chronicle says only that she came up three days later, alive, with a pearl the size of a child's fist and the first sea-pact any Landing family had made. Nobody has ever been told what she promised.

**Nacre (about 12 EC).** With the pearl, Ilsa bought the small island of Nacre on the Coral edge, and the pearl-clans of the coast came to dive under her protection, because the courts below let her divers come home. The Council raised her to the peerage for the trade she opened, and the house has been noble since.

**The sea-pacts (from about 15 EC).** Pelagar keeps the oldest land-side sea-pacts in the islands. The port gives the first catch of each season, the true names of its ships, and burial rights over its drowned. The court gives safe water, storm-warning, and the drowned returned. Every Pelagar ship is named twice, once for the land and once for the sea.

**The deep trade (from about 40 EC).** With Belmaris casting the bells, Pelagar began to carry the courts' goods to the land and the land's to the courts: pearls, shell, and reefpurple up; worked silver, bronze, and brass down, valued by the sound they make. The Coral courts trade almost wholly with the Heartland, through Pelagar and Belmaris.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Castor rules Nacre. He has two children. The house's pearl-ships come in at night with their lamps out, and the Glass Gardens, the clearest of the courts, have stopped trading with Pelagar this year, which the Heartland has noticed.

sections.title: Nacre and the Coral edge
list: **Nacre** is a small island off the Heartland's eastern coast, on the Coral edge, near Pearl Groove.
**The pearl-houses**, long low buildings on the shore where the pearls are sorted, graded, and drilled, and where the windows face the sea.
**The sea-gardens**, beds of shell and weed tended underwater by the Pelagar divers, and by others who are not seen.
**The night harbor**, where the pearl-ships come in with their lamps out, because the courts below dislike lights on the water at night.
**The Pelagar house**, a white house of shell-lime on the island's seaward point, with a stair cut down into the water.
**The Pearl Shallows**, the beds off the coast where Pelagar's divers work, above one of the Coral courts, whose Matron the divers do not name aloud.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 14,000 Orsals a year.
list: **Pearls.** A pearl sells for 10 to 500 Anchors, and the best never reach the market at all.
**The deep trade.** The house carries the courts' goods up and the land's goods down, and takes its share of both.

**Reefpurple.** A vial of the murex-dyed purple for one sash costs 30 Anchors. By custom it is worn by Council seats and high clergy, and anyone else risks the room going quiet. Pelagar and Belmaris share the trade.
**Shell-craft.** Mother-of-pearl, buttons, inlay, and the shell lamps of the Heartland's salons.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Seven houses are sworn to Pelagar, most of them pearl-clans of the coast who were raised with the house.
list: **House Seaholm**, Holder. Pearl-captains, who sail the pearl-ships and know every ship's second name.
**House Tidewell**, Banneret. Keepers of the sea-gardens, who tend the beds and sometimes see the others who tend them.
**House Saltmere**, Banneret. The divers' families, whose children learn to hold their breath before they learn to read.
**Four more**, pearl-clans of the Coral edge.
**House Belmaris** of Pearl Groove is not sworn to Pelagar. It is a merchant house of its own, and one of the Twelve Flags, and would be insulted to be counted.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Pelagar keeps a small force, and the sea keeps it safer than any army.
list: **The Nacre Guard:** about 500 soldiers and marines in sea-green, who keep the island and the night harbor.
**The full muster:** about 2,000 with the bannermen's levies, most of them divers and sailors.

**At sea:** three warships in the Castellan's Register, the frigate *Return* (the flagship) and the sloops *Ilsa* and *Tide's Due*, each with its sea-name painted below the waterline. About twenty-two pearl-ships.

**The sea-pacts:** in waters where Pelagar's pacts hold, the house's ships have safe water and warning of storms. The Armada's Third Fleet, the Last Psalm, which enforces the Concord's sea-pacts, knows this well.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war, the house's warships answer the Armada, and the house has asked, each time, to sail with the Last Psalm.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **Two names.** Every Pelagar ship, and every Pelagar child, has two names, one for the land and one for the sea. The sea-name is never spoken on land.
**The first catch.** The first catch of every season goes back into the sea, at the night harbor, by lamp-less boat.
**No lamps on the water.** Pelagar ships come in at night with their lamps out.
**The drowned.** The house claims burial rights over the drowned of its waters, and Pelagar funerals are held at the water's edge, at low tide, so that the sea can come for what it is owed.
**The pearl at birth.** Every Pelagar child is given a pearl at birth by the head of the house, and keeps it for life.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
list: **Lord Castor.** Castor Pelagar is a quiet, brown, weathered man who looks more like a pearl-captain than a lord. He is said to know every pearl-clan's elder by name and to have never once been seen to bargain. He swims alone at night, and the boatmen say he comes back drier than he went in.

**The family.** Lord Castor has two children, and the house is careful not to say much about either of them in Goldwind. The salons have noticed that the house's children are always at Nacre for the King Tides.

**An evening at Nacre.** Guests arrive before dark, because no boat comes in after. Dinner is served on the terrace above the stair into the sea, and the shell lamps are put out at the second course. In the dark the water below the terrace glows faintly, and sometimes something sings, and the Pelagars go on eating as if nothing were happening, which, for them, is true.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: House Belmaris is Pelagar's partner and rival: Pelagar keeps the sea-pacts while Belmaris supplies the gifts, and the two houses compete for every pearl. The Concord and its Third Fleet respect the house's pacts. The Council would like to know what they say. The Glass Gardens have stopped trading with Pelagar this year, and nobody on land knows why.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Pelagar has been buying the Starfall coral in bulk. The Glass Gardens have stopped trading with Pelagar in return.” (heard in the Sea and the Coral Kingdoms)
“Lord Castor swims alone at night, and comes back drier than he went in.” (a Pelagar boatman)
“Every Pelagar generation, one of the children goes away to be schooled, and none of them come back to Goldwind.” (a Goldwind tutor)
“Ilsa Pelagar did not come back from the sea. Something came back that looked like her.” (a Pearl Groove diver's grandmother)
“The Hunter they call the Helping Tide swims like a Pelagar.” (a Lodge diver)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A sealed casket that must reach the Coral edge unopened, and very little else in the instructions.
A pearl-diver has not come up, and the Pelagar house will not send anyone down.
Someone wants to know who Pelagar's buyer is, and Pelagar will not say.
A Pelagar ship has come in at night with its lamps lit, and the house wants to know who lit them.
A Belmaris bell has gone missing on its way to the courts, and both houses blame the other.

title: House Quillane
subtitle: The Coin-Made Lords
summary: The Coin-Made Lords: the only Warden-rank house counted among the Twenty, by wealth and not by worth, which has spent two generations selling titles to anyone with coin and a use for one, and is the chief author of the bannermen glut.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Quillane is the only Warden-rank house counted among the Majors, by wealth and not by worth. Its sigil is a quill crossed with a key, on muddy gold, and its motto is the one honest thing it has ever said in public: *"Title for the Taking."*

It is wealthy, careless, and grasping, and the chief author of the bannermen glut. Where responsible houses grant title rarely and vet ruthlessly, Quillane has spent two generations, in effect, selling bannerets to anyone with coin and a use for one, flooding the south with petty, under-resourced nobles of dubious quality. The old houses despise it. The Council cannot stop it. And Quillane keeps minting lords, because every new banneret owes it.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Quillanes were notaries of the continent, the people who drew up and sealed the papers that made other people's claims true.

**The wardenship (about 90 EC).** During the Plague of the Burning Sea, a Quillane notary kept the south's land-registers when half the clerks of Southhaven were dead, and the Council made him a Warden for it, holding directly of the Council. It is the only wardenship in the islands granted that way.

**The grant clause.** To ennoble, a granting lord must be Warden or higher, hold the land and wealth to back the grant, command the standing to make it stick, and secure their own liege's assent. Quillane's liege is the Council, and by an old article of the land code, the Council's assent is given unless the Council objects within one Cycle of the grant being filed. The Council has never once objected in time.

**The glut (from about 140 EC).** Lord Pellam's father saw what the clause meant, and began to mint bannerets: first for merchants who wanted a seat at the lords' table, then for anyone who could pay. Lord Pellam has done it by the dozen. Half the bannerets House Quillane has minted are in some merchant house's books.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Pellam rules the Quill House. A Pocchin spice merchant named Pobbo has bought a banneret from him and styles himself *Lord of Nothing in Particular*. The old houses are appalled, and buy his spices anyway.

sections.title: The Quill House
list: **The Quill House** stands in Southhaven's upper town: a large, new, gaudy house with too many windows, built in the style of a great Heartland seat and furnished with the gifts of grateful lords.
**The grant-room**, where titles are written, sealed, and handed over, with a ceremony that the house has made a little longer and a little more expensive every decade.
**The roll**, a great book of every banneret the house has minted, with their arms painted in, which grows by several pages a year.
**The garden**, where the new bannerets are presented to the house at a party every Landing-Day, and where the old houses' servants come to watch and laugh.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 12,000 Orsals a year, more than many Highlords take.
list: **Titles.** A banneret from Quillane costs from 100 to 500 Orsals, depending on the buyer and the land, and the land is usually very little.
**Dues.** Every banneret the house has minted pays it a small due each year, as bannermen do. Seventy small dues make one large income.
**Credit.** The house lends to its own bannerets, at the merchants' rates, to keep them in the style their titles promise.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: About seventy houses are sworn to Quillane, more than to any house in the islands. Most of them are bannerets of no land worth the name, and few could raise a dozen soldiers.
list: **House Marrow**, Banneret. A southern house of Quillane's minting, living well beyond its land on Fennick credit and lending the Fennick factors its seat at the planters' table.
**Pobbo, Lord of Nothing in Particular**, Banneret. A Pocchin spice merchant who bought the title as a joke, uses it in every letter, and is the most solvent banneret on the roll.
**Sixty-odd more**, merchants, planters, factors, and adventurers, most of them in a merchant house's books, and a few of them, the old houses admit, rather good.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Quillane has almost no strength of its own, and a great deal on paper.
list: **The Quill Guard:** about 300 guards who keep the Quill House and the grant-room.
**The full muster:** about 9,000 on paper, if every banneret on the roll raised the levy its title promises. In truth, perhaps 2,000, and many of those would ask to be paid first.
**At sea:** no warships in the Castellan's Register. About four merchant hulls.
**The real strength:** seventy votes at every lords' table in the south, and every one of them owed.
**The Charter Call** asks nothing of it. The house has offered the Council letters of nobility for any captain who distinguishes himself, and the Council has not replied.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **The longer ceremony.** Every decade the house adds a step to the grant ceremony. There are now eleven, including a sung oath and a gift of gloves.
**Landing-Day.** The house presents its new bannerets in its garden every Landing-Day, and pays musicians to play loudly enough to drown out the laughter.
**The gloves.** Every Quillane banneret is given a pair of muddy-gold gloves at their making, and is expected to wear them at the lords' table. Most do, once.
**Never refuse coin.** A Quillane never refuses a buyer who can pay. The house has been known to refuse buyers who cannot pay enough.
**The roll.** Every banneret's arms are painted into the roll by a Quillane hand, and the house has never once painted them well.

**The bloc.** At the Choosing, every five years, every banneret at the Moot may cast a voice for ten Orsals. Quillane's seventy vote as one, their voice-money is always paid, and the house says they vote for the good of the peerage.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
list: **Lord Pellam.** Pellam Quillane is a round, cheerful, expensively dressed man who is delighted by everything, including the contempt of the old houses, which he says is good for business. He is not stupid, which is the thing the old houses find hardest to forgive. He has six children, and has made each of them a banneret of their own.

**The roll.** The salons read the Quillane roll the way they read the Gift-Book of Varselis, for scandal. Every Landing-Day someone new is on it, and someone in Goldwind is mortified to learn that their grocer is now a lord.

**A Landing-Day at the Quill House.** The garden is full of new lords in new gloves. The ceremony takes an hour and a half. Lord Pellam makes a speech about the dignity of the peerage. Across the street, the servants of three old houses watch from a balcony with a bottle of wine, and the Quillane musicians play louder.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: Every old house in the islands despises Quillane, and every one of them has, at some point, had a cousin who bought a title from it. The Council cannot stop it. The merchant houses hold half its bannerets' paper, and Blackstrand holds theirs. The southern tyrant-houses have minted bannermen by the fistful too, and are happy to have Quillane take the blame.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Quillane has sold a title to a pirate, and the pirate sat at a Southhaven lords' table last month in muddy-gold gloves.” (a Southhaven footman)
“Half the bannerets on the Quillane roll could not raise a dozen soldiers between them.” (a Faust bannerman, at Bastion)
“Pellam Quillane keeps a second roll, of the titles he has sold that are not on the first.” (a Quill House clerk)
“The Council has tried to close the grant clause three times, and each time the motion was filed one day late.” (a Holst clerk)
“Pobbo is the most solvent lord in the south, and the old houses borrow from him.” (a Southhaven factor)
“At the Choosing of 173 EC the Quillane bloc voted for Halsof Varselis, and somebody paid for every vote.” (a Mardle vote-counter)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A title for sale, cheap, and a seller who cannot quite explain why it is cheap.
A Quillane banneret is calling up his levy for a private war, and his levy is the party.
Someone wants their name struck from the Quillane roll, and the house does not strike names.
The Council wants proof that a Quillane title was sold to a pirate before it can act.
Pobbo, Lord of Nothing in Particular, needs a herald, and pays well.

a quill crossed with a key, on muddy gold
the Quill House, in Southhaven's upper town
the Quill House and a scatter of small estates across the south, most of them granted away again

about 12,000 Orsals a year (the Reckoners' guess), more than many Highlords take
about seventy on paper, more than any house in the islands
about 9,000 on paper; perhaps 2,000 in truth
about 300 younger sons of its bannerets, who want glory; most come home
the bannerets it has made, when it suits them; the merchant houses that hold their paper

epigraph.quote: Every new banneret owes us. That is the whole of the business.
epigraph.by: Lord Pellam Quillane, at a Southhaven dinner

title: House Silverthorn
subtitle: The Quiet Knife
summary: The Quiet Knife: a discreet house of arcane operators in walled Briarcrown, makers of the Heartland's best locks, keepers of the register of its shadow markets, and the cold rival of the Rose House.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Silverthorn is a house of arcane spies and quiet operators, one of the ten Highlords. Its sigil is a silver thorn-branch on midnight blue, and its motto, *"Spoken Soft, Cut Deep,"* is the only loud thing about it.

It is the smallest of the great houses in land and men, and one of the hardest to read. It makes the best locks in the Heartland, carries letters nobody else can be trusted with, and keeps a register of everyone who buys or sells in the Heartland's shadow markets. The salons say Silverthorn knows something about every house in the islands. Silverthorn says nothing, which the salons take as agreement.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Silverthorns say they were locksmiths. Their enemies say they were the people locksmiths were hired to keep out. Both may be true, and the house has never corrected either story.

**Briarcrown (about 25 EC).** The house built Briarcrown on a hill above the eastern shore, a walled town with one gate, and was granted the hill-country around it when its first lord, Orrel Silverthorn, delivered a letter to the Council that four other couriers had died carrying. Nobody ever learned what was in the letter, and that was the point.

**The quiet war (from about 70 EC).** When the Rose House rose into the Five, Silverthorn was the first house to notice how it had happened. The cold war between them dates from that year. Neither house has ever struck the other in public, and both houses have buried agents whose names the other knows.

**The Ascendant's War (105 EC).** Silverthorn sent no soldiers to the Coalition. It sent the Coalition's generals the names of three of Morvane's captains who were willing to change sides, and all three did. The house has never claimed the credit, which is why everyone gives it.

**The Registry's founding (after 105 EC).** When the Arcane Registry was founded, Silverthorn registered every caster in the house within the first month, and the Registry has been suspicious of it ever since, because no one is that obedient without a reason.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Silas rules from Briarcrown. The register of the shadow markets grows every year, Cedric's workshop takes commissions from three great houses at once, and the Rose House and Silverthorn are, as always, perfectly polite.

sections.title: Briarcrown
list: **Briarcrown** is a fortified town on a hill above the eastern shore of the Heartland. It has one gate, high walls, and silent gardens, and its streets are so quiet that visitors notice it. They usually notice it on their way out.
**The Thornhouse**, the family's seat at the top of the hill: a plain grey house behind a wall of briar, with no windows on the street side.
**The lock-works**, a row of workshops below the Thornhouse where the Ferrant smiths make Silverthorn locks and strongboxes, and where every apprentice signs an oath before touching a key.
**The register-house**, a building no one enters but the Mornes and the family, where the register of the shadow markets is kept.
**The courier yard** by the gate, where the house's sealed couriers come and go at every hour, and where no one asks where they are going.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 9,000 Orsals a year, and does not believe it.
list: **Locks.** A Silverthorn lock costs from 5 Anchors for a door to 50 Orsals for a vault. The great houses of the Heartland buy them because they are the best. Goldwind's joke is that the house can open every one of them, and the house has never once denied it.

**Couriers.** The house's sealed couriers carry letters, contracts, and small parcels between the great houses, for a fee of 1 Anchor a day of travel and much more for silence. A Silverthorn courier has never lost a letter, and two have died keeping one.
**Cedric's work.** Enchanted devices, registered and unregistered, made to order.
**The register.** The house does not sell the register. It sells a single answer from it, once, to someone who can pay, for a price nobody repeats.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Five houses are sworn to Silverthorn, all small and all quiet.
list: **House Ferrant**, Holder. The lock-smiths of Briarcrown, who have made every Silverthorn lock since the first, and who keep the house's keys.
**House Morne**, Banneret. Keepers of the register-house. A Morne writes every entry and forgets nothing, and the family's children are taught to read before they are taught to speak in company.
**House Lanthis**, Banneret. The couriers. A Lanthis rider on a domestic auroc can cross the Heartland in two days, and will not tell you which road they took.
**Two more**, Bannerets of the eastern hills.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Silverthorn keeps almost no army. It does not fight wars. It ends them before they start, or makes sure they happen to someone else.
list: **The Briar Guard:** about 400 soldiers in midnight blue, who keep Briarcrown's walls and gate and the Thornhouse.
**The agents:** uncounted. The house's people are in every great port, every salon, and, the salons say, every other house's kitchen.
**The full muster:** about 1,500 with the bannermen's levies, on paper. In a war, Silverthorn would send far fewer soldiers and far more letters.
**At sea:** one warship in the Castellan's Register, the sloop *Hush*, the fastest hull in the eastern Heartland, and about four merchant hulls.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war the *Hush* answers the Armada. The house has offered, each time the Call has been drilled, to send information instead.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **No raised voices.** Nobody in the Thornhouse raises their voice, and a servant who does is dismissed with a year's wages and a reference.
**The one gate.** Briarcrown has one gate, and every person who passes it is written down, coming and going.
**The thorn.** A Silverthorn who means to threaten someone sends them a silver thorn, unwrapped, with no note. It has happened eleven times in the house's history. The salons know all eleven.
**The silence of the dead.** The house buries its dead at night, without a service, and does not say their names aloud again for a year.
**Courtesy to the Rose House.** A Silverthorn is perfectly polite to an Alastor at all times, and a Silverthorn who is not is called home.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
list: **Lord Silas.** Silas Silverthorn is a slight, grey, pleasant man who looks like a clerk and listens like a confessor. He goes to every salon, says little, and leaves early. The salons have never caught him in a lie, and have never been sure they have heard him tell the truth. He is a widower with no children the salons know of, which the salons find the most suspicious thing about him.
**The family.**
**Lady Vivian,** said to be a master of the shadows, and whatever else the salons whisper when she has left the room. She is very beautiful, very still, and has never been seen to eat at a party.
**Cedric,** an artificer, the maker of most of the family's magical creations, who will buy a strange object you found and pay too much for it.
**Elowen,** a necromancer, rumored to command the dead. Her household staff has not changed in forty years.
**Lucan,** a charismatic bard and a master of deception, the only Silverthorn who is loud, and the salons suspect he is loud on purpose.

**A visit to Briarcrown.** You give your name at the gate and watch it written down. The streets are clean and empty. A Lanthis rider passes you without a sound. At the Thornhouse you are given tea in a room with no windows, and Lord Silas asks after your family, by name, including the cousin you have not spoken to in years.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: Silverthorn and the Rose House both deal in shadows, and neither trusts the other an inch. Their cold war is the longest-running quiet feud in the Heartland. The Registry suspects the house and cannot prove anything. Every great house buys Silverthorn locks, and every great house wonders, sometimes, what that means.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Half the unregistered magic sold in Goldwind ends up in Briarcrown. The other half started there.” (a Goldwind fence)
“Elowen Silverthorn's household staff has not changed in forty years. Neither have they.” (a Briarcrown carter)
“Every Silverthorn lock has two keys, and the house keeps the second.” (a Goldwind locksmith, out of work)
“The Briarcrown register has a page for every lord in the Council, and Lord Silas reads one of them every night before he sleeps.” (a Morne servant, dismissed)
“There is a reading-room under Goldwind where the dead tell their secrets, and a Silverthorn keeps the book.” (a gravedigger)
“Lord Silas has had a Lanthis rider watching the Strangers' Roads since 171 EC, and the rider has never once seen the imperial ships' boats come back the way they went.” (a Briarcrown carter)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A Silverthorn wants something stolen back from the Rose House, and swears it was theirs first.
Cedric Silverthorn will buy a strange object you found, and will pay too much.
Your names are in the Briarcrown register, and someone has paid to read them.
A Silverthorn courier has been killed on the road, and the letter is missing. The house wants the letter more than the killer.
Someone has received a silver thorn, and wants to know what they did.

title: House Solenne
subtitle: The Faithful Seat
summary: The Faithful Seat: the devout house of Sunhold, bound to the Concord more closely than to the Council, host of the Sunhold Accord, and the great faith's noble voice.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Solenne is the devout house, one of the ten Highlords, bound to the Concord more closely than to the Council. Its sigil is the Concord's own sign, a sun rising over a wave, on white and deep blue. No other house would dare. Its motto is *"Sun, Sea, and Order."*

It is the nearest thing the great faith has to a noble voice. Solenne lends the Concord legitimacy in the peerage, and lends the peerage a thread to the Concord. Its first loyalty, everyone understands, is to the faith. Some in the Council find a great house whose true allegiance lies outside the Council deeply unsettling, which is rather the point.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Solennes were a temple family of the continent, keepers of a sun-shrine on the coast, and when the Exodus came they carried its altar-stone south in the hold of the first convoy. The stone stands in the Dawn House today.

**Sunhold (about 25 EC).** The house was granted the bright western terraces of the Heartland, and built Sunhold there, a town of white walls above the sea, where the dawn comes up over the hills behind it and lights the water in front. The Concord's first great shrine in the Heartland stood in Sunhold before Goldwind's Grand Temple was built.

**The Sunhold Accord.** On Veriden 6th every year, the Concord and the Council meet at Sunhold to renew the Sunhold Accord, the treaty that keeps each out of the other's house. Solenne hosts it, and has hosted it since the first.

**The Last Psalm.** When the Armada's Third Fleet was given to the Concord's sea-pact work, a Solenne frigate was the first house ship to sail with it, and a Solenne ship has sailed with the Last Psalm ever since.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Aurelian Solenne rules Sunhold. The Concord is led by Sunward Alesse Brightwater and Tidecaller Ondrel Greywake. When the Concord needs a door opened in the peerage, Solenne opens it. When the peerage needs a word with the Concord, Solenne carries it.

sections.title: Sunhold and the Dawn House
list: **Sunhold** is the brightest town in the Heartland, a town of terraces and white walls above the western coast. Its hills grow the brightleaf that the Terrace Guild presses into leaf-bricks, and its vines produce the Sunhold wines that the Goldwind banks judge by taste.
**The Dawn House**, the house's seat, a white hall with its great windows facing east, where the family rises before dawn to greet the sun.
**The altar-stone**, carried from the continent in the Exodus, which stands in the Dawn House's chapel and is the oldest worked stone of the Concord in the islands.
**The Accord Hall**, where the Concord and the Council meet every Veriden 6th, with two doors, one for each, and a single table.
**The temple-terraces**, vineyards and brightleaf fields that the house holds for the Concord and works for it.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 9,000 Orsals a year, and most of it is not the house's to spend.
**Temple-lands.** The terraces the house holds for the Concord, whose wine and brightleaf it sells, keeping a part and giving the rest to the faith.
**Tithes.** The faithful of Sunhold tithe to the Concord through the house.
**The Accord.** The Council and the Concord both pay the house to host the Accord, and both suspect the other pays more.
The house spends heavily on the faith, on the Accord, and on the *Dawnsong*, and lives plainly. A Solenne at a Goldwind ball is the only noble in the room wearing no jewelry but a sun-pin.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Seven houses are sworn to Solenne, most of them families of the faith.
list: **House Ammeline**, Holder. Keepers of the altar-stone and the Dawn House chapel, a family of Sunwards.
**House Teyl**, Banneret. Captains of the Dawnward, the temple guard.
**House Calloh**, Banneret. Vintners of the temple-terraces, whose wine is poured at the Accord.
**Four more**, families of the western terraces.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Solenne keeps a guard for its shrines and a ship for the faith.
list: **The Dawnward:** about 500 temple guards in white and deep blue, who keep the Dawn House, the Accord Hall, and the shrines of the terraces.
**The full muster:** about 2,200 with the bannermen's levies, which the house would call only with the Concord's blessing.

**At sea:** one warship in the Castellan's Register, the frigate *Dawnsong*, which sails with the Last Psalm under a Solenne captain, with a Tidecaller aboard. About three merchant hulls carry wine and brightleaf.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war, the *Dawnsong* answers the Armada, and is already in it.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **Dawn.** The family rises before dawn every day, and greets the sun from the Dawn House's east windows. A Solenne who sleeps through the dawn fasts until noon.
**The sun-oath.** Every Solenne takes the sun-oath to the Concord at fifteen. A few take it again later, as if the first had worn thin.
**Two doors.** At the Accord, the Concord and the Council come in by different doors and sit at one table. The house says the doors are the point and the table is the hope.
**No jewels.** A Solenne wears only a sun-pin, and the house gives its jewels to the faith.
**The first sail.** Every ship launched from Sunhold's harbor is blessed by a Solenne before a Tidecaller blesses it, so that it has both.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
list: **Lord Aurelian.** Aurelian Solenne is a tall, grave man with a kind face and a voice that carries. His first loyalty, everyone understands, is to the faith, and he has never pretended otherwise. He took the sun-oath again at fifty, and the salons are still guessing why. He has nine children, and the third is the one the salons whisper about.

**The family.** The Solennes are many and devout, and the salons have only one complaint about them: that they cannot be gossiped about. The one exception is the heir who is said to want to leave the faith, and to have asked a Hunter how it is done.

**The Accord.** On the morning of Veriden 6th, Sunhold's bells ring at dawn. The Sunward comes in by the east door, the Council's delegation by the west, and they sit at the single table under the windows. Lord Aurelian reads the Accord aloud, as a Solenne always has. Both sides sign. At the dinner afterward the wine is from the temple-terraces, and nobody mentions the Registry.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: The house is the Concord's friend in the peerage and its door into the Council. It sails with the Last Psalm. It has no rival it would name, but the Arcane Registry and the Concord are about to collide over the Concord's unregistered priests, and Solenne is standing between them.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Lord Aurelian took the sun-oath again at fifty, as if the first one had worn thin.” (a Goldwind acolyte)
“Solenne has been sheltering the Concord's unregistered priests, and the Registry knows exactly where.” (heard in the Central Heartland)
“A Solenne heir wants to leave the faith, and has been asking how.” (a Hunter of the Goldwind Lodge)
“The altar-stone in the Dawn House is not from the continent. It was here when the Solennes came.” (a Sunhold stonemason)
“The Dawnsong sails with the Last Psalm, and the Last Psalm has been sailing to places the Armada's charts leave blank.” (a Third Fleet sailor)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: The Concord needs something carried to a noble house, and Solenne needs it to look like an accident.
A Solenne heir wants to leave the faith, and asks you how.
The Registry and the Concord are about to collide, and Solenne is standing between them.
Someone wants to disrupt the Sunhold Accord, and the house needs guards who are not its own.
A Tidecaller of the *Dawnsong* has come home with a story the Concord wants buried and Lord Aurelian wants told.

title: House Starborn
subtitle: The Watchers of Heaven
summary: The Watchers of Heaven: the astronomer house of Highspire, whose star-charts and lenses every navigator wants, whose almanac tells the islands their tides and weather, and whose partnership with the Aethyn each side tells differently.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Starborn is the astronomer house of the spire-island, one of the ten Highlords. Its sigil is a silver star over a tower, on deep indigo, and its motto is *"We See Far."* The Starborn observatories are the best in the islands, and navigators pay dearly for their charts.

It is a small house with a long reach. There is a Starborn chart in the chart-room of nearly every great ship in the islands, a Starborn lens in nearly every good spyglass, and a copy of the Starborn Almanac in every harbor-master's office from Ironfort to Southhaven. The house is quietly entangled with the Aethyn, the winged folk who watched Highspire's skies long before any house was raised there. Whether the Starborn learned the stars from the skykin or merely beside them, the two sides tell it differently, and both tell it politely.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Starborns were scholars of the Star Tower at Berith, the floating school above the Front, where the Weathermakers are trained. When the great houses fled south, three of the family's astronomers left Berith with their instruments and their notebooks, and Berith has never quite forgiven the loss of the instruments.

**Highspire (about 20 EC).** The family found a cliff-shelf above the clouds where the sky was clearer than anywhere in the islands, and the Aethyn already nesting in the cliffs above it. The first Lady Starborn, Ysolwen, climbed to the Aethyn eyries alone and came down three days later with an agreement. Nobody has ever seen it written down. The Aethyn say it was a conversation.

**The great chart (about 60 to 90 EC).** Over thirty years the house and the Aethyn charted every star visible from the islands, and the Starborn star-chart became the standard by which the Armada's chartmasters are taught. The chart has been corrected eleven times since. The house will tell you about every correction.

**The Almanac (from about 95 EC).** The house began to publish the Starborn Almanac each Landing-Day: the year's tides, moons, eclipses, and festival dates, with the weather Highspire's harbor-masters read from the Singing Cliffs. Sailors call it *the Book*, and a ship without one is thought unlucky.

**Today (175 EC).** Lady Astraea rules Highspire. Lord Orion has not made a prediction since he named the hour of the last King Tide, Altair is preparing another voyage, and Relbic works in the observatories beside the Aethyn and the gnome lens-makers.

sections.title: Highspire
list: **Highspire** is a walled tower-city on a narrow shelf halfway up a colossal cliff, above the cloud-line. Its harbor lies far below, often lost in fog, and a long cliff-road and a hauling-lift connect the two.
**The observatories**, copper domes across the rooftops, with brass telescopes that open at dusk. The great dome at the center, the Eye, holds the largest lens in the islands.
**The lens-works**, where gnome and Aethyn grinders shape Highspire's lenses, in rooms kept so clean that visitors are asked to leave their boots at the door.
**The Starborn house**, a palace of slender spires set against the cliff, where the family dines at noon and works at night.
**The Singing Cliffs** above the city, wind-bored crags full of holes where the Aethyn nest. When the wind turns, the cliffs sing, and Highspire's harbor-masters read tomorrow's weather by the pitch.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 8,000 Orsals a year.
list: **Star-charts.** A Starborn chart for a ship costs 20 to 50 Anchors, and the Armada buys a new set for every hull it commissions.
**Lenses and spyglasses.** A Highspire spyglass costs 100 Anchors, and the best captains will pay twice that for one ground by Relbic.
**The Almanac.** A copy costs 5 Tides, and the house sells some thirty thousand every Landing-Day.
**The harbor.** Highspire's harbor dues, collected by the Sennet harbor-masters.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Five houses are sworn to Starborn, all small, and most of them have more instruments than land.
**House Sennet**, Holder. The harbor-masters of Highspire, who read the weather from the cliffs' pitch and write the weather pages of the Almanac.
**House Quarle**, Banneret. A gnome family of lens-grinders, the best in the islands after Relbic, and the only gnomes in the peerage who still grind their own glass.
**House Aldmere**, Banneret. The printers of the Almanac, who set its tables by hand and have never let a misprint through, except once, in 131 EC, which the family still talks about.
**Two more**, Bannerets of Highspire's harbor and the cliff-road.
The **Aethyn** are not sworn to anyone. They share the watch.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Starborn keeps almost no soldiers and needs few. Highspire stands on a cliff above the clouds, and the only ways up are the cliff-road and the lift.
list: **The Tower Watch:** about 300 soldiers in indigo, who keep the cliff-road, the lift, and the city's wall.
**The cliff itself:** the hardest seat in the islands to take, and the house knows it.
**The full muster:** about 1,200 with the bannermen's levies.

**At sea:** one warship in the Castellan's Register, the courier *Meridian*, the fastest hull in the house's waters, which carries the Almanac's first copies to Goldwind every Landing-Day. About three merchant hulls carry lenses and charts.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war, the *Meridian* answers the Armada, and the house's charts and weather-readings go to the Admiralty first.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **Noon and night.** The family dines at noon and works at night, and a Starborn who sleeps through a clear night is teased for a year.
**A star at birth.** Every Starborn child is given a star on the great chart at birth, and the star's name is written beside theirs in the house's book.
**The first copy.** The first printed copy of each year's Almanac is carried up to the Singing Cliffs and left for the Aethyn. In the morning it is gone.
**The corrections.** When the house corrects the great chart, it publishes the correction with the name of the person who found the error, whoever they were.
**No prophecy for coin.** A Starborn may read the stars for anyone, and may never take money for it. Orion's predictions have made the house famous and never once made it richer.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
list: **Lady Astraea.** Astraea Starborn is a tall, sharp-eyed woman who looks at people as if measuring their distance. She runs Highspire like an observatory: everything in its place, everything recorded, and nothing hurried. She comes down to Goldwind twice a year, for the University's councils, and is home before the next clear night. She has two sons, both astronomers; the elder keeps the Eye.
**The family.**
**Lord Orion,** an astrologer known for predictions that come true. He named the hour of the last King Tide, and has predicted nothing since.
**Lyral,** an enchantress of astral magic, whose wards on the observatories have kept the lenses clean of frost for twenty winters.
**Cassiopeia,** a researcher of the cosmos and its mysteries, who is said to have found a star that crosses the sky the wrong way.
**Altair,** an explorer who goes wherever the stars point, and who has been to more uncharted islands than any Starborn before him.
**Relbic,** the youngest, a lens-grinder who works in the observatories beside the Aethyn and the gnome lens-makers, and the only Starborn the Aethyn call a friend.

**A night in Highspire.** At dusk the domes open with a sound like a field of shutters. The city goes dark, by law, so that the lenses can see. On the rooftops the astronomers call numbers to their clerks, and above them, against the stars, the Aethyn glide out from the Singing Cliffs to keep their own watch. Nobody speaks loudly. Somewhere a lens-grinder is still working by a hooded lamp.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: Starborn keeps a friendly competition with Caelvaron over the magical arts, and both sit with Varselis in the University bloc. The Armada is its best customer. Berith wants its instruments back. The Aethyn are partners, and the house is careful never to call them anything else.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Highspire's astronomers keep one star on their charts that crosses the sky the wrong way.” (a Starborn page)
“Orion Starborn named the hour of the last King Tide. He has not predicted anything since, and he will not say why.” (a Highspire navigator)
“The Aethyn have their own star-chart, older than the house's, and they have never shown it to a Starborn except Relbic.” (a Quarle lens-grinder)
“Altair Starborn came back from his last voyage with one fewer sailor and one more island, and the island is not on the great chart.” (a Highspire dock-hand)
“The Almanac for 177 has already been printed, and Lady Astraea locked it away.” (an Aldmere apprentice)
“The imperial Survey bought a Starborn chart through a Goldwind dealer, and sent it back a month later with a correction in the margin. Lady Astraea checked it. It was right.” (an Aldmere apprentice)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A Starborn chart with an island on it that no ship has ever reached.
Altair Starborn is going where the stars point, and needs a crew.
Relbic Starborn asks you to carry a lens to the Aethyn, and not to look through it.
A misprint in this year's Almanac has put a festival on the wrong day, and someone did it on purpose.
The great lens in the Eye has cracked, and the house needs glass from somewhere dangerous.

star-charts and lenses; Highspire spyglasses; the Starborn Almanac; Highspire's harbor dues

epigraph.quote: The stars are dead gods. We are only reading their letters.

title: House Stormweaver
subtitle: The Storm-Sung
summary: The Storm-Sung: the storm-sorcerer Marchlords of Greyhaven, whose mages keep the harbor-lights burning through the Murk, whose bells guide the fishing fleets home, and whose old rivals hold the strait next door.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Stormweaver is the storm-sorcerer house, a Marchlord line of the Northern Frontier. Its sigil is a forked bolt over a lighthouse, on grey and pale gold, and its motto is *"We Sing the Storm."*

Its mages keep Greyhaven's harbor-lights burning through the famous Murk, the fog that lives on that coast, and the Brine Brotherhood's fishing fleets pay them to keep their boats off the rocks. It is a small house with an old trade and a hard coast. Its neighbors and old rivals are the Vanris of Stormreach, two maritime houses on one stretch of fog-bound coast, which has never once gone smoothly.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Stormweavers were Weathermakers of Berith's Storm Spire, the college of storm-callers that every navy wants. When the Exodus came, two of the family's storm-callers sailed with the convoys to keep the weather off them, and stayed.

**Greyhaven (about 10 EC).** The fishing families of the Frontier had found the ring-harbor of Greyhaven and were losing boats on the Widow's Teeth every winter. The first Lady Stormweaver, Halcyra, lit the first light on the last of the Teeth, and the fishing fleets have paid the house to keep it lit since.

**The captive storm (about 31 EC).** Halcyra's grandson, Lord Taran, caught a storm and set it in the lantern of the Stormweaver light, where it has burned ever since: pale blue-white lightning crackling in a glass that has never been opened. The light can be seen through the Murk when no flame could.

**The rivalry (from about 40 EC).** When Vanris lit its own lantern on Stormguard Hold, Greyhaven took it as a challenge, and Stormreach took Greyhaven's answer as an insult. The two houses have argued since over whose lights the north's sailors should trust, and the sailors trust both and say so to neither.

**The Plague (about 90 EC).** When the Plague of the Burning Sea came north, the house kept the lights lit through a winter in which half Greyhaven was sick, with three mages who had not slept in a week. Greyhaven has never forgotten it, and the house has never let it.

**Today (175 EC).** Lady Elara rules Greyhaven. When Vanris went to war with the Stormchanters this year, it asked the house for storm-mages, and Elara refused. *"We do not fight storms with storms,"* she wrote, and Stormreach has not forgiven the letter.

sections.title: Greyhaven and the Widow's Teeth
list: **Greyhaven** is a grey, hard port that lives inside the fog, built in a ring of sheer cliffs around a round, calm harbor. Its harbor is the richest salt-fish harbor in the Frontier, and its bells never stop during the Murk.
**The Widow's Teeth**, a row of jagged sea-stacks at the harbor mouth. On still nights the wind moves through the holes in the rock and makes a chord.
**The Stormweaver light**, on the last of the Teeth, a stone tower whose lantern holds the captive storm.

**The bell-towers** on the stacks and the bell-buoys in the channel, which ring the bell-codes. Every Greyhaven child learns the codes before their letters, because a boat that cannot read the bells cannot find the harbor.
**The widows' chapel** on the cliff above the old quarter, where the widows of the lost light lamps for the boats that have not come home.
**Storm House**, the family's seat on the cliff-top, a grey hall full of barometers, wind-gauges, and storm-glasses, where the windows rattle in every wind.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 7,000 Orsals a year.
list: **The lights.** The Brine Brotherhood's fishing fleets pay the house a fixed sum a season for the lights and the bells, and the Hallorn house of Saltreach helps to pay for them.
**Salt-fish.** The house takes a share of Greyhaven's salt-fish, the richest catch in the Frontier, which feeds Faust's garrisons and half the north.
**Weather.** The house's storm-mages read the weather for any captain who asks, for a fee, and are very rarely wrong.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Seven houses are sworn to Stormweaver, all of them families of the fog-coast.
list: **House Skerrin**, Holder. Captains of the house's ships, and its link to the fishing fleets.
**House Thole**, Banneret. Keepers of the bell-towers and the bell-codes. A Thole can ring a boat home through the Murk by ear.
**House Gannet**, Banneret. Keepers of the widows' chapel and the lamp-rolls, which record every boat lost off Greyhaven since 10 EC.
**Four more**, Bannerets of the fishing coast.

sections.title: Strength
list: **The Greyhaven Guard:** about 550 soldiers in grey and pale gold, who keep Storm House, the light, and the harbor.
**The storm-mages:** about fifty registered casters, the house's own, who can call wind, fog, and lightning, and who keep the lights.
**The full muster:** about 2,400 with the bannermen's levies, most of them fishermen.

**At sea:** four warships in the Castellan's Register, the frigates *Forked Light* (the flagship) and *Halcyra*, and two sloops. About five merchant hulls, and every fishing boat in Greyhaven would sail for the house if asked.
**The Murk:** the house's real defense. No fleet can find Greyhaven in the fog without the bells, and the bells answer to the house.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war, the house's warships answer the Armada, and its storm-mages are the first casters the Admiralty asks for.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **The bells first.** Every Stormweaver child learns the bell-codes before their letters, like every Greyhaven child.
**The night on the light.** Every Stormweaver mage spends one night alone in the Stormweaver light before taking their rings, with the captive storm a hand's breadth away.
**Never a storm against a storm.** The house does not turn its weather against another weather-calling people. Elara's letter to Stormreach quoted the rule exactly.
**The widow's lamp.** When a Stormweaver dies at sea, the head of the house lights a lamp in the widows' chapel herself, and leaves it to burn out.
**Grey and gold.** The family wears grey on land and pale gold at sea, so that a boat can tell a Stormweaver from a distance.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: **Lady Elara.** Elara Stormweaver is a weathered, white-haired storm-sorcerer with a sailor's laugh and a sailor's language. She has never been to a Goldwind ball, and has sent a different relative to each one she was invited to. She is the only head of a house who has publicly refused Mortimer Vanris anything, and the north loves her for it. She has outlived her husband and two of her children, and has eleven grandchildren, every one of whom learned the bell-codes before their letters.
list: **The family.**
**Lord Corvus,** a naval commander and an evoker, who captains the *Forked Light* and has twice turned a Vanris squadron with a single squall.
**Vesper,** an explorer and cartographer, who charts the fog-coast and the north's uncharted rocks.
**Maelstrom,** a druid who can call the weather, and who has lately been spending a great deal of time alone in the Stormweaver light.
**Isadora,** an enchanter and the house's diplomat, who is sent to the Goldwind balls and enjoys them more than she admits.

**A night in the Murk.** The fog comes in at dusk and does not lift. The town goes dim; the harbor goes white. On the stacks the bells start, a code for every channel, and out in the fog the fishing boats answer with horns. On the last of the Teeth the Stormweaver light flickers blue, and the whole harbor watches it the way a household watches a fire.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: House Vanris shares the foggy coast and an old rivalry, and this year it has a new grievance: Elara's letter. House Emberheart quarrels with Stormweaver over the elemental forces both houses claim. The Brine Brotherhood and the Hallorn house pay for the lights, and House Faust's garrisons eat Greyhaven salt-fish. The Fogrunners of Black Harbor thread the Widow's Teeth blind by the same bell-codes, and the house has never asked how they learned them.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The storm in the Stormweaver light is alive, and on still nights you can hear it ask to be let out.” (a Greyhaven fisherman)
“Elara Stormweaver told Mortimer Vanris no, in writing, and he had the letter framed so he could throw things at it.” (a Coilward clerk)
“The Fogrunners learned the bell-codes from a Thole who was paid very well, and the Tholes know which one.” (a Black Harbor smuggler)
“Corvus Stormweaver turned a Vanris squadron with a squall in 171 EC, and both houses swear it never happened.” (a Greyhaven pilot)
“There are more lamps in the widows' chapel this year than there were boats lost.” (a Gannet keeper)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: The Murk has come down early, and a ship carrying something important is out in it without the bell-codes.
Maelstrom Stormweaver needs someone to sit a night in the light with him and tell him what they hear.
A bell-tower on the Teeth has gone silent, and the Tholes say it was not the weather.
Vanris wants storm-mages for the Stormchanter war and has stopped asking politely.
A Gannet keeper wants to know who has been lighting the extra lamps in the widows' chapel.

title: House Sunforge
subtitle: The Golden Hammer
summary: The Golden Hammer: the master-smith house of Aurelion, fabulously rich from its forges, firearms, and goldwork, keeper of the only proof-house in the Heartland, and the noble house closest to the Mercantile Congress.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Sunforge is the master-smith house of the Heartland, one of the ten Highlords, fabulously wealthy from Aurelion's forges and goldwork and deeply tied to the Mercantile Congress. Its sigil is a golden hammer over a sunburst, on gold and white, and its motto is *"By Hand and Fire."* The golden hammer is stamped on more fine metal than any other mark in the islands.

It is the noble house that most resembles a merchant house, and the one the merchant houses trust most. Its forges, the Sunforge works, are the only place in the Heartland where a firearm can be made to proof standard, and the Aurelion smiths guard the secret of that proof as closely as the Council guards its seats.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Sunforges were master-smiths of the continent's Free Cities, a guild family raised to the nobility for arming the Alliance in a war it nearly lost. They took the Exodus with their tools, their apprentices, and the house's most valuable possession: the notebooks of the proof.

**Aurelion (about 12 EC).** The house found coal, iron, and a deep harbor together on the north coast of the Heartland, and built Aurelion around them. The first forge was lit on the day the town was named, and the house says it has never gone cold.

**The proof (from about 30 EC).** The Smiths' Guild was founded in Aurelion, under Sunforge patronage, to stamp honest work. Proof make, the guild's stamp and guarantee, began here. Today everything ordinary in the islands comes in harbor make or proof make, and the best proof is Aurelion's.

**The Ascendant's War (105 EC).** Aurelion armed the first Grand Coalition. The house worked its forges day and night for a year, and the bells of the works rang the shifts so often that Aurelion children born that year were nicknamed *bell-babies*. Some of them are still alive and still answer to it.

**The Congress.** As the Mercantile Congress grew, Sunforge became the noble house closest to it. Its goods fill the Congress's warehouses, and its lords sit at the Congress's table as guests, which no other noble house is offered.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Eamon rules Aurelion. Fergus has not signed a blade in three years, Niamh's draughts are bought by the Hunters by the crate, and Declan's designs keep the works ahead of everyone else's.

sections.title: Aurelion
list: **Aurelion** is the forge-city of the north coast, and its smoke is visible from Goldwind on a clear day. The city smells of coal and hot brass, and the bells of the works ring the shifts.
**The Sunforge works**, the great forges along the harbor, where blades, firearms, and fine metal are made. Every forge has its bellows toad, which blows the fire, and every toad has a name.

**The proof-house**, a squat stone building in the middle of the works where the guild's stamp is struck and where firearms are proved. Only Sunforges and the masters of House Anvell may enter its inner room.
**The Golden Hall**, the house's seat above the city, a palace of white stone with a gilded hammer over the gate, where the Congress's merchants dine as guests.
**The jewelers' row**, a street of goldsmiths and gem-setters under the Golden Hall, where Lady Branwen keeps her workshop.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 19,000 Orsals a year.
list: **Fine metal.** Jewelry, goldwork, and plate, sold through the Congress and to every great house. Lady Branwen's pieces are worn at every Council session.
**Blades.** A good sword costs 20 to 100 Anchors and up; a Sunforge blade costs more, and Fergus's own are not sold at all, only given.
**Firearms.** An Aurelion fine-work pistol costs 200 Anchors and up, and is the most coveted firearm in the islands. Muskets, locks, and barrels follow.
**War-gear.** House Faust buys its finest gear from Aurelion every year, and has never once admitted it is the best.
**The guild.** The Smiths' Guild pays the house for its hall, and the house takes a small fee for every stamp struck in Aurelion.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Eight houses are sworn to Sunforge, most of them guild families raised to the nobility for their craft.
list: **House Anvell**, Holder. Masters of the proof-house. An Anvell proves every Aurelion firearm and keeps the proof's secret with the family. There has never been an Anvell who could not keep a secret.
**House Sorrend**, Banneret. Gold-assayers of the jewelers' row, who test every ingot that comes into Aurelion and many that only pass through.
**House Colliss**, Banneret. Coal-masters of the hills behind the city, who keep the forges fed.
**Five more**, Holders and Bannerets of Aurelion and the north coast.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Sunforge keeps a small force, armed better than anyone's.
list: **The Hammer Guard:** about 800 soldiers in gold and white, every one with a proof-made blade, a Sunforge breastplate, and an Aurelion musket. Man for man they are the best-armed soldiers in the islands, and they cost the house more than an army twice their size would.
**The works:** in a war, Aurelion's forges arm everyone else, and that is the house's real strength.
**The full muster:** about 3,000 with the bannermen's levies, most of them smiths' journeymen who can shoot.
**At sea:** two warships in the Castellan's Register, the frigates *Proof* and *Assay*, which escort the house's cargoes. About eighteen merchant hulls carry Aurelion's work.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war, the house's frigates answer the Armada, and its forges work for the Council at cost, as they did in 105 EC.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **By hand.** Every Sunforge, of every branch, learns a craft at the forge or the bench before they learn to ride. Lord Eamon is a fair locksmith. Lady Branwen is a great one.
**The bell-names.** Aurelion children are named at the works, under the shift-bells, and the bell that rings at the moment of naming is written on the child's record.
**The invoice.** The house writes the Faust invoice by hand every year, and always adds a line. One year it was *"adequate"*. Faust has paid every one.
**The given blade.** A blade by Fergus Sunforge is never sold. It is given, to someone the house judges worthy, and the gift is recorded in the guild's book.
**The cold forge.** On the day a head of the house dies, every forge in Aurelion is let go cold for one hour. It is the only hour in the year when the city is quiet.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: **Lord Eamon.** Eamon Sunforge is a broad, loud, cheerful man with burn-scars on both hands, who dines with merchants and talks prices at balls. The old houses find him vulgar and buy everything he makes. He is the best-liked noble in the Congress and does not care much what the peerage thinks of him. He has four children, all still minors, each apprenticed at a bench. He drives to the Council in a gilded carriage behind four aurocs, which the old houses call vulgar and the Congress calls a bargain.
list: **The family.**
**Lady Branwen,** a jeweler whose pieces are worn at every Council session, and who can tell from across a room whose necklace is false.
**Fergus,** a master weaponsmith, the hand behind many of the islands' legendary blades. He has not signed a blade in three years, and says the next one will be his last.
**Niamh,** an alchemist whose potions and elixirs the Hunters buy by the crate. Her newest draught is sold only to Gold Hunters.
**Declan,** an engineer whose designs keep Aurelion's forges ahead of everyone else's, and who has opinions about every gun in the islands.

**A day at the works.** The first bell rings before dawn, and the bellows toads start before the smiths do. By midmorning the harbor is loud with hammers and the air tastes of coal. A Congress factor comes up to the Golden Hall to haggle with Lord Eamon over lunch, and loses, and enjoys it. At the proof-house a pistol is fired into a sand-box, and an Anvell writes a number in a book nobody else may read.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: House Faust buys Sunforge war-gear and has never admitted it is the best. The rivalry is friendly, loud, and one of the oldest in the peerage. The house is the noble friend of the Mercantile Congress and the patron of the Smiths' Guild. It competes with Everfall's Anvilworks for the Armada's gun contracts, and the two houses are civil about it in the way of people who know exactly how good the other is.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Fergus Sunforge has not signed a blade in three years. He says the next one will be his last.” (an Aurelion apprentice)
“Niamh Sunforge's newest draught is sold only to Gold Hunters. Nobody below Gold has seen the label.” (a Lodge quartermaster)
“There is a family in Aurelion that buys more silver than the jewelers' row and makes no jewelry with it.” (a Sorrend assayer's boy)
“Declan Sunforge has seen a gun that loads from the back, and he went very quiet.” (an Aurelion barrel-maker)
“Somebody is stamping the golden hammer on blades that never saw Aurelion, and they are good enough to fool a Sunforge.” (a Goldwind sword-seller)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A Sunforge blade with a forged mark, and a Sunforge who wants to know who made it.
Declan Sunforge needs a rare ore from somewhere no sane person goes.
Lady Branwen's newest piece goes missing the night before a Council session.
Fergus Sunforge is looking for the person worthy of his last blade, and he has heard of one of you.
A cargo of Aurelion pistols has gone missing between the works and the Congress warehouses.

title: House Vanris
subtitle: Unyielding as the Storm
summary: Unyielding as the Storm: the maritime Archlords of Stormreach, who hold the strait between the Frontier and the Heartland, build the best storm-hulls in the islands, keep the largest house fleet afloat, and sit under a weak lord.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Vanris is one of the Five, the great maritime Archlord. It holds Stormreach, the strait between the Northern Frontier and the Central Heartland, and so holds a great deal of who and what moves between them. Its sigil is a coiled sea-serpent about a tower, on storm-grey and deep green, and its motto is the one the ferrymen like to finish for it: *"Unyielding as the Storm."*

It is the house of the sea. It builds the best storm-hulls in the islands and charges a premium for them, it keeps more warships than any other house, and its pilots are the only safe way through the reefs below its seat. The Armada's Ninth Fleet, the Standing Storm, is stationed in its waters, and the two have learned to share a harbor.

The house's tragedy is its head. Lord Mortimer is a weak and vain lord sitting on a mighty seat, and the real work of holding Vanris together falls to his brother Rodrick and his spymaster Cassandra. Everyone in Stormreach knows it. Mortimer may be the only one who does not.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: **Before the Landing.** The Vanris were shipowners of the continental coast, captains and builders who carried a share of the Exodus south on their own keels and charged for it. The house's chronicle says it never charged a family that could not pay. Varselis keeps the passage-lists, and has never said whether that is true.

**The serpent (about 6 EC).** Lord Valdar Vanris, then a convoy-captain, lost his way in a storm in the strait and followed a sea serpent through the reefs to a rock above calm water. He built the first tower of Stormguard Hold on that rock. The reefs below have been called the Serpent's Coil ever since, because from the Hold's top they look like a serpent coiled about a tower, and the house took the shape for its sigil.

**The strait-money (about 12 EC).** The Council granted Vanris a toll of one Tide a mast on every ship passing the strait, in return for charting the Coil and lighting it. The house calls the toll *the serpent's due* and says it is owed to the serpent, not to Vanris. The serpent has never come to collect.

**The yards (from about 20 EC).** Keelhaven grew under the Hold, and the Vanris yards became the largest in the north. The house learned to build for the strait's weather, and its storm-hulls have been the envy of every shipwright in the islands for a hundred and fifty years.

**The Ascendant's War (105 EC).** Vanris carried the Frontier's soldiers south through the strait to the first Grand Coalition, Faust's among them, and charged the Council for every passage. The Council paid. Faust has never stopped mentioning it.

**The Kraken's Maw (165 EC).** Sir Rodrick, then a young captain, commanded the house's three heavy frigates in the Coalition line, and brought all three home. That is the day the house's captains began to follow him.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Mortimer holds the seat and a high post in the Armada that his father's name earned. This year he wanted a port on the Stormchanters' island, and when the islanders asked him to build elsewhere, he took it as an insult. At his urging the Council declared the Stormchanters enemies of Kalvatar, and ships of the First Fleet and Hunters on Vanris coin made the first attacks. He has also petitioned the Admiralty to give his brother a squadron in the far south. House Varselis's Strait Case, which argues that the strait-money has no basis in the Charter, is still before the Council.

sections.title: Stormreach
list: **Stormguard Hold** is a fortress on a rock above the strait: grey towers, green banners, and a lantern at the top that has been lit every night since 12 EC. From its upper walls a watcher can see both shores of the strait, every sail in it, and the pale shape of the Coil under the water.

**The Serpent's Coil** is a ring of reefs in the strait, shaped like a serpent coiled about a tower. Ships pass it with a Vanris pilot or not at all. The ones that tried without are still there, and the pilots point them out.

**Keelhaven** is the yard-town on the northern shore, the largest shipbuilding yard in the north: slipways, ropewalks, timber-ponds, and sail-lofts, and the noise of hammers from before dawn to after dark. Its people say they can tell the hour by which yard is hammering.
**Pilot's Isle** is a small island in the strait where the Vanris pilots live and train, and where no one else is allowed to learn the Coil's channels.
**The Coilward** is a fort and harbor on the southern shore, where the Heartland begins and the strait-money is counted.
**The Floating Pavilion** is not in Stormreach at all. It is Mortimer's palace on the sea, moored off Goldwind, built to prove a point to a gala.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 70,000 Orsals a year, second of the Five.

**The yards.** An ocean merchantman costs 800 to 1,500 Orsals; a Vanris storm-hull costs a fifth more and is worth it. The yards build House Corvane's great hulls, and the Armada's heavy frigates under contract. Keelhaven launches some thirty hulls in a good year.
**Pilotage.** Every ship that passes the Coil takes a Vanris pilot, at 5 Anchors for a coaster and up to 5 Orsals for a great ship. This is the real money of the strait.
**The strait-money.** One Tide a mast, collected at the Coilward. It is small coin. The house counts every mast that pays it, and keeps the count.
**Timber and cordage.** The yards buy more timber than any other buyer in the north, and sell their offcuts, rope, and sailcloth to every yard that cannot match them.
The house spends lavishly. The Floating Pavilion cost more than the Stormguard's new wall, and the masons say the wall needed it more.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Sixteen houses are sworn to Vanris. Most of them are sea-families of the strait: shipwrights, pilots, captains, and rope-makers, who swore to the serpent before they swore to the man.
list: **House Brenning**, Holder. Master-shipwrights of the Keelhaven yards for five generations. A Brenning drew every Vanris storm-hull since the first, and old Master Odda Brenning still signs every keel.
**House Quellin**, Warden of Pilot's Isle. The pilots. A Quellin knows every channel of the Coil by night and by fog, and teaches them only to Quellins and to those the house names.
**House Thalwen**, Holder. Captains of the house's marines, the Coil Marines, and the bannermen closest to Sir Rodrick.
**House Callant**, Warden of the Coilward. Keepers of the southern fort and the toll-house, who count the masts and know which ships passed twice.
**House Daskell**, Banneret. Rope-makers and sail-makers of Keelhaven, rich, quiet, and owed money by everyone on the slipways.
**Eleven more**, Holders and Bannerets of both shores.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Vanris keeps the largest house fleet in the islands, and a small army to go with it.
list: **The Coil Marines:** about 2,200 marines in storm-grey and green, who man the house's warships, garrison Stormguard and the Coilward, and board anything that does not stop. Most of them follow Sir Rodrick.
**The Hold Guard:** about 600 soldiers who keep Stormguard Hold and Keelhaven, under the master of arms, Gideon.
**The full muster:** about 8,500 with the bannermen's levies, most of them sailors who can also fight.

**At sea:** twenty-four warships in the Castellan's Register, the largest house fleet afloat: three heavy frigates built in the house's own yards to the Armada's storm-runner pattern (the flagship *Unyielding*, the *Valdar's Coil*, and the *Green Squall*), nine frigates, eight sloops, and four cutters. About sixty merchant hulls fly the green pennant.
**The strait itself:** the Coil, the pilots, and the guns of the Hold and the Coilward make the strait the hardest water in the islands to force, and the house knows it.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war the house's warships answer the Armada and join the Ninth Fleet, the Standing Storm, which is already in its waters.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **The heir's passage.** At twelve, every Vanris heir is rowed out to the edge of the Coil and must take a small boat through it alone. Most do it in an afternoon. The house does not say how long Mortimer took.
**The serpent's due.** Every new Vanris hull, on its first voyage, passes over the Coil and drops a single silver Tide into the water for the serpent.
**The lantern.** The lantern on Stormguard Hold is lit every night by a member of the family, or by whoever the family has failed to send.
**The hammers.** The Keelhaven yards start their hammers before dawn, and on the day a head of the house dies, they do not start at all.
**Green at sea.** A Vanris wears green only at sea. On land the family wears grey, and a Vanris in green at a Goldwind ball is understood to be making a point.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: **Lord Mortimer.** Mortimer Vanris is arrogant, complacent, and well out of his depth. He is handsome in the way of men who have been told so, generous in the way of men who have never had to count, and quick to take offense at anything he does not understand, which is a great deal. He holds a high post in the Armada that his father's name earned, and spends his money proving points: the Floating Pavilion was built to outshine a gala, and the Stormchanter war began because he was asked, politely, to build his port somewhere else. He married late, a young Daskell daughter, and has no children yet, which is why his brother is next of the blood.
**The people who hold it together.**

**Sir Rodrick Vanris,** his younger brother, a brilliant naval officer and tactician, and the man the house's captains actually follow. He is quiet, tired, and loyal, and has never once said a word against his brother in public. The salons say he does not need to. He has never married. The salons say he is married to the fleet, and the fleet would agree.

**Lady Cassandra Dosslas,** the house's spymaster. Born a Dosslas, she married into a minor branch of the house, kept her own name, and keeps her own counsel. Goldwind is afraid of her and cannot say why.
**Mortis,** Mortimer's assistant, shrewd and manipulative, who handles the family's affairs and is said to decide more of them than his lord knows.
**Gideon,** master of arms and Mortimer's bodyguard, a formidable warrior whose loyalty is to the house more than to the man.

**A night at the Floating Pavilion.** The barges leave the Goldwind quay at dusk, lit green. The Pavilion rides at anchor in the gulf, three decks of gilt and glass, with an orchestra on the top deck and a fountain on the middle one that pumps seawater and calls it a feature. Mortimer greets every guest and tells each of them a different story about the serpent. Rodrick is never there. Cassandra always is, and nobody ever sees her arrive.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: House Stormweaver shares the foggy coast and an old rivalry over who keeps the north's lights. House Varselis challenges Vanris's hold on the strait, and the Strait Case has been before the Council since 168 EC. House Faust needs the strait open and has never liked paying for it. House Corvane needs the yards and pays for them. The Blackstrand house holds a great deal of Mortimer's paper, and the house does not discuss how much.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Mortimer Vanris will sell the Stormguard to the Heartland before the year is out. His brother has already written to the Council about it.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“The Floating Pavilion cost more than the Stormguard's new wall. The masons say the wall needed it more.” (a Stormreach mason)
“Mortimer wants Rodrick sent south because the captains cheer when Rodrick comes aboard and only salute when Mortimer does.” (a Coil Marine)
“Mortis meets a man with a knotted thread on his cuff, in a different tavern every time.” (a Keelhaven tavern-keeper)
“When Mortimer took his heir's passage, his brother rowed out and towed him through the Coil, and the whole of Pilot's Isle was paid to forget it.” (a Quellin pilot, very drunk)

“The imperial survey ships take a Quellin pilot through the Coil like everyone else, and pay in Orsals, and the pilots say those ships answer the helm faster than anything they have ever steered.” (a Pilot's Isle pilot)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: Sir Rodrick needs something done that his brother must not hear about.
Passage through the strait, and a Vanris pilot who wants a favor first.
Hunters are being hired for the Stormchanter campaign, at very good rates.
A Callant toll-clerk has noticed a ship that passed the Coil twice in one night, paying both times.
An invitation to the Floating Pavilion, and a request from someone else to search Mortimer's study while he is dancing.
