epigraph.quote: Unyielding as the storm. Mostly the storm.

title: House Varselis
subtitle: The Even Hand
summary: The Even Hand: the Archlords of law and balance, the nearest thing the peerage has to a conscience, keepers of the Hall of Scales, and the house that holds the Nobles' seat on the Council.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Varselis is one of the Five, and the house of justice, law, and balance. It holds the Nobles' seat on the Council of the Charted Isles, keeps the Hall of Scales where any petitioner may be heard, and stands as the chief lawful check on Vol Kaern's ambition. Its sigil is a set of silver scales over an open book, on grey-blue, and its motto is *"Weighed, Not Wagered."*

It is the poorest of the Five and the most quoted. Its sigil hangs in more courtrooms than any other house's, its law-school trains half the advocates in the islands, and a Varselis seal on a ruling is the closest thing the peerage has to a final word. Other houses are feared for what they can do. Varselis is feared for what it can prove.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: **Before the Landing.** The Varselis were magistrates of the Free City of Castia, where the Exodus took ship. When the great houses fled south, someone had to keep the lists: who sailed, on which hull, with what, and what they owed for their passage. The Varselis kept them for fifteen years, from the first wave to the last, and they still have every page.

**The Charter (1 EC).** The first Lord Varselis, Corvin, sat with the committee that wrote the Charter's articles of law, and the house has been reading them aloud to the other houses ever since. When the Landing was declared complete, the Nobles chose a Varselis to speak for them on the new Council, and with two short gaps a Varselis has held the Nobles' seat since.

**The Abolition (about 60 EC).** When the enslaved of the young federation rose, it was Lady Sereth Varselis who argued the Abolition through the Council, against the votes of half the peerage. Slavery ended in Council lands that year. It did not end in the south, and the house has never stopped saying so in the Council, which the southern houses have never forgiven.

**The Ascendant's War (105 EC).** The Hall of Scales was the one great seat in the central Heartland that Morvane's mage-army did not take, and the house's guard held it for forty days. After the war, the Hall heard the trials of the Ascendant's captains, and every one of them was heard in full.

**The Kraken's Maw (165 EC).** The frigate *Even Keel* sailed with the Coalition and came home with a hole in her side that a cart could have driven through. The house had her mended rather than replaced, and the patch is still painted a different grey, so that everyone who sees her knows.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Linus is old and still rules. His heir Halsof holds the Nobles' seat and is the face of the nobility in a fracturing age. This year Halsof carried Mortimer Vanris's motion against the Stormchanters to the Council, which declared them enemies of Kalvatar. The house has an older case before the Council, the Strait Case, which argues that Vanris's strait-money has no basis in the Charter. Both things are true at once, and the salons have noticed.

sections.title: The Hall of Scales
paragraphs: The house's seat is the Hall of Scales, on a rise above the town of Varhall: a long hall of grey stone with no towers and no wall, because a court should not look like a castle. A great pair of silver scales hangs over its doors, always level, so that everyone who enters walks under it. The scales are dusted every morning and checked with a plumb-line every Restday, and the day they are found uneven, the house says, the Hall will close.

Petitioners of any rank may be heard. They queue from before dawn on the Hall steps, and the order in which they are heard is drawn by lot, so that a fishwife may be heard before a Highlord. A Hall saying goes: *"The lot does not know your name."*
Behind the Hall stand the Record-House, where the Exodus lists and every judgment since the Charter are kept, and the house itself, which is plain, cold in winter, and full of books.

sections.title: Varhall and the Inns
paragraphs: The house's Dominion is the isle of Varhall and its small sister, Lesser Varhall.
list: **Varhall**, a broad green island of sheep-downs and wheat, with the town of Varhall under the Hall and a harbor that ships wool to Goldwind.
**Lesser Varhall**, an island of orchards and quiet houses, where old judges of the Hall go to retire, and where the house sends its young to read.

**The Inns of the Scale**, in Goldwind's banking quarter: the law-school of the Varselis, a warren of lecture rooms and moot courts where some three hundred students read the Charter and the codes at a time.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 35,000 Orsals a year, the smallest of the Five. It comes from:

**Arbitration.** Merchant houses, guilds, and noble families bring their disputes to a Varselis arbiter rather than to the Council's courts, because a Varselis ruling is final and fast. The fee is one in every hundred of the sum in dispute, from both sides, win or lose.
**Court fees.** A petition at the Hall costs one Bit for the poor and a great deal more for everyone else, by a scale nailed to the door.
**The Inns of the Scale.** Five Orsals a year for a student, and the Inns are never short of them.
**Varhall.** Wool, wheat, and mutton from the downs, shipped on the house's own hulls.

Varselis does not lend, does not trade in titles, and does not take gifts without writing them down. That is why it is the poorest of the Five, and the house considers it the best investment it ever made.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Fourteen houses are sworn to Varselis. Most are families of law: advocates, recorders, bailiffs, and judges, who swore to the Even Hand because it was the only great house that would never ask them to lie for it.
list: **House Ystrel**, Holder. The house's chief advocates for four generations. An Ystrel has argued for Varselis in every great case since the Abolition, and lost two.
**House Tamsor**, Warden of the Downs on Varhall. Sheep-lords who raise the largest share of the house's levy, and the only Varselis bannermen who have never read a law-book and are proud of it.
**House Ardith**, Holder. Keepers of the Record-House. Lady Fenna Ardith knows where every judgment since 1 EC is shelved, and has read most of them twice.
**House Selvane**, Banneret. The Hall's bailiffs, who carry its summons. A Selvane summons has been served on a Highlord in his bath, on a pirate at sea, and once, famously, on a Vol Kaern at a ball.
**House Dunholt**, Warden of Lesser Varhall. A family of sea-captains who command the house's three warships, and grumble that there are only three.
**House Crest**, Banneret. A respectable old house of the Heartland, honest, poor, and proud. Sir Rikard Crest has never asked Varselis for anything, and would be offended to be offered it.
**Eight more**, Holders and Bannerets of Varhall and the Goldwind courts.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Varselis keeps the smallest force of the Five, and says it needs no more, because its real strength is the law and everyone's need of it.
list: **The Scale Guard:** about 1,200 pikemen and crossbowmen in grey-blue, under Aelius Varselis, who keep the Hall, the Record-House, and the harbor of Varhall. In the Ascendant's War they held the Hall for forty days.
**The bailiffs:** some sixty Selvane-trained officers who serve the Hall's summons across the islands and are not soldiers, though they are often mistaken for them.
**The full muster:** about 5,000 with the bannermen's levies, most of them Tamsor shepherds with long spears.

**At sea:** three warships in the Castellan's Register, the frigate *Even Keel* (the flagship, with her grey patch) and the sloops *Witness* and *Summons*, under Dunholt captains. About twelve merchant hulls carry the house's wool and grain.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war its warships answer the Armada, and the house has said it would answer first.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **The Gift-Book.** Every gift a Varselis receives, from a bribe to a birthday cake, is written in the Gift-Book with the giver's name, and the Gift-Book lies open in the Hall for anyone to read. A great deal of Heartland politics has been decided by people reading it.

**The second name.** Every head of the house takes *Varhall* as a second name on the day of his seating, to remind him whose ground he stands on. That is why the head is Lord Linus *Varhall* Varselis, and why Halsof is not yet.
**The year of clerking.** Every Varselis child serves a year as a clerk of the Hall, copying judgments by hand, before being allowed to give one.
**No duels.** A Varselis does not fight for honor. A Varselis files. Several duelists have been more frightened by that than by a blade.
**The level coins.** The house's dead are buried with one coin in each hand, of the same weight, so that they arrive even.

**The chair of the Moot.** The holder of the Nobles' seat presides at the Moot of Banners, and Selvane bailiffs keep its order. A Varselis has presided over more Moots than any other house, and the other houses have never let it forget it.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: **Lord Linus.** Linus Varhall Varselis is old, austere, and genuinely principled, a thin man in grey who eats little and listens a great deal. The salons find him tiresome and trust him completely, which they say about no one else. He has never been known to take a side before he has heard both, and has sometimes been known to take neither.

**Halsof.** His heir holds the Nobles' seat: young, ambitious, calculating, and serious, and often colder than he is. Halsof wins votes his father would have lost, and the salons are not sure his father is pleased. Whether he keeps Linus's principles or sharpens them into something colder is one of the open questions of Kalvatari politics, and the Stormchanter motion has made it a louder one. The peerage chose him for it at the Moot of 173 EC, and the next Choosing is at the Moot of 178. He married a Tamsor daughter in 172 EC, and their son is two.
**The family.**

**Lady Octavia,** the house's diplomat, who spends her life keeping the noble families out of each other's throats. She has ended more feuds than the Council has heard, mostly over tea, and never with a ruling.

**Julius,** a wizard devoted to knowledge and the house's bridge to the University. He is the only member of the family who laughs at dinner, and the only one with a key to the Record-House's locked room.

**Calista,** a rogue and a gifted negotiator, who is said to do the work her family's principles would rather not look at. She is the one Varselis the Gift-Book has never recorded a gift for, which the salons find suspicious.
**Aelius,** a seasoned warrior who commands the Scale Guard and defends the house's interests when words run out. He has asked for more ships every year for a decade.

**A morning at the Hall.** The queue starts in the dark. At first light a Selvane bailiff draws the lots from a grey urn, and the names go up on a board by the door. A fishwife with a stolen net is heard third; a Highlord's steward is heard eleventh and leaves furious. The arbiter does not look up when a petitioner raises their voice, and does not look away when they cry. At noon the Hall closes for one hour, and the arbiters eat bread and cheese at the same table as the petitioners, because the house says a judge who has not eaten with you should not judge you.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: With House Caelvaron, House Starborn, and the University, Varselis makes the University bloc. It is the chief lawful check on Vol Kaern, and Kastan treats it with perfect courtesy, which the house finds more alarming than threats. It challenges House Vanris over the strait in the Strait Case, and Vanris has never forgiven it. The southern plantation houses have never forgiven it for the Abolition.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Halsof carried the Stormchanter motion because Vanris promised him something about the strait. Ask what the Strait Case is waiting for.” (a Hall of Scales clerk)
“Lord Linus left the table the night the Stormchanter motion passed, and did not come back for dessert.” (a Hall of Scales footman)
“The Gift-Book has a second volume, and Calista keeps it.” (a Goldwind advocate)
“Julius Varselis has been reading the Exodus lists in the locked room. Somebody's great-grandfather never paid for his passage.” (an Inns of the Scale student)
“Aelius Varselis asked his father for a second frigate again, and got the lecture again.” (a Scale Guard sergeant)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A petition to be heard at the Hall of Scales, and an opponent who has already been heard first.
Calista Varselis needs something done that her family cannot be seen to do.
Lady Octavia wants a feud between two bannermen ended before it reaches the Council.
A Selvane summons must be served on someone who has sworn never to be served.
The Strait Case needs a witness who has counted the masts at Stormreach, and Vanris would rather that witness never reached the Council.

title: House Veldane
subtitle: The Marriage-Web
summary: The Marriage-Web: the courtly house of diplomacy and marriage, related by blood or wedding to half the peerage, whose weddings are where the islands' alliances are made and whose seating plans are read like treaties.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Veldane is the courtly house of diplomacy and marriage, one of the ten Highlords. Its sigil is two clasped hands ringed in laurel, on cream and rose-gold, and its motto is *"Kin to All, Kept by None."*

It is related by blood or wedding to half the peerage, and its power runs entirely through kinship, obligation, and the things people tell their in-laws. It keeps no army worth the name and needs none. A house tied to everyone is a house no one can afford to move against.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Veldanes were a minor house of the continent with a great many daughters. They married them into nearly every house that took the Exodus, and arrived in the islands as everyone's cousins.

**Laurelmere (about 35 EC).** The house built Laurelmere, a long, pale house on a lake in the central Heartland, with a hall large enough to seat four hundred. The first wedding held there joined two houses that had been at feud since the Landing, and the seating plan, which put the two mothers side by side, is still kept.

**The web (from about 50 EC).** Over the following century the house made a profession of the thing it had always done. A Veldane arranged marriages for houses that could not speak to each other, hosted the weddings, and kept the record of who was kin to whom, and the peerage came to rely on all three.

**The Garland Register.** The house's register of the peerage's marriages and descents, kept since the Landing, is the most complete in the islands. When two houses dispute an inheritance, both send to Laurelmere first.

**Today (175 EC).** Lady Mirabel rules the house. Grand Dame Ottilie, its memory, draws the seating plans herself, and has kept every one for forty years. Horace Goldspire's late wife was a Veldane. So, at some remove, is nearly everyone else.

sections.title: Laurelmere
list: **Laurelmere** is a long, pale house of cream stone on the shore of a still lake in the central Heartland, surrounded by laurel hedges and lawns that run down to the water.
**The Garland Hall**, the great hall where the weddings are held, which seats four hundred and has been redecorated for every wedding since 35 EC.
**The plan-room**, where Grand Dame Ottilie draws the seating plans on a long table, and where the plans of every wedding are kept in cabinets by year.
**The Register-room**, where the Garland Register is kept, and where the house's clerks answer letters from every house in the islands about who married whom.
**The lake**, where the house's two pleasure-barges carry wedding guests out at dusk, and where, the salons say, more marriages have been agreed than at the altar.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The Reckoners' Hall puts the house's income at about 7,000 Orsals a year, and the house could raise ten times that in a week by asking its relatives.
list: **The Veldane portion.** When the house arranges a marriage, it takes the customary portion of one in fifty of the dowry. A great house's dowry runs to thousands of Orsals.
**Weddings.** A wedding at Laurelmere costs a fortune, and the house provides everything.
**The Register.** A search of the Garland Register costs 5 Orsals; a certified descent, sealed for a court, costs 20.
**Gifts.** Every family the house has married well sends a gift every Landing-Day, and the house has not had to buy its own wine in a century.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Six houses are sworn to Veldane, all of them small, all of them married to someone important.
list: **House Amberlin**, Holder. Stewards of Laurelmere, who run the weddings and have never once run out of anything.
**House Pennard**, Banneret. The Register's clerks, who can trace any noble descent in the islands back to the Landing in an afternoon.
**House Wendle**, Banneret. Musicians and dancing-masters, who teach the peerage's children the steps every wedding expects.
**Three more**, Bannerets of the lake country.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Veldane keeps no army worth the name, and needs none.
list: **The household:** about 150 guards and stewards who keep Laurelmere, and who are better at seating people than at stopping them.
**The full muster:** about 900 with the bannermen's levies, which the house has never called.
**At sea:** no warships in the Castellan's Register. Two pleasure-barges on the lake.
**Its real defense:** every army that could march on Laurelmere is commanded by someone with a Veldane cousin.
**The Charter Call** asks nothing of it. The house sends a wedding gift to every ship that answers.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **The plan is the ceremony.** At a Veldane wedding, the seating plan is the real ceremony. Who sits beside whom is a message to every house at the table, and some of those messages are jokes.
**Never decline.** A Veldane never declines an invitation, and always sends someone.
**The cousins.** Every Veldane child learns the names of three hundred cousins before the age of twelve, and is tested on them at dinner.
**The margins.** Grand Dame Ottilie writes notes in the margins of every seating plan. Nobody has ever read them.
**The laurel.** Every bride married at Laurelmere is given a sprig of laurel from the house's hedges, and the hedges have never been allowed to grow thin.
**The Stands.** Veldane seats the Stands at the Moot of Banners, and the bannerets read their places the way the houses read a wedding plan.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: **Lady Mirabel.** Mirabel Veldane is a plump, cheerful, very shrewd woman who remembers everyone's children's names and everyone's grandmother's grievances. She is the head of the house, and she runs it like a hostess, which is to say she is always smiling and always in control. She has six children, all married, every one of them into a different great house.

**Grand Dame Ottilie.** The family's memory, and the most feared hostess in the Heartland. She is very old, very small, and draws every seating plan herself. She has kept every one for forty years, and nobody has ever read the margins. Half the peerage is afraid of her, and the other half has not been seated badly yet.

**A Veldane wedding.** Four hundred guests, a lake at dusk, laurel at every door. The seating plan is posted in the hall at noon, and by one o'clock every house in the room has read it twice and decided what it means. At the long table a Highlord finds himself beside the woman whose father ruined his. Two houses at feud are seated so close that they must pass each other the salt. Across the hall, the Rose House's diplomat is seated beside the Hundred-Year House's historian, as she was six years ago. Grand Dame Ottilie watches from the head table and writes something in a small book.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: Veldane is kin to the Rose House and to Vol Kaern, which has married in twice under Kastan. It is kin to the Goldspire Exchange through Horace's late wife, and kin, at some remove, to nearly everyone else. Its rivals are the houses that make marriages without it, and there are very few.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Lady Xanthea Alastor and Lady Lysandria Caelvaron dance together at every Veldane wedding, and at no other.” (a Veldane wedding-guest)
“Grand Dame Ottilie has kept the seating plan of every wedding for forty years. Nobody has ever read the margins.” (a Veldane steward)
“The Garland Register has a page that says a great house is not who it says it is.” (a Pennard clerk)
“Lady Mirabel and the Grand Dame have not agreed about a seating plan in ten years, and the Grand Dame has won every time.” (an Amberlin steward)
“The Veldanes know which marriage contract the Rose House has drawn up for its heir, because they were asked to host the wedding.” (a Laurelmere seamstress)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: An invitation to a Veldane wedding, and a seat that is plainly a message.
Two houses want a marriage, and one of the couple wants out.
A seating plan has gone missing, and its margins name names.
A disputed inheritance hangs on a certified descent from the Garland Register, and the page has been cut out.
Grand Dame Ottilie wants someone to sit beside a particular guest at the next wedding and remember everything he says.

title: House Vol Kaern
subtitle: The Crown That Isn't
summary: The Archlords who crown Goldwind's heights: mages and statesmen of old Korvan blood, landlords of the capital's highest ground, and the most patient ambition in the islands.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Vol Kaern is one of the Five, the Archlord houses that stand just below a crown the islands do not have. It holds the castle-heights at the top of Goldwind, the highest ground in the capital, and a small Dominion of islands at the mouth of the gulf. Its sigil is a black tower crowned with a silver flame, on deep violet. Its motto, *"One Hand, One Helm"*, is the only thing the house has ever said aloud about what it wants.

It is a house of mages and statesmen. Its children learn the Registry's copper rings before they learn to dance, and its heads have sat on every great committee of the Council and in none of its seats. It lends, it marries, it builds, and it waits. The salons say it has been waiting for a hundred and twenty years, and that it is very good at it.

The name gives the blood away. *Vol* is the Korvane particle for "of the line of", and Vol Kaern is a house of old Korvan descent that came south with the Landing like everyone else. In a federation founded by people running from the Sun-Throne, that is a hard thing to carry. Goldwind has never quite forgotten it, and Vol Kaern has never once mentioned it.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: **Before the Landing.** Two stories are told. The house's own says the Kaern line held lands on the southern coast of Assios and broke with the Sun-Throne over the burning of a library, and that it chose the Exodus with its eyes open. The other, told in Frontier taverns, says the Kaern were imperial governors who backed the wrong prince and ran south one step ahead of the headsman. Both stories agree that the Kaern ships sailed from Castia, and that Kaern mages warded the convoys they sailed in.

**The Landing (about 15 years before the Charter to 1 EC).** Vol Kaern came in the last waves, to Ironfort, with fewer ships than its name deserved and more mages than anyone else. For the fifteen years of the crossing there were Kaern wards on the hulls of the convoys the Hunters escorted, and the house still keeps the list of every ship it warded. None of them, it says, was lost to anything but the sea.

**The worthless rock (about 30 to 55 EC).** When Archmage Eamos founded Goldwind, the great houses bought the harbor and the gentle slopes. Vol Kaern bought the bare rock above the city, which had no water, no road, and no use. The house cut the Violet Stair up its face and built on the top, and for twenty years the Heartland laughed at a castle with nothing under it. Then the Council's seat moved to Goldwind, the city climbed the hill in rings, and the worthless rock became the top of the capital. The chronicles date the house's long climb from that year.

**The rent (about 55 EC).** The Council's white halls were raised on ground that Vol Kaern still owns. The house leased it to the federation for one Orsal a year, forever. Every Landing-Day the head of the house walks down the Violet Stair alone and lays the coin on the Council table. It is the smallest rent in the islands and the one most talked about.

**The Ascendant's War (105 EC).** When Eldric Morvane's mage-army came within sight of Goldwind, Vol Kaern's mages held the heights and the Stair, and the heir of the day, Lord Halthor Vol Kaern, died on the Stair's lowest landing. The Arcane Registry was founded in the war's ashes, and Vol Kaern was the first great house to enter its children on the rolls. The Registry has never forgotten it, and the other mage-houses have never forgiven it.
list: **The Kraken's Maw (165 EC).** Vol Kaern paid for two of the Coalition's hulls and sent none of its own, and Goldwind remembered both.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Kastan has held the seat for more than twenty years. In that time the house has married into Veldane twice, lent to half the Heartland, and never lost a vote it cared about, mostly because it never calls one it might lose.

sections.title: The castle-heights
paragraphs: The heights crown Goldwind's highest ring: a castle of blue-grey stone and many spires around the Black Tower, which flies the violet banner and is the first thing a ship sees from the gulf on a clear day. Inside the walls are the house's gardens, the Hall of Masks where the balls are held, the archive that no one outside the family has seen, and the barracks of the Violet Guard.

There is one way up for a cart and one for a person. The carriage road winds around the back of the rock, and the house's carriages climb it behind teams of aurocs in violet harness, the only auroc-teams kept in the capital. The Violet Stair climbs its face in nine hundred and twelve steps, with a guard-post at every hundredth. Goldwind has a saying for it: *"Nobody visits the heights by accident."*

On ball nights the castle is lit in violet, and the whole city can tell from the harbor that the house is receiving. Masks are expected, and so is the suspicion that the person behind yours is not who they seem.

sections.title: The Kaern Isles
paragraphs: The house's Dominion is a cluster of five islands at the mouth of the gulf, the first land a ship passes on the way into Goldwind and the last on the way out.
list: **Ardholm**, the largest: wheat, orchards, and the seat of House Ardholm.
**Caskmere**: terraced vineyards whose dark wine the house pours at every ball and sells to no one for less than a favor.
**Whitecut**: a marble island, half quarried away. The white halls of the Council are Whitecut stone.
**Vardrel's Isle**: horse-pastures and hound-kennels behind a sea-wall, where no boat lands without a Vardrel pass.
**The Kaernstone**: a bare rock with a lighthouse and a signal tower that sees every sail that comes into the gulf, and sends word up to the heights before the ship has reached the harbor.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: Vol Kaern is one of the three richest of the Five. The Reckoners' Hall puts its income at about 75,000 Orsals a year and is careful to say it is guessing.

**Ground-rents.** Most of the ground of Goldwind's two highest rings is Vol Kaern's, leased by the generation to great houses, guild halls, and the University's newer colleges. Somewhere, a lease comes due every year.
**The Isles.** Ardholm grain feeds the upper city, Caskmere wine fills its glasses, and Whitecut marble builds its halls.

**Wardwork.** The house's mages set and keep wards on vaults, archives, and great houses all over the Heartland, at registered rates, with the house's mark on every ward. The wards are excellent. What else they may tell the people who made them is a question the salons enjoy.

**The Violet Counter.** Vol Kaern lends from a narrow office in the banking quarter, at no interest at all. Its loans are repaid in favors, named later. The Counter makes no money, and the Reckoners' Hall dislikes it the way fishermen dislike a man who gives fish away.
The house spends freely on three things: its mages, its balls, and its Guard. What else it spends on, no ledger in the banking quarter shows.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Eighteen houses are sworn to Vol Kaern, more than to any other house of the Heartland. Vol Kaern has never sold a title and never granted one by accident, and its bannermen are known for being few in each generation, well married, and loyal.
list: **House Ardholm**, Warden of Ardholm. The oldest of the sworn houses, which sailed with the Kaern from Castia and reminds them of it at every feast. Lord Edvar Ardholm commands the house's levy and has never been asked his opinion of anything else.
**House Oskereth**, Holder. Captains of the Violet Guard for four generations. An Oskereth has never sat at the high table, and has never been off duty in a room where it stands.
**House Tellisand**, Holder. Keepers of the Violet Counter. Lady Ilvessa Tellisand can tell you to the day what you owe Vol Kaern, and will not, unless Kastan asks her to.
**House Vardrel**, Warden of Vardrel's Isle. Breeders of horses and hounds, and the most private family in the Isles.
**House Saelwin**, Banneret. Keepers of the gardens and of the ball nights. A Saelwin decides which lamps are lit violet, and a Saelwin writes the invitations.
**House Kessaly**, Banneret. A river family who run the house's barges and know every wharf-master on the river by his debts.
**Twelve more**, Holders and Bannerets of the gulf shore and the Isles.

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: Vol Kaern does not look like a martial house, and it is not one. It does not need to be. The Armada's First Fleet, the Iron Wall, lies in Goldwind's own harbor, and Kastan has never needed to own what he can borrow.
list: **The Violet Guard:** about 1,400 halberdiers and musketeers in violet coats and black breastplates, who hold the castle and the Stair. It is known for discipline and silence, and for never having had to fight in the streets of the capital, which is the point of it.
**The Stair Watch:** about 800 more, who keep the gates, the carriage road, the barges, and the harbors of the Isles.
**The house mages:** some forty registered casters in house service, more copper rings than any other house can put in one room. In the Ascendant's War they held the Stair.
**The full muster:** about 7,000 with the bannermen's levies, of which Ardholm raises the largest share.

**At sea:** eight warships in the Castellan's Register: the frigates *Patience* (the flagship) and *Courtesy*, four sloops, and two cutters, all moored under the guns of the Iron Wall. About twenty-five merchant hulls fly the violet pennant under flag-captains.

**The Charter Call:** like every house's, Vol Kaern's warships answer the Armada in a declared war. The Kraken's Maw was a coalition, so the Call was never made, and Vol Kaern sent coin instead of ships.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **The first two lessons.** A Vol Kaern child learns two things before learning to read: never to raise your voice, and never to sign first.
**The copper.** The family wears its Registry rings openly, and a Vol Kaern hand often carries more copper than a University bench.

**The walk.** Every Landing-Day the head of the house walks down the Violet Stair alone, carrying a single Orsal for the Council. Goldwind lines the Stair to watch, and no one has ever seen a Vol Kaern stumble on it.
**Masks.** Masks are worn at every ball on the heights. It is bad manners to recognize anyone before the last dance, and worse manners to say afterwards whom you recognized.

**What is never said.** The house never speaks of Assios, of its Korvan blood, or of what its motto means. Ask a Vol Kaern about any of the three and you will hear about the weather, which in Goldwind is always good.

**The Moot ball.** On the last night of the Moot of Banners, the peerage climbs to the heights for the closing ball. Vol Kaern has hosted it since 56 EC. At the Moot itself the house never speaks first, only last.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: **Lord Kastan.** Kastan Vol Kaern is charming, soft-spoken, and patient, and people who meet him leave feeling that he agreed with them. No one in Goldwind has seen him hurry, lose his temper, or lose. He takes his wine watered and his advice from his sister. The salons call him the most dangerous man in Kalvatari politics, usually after he has left the room. He has never married and has no children, and Goldwind stopped asking why a long time ago.

What he wants, he has never said. Goldwind has a guess, and it is the one thing the Landing was meant to make impossible: one hand on the whole archipelago. The motto says *one hand*. Nobody at the balls is rude enough to ask whose.
**The family.**

**Lady Vaela,** his sister and heir presumptive, a diplomat and an enchanter of rare subtlety, married to a Veldane cousin, with two children still in the schoolroom. She opens the doors her brother walks through, and no one has ever seen her lose her temper, or seen what she does with it instead.
**Nyssara,** a sorceress of illusions and the family's mask-maker. Half of what Goldwind thinks it saw at a Vol Kaern ball was hers, and the other half was the wine.
**Lord Arkos,** a wizard and Kastan's closest advisor, the one sibling who argues with him, and only ever in private. When Arkos leaves a council in silence, the house's plans change by morning.

**Draven,** who is said to keep a ledger of other people's secrets and to trade one only for something better. He is always at the balls and never in a mask, because, the salons say, he wants you to know who saw you.

**An evening on the heights.** The invitation comes sealed in violet wax, in a Saelwin hand, with no name inside: whoever carries it is the guest. Carriages take the road; the proud walk the Stair and arrive out of breath. In the Hall of Masks the music is excellent, the Caskmere is poured without stint, and somewhere a Tellisand clerk is writing down who danced with whom. Kastan greets every guest by name, through their mask, and that is the moment most of them decide never to cross him.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: House Varselis is the lawful check on Vol Kaern, and House Alastor opposes it for reasons of its own. Kastan lets them both believe that this is the whole of the game. Veldane is kin twice over and has been useful three times. The house is polite to Blackstrand, whose Reckoners hate the Violet Counter, and friendly to the University, whose newer colleges stand on Vol Kaern ground and pay Vol Kaern rent.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Kastan Vol Kaern is buying Bastion's debts through the Zane house. He will own the Frontier's gate before the Council knows he has begun.” (heard in the Central Heartland)
“Tana Sukuun has sold a Dreadmaw to the Heartland. The buyer is a Vol Kaern agent, and the saurian is named after the Vol Kaern tower.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“A Vol Kaern scrivener left the Rose House gardens at dawn with a sealed contract case. The gardeners swear he was not smiling.” (a Goldwind gardener)
“Nobody lands on Vardrel's Isle, but the feed barges go out every day, and there is more on them than a hound eats.” (a Kessaly bargeman, in drink)
“Every ward on every vault in the banking quarter has a Vol Kaern mark on it. Ask yourself who checks the wards.” (a Reckoners' counter)
“The imperial envoy dined on the heights last Okram, masked like everyone else, and Kastan seated him at his own right hand.” (a Saelwin footman)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: An invitation to a masked ball on the heights, where nothing you saw can be trusted later.
A loan from the Violet Counter, at no interest at all. The price is a favor, named later.
Draven Vol Kaern wants something one of you knows, and he has something to trade for it.
Someone needs a Vardrel pass, and no Vardrel has ever sold one.
Guard the Landing-Day walk: one Orsal, nine hundred and twelve steps, and someone who would like to see a Vol Kaern stumble.

title: House Vossreth
subtitle: The Hollow Crown of the South
summary: The Hollow Crown of the South: the southern Marchlords grown obscenely rich on Krysta and coffee worked by the unfree, who rule their mining holding at Karn Sorroch as a private kingdom, and the respectable face of the southern tyrant-houses.

sections.title: The house
paragraphs: Vossreth is the dark mirror of Greymoor, a southern Marchlord house and the mortal, respectable face of the Southern Merchant-Noble tyrants. Its sigil is a red gem in a black hand, on bruise-purple, and its motto is the house's whole program: *"What Is Mine, I Keep."*

It has grown obscenely rich on southern Krysta and plantation crops worked by the unfree, and it rules its holding as a private kingdom. Slavery ended in Council lands in the Abolition; it never ended at Karn Sorroch, and the Council has never found the will to make it. In the Heartland, the house's name is spoken quietly, because half the Heartland buys what it sells.

sections.title: History
list: **Before the Landing.** The Vossreths were a mining family of the continent, owners of a silver-mine and the people in it. They came south with the Exodus, and then south again, early, looking for something to own.

**Karn Sorroch (about 45 EC).** The house found the Krysta seams on a jungle river-bend in the deep south and built a fortified mining-camp there, Karn Sorroch, which became a town without ever ceasing to be a camp. Its streets are lit by the blue glow of unrefined Krysta, and its gates are kept by the house's thralls.

**The Abolition (about 60 EC).** When the Great Slave Rebellion ended slavery in Council lands, the Vossreth of the day declared that his holding was not Council land in the sense the Council meant, and the Council, which needed his Krysta, did not test the point. It has not tested it since.

**The south's Krysta (from about 70 EC).** Karn Sorroch became the great Krysta source of the south, and the Krysta of the Darlath mines reaches the south by way of Karn Sorroch. The house grows richer on both.

**Today (175 EC).** Lord Caldren Vossreth rules Redhand. The unfree estates border Greymoor's fair ones, and the road between them runs past Fairhand's veranda. The southern boycott names Greymoor, and Vossreth's coffee is sold anyway, under other names.

sections.title: Karn Sorroch and the estates
list: **Karn Sorroch** is a fortified mining-town on a jungle river-bend, its gates kept by the house's thralls and its streets lit by the blue glow of unrefined Krysta. It has walls on the jungle side and the river side, and the walls face inward as much as out.
**Redhand**, the house's seat, a black-and-purple palace on the high ground above the mines, with a red gem the size of a fist set over its door.
**The Deeps**, the house's Krysta-mines, worked by the unfree, which run under the town and the river.
**The river gate**, where the Krysta barges leave for the coast and the supply barges come in.
**The unfree estates**, the house's coffee, cane, and cotton plantations in the coffee country, which border Greymoor's.

sections.title: Wealth
paragraphs: The house declares about 16,000 Orsals a year. The Reckoners' Hall does not believe it, and does not say so.
list: **Krysta.** Raw Krysta from the Karn Sorroch mines, sold through brokers at the broker's price, plus the Registry's tenth, which the house pays on some of it.
**Coffee and cane.** From the unfree estates, sold through the Fennick factors of Southhaven and others.
**Cotton.** From the estates' lower fields.
**Labor.** The house sells the work of its unfree to other southern estates, which the Council does not call by its name.

sections.title: Bannermen
paragraphs: Eight houses are sworn to Vossreth, and a crowd of bought bannerets lives on its credit.
list: **House Veck**, Holder. Overseers of the Deeps for three generations, and the cruelest family in the south by the south's own reckoning.
**House Crell**, Banneret. Keepers of the river gate and the Krysta barges.
**House Ashvane**, Banneret. Planters of the unfree estates nearest Greymoor's, who have been in a boundary dispute with House Lumaren for forty years.
**Five more**, Holders and Bannerets of the south, and many more bannerets minted by the house and its allies, who owe it everything.

sections.title: Strength
list: **The Redhand Guard:** about 1,000 soldiers in purple and black, who keep Redhand, the walls, and the river gate.
**The overseers:** about 800 armed overseers on the mines and the estates, whose work is to keep the unfree from leaving. They are not soldiers, and the house counts them as if they were.
**The full muster:** about 4,500 with the bannermen's levies and the bought bannerets.
**On the rivers:** three warships in the Castellan's Register, the frigate *Keeping* (the flagship) and two river gunboats. About nine merchant hulls carry Krysta and coffee to the coast.
**The Charter Call:** in a declared war, the house's warships owe the Armada service. The Emerald Wrath, which would command them, has made it clear what it thinks of that.

sections.title: Customs of the house
list: **The red gem.** Every Vossreth wears a red gem set in a black ring on the right hand, and never takes it off.
**The count.** The head of the house counts the Deeps' output himself, every Restday, by Krysta-light.
**No guests after dark.** Redhand receives no visitors after sunset, and none have ever been allowed to stay the night.
**The new moon.** Lord Caldren travels upriver alone on the night of every new moon, and the house does not explain it.
**What is kept.** Nothing that comes into Karn Sorroch leaves it without the house's leave, whether it is Krysta, coin, or a person.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
list: **Lord Caldren.** Caldren Vossreth is a pale, elegant, soft-spoken man who dresses in purple and is unfailingly courteous. He visits Goldwind rarely and is received everywhere, because half the Heartland buys what he sells and the other half buys it through someone else. He goes upriver every new moon and comes back paler, and the salons find that more interesting than anything else about him.
**The family.** The Vossreths are few, quiet, and rarely seen outside Karn Sorroch. The salons have noticed that the family's young do not seem to age much, and that its old do not seem to die.

**An audience at Redhand.** You are brought upriver by day, and through the river gate by a Crell. The town smells of wet stone and Krysta. At Redhand, Lord Caldren receives you in a cool room with the shutters closed, and is charming, and offers you wine he does not drink. At sunset you are shown, politely, to the barge.

sections.title: Friends and rivals
paragraphs: Vossreth is the dark mirror of Greymoor, and the two houses are each other's oldest enemies in the south. The tyrant-houses and the Merchant-Nobles are its allies; the slaver-rings are its customers and suppliers; the abolitionists, the Verdant Pact, and the Emerald Wrath are its enemies. The Fennick factors buy from both Vossreth and Greymoor, and are the only factor both houses will receive.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Caldren Vossreth goes up the river every new moon and comes back paler.” (heard in the Southern Wilds)
“The Vossreths don't age. Ask anyone in Karn Sorroch how old the old lord's sister is.” (a river trader)
“Some of the University's best-funded expeditions are paid for by people who have never been to Goldwind, and the money comes from the south.” (a University porter)
“The coffee Fennick sells as Greymoor's has never been to Greymoor.” (a Southhaven warehouse guard)
“There is a second town under Karn Sorroch, older than the house, and the house did not build it.” (a freed miner, upriver)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A freed worker from the Deeps needs to be gotten out of the south before the house's overseers find them.
The Registry wants proof that Vossreth is selling unregistered Krysta, and nobody it sent has come back.
A University expedition, funded by a donor nobody has met, needs a guide to Karn Sorroch.
Lord Caldren offers the party a great deal of money to carry a sealed box upriver on the night of the new moon.
House Ashvane and House Lumaren's boundary dispute has turned bloody.

epigraph.quote: What is mine, I keep. What is yours, we can discuss.
epigraph.by: Lord Caldren Vossreth, to a Council envoy

title: The Noble Houses
subtitle: A noble house
summary: The twenty Major Houses, the Five among them, and the hundreds of lesser houses beneath them.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: There are twenty Major Houses. Five are first among them:
Vol Kaern: the Crown That Isn't, whose castle looms over Goldwind.
Varselis: the Even Hand; holds the Nobles' seat on the Council.
Faust: the Gate of the North, at Bastion.
Vanris: Unyielding as the Storm, at Stormreach.
Alastor: the Rose House.

The Highlords: Caelvaron, the Hundred-Year Throne of the high elves; Emberheart, the Fire Beneath; Silverthorn, the Quiet Knife of Briarcrown; Sunforge, the Golden Hammer; Starborn, the Watchers of Heaven; Holst, Order Before Mercy, keepers of the customs-codes; Blackstrand, the Ledger's Lord; Pelagar, the Deep Trade; Veldane, the Marriage-Web; and Solenne, the Faithful Seat.
The Marchlords: Stormweaver, Kaldmark, Greymoor (the Fair Hand of the South), and Vossreth.
The Warden: Quillane, the Coin-Made Lords, who sell bannerets to anyone with coin.
The bannermen: beneath the Twenty swarm more than two hundred minor houses, each granted land or title by a greater lord.
Knightly orders: the Knights of the Pale Rose (sworn to Alastor), the Sapphire Guard, the Shieldmaidens, and the Knights of Dawn.
Grand Dame Ottilie Veldane arranges half the weddings in the Heartland.

title: Abysm
subtitle: Domination, strength, and slavery
summary: Abysm is the god of absolute power over others. Slavers and despots are Abysm’s, and the faith teaches that owning another person is the natural reward of being stronger.

sections.title: What Abysm keeps
paragraphs: Abysm keeps domination, strength, and slavery. Where Vautun is the chain that is legal, Abysm is the chain itself, with no argument offered. The faithful hold that the weak exist to be used.

sections.title: Who turns to Abysm
paragraphs: The slaver-rings of the south and the masters of bound labor. Abysm’s worship is the reason the Hearthkeepers bar their orphanage doors at night, and the reason the Chainbreakers do not take prisoners among overseers.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The wound chain.** A length of chain wound three times around the wrist, under the sleeve.
**The marked collar.** A slaver who stamps a collar with the fist and chain is naming his god as well as his property.
**The answer.** Sevrin’s faithful break every such collar they find, and leave the pieces on the slaver’s own door.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The rings have a temple, a real one, with a roof. It’s on an island the Armada patrols twice a year and has never landed on.” (a Chainbreaker)
“Some of the names in his ledgers are of people who think they are free.” (a Southhaven dock-clerk)

facts: a chain wound around a fist
among the slaver-rings, and never openly in Council lands

epigraph.quote: He didn’t hate us. That would have meant we were people.
epigraph.by: a freed thrall of the southern mines

title: Aoifel, the Green Laugh
subtitle: Archfey of Spring: sovereign of the First Bloom
summary: Aoifel is the Archfey-Queen of Spring, sovereign of the Court of the First Bloom: renewal, youth, and games. She is the gentlest of the four sovereigns, by fae standards, which is to say her games can still kill.

sections.title: Who she is
paragraphs: Aoifel rules the Faewild’s Spring. Hers is the Court that best preserves the old innocence of the fae, or best pretends to. It plays the old games, with the old delight, and the players do not always get up afterward.

sections.title: Her Court and the islands
paragraphs: The Liriath and the Florians honor the Spring Court beside the Green Fire and their own Yarrowen. Of the four Courts, hers is the one a lost child is most likely to come back from, and the one most likely to have taken the child in the first place.

sections.title: If you meet her Court
list: **Never give a true name.**
**Never say thank you.**
**Count every bargain three times.**
**Do not agree to play.** Not a game, not a riddle, not a race. If you must, ask how it ends before it starts.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Something of her Court’s was lost in the islands long ago, and one of her own is here looking for it, wearing whatever face is useful.” (a Jakupur art dealer)
“She laughed at the Winter Queen once, to her face. Spring has been short ever since.” (a Florian elder)

facts: the Spring Court; honored by the Liriath and the Florians

epigraph.quote: Laugh at the frost, child. It cannot understand a joke, so it will simply go away.
epigraph.by: A Florian child of the Spring Court's edge, at the Laughing Thaw, to a grandfather who had been afraid of the late frost

title: Asmodul
subtitle: Necromancy, pestilence, and decay: plague as deliberate cruelty
summary: Asmodul is the god of rot brought on purpose. Death, decay, and disease are Asmodul’s tools, and the plague-bringers who serve the god spread sickness as a weapon.

sections.title: What Asmodul keeps
paragraphs: Asmodul keeps necromancy, pestilence, and decay. The islands tell two plague-gods apart. **Khagun** is plague as blind nature, the swarm and the famine. Asmodul is plague as intent: sickness aimed at someone.

sections.title: Who turns to Asmodul
paragraphs: Very few, and none openly. A besieger who fouls a well, a poisoner who works slowly, and a necromancer who has left the Pale Man’s rules behind. Maela’s healers are the god’s sworn enemies, and are usually the first to recognize the work.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The wilted wreath.** Left on a door before the sickness comes, and not after.
**The pattern.** A sickness that respects walls, banners, or debts.
**The clean hands.** The god’s servants never fall ill themselves, and that is how they are found.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Plague of the Burning Sea had a wreath on the first door. The Menders took it down and never said so.” (an old Hearthkeeper)
“The Pale Man’s priests give his people up to the Registry without being asked. It’s the one thing the two faiths agree about.” (a Registry examiner)

facts: forbidden; the Menders and the Registry both hunt it
plague-bringers, poisoners of wells, the cruelest necromancers

epigraph.quote: A fever that follows the wells and skips the garrison isn’t a fever. It’s a plan.

title: Athuraz
subtitle: Destruction, chaos, and tyranny: tearing down for gain
summary: Athuraz is the god of the raider: of tearing down what others built and taking what is left. Raiders and warlords pray to Athuraz before a burning.

sections.title: What Athuraz keeps
paragraphs: Athuraz keeps destruction, chaos, and tyranny. Elros wants to rule what is conquered. Athuraz wants it broken. The faithful measure a leader by what burned.

sections.title: Who turns to Athuraz
paragraphs: Raiding bands, wrecker crews, and the worst of the pirate captains. The Twelve Flags of the Freeholds, who want ports to sell in, do not love these raiders, and more than one has been handed to the Armada by other pirates.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The beach fire.** A fire lit on the landing beach before a raid, and fed with something taken in the last one.
**The tower mark.** Burned into a door, it means the house is to be left standing as a message.
**No ransom.** The faithful take no ransom. It is how the Armada tells them from ordinary pirates.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “One warband on the Frontier carries his mark and has started leaving the granaries alone. Somebody is paying them to be choosy.” (a Bastion scout)
“He and Chaos aren’t the same. His people want something. That makes them worse.” (a Knight of Dawn)

facts: among raiders, on beaches, before a landing
raiders, wreckers, warlords of the unruled islands

epigraph.quote: They didn’t want the town. They wanted to have taken it.
epigraph.by: a survivor of a Frontier raid

title: Brakkundr, the War-Forge
subtitle: The War-Forge: war-smithing and the armed host
summary: Brakkundr is the smith-god of war: the forging of weapons and the spirit of the army that carries them. He blesses the blade as it is quenched and the host as it marches.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Brakkundr keeps war-smithing and the armed host. He is not Rhor, the god of lucky craft, and he is not the dwarves’ eternal anvil. He is the god of the weapon made to be used, and of the discipline that makes an army more than a crowd.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: He is sacred to House Emberheart and House Sunforge, to the Armada’s armorers, and to any smith who makes war-gear. Garrison forges on the Frontier keep his anvil by the door.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The quenching.** A blade is quenched in silence, and named only after it has cooled.
**The marching blessing.** A host is blessed as it sets out, never as it returns.
**The broken blade.** A weapon that fails its bearer is brought back to the forge that made it, and the smith answers for it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A blade quenched in his name can’t be surrendered. It can be taken, but the hand has to be opened by someone else.” (a Bastion armorer)
“Emberheart and Sunforge each say he favors their steel. They’ve settled it with duels four times and with a marriage once.” (a Heartland herald)

facts: a sword cooling on a black anvil
the first blade of a forging, given to someone who will need it
armorers, weaponsmiths, sergeants, House Emberheart, House Sunforge

epigraph.quote: Quench the blade in the same water you will drink from tomorrow. Then you will know what it is for.
epigraph.by: An armorer of the Frontier garrison, to a young recruit who had broken his first sword

title: The Breath That Wanders
subtitle: The Aspect of Sky: wind, storm, breath, and freedom
summary: The Breath That Wanders is the Aspect of Sky: wind and storm, breath and freedom, and the five layers of the heavens. Sailors and the free-spirited honor it, and the winged Aethyn revere it above all.

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: Sky is the Aspect nobody holds. It fills a sail or does not, and it is in every chest that is still alive. Its faithful say the first thing a child does is take some of it, and the last thing anyone does is give it back.

sections.title: Its names
paragraphs: Its primal names are Aëthyr-Vol, the Five Skies, and the Open Mouth. At the hearth it is the Wind, the High Blue, and the Wanderer.

sections.title: The Five Skies
paragraphs: The old teaching counts five layers of heaven, one above another, each with its own winds. The Aethyn, who fly the lower ones, say the upper skies are no place for anything with a name. Kayuntu, the Violent Monarch of the Five Skies, is said to rule them all.

sections.title: Rites and customs
list: **The first breath.** A newborn is carried outdoors for its first full breath.
**The whistle.** Sailors whistle for wind in a calm and never in a blow.
**The far view.** The Aethyn’s faith is one of long patience: seeing the storm while it is still a smudge on the horizon.
**Storm and Spirit.** Shamans call on its lesser children: Storm with Water, Spirit with Life.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The fifth sky has a floor. An Aethyn flew high enough to touch it, and came down unable to say what it was made of.” (an Aethyn star-reader)
“Two great things are fighting up there, and have been for years. The weather in the south is what falls off the table.” (a Galven storm-pilot)

facts: Aëthyr-Vol, the Five Skies, the Open Mouth
the Wind, the High Blue, the Wanderer
wind, storm, breath, freedom, the five layers of the heavens
a breath, held and let go
the native peoples, the Aethyn, the Galven, sailors

epigraph.quote: Whistle for it if you like. It was coming anyway, or it wasn’t.

title: Brother Dog
subtitle: Travel, animals, and companionship: loyalty and the joy of the road
summary: Brother Dog is the god who walks beside you. Loyalty, the road, and the animals who share both are his, and travelers and herders pray to him the way they would talk to a friend.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Brother Dog keeps travel, animals, and companionship. In a land where nearly everyone has a small companion with a job, he is prayed to more often than most of the great gods, and less formally. He asks for one thing: do not leave behind what trusted you.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: He has no temples. He has wayside posts with a water bowl at the bottom, which whoever passes is expected to fill. Halflings count him among their three, with Eo and Castellyn. People say the lodge hound is his own breed.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The bowl.** Fill the bowl at a wayside post, even if you have no animal with you.
**The shared crust.** The last of a traveler’s food is split with their companion before the traveler eats.
**The gate.** A dog that waits at a gate for someone who is not coming back is fed by the whole street.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A stray that follows you three days is his. Turn it away and see how your roads go after that.” (a Tarvan drover)
“He’s the only god nobody has ever been afraid of. The priests of the dark ones can’t stand it.” (a halfling innkeeper)

facts: the last of your food, shared with an animal
travelers, herders, halflings, anyone with a companion

epigraph.quote: He does not care where you are going. He only wants to know whether you will be coming back, and he will wait by the gate until you do.
epigraph.by: A herder of the Tarvan moors, to a child who had lost the family's dog on the road

title: Cael the Vintner
subtitle: Revelry, wine, joy, and festival
summary: Cael is the god of the feast and the cup, of laughter that defies a hard world. His festivals are sacred riots of joy, and every islander pours a cup for him whatever other gods they keep.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Cael keeps revelry, wine, joy, and festival. He is no trickster: his chaos is pure celebration. His teaching is that joy is a kind of courage, and that a people who can still throw a feast have not been beaten.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Vintners and brewers keep his altars, which are usually a cask. Sunhold’s terraces and the wine-houses of the Heartland are his country, and no festival in the islands begins without a cup poured on the ground for him.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The poured cup.** The first cup of any new cask goes on the ground.
**The order of toasts.** Drink to the living first, then to the dead, and then to whoever is left.
**The riot.** At his festivals rank is set aside until dawn, and what was said is not held against anyone.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “What’s said at Cael’s feast can’t be used in a court. Three magistrates have tested it, and all three were at the feast.” (a Sunhold vintner)
“The only year Goldwind skipped the Riot of Cups was the year of the plague. Some say the order was the other way round.” (a Goldwind tavern-keeper)

facts: the first cup of a new cask, poured out
vintners, brewers, revelers, anyone at a festival

epigraph.quote: Drink to the living first, then to the dead, and only then to whoever is left. The cup is always fuller than the grief.
epigraph.by: A Heartland vintner at the Riot of Cups, pouring for the widows of the Long Night

title: Castellyn, the Open Hearth
subtitle: The Open Hearth: hospitality and guest-right
summary: Castellyn is the god of the bond between host and guest. He is the silent witness wherever a stranger is fed, and to harm someone you have fed, or someone who has fed you, is among the gravest sins an islander can commit.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Castellyn keeps hospitality and guest-right. In the Icy Expanse, to deny a traveler food is murder, and Castellyn is the witness to that law everywhere it is honored. In the villages of the south, strangers are welcomed, or judged, at the communal heart-fire first, and guest-right there is his.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Every innkeeper is his priest whether they know it or not. Halflings count him among their three, with Eo and Brother Dog. He has no temples, because any house with bread on the sill is one.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **Bread on the sill.** Bread left on a windowsill says a stranger may ask here.
**The first bite.** Once a guest has eaten in a house, host and guest are bound, and neither may harm the other under that roof.
**The parting cup.** A guest who leaves without the parting cup has left a quarrel behind.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Two houses at feud once ate at the same table by mistake. They had to stop the feud until morning, and by morning they’d forgotten why they started.” (a Heartland innkeeper)
“The man who broke guest-right at Kaldmark is still alive. Nobody will sell him bread. That’s the punishment.” (a Frontier carter)

facts: an open door, with bread upon the sill
a place at the table for whoever knocks

epigraph.quote: Feed the stranger at your table, and nobody in the village will ever harm him. It is the only law anyone has ever needed.
epigraph.by: An innkeeper of the Heartland, to a visiting Navy officer who had asked why she never turned away a beggar

title: Chaos
subtitle: The caged first being: destruction and madness
summary: Chaos is the oldest thing the pantheon names: the first being, vast and unbound, caged by its own children before the world was finished. It is counted among the five Greater Gods, and only the mad and the desperate pray to it.

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: The old account says that Chaos came first, that Law and the other deep powers came out of it, and that together they caged it, because Chaos unbound would have dissolved everything they had named. The cage is the heart of the story: the first being still exists, and the world was built with it shut inside.

sections.title: Who prays to it
paragraphs: No temple stands to Chaos and no priest admits to serving it. A prayer to Chaos comes from the far edge of desperation: a ruined gambler, a prisoner before the rope, someone who wants a thing destroyed and no longer cares what goes with it.

sections.title: Signs and customs
list: **The broken ring.** A circle scratched with a gap in it, found on cell walls and the undersides of tables.
**Naming it.** Sailors will not say its name aboard ship. They say *the First* and spit to leeward.
**The answer.** Folk wisdom holds that Chaos always answers, and never with what was asked.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Concord preaches against it without much effort, since almost nobody needs persuading. Its real place in island life is as a curse and a warning: *Chaos take it* is what a captain says when a plan is past saving.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A cage that old leaks. Ask the priests what the Void is and watch them change the subject.” (a University lecturer)
“There’s a crew in the Freeholds that sails under the broken ring. They’ve never lost a ship. They’ve lost everything else.” (a Hollowkey fence)

facts: none; its faithful draw a broken ring
no temple, no priest, and shunned on every coast
the mad, the ruined, and the desperate

epigraph.quote: Nobody prays to it first. It’s the name you get to when you’ve run out of the others.

title: Daelhir
subtitle: Sand, time, death, and destiny
summary: Daelhir is the keeper of time: destiny written in falling sand. Where Fortura rolls, Daelhir counts, and everything that has a length belongs to this god, a watch, a contract, a life.

sections.title: What Daelhir keeps
paragraphs: Daelhir keeps sand, time, death, and destiny. The faith holds that every life has a measure, already poured, and that the only choice is what is done while it runs. It is a calm faith, and not a comfortable one.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Clockwrights keep a pinch of sand from their first glass. Ships’ timekeepers, who turn the watch-glass through the night, say a word to Daelhir at every turn. The gamblers of Fortura and the counters of Daelhir are old rivals: she rolls, and he counts.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The turning.** The glass is turned with the left hand, and never early.
**The last sand.** A pinch of sand is put in the hand of the dying, so that they arrive with something to show.
**The given hour.** An hour spent on someone who can never return it is the usual offering.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There’s a glass in his shrine at Goldwind that has been running since the Landing and hasn’t emptied. The priests won’t let anyone weigh it.” (a Goldwind lens-grinder)
“A priest of Daelhir can tell you how long you have. The honest ones refuse.” (a Fifth Fleet timekeeper)

facts: an hour given to something that cannot repay it
clockwrights, timekeepers, the old, those who know their time is short

epigraph.quote: Turn the glass if you like. It’s the same sand.

title: The Drowning Mother
subtitle: The Aspect of Water: where everything begins and ends
summary: The Drowning Mother is the Aspect of Water, and the most revered Aspect in Kalvatar, where everything begins and ends at the water’s edge. The native peoples pray to her directly, with no god’s mask between: oceans, rain, rivers, blood, birth, and dissolution are all hers.

sections.title: What she is
paragraphs: The old peoples of the islands never bothered with the gods’ masks. They pray to the deep powers themselves, as Aspects, and Water is the first of them. She gives the fish and takes the boat, and her faithful do not see two acts there. Her name says both.

sections.title: Her names
paragraphs: In the deep places she is called by her primal names: Ysra-Deep, the Unending Grey, She-Who-Was-First. At the hearth she is the Tide, the Old Wet, and Grandmother Salt, and a fisher’s child learns the hearth-names before their own.

sections.title: Rites and customs
list: **Salt back.** A pinch of salt is thrown to the sea before a boat is launched.
**The sea-burial.** The whalers of the Icy Expanse give their dead to her, weighted, with their names said three times.
**The first water.** A newborn is washed in seawater before fresh.
**Storm and Ice.** Shamans call on her lesser children for particular work: Storm with the Sky, Marsh with the Earth, Ice with Death.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The coral courts are born from her and honor her in the light, beside their own Coral Sovereign. The Concord’s sea gods are, to her faithful, three of her moods given faces: the one that feeds, the one that judges, and the one that devours.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “She has a heart, a real one, and it is somewhere in the far south. The old songs say it heals whatever is carried to it.” (a chant-keeper of the Wilds)
“The sea-peoples say she is only half of the sea, and they will not name the other half.” (a coral speaker, off duty)

facts: the Tide, the Old Wet, Grandmother Salt
oceans, rain, rivers, blood, birth, dissolution
salt, given back to the sea
the native peoples, the whalers, the coral courts

epigraph.quote: She was here before the first boat, and she will be here after the last one sinks. Bring her salt and she will not take the boat.
epigraph.by: A fisher's widow of Goldwind's Lower Harbor, to a son who wanted to sail in Storm Water

title: Elcifer
subtitle: Illusion, trickery, charm, luck, and lies
summary: Elcifer is the trickster of the pantheon: the god of the illusion, the charming lie, and the luck of whoever is quick enough to use it. Rogues, gamblers, and illusionists count themselves Elcifer’s.

sections.title: What Elcifer keeps
paragraphs: Elcifer keeps illusion, trickery, charm, luck, and lies, and takes a trickster’s delight in the mess. The faithful insist there is a creed under the laughter: the proud should be tripped, and nobody should be so sure of what they see.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Card-sharps, confidence players, and the illusionists of the theaters, who are the only casters in Goldwind applauded for their work. Elcifer’s shrines are never where they were last week.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The harmless trick.** A prank that costs the victim nothing but dignity is an offering.
**The false bottom.** Every shrine has one, and something is always in it.
**The honest hour.** Once a year the faithful tell the truth for an hour. They do not say which hour.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Fortura’s people say Elcifer cheats. Elcifer’s people say thank you.” (a Slatemouth dice-maker)
“The Registry licenses illusionists more strictly than fire-casters. They know which one empties a bank.” (a Registry examiner)

facts: a trick that hurts nobody, played on someone who deserves it

epigraph.quote: I never lied to you. I let you finish the sentence yourself.

title: Eliol
subtitle: Chart and Star: magic, knowledge, and time
summary: Eliol is the god of magic and knowledge: the spell, the book, and the patient hours both of them cost. He is the patron of the University in all but name, and the second month of the year, the month of long nights and study, is his.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Eliol keeps magic, knowledge, the spell, and time. His teaching is that magic is a tool and takes no side: what matters is whether the working is true. Scholars and arcane casters are his, and so is anyone finding their way with a chart and a star.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The University of Goldwind is his house in practice, though it has never said so in its statutes. Gnomes lean toward him beside Rhor and their own Tik. His priests are more often librarians and examiners than preachers.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **The convocations.** In his month the University holds its convocations and investitures.
**The copper examinations.** The Arcane Registry examines its new casters in Eliol.
**The binding.** Apprentices are bound to their masters in his month, in every trade.
**The long nights.** His month falls in Closed Water, when the lanes are shut and there is nothing to do but study.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: A student carries a stub of candle from the last examination they passed. Starfall, on Eliol 30th, falls in his month and belongs to Skaia, and the two priesthoods have shared the night without a quarrel for longer than the Charter.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “He isn’t on the University’s seal because the Registry wouldn’t have it. A god of magic on the door, in Goldwind?” (a University porter)
“Every book ever burned is still in his library. The trick is the door.” (a Goldwind bookbinder)

facts: an open book under a single star
a candle burned to the end over honest work

epigraph.quote: Eliol doesn’t care what you do with it. He cares whether you got it right.

title: Elisse
subtitle: Envy, lust, passion, and fire: the desire that consumes
summary: Elisse is the power of the desire that devours: jealousy, obsession, the wanting that burns down what it wants. The islands set Elisse against Liora, whose love frees. Elisse’s keeps.

sections.title: What Elisse keeps
paragraphs: Elisse keeps envy, lust, passion, and fire. This is not the power of wanting something. It is the power of wanting it because someone else has it, and of being unable to stop.

sections.title: Who turns to Elisse
paragraphs: The cults run among the ambitious elite: salons within salons, where a rival’s ruin is planned as carefully as a wedding. A lover refused, a younger heir, and a courtier passed over have all lit a candle to Elisse and regretted where it led.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The burned letter.** A letter is written to the one envied and burned unsent. The ash is kept.
**The red thread.** Tied where the wearer will see it every day, until the thing is had or the rival is gone.
**The candle.** One lit for Elisse is never blown out. It is left to burn down.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Half the duels of the Goldwind season start at one salon. The hostess has never been challenged herself.” (a Goldwind dancing-master)
“A knot tied on Liora 1st can be burned. That’s Elisse’s rite, and it’s the only way.” (a Goldwind ropemaker)

facts: a flame shaped like a hand
the jealous, the obsessed, rivals in love and in rank

epigraph.quote: Liora’s lovers write to each other. Elisse’s write about each other.

title: Elros
subtitle: Tyranny, war, law, and tempest: power through force and fear
summary: Elros is the god of rule by force. Warlords and dictators pray to Elros, and so does every officer who has decided that fear is quicker than loyalty.

sections.title: What Elros keeps
paragraphs: Elros keeps tyranny, war, law, and tempest. This is law of a particular kind: the rule that exists because someone strong enough said so. The faith is honest about itself. It promises order, and it does not pretend the order is for the good of the ordered.

sections.title: Who turns to Elros
paragraphs: Warlords of the unruled islands, captains who rule by the lash, and now and then a lord who has lost patience with a council. Soldiers serving under such a commander learn the signs quickly.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The closed fist.** Worn on a ring turned inward, shown only to those who already know it.
**The storm-oath.** Elros’s followers swear obedience in bad weather, outdoors, and call the thunder to witness.
**The tenth.** A commander who punishes one man in ten for the failure of all is keeping the rite, whether or not the god is named.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There’s a fist ring on at least one hand in the Admiralty. The Shieldmaidens know whose.” (an Armada purser)
“Lilim’s storms judge. Elros’s just arrive. Sailors say you can tell which is which by whether there was a warning.” (a Tidecaller)

facts: a mailed fist closed on a lightning bolt

epigraph.quote: He kept perfect order. You could hear it from the next island.
epigraph.by: a refugee from a Frontier holdfast

title: Eo
subtitle: The hearth-mother: family, earth, healing, and the first fire of the year
summary: Eo is the Greater God of the good: the family, the tended earth, the healing that a community does for its own. The year opens in her month, and its first day, Landing-Day, begins with a fire lit in her name in every house in the islands.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Eo keeps the things that hold people together: the family, the house, the field that feeds it, and the care a community gives its sick and its old. She is the most loved god in the islands and the least argued about. Farmers and common folk pray to her first, and the halflings count her among their own.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: She has few great temples and a hearth in every home. Her best-known servants are the **Hearthkeepers**, the humble order of Eo and Maela that runs the orphanages, hospices, and shelters of the archipelago. The Slaver Rings prey on those orphanages, which has made a gentle order the patient enemy of organized crime.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **Landing-Day, Eo 1st.** The first fire of the year is lit at dawn. The day is solemn in the morning and rowdy by night.
**Hearth and Home.** All through her month families gather, and old quarrels are supposed to stay outside.
**Ironwake.** On the Frontier, the garrisons light bonfires in her month for their dead.
**The hearth-rite.** A new house is not lived in until a coal from the old one has been carried to its hearth.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Concord keeps an altar to Eo in every one of its temples. The Heartland has its hearth-cults, and in the Icy Expanse, where a dead fire can kill a household, her hearth-rites are kept more strictly than anywhere else.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Hearthkeeper will take in anyone, and I mean anyone. Ask the Watch how many wanted men have wintered in an orphanage kitchen.” (a Goldwind watch-sergeant)
“Let the first fire of the year go out before noon and the house loses someone before the year ends. My grandmother sat up with ours.” (a Greyhaven fishwife)

facts: the first bread of a new oven; a place laid for whoever is missing
families, farmers, healers, halflings, the Hearthkeepers

epigraph.quote: You can tell how a house is doing by its hearth. Eo can tell from further off.

title: Ezra
subtitle: Mast and Sail: protection, courage, and the Shield
summary: Ezra is the goddess who guards the weak and asks the strong to stand in front of them. She is the Armada’s own goddess, and the third month, when the lanes open and the ships go out, carries her name.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Ezra keeps protection and courage. Her sign is the Shield, and her teaching is plain: strength exists to be put between harm and those who cannot stop it. She is also the goddess of setting out, because leaving harbor is the first brave thing most islanders do.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The Armada reveres her above its other gods. The **Shieldmaidens**, a martial sisterhood devoted to her, serve as bodyguards, escorts, and shield-line defenders, and it is said of them that a Shieldmaiden’s charge is safe or the Shieldmaiden is dead. Several great houses and Concord temples retain them.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **First-Sail.** The spring blessing of the ships, when the Armada’s fleets leave their winter stations and the long-haul convoys depart.
**The Bastion tourneys.** Held in her month at Bastion, the seat of House Faust.
**The Trials of Ascension.** The Hunters hold their yearly examination in Ezra.
**The shield-vow.** A guard taking a charge says so aloud, in front of the person guarded.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The companies of the Front Levy sail at First-Sail, under her blessing. Her chapels stand in every Armada station, and a shield hung face-out over a door means the house will shelter whoever asks.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Shieldmaidens keep a book of every charge they ever lost. It’s a short book, and they read it aloud once a year.” (a house steward of the Heartland)
“Half the Armada prays to Ezra and the other half to Lilim, and the admirals know exactly which captains are which.” (an Armada purser)

facts: a vow made aloud, with a witness
the Armada, the Shieldmaidens, guards, escorts, anyone setting out

epigraph.quote: Ezra’s children don’t stay home.
