title: Fortura the Fickle
subtitle: Luck, chance, and gambling: pure chance made divine
summary: Fortura is chance itself. She does not love or hate; she rolls. Gamblers, pirates, and the desperate pray to her knowing she answers at random, and pray anyway.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Fortura keeps luck, chance, and gambling. She cannot be bribed, flattered, or earned. Her faithful find that restful: whatever else is rigged in the islands, the dice in her temple are not.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Her priests run the fairest tables in any port and feed the fortune geckos that live in the rafters. The faithful say the gecko chooses the lucky, and not the other way round. The cat-kin honor her beside their own Mishri the Nine-Lived. Her old rivalry is with Daelhir: she rolls, and he counts.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The lost stake.** A small bet lost on purpose, to remind yourself whose dice they are.
**The single throw.** A question put to her is settled by one throw, and not thrown again.
**The gecko.** Win a bet with a gecko watching, and it may follow you home.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Her temple in Goldwind has never once been robbed. The thieves’ own odds-makers won’t take the bet.” (a Goldwind pit-boss)
“There’s a pair of dice that always comes up the same. She had them made, to see who would be fool enough to trust them.” (a Freehold quartermaster)

facts: the fortune gecko, which her priests feed
a stake you can afford to lose, lost on purpose
gamblers, pirates, the desperate, the cat-kin

epigraph.quote: I do not love you. I do not hate you. I roll, and you live with what comes up. Pray to me if you like. I will not listen any harder for it.
epigraph.by: A pit-boss of the Heartland's gambling halls, to a sailor who had bet his ship on a single throw

title: The Gods of the Pantheon
subtitle: The gods of the Council’s peoples
summary: The pantheon of the imperials and the Council's peoples: five Greater Gods over the Named Gods, by alignment, and the ten gods of the months.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The pantheon of the imperials and the Council's peoples, by alignment. Most islanders are practical polytheists: a fisherman thanks Okram, fears Mhavros, respects Lilim, and pours a cup for Cael at festival, and sees no contradiction. Gods marked with a month are the patrons of the Charter calendar (Part Five).

sections.title: The Greater Gods
paragraphs: Eo: family, earth, healing, community. The year opens in her month.
Law the Sun King: law, sun, fire, purification. The First Namer, as the faithful know him.
Skaia: dreams, fate, sky, stars. She touches the oldest sorrow of all, for every star is a dead god.
Chaos: destruction and madness. The caged first being, prayed to only by the mad and the desperate.
Mhavros: the ocean depths, hatred, suffering, the abyss. Lord of the things in Abyssara.

sections.title: The gods of the months
paragraphs: The Charter calendar names each month for a god and the part of life that god keeps (Volume XV).
| Month | God | Keeps | Season | |

title: The Green Fire
subtitle: The Aspect of Life: growth, hunger, and the jungle’s reach
summary: The Green Fire is the Aspect of Life: plants, beasts, fertility, hunger, and the jungle’s relentless reach. It is strongest in the Southern Wilds, where a cleared field is a forest again in a few years.

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: Life, to its faithful, is a fire that burns green. It spreads, it eats, and it does not stop. The Aspect is as much hunger as growth, and its primal names say so.

sections.title: Its names
paragraphs: Its primal names are Ilavash, the Spreading, and the Thousand Mouths. Its hearth-names are the Growth, the Green, and Mother Leaf.

sections.title: Rites and customs
list: **The grave-planting.** The dead are put in the earth with a seed. The Liriath say you can hear the green answering.
**The uninvited seed.** A seed pressed into the ground somewhere it was not asked for, as an offering.
**The clearing-word.** Before ground is cleared, it is told why, and told when it may have itself back.
**Spirit.** Shamans call on its lesser child, Spirit, with the Sky.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Liriath and the Florians keep it beside their own Yarrowen, the Rooted Crown, and the Spring Court. The Green Hunter is this Aspect made into a wild god, and the faithful of Ilis are its bookkeepers.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There are places in the Wilds where it grows fast enough to watch. The guides won’t camp there.” (a Jakupur guide)
“The Lords’ countries are greener than they should be. The Green Fire likes whatever a Lord is doing.” (a Verdant Pact warden)

facts: Ilavash, the Spreading, the Thousand Mouths
the Growth, the Green, Mother Leaf
plants, beasts, fertility, hunger, the jungle’s relentless reach
a seed planted where nobody asked for one
the native peoples, the Liriath, the Florians, druids

epigraph.quote: Put your dead in the earth and listen. You will hear the green answering.
epigraph.by: A grove-mother of the Liriath, at a planting, to a human settler who wanted to bury his dead in stone

title: The Green Hunter
subtitle: The free hunt and the wild beasts
summary: The Green Hunter is the Aspect of Life made into a wild god: neither cruel nor kind, the joy of the chase under an open sky. Wood elves, free hunters, and Hunters who hunt for the love of it honor him.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: The Green Hunter keeps the free hunt and the wild beasts. He is the Green Fire with a spear in its hand. A clean kill honors him and a wasteful one insults him, and he makes no promise that the hunter will not be the prey next time.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Wood elves honor him beside Ilis and their own Aelthuvar. Some of the cults of the Savage Lords run him together with the great beasts themselves, which his own faithful think is a mistake a hunter makes once.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The clean kill.** One arrow if you can. Nothing wasted.
**The heart.** The heart of the first kill of a season is left for the forest.
**The run.** At the turn of the year his faithful run a day’s chase with no weapon, to remember how it feels from the other side.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “He’s been seen. Antlers, no face, running with the pack. The ones who saw him gave up hunting for coin.” (a Hunter Scout)
“The Lords’ cults say he is their Lord’s shadow. Ask which Lord and you get a different answer in every valley.” (a Verdant Pact warden)

facts: the heart of a clean kill, left for the forest
wood elves, free hunters, trackers, some Hunters

epigraph.quote: The chase is joy. It is not cruelty and it is not kindness. Run, and let the sky watch you run.
epigraph.by: A free hunter of the Southern Wilds, at the end of a day's chase, to an Ilis druid who had asked him to stop

title: Halvenir, the Reaper of Grain
subtitle: Salt and Harvest: plenty, and keeping it
summary: Halvenir is the god of the planted field and the turning year: harvest, seasons, plenty, and toil. He is the most worshipped god nobody tells stories about, because his followers are too busy working. The eighth month, when the harvest of land and sea comes in, is his.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Halvenir keeps the harvest and the labor that earns it. In the islands that means the sea’s harvest as much as the land’s, and his month is called Salt and Harvest for both. His one teaching is that plenty is only half the work, and keeping it is the other half.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: He has almost no priests. His rites are led by whoever owns the field or the boat, and they are short, because there is work waiting. The Concord keeps his altar among its gods of Sun, Sea, and Order.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **The Bounty of the Sea.** The great autumn festival of his month.
**The putting-by.** Salting, smoking, and storing fill the month, and every windowsill overflows.
**The last sheaf.** The last sheaf cut is left standing in the field for him.
**The first barrel.** The first barrel salted in a season is given to a house that has none.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: His month opens Storm Water, and everyone works against the weather. A village that brings its harvest in before the first storm is said to have been early for Halvenir, which is the highest praise a farmer gives.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The year the last sheaf is cut, the next harvest fails. Nobody has tested it in my lifetime, and nobody’s going to.” (a Kaskan farmer)
“He does have one story. The farmers know it, and they aren’t telling.” (a chant-keeper of the Wilds)

facts: the last sheaf; the first barrel salted
farmers, fishers, salters, anyone with a winter to get through

epigraph.quote: Nobody writes stories about the harvest. We are too busy bringing it in.
epigraph.by: A farmer of the Heartland's Storm Water fields, at the last sheaf of the season

title: The Hunger That Warms
subtitle: The Aspect of Fire: the hearth and the volcano
summary: The Hunger That Warms is the Aspect of Fire: warmth and destruction, the forge, passion, and the volcano. It keeps a house alive and it eats a forest, and its faithful are taught from childhood that these are the same appetite.

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: Fire is the Aspect that must be fed. Treated well it warms, cooks, and forges. Forgotten once, it remembers. The southern elders say the imperials’ god of war is only this: *Fire that learned to walk.*

sections.title: Its names
paragraphs: Its primal names are Kel-Vorrath, the First Spark, and the Ever-Eating. At home it is the Hearth, the Red Tongue, and Old Ember.

sections.title: Rites and customs
list: **The Keeping.** Its humblest rite, and the commonest in the islands: the household fire is banked each night so that it never quite dies.
**The heart-fire.** In the villages of the south a communal hearth is tended in rotation and never put out. To let it die is the worst of omens.
**The forge-word.** A smith speaks to the fire before the first heat of the day.
**Ash and Magma.** Shamans call on its lesser children: Ash with Death, Magma with the Earth.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: It is sacred to the Cindren, who say the Hunger is their fire and Sathrun its steady flame, and to House Emberheart at Everfall. The cults of KakanKal, the Emperor of Flames, hold that their Lord sleeps in its lap.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The fire under Everfall has been fed on purpose for a hundred years. Ask the Emberhearts what with.” (an Everfall glassblower)
“A house fire that starts on the one night the hearth went cold isn’t an accident. It’s a reminder.” (a forge-mother of Everfall)

facts: Kel-Vorrath, the First Spark, the Ever-Eating
the Hearth, the Red Tongue, Old Ember
warmth, destruction, the forge, passion, the volcano, transformation
a little fuel every night, without fail
the native peoples, the Cindren, smiths, the Emberhearts

epigraph.quote: Feed me a little each night and I will keep your children warm. Forget me once and I will remember you.
epigraph.by: A forge-mother of Everfall, to a Heartland apprentice who let his hearth go out

title: Idel
subtitle: Coin and Cargo: the honest deal and the clever one
summary: Idel is the god of trade, travel, trickery, and music: the bargain struck fairly, and the one struck cleverly, which the markets hold to be nearly the same thing. The sixth month, high summer and the fattest weeks of the trading year, is Idel’s.

sections.title: What Idel keeps
paragraphs: Idel keeps trade, trickery, travel, and music, and sits at the heart of the trade routes and the festivals that grow along them. A hard bargain honors Idel. A cheat does not, and the difference is the subject of most of the god’s parables.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Merchants touch the doorpost of the market shrine on the way in. The Pocchin, who pray to whichever god seems likeliest to improve the next deal, pray to Idel more often than not.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **The great markets.** Held all through the month, in every port with a quay to hold one.
**The Festival of Winds.** Kites, regattas, and the season’s Long Pull.
**The caravan weeks.** The Pocchin caravans’ fattest weeks of the year.
**The first coin.** The first coin of a day’s trade buys something for someone else.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: A deal closed with music playing is held to be luckier, which is why no great market is ever quiet. Idel’s priests settle small disputes on the spot, for a fee, and are rarely appealed.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Idel has no temple in Goldwind because the banks wouldn’t sell the land. The banks say it was the other way round.” (a Reckoners’ clerk)
“The best cheat in the islands tithes to Idel every year, on time and in full. Make of that what you like.” (a Slatemouth broker)

facts: the first coin of a day’s trade, spent on a stranger

epigraph.quote: Idel blesses the honest deal and the clever one. If yours was neither, don’t bring it to the altar.

title: Iliriel, the Perfect Form
subtitle: The Perfect Form: beauty, art, and aesthetic glory
summary: Iliriel is the goddess of beauty made manifest: the painted masterwork, the flawless line, the terrible loveliness of a thing with nothing wrong in it. She is indifferent to whether that perfection comforts or wounds.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Iliriel keeps beauty, art, and aesthetic glory. Where Khadras is the joy of art, Iliriel is its perfection. Her faith asks one question of any made thing, *is it right*, and does not ask whether anyone was happy making it.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Goldwind’s fashion-courts bow to her, and so do the great architects. A dressmaker of the salons, a sculptor of the Mirror Hall, and a jeweler cutting a stone for the third time are all at prayer.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The breaking.** A work that falls short is destroyed by the hand that made it. Selling it is the sin.
**The mirror.** Her mirrors are kept covered, and uncovered only to judge a finished work.
**The season.** Goldwind’s salons open their season with a single dress shown in silence.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Rose House’s beauty is hers, and it isn’t natural. Look at a portrait of any Alastor from a hundred years ago, and then at the one in front of you.” (a Goldwind portrait-limner)
“There’s a statue in the Mirror Hall kept under a cloth. The last apprentice who looked hasn’t worked since.” (a Goldwind stonecutter)

facts: a flawed work destroyed by its maker
artists, architects, Goldwind’s fashion-courts, the exacting

epigraph.quote: Perfection does not comfort. It cuts clean, and it leaves you with the cut. Learn to love the edge.
epigraph.by: A sculptor of Goldwind's Mirror Hall, to an apprentice who had wept at the first finished statue

title: Ilis
subtitle: Animals, balance, life, and plants
summary: Ilis is the god of the balance of living things: what grows, what feeds on it, and what the land can bear. Druids and keepers of the wild places are the faithful of Ilis.

sections.title: What Ilis keeps
paragraphs: Ilis keeps animals, balance, life, and plants. The faith has no quarrel with the axe, the net, or the plough. Its quarrel is with taking more than comes back. A forest cut faster than it grows is, to the faithful, a debt, and Ilis collects.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The druids are the faithful of Ilis. With wood elves and certain tribes they make up the **Verdant Pact**, the coalition sworn to protect the Wilds from over-exploitation, which sabotages loggers, miners, and slavers. Wood elves honor Ilis beside the Green Hunter, and the Liriath say the name at every planting.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The planting.** A tree is planted for a birth, and its fruit is not picked by the one it was planted for.
**The leaving.** A tenth of any harvest from wild land is left where it grew.
**The saying.** *Ilis anneth, Ilis shorra:* Ilis gives, Ilis takes.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Pact doesn’t only burn logging camps. Ask the Charterhouse how many surveyors it has lost.” (a Jakupur timber-factor)
“The druids say there is a count of every living thing, and that it has started going down.” (a Liriath grove-mother)

facts: a leaf and a tooth, balanced
something planted that you will not live to harvest
druids, the Verdant Pact, wood elves, the Liriath

epigraph.quote: Ilis gives; Ilis takes.
epigraph.by: a Liriath saying, spoken at a planting and at a death

title: Kessa of the Crossroads
subtitle: Travel, choice, and chance meetings
summary: Kessa is the goddess of the decision not yet made and the stranger you meet on the road. Wanderers leave coins at crossroads for her.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Kessa keeps travel, choice, and chance meetings. She has nothing to say about which road is right. Her gift is the moment before the choice, and the person you would not have met if you had chosen otherwise.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Her shrines are the crossroads themselves, marked with a post or a pile of small coins. A wayside shrine-keeper tends each one, takes nothing from the pile, and somehow never goes hungry.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The coin.** Leave a coin before you choose your road. Never take one.
**The stranger’s due.** The first stranger met after a crossroads is given a fair hearing, whatever they look like.
**The third road.** When two choices are both bad, her faithful say there is a third road, and stop to look for it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The coins at a crossroads are never stolen. Now and then someone tries, and is met on the road by someone.” (a Heartland shrine-keeper)
“Idel’s merchants leave her a coin going out and nothing coming back. She’s noticed.” (a Pocchin caravan-master)

facts: a coin left at a crossroads
wanderers, messengers, runaways, anyone who has not decided

epigraph.quote: Every road has three ways out of it. Choose one, and you will meet someone who chose another. Leave a coin for her before you choose.
epigraph.by: A wayside shrine-keeper of the Heartland's southern roads, to a young wanderer who could not decide which road to take

title: Khadras
subtitle: Life, glory, music, and magic: joy through art and bravery
summary: Khadras is the god of joy made on purpose: the song, the brave act, the healing that comes from being lifted up. Bards, healers, and everyone whose work is to put heart into other people look to Khadras.

sections.title: What Khadras keeps
paragraphs: Khadras keeps life, glory, music, and magic. The faithful say there are three ways to be healed: Eo heals through community, Maela through skill and sacrifice, and Khadras through art. A crew that sings pulls harder, and a sickroom with music in it loses fewer.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Khadras has more singers than priests. Shanty-singers, tavern players, and the heralds of the great houses all count themselves in. So do the players of Tidecall, who win for their towns and are loved for it.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The whole song.** A song begun in Khadras’s name is finished, whatever interrupts it.
**The brave cup.** After a rescue, the one rescued buys the first drink and the rescuer sings for it.
**The gold string.** A player’s instrument carries one string wound with gold thread, for luck and for show.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There’s a song that stops bleeding. Three people in the islands know all of it, and they don’t like each other.” (a University music-master)
“Iliriel’s people say art should be perfect. Khadras’s people say it should be loud. The two temples in Goldwind share a wall.” (a Goldwind stagehand)

facts: a song sung in full, to whoever is there

epigraph.quote: Anyone can sing when the ship’s dry. Khadras listens for the ones who sing while they bail.
epigraph.by: a ship’s fiddler of the Fifth Fleet

title: Khagun the Rotmother
subtitle: The Rotmother: plague, famine, and the swarm
summary: Khagun is disease as a force of nature: the locust cloud, the wasting sickness, the famine that follows war. She does not hate. She only eats, and what she eats feeds something else.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Khagun keeps plague, famine, and the swarm. The islands tell her apart from **Asmodul**, whose plague is deliberate cruelty. Khagun has no aim. She is what happens when there are too many mouths, too little rain, or an army that leaves its dead in the fields.

sections.title: Who turns to her
paragraphs: People pray to Khagun to ask her to go somewhere else. In the dry years the Heartland’s famine-priests walk the fields with a covered dish and bury it at the boundary. It is one of the few dark faiths the Concord tolerates, because nobody has thought of anything better to do.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The buried dish.** A portion of the last good harvest, buried at the field’s edge so that she eats there first.
**The fly.** Killing a fly in a sickroom is bad luck. It is put out of the window.
**The fallow year.** A field she has taken is left a full year before anyone plants it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Halvenir’s story, the one the farmers won’t tell, has her in it.” (a chant-keeper of the Wilds)
“The Sporrn don’t fear her at all. They say she is half of something, and they keep the other half.” (a Hunter of the southern Board)

facts: by famine-priests, in bad years, to ask her to pass by
famine-priests, plague-ward keepers, those who live where the swarm comes

epigraph.quote: Nature does not hate you. It only eats. Learn to be eaten gracefully, and you may yet feed something worth feeding.
epigraph.by: A famine-priest of the Heartland's dry years, at a field of blackened grain, to a farmer who had asked why the swarm had come

title: Korthax the Iron Crown
subtitle: The Iron Crown: conquest, empire, and dominion
summary: Korthax is the god of the conqueror’s right: that the strong civilization may rule the weak, or erase it. In the Imperium, Magnus is the public face of the faith, and Korthax is the whispered truth behind it.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Korthax keeps conquest, empire, and dominion. His creed says that history belongs to whoever writes it, and that being conquered is proof of having deserved it. Memnara’s faithful, who remember what conquest erases, count him their particular enemy.

sections.title: Who turns to him
paragraphs: Across the water, the Imperium’s officers and great houses. In the islands, founded by the houses that fled the Imperium, his worship is close to treason, and is found mostly among those who think the islands would be better run by one hand.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The private feast.** A dinner with no servants in the room and one empty chair at the head.
**The iron band.** A plain iron ring worn on the hand that signs orders.
**The word.** His followers speak of *order restored* where anyone else would say *conquest*.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There’s an island house that keeps his feast. The same night every year, the lamps on the top floor burn until dawn.” (a Goldwind lamplighter)
“Memnara’s priests keep a list of everyone who has ever toasted him in the islands. It is shorter than you’d fear and longer than you’d like.” (a Goldwind archivist)

facts: in private; in the Imperium his feast is held behind closed doors, and every great house attends
conquerors, imperial officers, those who believe in the right of the strong

epigraph.quote: The strong civilization rules. The weak civilization is erased. This is not cruelty. It is history, and history is merciful to those who write it.
epigraph.by: A Korvan officer of the imperial frontier, in private, to a native guide who had asked why his village was being burned

title: The Laughing Beast
subtitle: Wild instinct and the untamed self
summary: The Laughing Beast is the god of throwing off civilization and running with the wild. Berserkers, shifters, and everyone who feels the animal under the skin know it.

sections.title: What it keeps
paragraphs: The Laughing Beast keeps wild instinct and the untamed self. It is no god of cruelty. It is the god of the howl, the sprint, and the meal eaten with the hands, and its creed is that a person who has never once been an animal is missing half of what they are.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Berserkers go into battle under it. **Shifters**, who are born with a beast in the blood, pray to it when they let the beast rise, and to something calmer when they need it to go back down.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The night outside.** A night with no roof, no fire, and no name.
**The howl.** Its faithful howl at a feast, once, all together, and then go on eating.
**The return.** Coming back is part of the rite. A worshipper who does not come back has stopped worshipping and started something else.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The cults of the Savage Lords use its rites and call them their own. The Beast doesn’t seem to mind. The Lords might.” (a Hunter Scout)
“A shifter who can’t bring the beast back down has gone to it for good. Their families leave food at the edge of the trees.” (a Southhaven midwife)

facts: a night spent outside every wall
berserkers, shifters, the were-touched, the restless

epigraph.quote: You were born with a tooth and a howl. Civilization made you forget it. Remember it, and run.
epigraph.by: A berserker of the Southern Wilds, after a feast, to a Council soldier who had asked him to sit still

title: Law, the Sun King
subtitle: The First Namer: law, sun, fire, and purification
summary: Law is the Greater God of order, the blazing ruler whose light sustains and burns. The faithful call him the Sun King and the First Namer. Judges, noble courts, and the Armada’s northern fleets swear by him, and so, across the water, does the Imperium.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Law keeps order, the sun, and the fire that cleans. His oldest title is the First Namer: in the oldest telling, to name a thing was to make it, and he named the world into shape. That is why a true name still carries weight in the islands, and why an oath sworn by name is the heaviest kind.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: He is the first god on the Concord’s altars, and the **Sunward**, the Concord’s high priest of the solar and order gods, speaks for him. The **Knights of Dawn**, a militant order of the sun, keep their vigil in his name; most islanders know them simply as sun-knights and monster-slayers.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The dawn oath.** A judge takes office at sunrise, facing east, and a verdict given in full daylight is held to be harder to overturn.
**Purification.** His priests cleanse with fire and light: a lamp carried through a house, a brand passed over a blade.
**The courts.** A sun is carved over the bench of every Council court.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Law is a god of the north and of the old houses more than of the fishing quays. The Imperium worships him too, as the Iron Sun whose light the Emperor carries on earth, and the islands’ priests are careful to say that the sun rises on everyone.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Knights of Dawn aren’t waiting for monsters. They’re waiting for a night, and they think it’s coming back.” (a Knight’s former squire)
“The Imperium’s Sun and ours are the same god. Ask a Sunward whose side he’s on and watch how long the answer takes.” (a Frontier chaplain)

facts: judges, noble courts, the Armada of the north, the Knights of Dawn

epigraph.quote: The sun does not hate what it burns. That is what makes it a judge.

title: Lilim
subtitle: The sea’s lawful wrath: tempest, sea, protection, and glory
summary: Lilim is the sea as law. Her storms are judgments, and sailors beg her mercy before dark waters. Where Okram feeds and Mhavros devours, Lilim decides.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Lilim keeps tempest, sea, protection, and glory. A crew that sails well, keeps its oaths, and respects the water has her protection. A crew that does not finds out what the other half of her domain means.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The Concord keeps her altar among its sea gods, under the Tidecaller. Captains make their vows to her, and the Armada honors her beside Ezra.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **First-Sail.** At the spring blessing of the ships, the youngest sailor of each crew throws a coin to Lilim.
**The dark-water prayer.** Said aloud by the whole watch before a crossing out of sight of land.
**The reckoning.** A ship that comes through a storm with all hands owes her a day ashore doing someone else’s work.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “She keeps a ledger. A captain who breaks a sea-pact gets one storm for each name on the wrong side of it.” (a Tidecaller)
“Stormcaller Vael’s people say Lilim is a magistrate with a wet coat. They say it ashore.” (a Hollowkey smuggler)

facts: a coin thrown by the youngest of the crew
captains, pilots, the Armada, anyone crossing deep water

epigraph.quote: You don’t ask Lilim for a fair wind. You ask her what you owe.
epigraph.by: a first mate of the Fifth Fleet

title: Liora of the Open Heart
subtitle: Heart and Hand: love freely given
summary: Liora is the goddess of love: romantic, familial, and found. Hers is the love that sets people free, and she is the patron of lovers, the wedded, and the lonely. The harbors say both moons are her lovers, and the fourth month is hers.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Liora keeps love, desire, union, and passion, and every kind of bond that is chosen. Her faithful set her against **Elisse**, the goddess of the desire that consumes: Liora’s love frees the one who is loved, and that is how they tell the two apart.

sections.title: Her lovers
paragraphs: The harbors say both moons love Liora. Valtaire comes full in her month to court her; Ciel wanders off and comes back. When both call on her at once, the King Tide rises with the quarrel.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **Friend-knots.** On Liora 1st, friends tie a knot together and each keeps half the cord.
**The Merrin Games.** All through her month the Heartland harbors hold twelve trials on the water, and each winner earns a merrin, a red kerchief.
**The Untying.** Under the full moon of Liora 18th, a girl who wants an evening on the water with a winner unties his merrin.
**Weddings.** The luckiest weddings of the year are held in Liora.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Her temples raise promise doves, which carry a pledge between two people and no one else. In Goldwind half the city’s romances travel by messenger squirrel, above all in her month.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A knot tied on Liora 1st can’t be untied by anyone but the two who tied it. People have tried, with knives.” (a Goldwind ropemaker)
“The priests of Liora marry anyone to anyone. The great houses hate that more than they hate piracy.” (a Sunhold notary)

facts: a knot tied by two people
lovers, the wedded, friends, the lonely

epigraph.quote: Love freely given is the only kind that does not turn into a debt. I have seen the other kind, and I will not pray to it.
epigraph.by: A Liora chaplain of the Heartland ports, at a wedding where the bride's family had demanded a dowry in writing

title: Lunia, the Lady of Light
subtitle: The Lady of Light: purity, exorcism, and the cleansing of corruption
summary: Lunia is the goddess who cleans what has gone wrong. Her clerics perform exorcisms and root out darkness, and where they go, things that were hidden stop being hidden.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Lunia keeps purity, exorcism, glory, and law. She stands close to Law the Sun King, and her faithful put the difference this way: his light judges, and hers cleans. A haunting, a curse, a rot in a house or a family are all hers to drive out.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Her clerics are few and travel constantly, because they are sent for. A Lunian exorcist arrives with a lamp, asks who has been lying, and usually has the worst of the work done before the rite begins.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The night lamp.** A house troubled by something unseen keeps a lamp lit from dusk to dawn in her name.
**The asking.** Before any rite, everyone in the house is asked, one at a time, what they have not said.
**White thread.** A length of white thread tied across a door after a cleansing, and left until it falls.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Lunian won’t take a fee. They take a promise, and they come back to see whether you kept it.” (a Goldwind landlady)
“Half of what they drive out was never a spirit. They know. They do the rite anyway, because the family needs it done.” (a Hearthkeeper)

facts: a lamp kept burning through one whole night

epigraph.quote: Light is not kind. It only shows you what you were hiding, and then it lets you decide what to do about it.
epigraph.by: A Lunian exorcist of Goldwind, to a Heartland widow who had brought her a husband's old ring, which the exorcist found to be cursed

title: Maela the Mender
subtitle: Medicine, healing, mercy, and childbirth: the goddess of the sickroom
summary: Maela is the quiet goddess of the sickroom and the midwife’s hands. She heals through skill and sacrifice, and her clerics run the hospices and plague-wards of the islands and never turn a patient away, friend or foe.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Maela keeps medicine, healing, mercy, and childbirth. Her rule is the hardest in the pantheon to keep: nobody is turned away. A pirate, a deserter, and the man who burned the village are all patients first, and whatever else they are can wait until they can stand.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: With Eo, she is the goddess of the **Hearthkeepers**, who run the orphanages, hospices, and shelters of the archipelago. Her traveling healers carry their herbs and salves on a chartback tortoise, so a healer smells like a spice market from twenty paces. Her hospices keep a moss sloth in every ward.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The reed cross.** Tied over a door, it means there is sickness inside and help is welcome.
**The watch.** Sitting up one night with someone else’s sick is the common offering to her.
**The first breath.** A midwife says Maela’s name before the child’s.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The plague-wards have taken in men the Armada was hunting, and the Armada waited outside. Nobody has ever gone in after one.” (a Southhaven harbor-watchman)
“There’s a hospice in the south where the worst cases go in by one door and come out by another, at night. I don’t ask.” (a Mender of Pearl Groove)

facts: a green cross of bound reeds
clean linen, and a night’s watch at a bedside

epigraph.quote: Let the enemy sleep in the sickroom too. A fever does not check whose side you are on.
epigraph.by: A Frontier surgeon of the Mercy House, at the bedside of a Navy prisoner

title: Magnus
subtitle: Destiny, civilization, courage, and humanity
summary: Magnus is the god of people building things: the city, the road, the law, the will to make a wilderness into a country. He is the public face of the Imperium’s faith, and the old imperial families of the islands still look to him.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Magnus keeps destiny, civilization, courage, and humanity. His faith holds that people were meant to build, and that a thing built well is a kind of virtue. It is a proud creed, and the native peoples of the south, who were here first, find it hard to listen to.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The imperial-descended humans of the north and the Heartland look to Magnus and to the memory of Korvan the Liberator. Some say Magnus is Korvan himself, made a god; the Imperium leaves that question open on purpose. In the islands his shrines stand in founding-squares, over the first stone of a town.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The first stone.** A new town lays its first stone in his name, with the founders’ names cut underneath where nobody will see them.
**The builder’s oath.** A master mason swears to leave the work stronger than the plan.
**Founding-day.** Each town keeps its own, and Goldwind keeps its in the month of Rhor.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Magnus is the face they show. There’s another god behind him in the Imperium, with a crown, and every great house over there dines with him in private.” (a Frontier chaplain)
“Ask a chant-keeper what was under Goldwind’s first stone before it was laid. Then ask a priest of Magnus, and compare.” (a University historian)

facts: a tower under a rising star
a stone laid in something that will outlast you

epigraph.quote: Every wall anyone ever raised is a prayer to Magnus. He isn’t particular about what the wall is for.

title: Memnara, the Unbroken Thread
subtitle: Bell and Remembrance: memory, lineage, and the true record
summary: Memnara is the goddess of memory: history, lineage, and the record kept true. She is the enemy of every forgery and every erased name. The ninth month, when the islands remember the dead and the drowned, is hers.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Memnara keeps what happened. Three kinds of people revere her for three reasons: the native peoples as the keeper of the ancestral chants, the nobles as the guardian of lineage, and the scholars as the patron of true history. All three agree that she remembers, whether or not anyone wants her to.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: In the villages of the south, a **chant-keeper** holds the whole history of a people in memorized chant: births, deaths, deeds, pacts, and grudges. In the north, the old houses keep their genealogies as a sacred duty to her. Her temples have bell-towers, and a gravedigger’s apprentice is given an owlet from the tower along with the spade.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **Storm-Watch.** The harbor lights are blessed before the fog comes in.
**The bells.** In every port a bell is rung for each name the sea took that year.
**The visiting.** Families visit their dead in her month.
**The Telling.** The orcs recite the Telling in Memnara.
**The finches.** During Storm-Watch, echo finches are set in the windows.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Her faithful and the Imperium are natural enemies: the Imperium erases what it conquers, and Memnara remembers it anyway. Her priests are the ones a court sends for when a document is in doubt.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There’s a roll in her temple at Goldwind with every house’s true line on it, bastards and all. Three houses have tried to buy it and one tried to burn it.” (a Goldwind genealogist)
“A bell that rings by itself in Storm-Watch is ringing for someone the sea hasn’t taken yet.” (a Greyhaven bell-ringer)

facts: Memory, history, lineage, the true record
an unbroken thread spun between two hands
the mirror plover; owlets are raised in her bell-towers

epigraph.quote: A name that is written down and read aloud is never quite dead. Write it, and I will keep it. Erase it, and I will ask why.
epigraph.by: A clerk of the Imperial Archives, copying the lineage of a noble house that had asked for a forgery

title: Mhavros
subtitle: The sea as an abyss: the depths, hatred, and suffering
summary: Mhavros is the Greater God of evil, and his country is the sea below the light. The drowned belong to his stories, and so do the things that live in Abyssara. Every sailor in the islands fears him, and almost none will admit to having prayed to him.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Mhavros keeps the ocean depths, and the hatred and suffering the old stories put there. Where Okram is the sea as a living and Lilim the sea as law, Mhavros is the sea as a mouth. His reach is tied to the drowned, to the Sunken Thrones, and to whatever lairs in Abyssara, the Black Below.

sections.title: Who prays to him
paragraphs: On the surface he has no open temples. He has wreckers, drowners, and captains who have run out of better gods. Under the water it is otherwise: the coral peoples honor the Drowning Mother and their own Coral Sovereign in the light, and in the dark of the deeps some courts keep Mhavros.

sections.title: Signs and customs
list: **The turned coin.** A sailor who has cursed the sea throws a coin over the wrong shoulder, face down, to pay him to look away.
**The unlit watch.** No lamp is shown over the side at night in deep water. Something might follow it up.
**The black wave.** His mark, cut into a keel, is a curse on the ship, and a shipwright who finds one burns the timber.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Tidecallers name him in their blessings only to shut him out. The Armada’s chaplains say that every man lost overboard is a man Tholmar has to take back from him.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Tide-Tyrant is his hand. When it rises, it’s because he reached.” (a Tidecaller of Pearl Groove)
“The deep courts have a name for the thing down there, and it isn’t Mhavros. Mhavros is just what we call it so we can sleep.” (a coral speaker, off duty)

facts: The ocean depths, hatred, suffering, the abyss
a black wave closing over a hand
nothing given willingly; sailors pay him to look away
the dark cults of the deep, and the desperate of every coast

epigraph.quote: Okram is the sea that feeds you. Lilim is the sea that judges you. Mhavros is the sea that wants you.

title: Morthryn, the Pale Empress of Air and Ending
subtitle: Archfey of Winter: sovereign of the Long Silence
summary: Morthryn is the Archfey-Queen of Winter, sovereign of the Court of the Long Silence: cold, cruelty, silence, and merciless survival. Hers is the Court most hostile to Kalvatar, the one that exiled the Frost Elves, and the only one that covets Krysta.

sections.title: Who she is
paragraphs: Morthryn rules the Faewild’s Winter, the Frost That Does Not Forgive. Her Court learned one lesson from the old war, that pity is death, and built a code around it. Winter is cruel, and it keeps its word exactly.

sections.title: Her Court and the islands
paragraphs: Winter exiled the forebears of the Frost Elves into the world, and their descendants no longer remember they were ever fae. Krysta does nothing across the Veil, so the Courts ignore it, all but hers: Winter understands what Krysta is worth on this side.

sections.title: If you meet her Court
list: **Never give a true name.**
**Never say thank you.**
**Count every bargain three times.**
**Do not ask for mercy.** In Winter it is an insult, and it is remembered.
**Carry iron.** Iron still limits where and how the fae may cross.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Something of hers was stolen at the last King Tide. A crown, they say. The Long Silence is patient, and it is looking.” (a Frosthold trader)
“There’s a hand behind half the trouble in the Icy Expanse, and it’s a cold one.” (a Knight of the Northern Lights)

facts: the Winter Court; once, the forebears of the Frost Elves

epigraph.quote: Spring forgets. Summer forgives, after a fight. Autumn sends a bill. Winter waits.

title: The Nameless God
subtitle: Hope, purification, and meditation: hope in the darkest hour
summary: The Nameless God is the god of hope when there is no reason for it. His name is lost to time and his mask has no face. People come to him last, and many say he was the only one who answered.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: The Nameless God keeps hope, purification, and meditation. Nobody knows what he was called. His images wear a smooth mask, and his faithful hold that this is the point: he can be hoped in by anyone, because he belongs to no one’s story.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: His servants are hermits and solitary keepers of small, bare shrines, most of them in hard places: an ice-cave on the Frontier, a rock off a lee shore, a cell at the end of a prison corridor. They do not preach. They sit with people.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The silent hour.** His one rite is an hour of silence, kept with someone else in the room.
**The blank stone.** A smooth stone with nothing carved on it, left where someone was lost with no body to bury.
**The washing.** Hands and face are washed before the silence, in whatever water there is.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Somebody knows the name. The ones who know don’t say it, and they won’t say why.” (a Frontier hermit)
“Memnara’s priests have gone looking for it more than once. Whatever they found, they didn’t write it down, and they write everything down.” (a Goldwind archivist)

facts: hermits, the grieving, prisoners, the besieged

epigraph.quote: I do not know my name. The priests who knew it are dead, and the ones who remember it do not say it aloud. But I am still here, and I am still hoping for you.
epigraph.by: A hermit of the Frontier's ice-caves, to a dying soldier who asked whether the god had a name at all

title: Naxithe the Dream-Eater
subtitle: The Dream-Eater: nightmares, madness, and fear
summary: Naxithe is the goddess who lives in the place where dreams turn rotten. Where Skaia keeps dreams and fate, Naxithe is the dream that hunts you. Those who make a weapon of terror serve her, and so do the mad.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Naxithe keeps nightmares, madness, and fear. Her faithful say that fear is the truest thing a person feels, and that she only shows people what was already there. Skaia’s faithful say she rots what Skaia keeps.

sections.title: Who fears her
paragraphs: Everyone who dreams, and the **kalashtar** above all, who dream every hour they sleep and fear her beyond any other power. Her priests hate the dreamcurl hedgehog, the little companion that sleeps on a child’s pillow and takes the bad dreams.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The shared nightmare.** The same dream, in the same street, on the same night.
**The open eye.** Her mark, drawn where a sleeper will see it on waking.
**The sleepless.** Her servants do not sleep, and can be known by it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A dream that comes back three nights isn’t yours. Something is dreaming it for you. Stay awake, and it has to find another.” (a dream-reader of Greyhaven)
“Her people can’t work under the wandering moon. When Ciel is up, sleep with the shutters open.” (a kalashtar net-mender)

facts: forbidden; Skaia’s dream-readers watch for it
those who weaponize terror, and the mad who serve her

epigraph.quote: You did not dream that. Something dreamed it for you, and it is hungry. Stay awake, child, and it will have to find another.
epigraph.by: A dream-reader of Greyhaven, at a bedside in the night, to a child who would not stop screaming in her sleep

title: Nethis, the Sealed Word
subtitle: The Sealed Word: pacts, bargains, and the price
summary: Nethis is the lord of the bargain with teeth: the warlock’s deal, the binding contract, the price that must be paid. Nethis does not care whether a pact is fair, only that it is kept. To sign in his name is to bind yourself beyond escape.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Nethis keeps pacts, bargains, the binding contract, and the price. He is set against Veriden, who keeps the oath honestly given: Veriden asks whether the word was true, and Nethis asks only whether it was signed.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The **Marked**, feared for their blood through no deed of their own, built the hardest-won culture in the islands under Nethis, whose law is that a debt is paid. A Marked door is never closed to a Marked stranger. **House Alastor**, the Rose House, names him its patron, and its motto is *All Power Has a Price*.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The margin.** A contract in his name is read aloud in full, margin and all, before it is sealed.
**The seal.** Once sealed it cannot be amended, only fulfilled or breached.
**The witnessed marriage.** Great houses sometimes marry by a Nethis-witnessed contract, which binds the heart’s conduct as well as the dowry.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Rose House knows another name for him, and only two of them are allowed to say it.” (a Heartland steward)
“When a Nethis contract is breached, nobody comes to collect. It simply gets collected.” (a notary of the Marked quarter)
“The Concord has never put him on its altars, and has never said why.” (a Concord deacon)

facts: Pacts, bargains, the binding contract, the price
a debt paid in full, on the day
the Marked, warlocks, House Alastor, contract-makers

epigraph.quote: Every bargain has a price, and the price is always written in the margin. Read the margin, or do not sign.
epigraph.by: A notary of the Marked quarters, to a young tiefling who had asked for a bargain that would save her mother

title: Oda
subtitle: Oracle, mystery, shadow, and knowledge
summary: Oda is the goddess of what is known and not said. She reveals only what she deems necessary, and seers and those who walk between look to her.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Oda keeps oracle, mystery, shadow, and knowledge. She is not a goddess of lies. She tells the truth, in pieces, when it is needed and not before. Her faithful say that most people who curse her were given the answer and wanted a different one.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Her oracles are scattered and seldom known by that name: a net-mender who is asked things, an old woman at a crossroads well. They share one rule, which is that an oracle never volunteers.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The one question.** You may ask her oracle once about any one matter. Asking twice cancels both answers.
**The veil.** An oracle covers her face to speak for Oda and uncovers it to speak for herself.
**The kept secret.** The offering is a secret told at her shrine and nowhere else, ever.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Skaia’s readers tell you what you dreamed. Oda’s tell you what you already know and won’t look at.” (a Greyhaven dream-reader)
“The oracles write to each other. Nobody has ever caught the letters, and the Chartwrights have tried.” (a postmaster of the Heartland)

facts: a veiled face with one eye open
a secret, told to no one else
seers, oracles, keepers of secrets, those who walk between

epigraph.quote: She answered. It took me nine years to work out which question.
epigraph.by: a pilgrim at the Veil of Shadows

title: Okram
subtitle: Harbor and Rest: the sea that feeds
summary: Okram is the salt-tongued patron of everyone who works the water: the coast, the fishers, survival, and protection. He is the sea as a living. The tenth month, when the fleets come home and the year is brought into harbor, is his.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Okram keeps the coast and the people who live off it. Where Lilim is the sea’s law and Mhavros its abyss, Okram is the sea that fills a net. He is blunt, patient, and practical, and so are his prayers.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The **Brine Brotherhood**, the fishers’ and whalers’ guild, is devout to him in every coastal town. The **Tidecallers**, the Concord’s sea-priests, serve Okram and the water: they bless fleets, read the moons and the tides, and mediate the sea-pacts with the coral courts.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **The homecoming.** In his month the fleets come home and the Returning Cups are turned up.
**The closing.** The year’s accounts are closed in Okram.
**The Lanterns of Unity.** On the last night of the month, lanterns are lit to guide the year into harbor.
**The first fish.** The first fish of the day is never sold. With a net cormorant aboard, it is the first one the bird brings up.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: A fisherman thanks Okram, fears Mhavros, respects Lilim, and pours a cup for Cael at festival, and sees no contradiction. The peerage holds its Moot of Banners in the first Cycle of his month, when everyone is home.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Brotherhood knows which boats are going to come home light before they leave. They say it’s Okram. I say it’s the Tidecallers.” (a Saltreach fish-buyer)
“A Returning Cup that’s still turned down on the last night gets a lantern of its own. Nobody says why.” (a Pearl Groove tavern-keeper)

facts: the Lanterns of Unity, the last night of Okram
the first fish of the day
fishers, whalers, the Brine Brotherhood, the Tidecallers

epigraph.quote: The first fish is never sold. You’d be amazed how many years a man can go without learning why.

title: Oorah
subtitle: Cold, community, courage, and glory: surviving together
summary: Oorah is the far south’s goddess of collective survival. Her country is the Icy Expanse, where nobody lives through a winter alone, and her whole teaching is that the cold is beaten by the number of people who face it.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Oorah keeps cold, community, courage, and glory. She is a goddess of law more than of kindness: her commandments are the rules by which a village on the ice stays alive, and breaking them kills other people.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Every long-house in the Expanse keeps her. Some of the Frost Elves, who lost their own god, have taken her up. She stands opposite **Volvieg**, the cold that kills, and the folk of the ice pray to the one and ward off the other in the same breath.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The Ghostlight Vigil.** When the aurora is strongest the people watch in silence and leave offerings, unsure whether they are thanking one goddess or warding off another.
**The count.** Every household is counted at dusk in deep winter. A missing name is everyone’s business.
**The neighbor’s fuel.** Fuel left at a door is never asked about and never refused.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The count at Snowvah came up one too many, three winters ago. They fed whoever it was until the thaw.” (a Frosthold trader)
“Oorah and Volvieg are the same cold. Which one you get depends on whether you shared your fire.” (an ice-fisher of the Expanse)

facts: a ring of joined hands around a flame
fuel left at a neighbor’s door
the folk of the ice, whalers, the long-house clans

epigraph.quote: The cold counts heads. Make sure it counts all of yours.

title: Orphanos
subtitle: Gluttony, greed, hunger, and envy: insatiable want
summary: Orphanos is the god of the appetite that cannot be filled. Hoarders consumed by want are Orphanos’s, and the faith is less a worship than a condition.

sections.title: What Orphanos keeps
paragraphs: Orphanos keeps gluttony, greed, hunger, and envy. Venkovolkos’s merchants want to win. The people of Orphanos only want more, and winning does not help. The old stories say the god was the first to be hungry and has never once been full.

sections.title: Who turns to Orphanos
paragraphs: Nobody decides to. A lord who cannot stop adding rooms, a miser with a cellar of spoiled grain in a hungry year, and a collector who steals what he could afford. Halvenir’s farmers, who know the difference between plenty and hoarding, call a locked granary in a famine an altar to Orphanos.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The locked store.** Food kept until it rots, with hungry people on the other side of the door.
**The count.** Counting it again, at night, alone.
**The empty plate.** The few real cultists eat from a plate with a hole in it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There’s a vault under a house in Goldwind that the family itself can’t open any more. They keep adding to it through a slot.” (a Goldwind locksmith)
“Ungoreth’s cult calls him a cousin. Emptiness that eats, and emptiness that is. He doesn’t like the comparison.” (a University lecturer)

facts: an open mouth with nothing behind it
none that anyone admits; the god is served by habit

epigraph.quote: He had enough for nine lifetimes and he died counting.

title: The Pale Man
subtitle: Necromancy, knowledge, death, and law: the cold intellect over the passage
summary: The Pale Man is the god of death understood: the passage from life to death, studied and kept in order. Necromancers and death-scholars are his, and so are the physicians who need to know exactly how a body fails.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: The Pale Man keeps necromancy, knowledge, death, and law. He is not the Quiet Door, which receives the dead, and he is not Tholmar, who carries the drowned. He is the mind that watches the crossing and writes down what it sees.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: His servants are scholars before they are priests: anatomists, embalmers, coroners, and the few necromancers who work inside the law. Surgeons who would never call themselves his still keep his small white hand over the dissecting table.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The true cause.** A death is recorded as it happened, whoever it embarrasses.
**The closed book.** His book is never shown open. What is in it is not for the living.
**The orderly dead.** Raising the dead outside his rules is an offense against him first, and against the Registry second.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Registry tolerates his priests because they report the other kind of necromancer. That’s the arrangement, and nobody wrote it down.” (a Registry examiner)
“There’s a company of surgeons in the south who honor him and nobody else, and they’re very interested in silver.” (a Southhaven apothecary)

facts: a white hand holding a closed book
a true record of how someone died

epigraph.quote: He isn’t cruel. He’s exact. People find that harder.

title: Patrons of the Peoples
subtitle: A god for every people
summary: Every people honors a patron of its own, or shares one, alongside the wider pantheon and the Concord.

title: Pyraxis, the Unbowed Flame
subtitle: Archfey of Summer: sovereign of the Burning Crown
summary: Pyraxis is the Archfey-Queen of Summer, sovereign of the Court of the Burning Crown: passion, glory, fire, and heroic war. She is the most martial of the four sovereigns. She duels for an insult and feasts on defeat.

sections.title: Who she is
paragraphs: The Archfey are the divine-tier rulers of the Faewild, and Pyraxis rules its Summer. Her Court is a place of golden knights and endless tourneys. It honors courage and despises weakness, and it has not forgotten the old war in which Summer fought hardest and bled most.

sections.title: Her Court and the islands
paragraphs: Summer trades with Kalvatar as every Court does: fae goods for worked iron, art, stories, and secrets. A mortal with a great deed to their name may find a herald of the Burning Crown at the door with a challenge, which is the highest compliment her Court knows how to pay.

sections.title: If you meet her Court
list: **Never give a true name.** Not to a knight, a page, or a horse.
**Never say thank you.** Thanks is an admitted debt.
**Count every bargain three times.**
**Do not insult anyone.** In Summer an insult is answered with a blade, and a refusal to answer is worse.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “She has never been beaten in a fair war. Everyone repeats that. Nobody asks about the unfair ones.” (a Caelvaron retainer)
“A dreamer with gold eyes won a Summer tourney in his sleep and woke with the scar.” (a kalashtar of Sunhold)

facts: the golden knights of the Summer Court

epigraph.quote: I have never once been defeated in a fair war. Fight me in the Burning Crown, and I will show you what it means to be remembered.
epigraph.by: A Faewild knight of the Summer Court, to a Heartland captain who had asked for a truce

title: The Quiet Door
subtitle: The Aspect of Death: the passage, memory, and the ancestors
summary: The Quiet Door is the Aspect of Death: death and decay, memory, the ancestors, and the passage. The native peoples do not fear it so much as respect it. Death is a guest who always comes, so one keeps a clean house.

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: The Door opens for everyone, once, and closes behind them. It is not an enemy and it does not bargain. Its faithful hold that the worst thing to do with a death is to cheat it, and the second worst is to be surprised by it.

sections.title: Its names
paragraphs: Its primal names are Morr-Ungal, the Last Cold, and the One Who Waits. At the hearth it is the End, the Long Sleep, and the Grey Guest.

sections.title: Rites and customs
list: **The clean house.** A household keeps its affairs in order, its debts short, and its quarrels mended, because the guest may come tonight.
**The guest’s place.** At a funeral meal one place is laid and left empty.
**The frame.** Nobody stands in a doorway while someone is dying in the house.
**Ash and Ice.** Shamans call on its lesser children: Ash with Fire, Ice with Water.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The Sporrn honor it as the compost of the next life, and are the calmest people in the islands about dying. Tholmar’s priests say their god carries the drowned as far as the Door and no further.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “In the far south some have come back through it. The Door didn’t send them. That’s the trouble.” (a Southhaven gravedigger)
“It took a girl halfway once, in the ice, and something else was holding the other half. She’s still there.” (a Frost Elf of the Unpainted)

facts: Morr-Ungal, the Last Cold, the One Who Waits
the End, the Long Sleep, the Grey Guest
death, decay, memory, ancestors, the passage
a clean house, and a place kept for the guest
the native peoples, the Sporrn, gravediggers, the old

epigraph.quote: The door opens for everyone, and it closes behind them with a sound like a latch. Do not stand in the frame.
epigraph.by: An old Frost Elf of the Unpainted, at a grave cut in the ice, to a child who wanted to follow a parent through

title: Rhor
subtitle: Net and Anvil: craft, and the luck to make a thing last
summary: Rhor is the god of the made thing: skill, artifice, and the fortune that lets good work outlive its maker. Artisans and inventors are his, and the fifth month, the first of the long working summer, carries Rhor’s name.

sections.title: What Rhor keeps
paragraphs: Rhor keeps craft, luck, artifice, and travel: the skill to make a thing, and the fortune to make it last. Rhor is no god of war-smithing, which is Brakkundr’s, and is not the dwarves’ eternal forge. Rhor is the god of the workshop and of a living honestly earned.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Every guild keeps a small shrine to Rhor, usually a shelf by the door with a tool on it that nobody is allowed to use. Gnomes lean toward Rhor beside Eliol and their own Tik, the Tinkering Spark.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **The Artisans’ Faire.** Held in Rhor’s month, in every town with a guildhall.
**The naming of masters.** The guilds name their new masters in Rhor.
**The Founding of Goldwind.** The capital keeps its founding day in Rhor’s month.
**The first piece.** A new master gives away the first thing made under their own mark.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: A maker’s mark is a small prayer to Rhor. A craftsman who signs bad work is said to have lied to Rhor, and no guild will defend it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The tool on the shrine shelf was the founder’s. In our hall it has moved twice, and both times the hall burned within the year.” (a Goldwind guild warden)
“Rhor’s luck is real, and the Lanternwrights have more of it than is decent.” (a rival glassblower)

facts: a hammer and a netting needle, crossed
the first piece a new master makes, given away

epigraph.quote: Skill gets it built. Rhor decides whether your grandchildren use it.

title: Saelthar the Cold Throne
subtitle: The Cold Throne: hierarchy, ambition, and bloodline
summary: Saelthar is the god of the noble who believes rank is divine right and rules through dread, and the whispered patron of the cruelest of the noble houses.

sections.title: What Saelthar keeps
paragraphs: Saelthar keeps hierarchy, ambition, and bloodline. The creed says that birth is a judgment already given, and that those born above are owed fear by those born below. It is a faith with no converts: you are born into its favor or you are not.

sections.title: Who turns to Saelthar
paragraphs: No house admits to it. The faith lives in private chapels, in a second altar behind the family’s public one, and in the way certain lords speak to their tenants. Memnara keeps lineages as a record. Saelthar’s faithful keep them as a weapon.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The cold seat.** One chair at the family table that is never warmed and never sat in by a guest.
**The frost mark.** A snowflake worked small into a signet, where a wax seal will not show it.
**The reminding.** A servant punished in front of the others, for nothing, on a regular day of the year.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Two houses at the Moot of Banners keep the cold seat. They sit on opposite sides of the hall and vote together.” (a Banner Hall usher)
“Winter’s court approves of him. Whether he approves of Winter’s court is a question nobody at the Moot will ask aloud.” (a Caelvaron retainer)

facts: in family chapels, behind the public altar
the proudest of the old blood

epigraph.quote: Rank is the will of the gods. The peasant who forgets it has already forgotten his place in the world, and I will remind him.
epigraph.by: A Heartland noble of an old house, at a feast, to a guest who had asked about the price of bread in the village

title: Sevrin the Chainbreaker
subtitle: Liberty, rebellion, and the broken yoke
summary: Sevrin is the god of those who refuse to kneel. The story says he was born from the first slave who killed a master. The Imperium has outlawed his worship, and in the islands he is the god of everyone who has ever broken a cage.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Sevrin keeps liberty, rebellion, and the broken yoke. His teaching is short: no one is owned. He is honored in the south above all, where the memory of chains is closest.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The **Chainbreakers**, the armed freedom-fighters who strike the slaver-rings and burn their ledgers, fill their ranks with his devout. Freed thralls keep the collar they were freed from, broken, and hang it by the door.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The breaking.** A collar is broken, never unlocked. The one freed keeps the pieces.
**The standing prayer.** Nobody kneels to Sevrin. His prayers are said on your feet.
**The open lock.** A lock left broken open on a gate is his mark, and a warning.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Across the water, worship of Sevrin is a hanging matter, and every collar-smith in the Imperium can tell you what a broken collar means. In the islands the Council does not forbid him, and the houses that keep bound labor wish it would.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “One of the great houses pays for the Chainbreakers’ powder. Everyone has a guess, and the guess is always the same house.” (a Southhaven dock-clerk)
“The first slave had a name. The Imperium burned every book it was in, and Memnara’s people are still looking.” (a chant-keeper)

facts: a lock broken and left open
freed thralls, the Chainbreakers, the rebels of the south

epigraph.quote: You kneel because they told you that kneeling was the law. I told you to stand. Stand, and see what the law does about it.
epigraph.by: A Southern Rebel, at the breaking of a slave-collar in the marsh, to a freed thrall who was afraid to walk away

title: The Six Aspects
subtitle: The old powers, prayed to directly
summary: Older and stranger than the Concord: Water, Fire, Earth, Sky, Life, and Death, prayed to directly by the native peoples.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The natives of Kalvatar never bothered with the gods' masks. They pray to the Primordials directly, as Aspects, by their primal names in the deep places and their mundane names at the hearth.

sections.title: At a glance
paragraphs: The derivative Aspects, lesser children of the six, invoked by shamans for particular work:
Storm: Water and Sky.
Ash: Fire and Death.
Marsh: Water and Earth.
Spirit: Sky and Life.
Ice: Water and Death.
Magma: Fire and Earth.
"You imperials pray to a man with a sword and call him War. We do not pray to War. War is just Fire that learned to walk." A southern elder.

rows: the Tide, the Old Wet, Grandmother Salt
Oceans, rain, rivers, blood, birth, dissolution. The most revered Aspect in Kalvatar
Kel-Vorrath, the First Spark, the Ever-Eating
the Hearth, the Red Tongue, Old Ember
Warmth, destruction, the forge, passion, the volcano. The Keeping is its humblest rite
Durn-Hakka, the Bone Below, the Stone That Dreams
the Ground, the Old Back, Mother Root
Mountains, stone, soil, endurance, the dead beneath, the giants of old
Aëthyr-Vol, the Five Skies, the Open Mouth
the Wind, the High Blue, the Wanderer
Wind, storm, breath, freedom, the five layers of the heavens
Ilavash, the Spreading, the Thousand Mouths
the Growth, the Green, Mother Leaf
Plants, beasts, fertility, hunger, the jungle's reach
Morr-Ungal, the Last Cold, the One Who Waits
the End, the Long Sleep, the Grey Guest
Death, decay, memory, ancestors, the passage

title: Skaia
subtitle: The Dreaming Sky: dreams, fate, and the stars
summary: Skaia is the Greater God who stands between: the keeper of dreams, of fate, and of the night sky. The pantheon teaches that every star is a dead god, so the lights sailors steer by are also a record of what the world has lost, and Skaia is the one who keeps it.

sections.title: What she keeps
paragraphs: Skaia keeps the sky after dark and everything that happens under closed eyes. Dreams are hers, and fate, and the long patience of the stars. She takes no side between the gods of order and the gods of ruin, and her priests say that is because she has seen how both stories end.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Her **dream-readers** in Greyhaven have counseled dreamers for as long as anyone has kept count, and a reader at a harbor fair will take a Bit for a dream. The Aethyn honor her beside the Breath That Wanders and Tramica. The kalashtar, who dream every hour they sleep, add her to whatever faith they were raised in.

sections.title: Rites and holy days
list: **Starfall, Eliol 30th.** The night the islands watch the sky. Lamps are put out, and the names of the year’s dead are said aloud under the stars.
**The told dream.** A dream that frightens you is told to someone before breakfast, so that it belongs to two people and weighs half as much.
**The star-reading.** A child’s stars are read at birth, and read again when they first go to sea.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Navigators give Tholmar the first cup and Skaia the last look at the sky before a crossing. Above every other power her faithful fear **Naxithe the Dream-Eater**, who rots the dreams Skaia keeps.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The stars are a graveyard, and the gods who are left know every grave. That’s why none of them will look up for long.” (a University astronomer)
“The readers in Greyhaven don’t only listen. They write the dreams down, and somebody comes for the books.” (a Greyhaven innkeeper)

facts: a ring of stars around a closed eye
dream-readers, star-readers, the Aethyn, the kalashtar

epigraph.quote: Count the stars if you like. She already has, and she remembers their names.

title: The Sleeping Giant
subtitle: The Aspect of Earth: stone, soil, and the dead beneath
summary: The Sleeping Giant is the Aspect of Earth: mountains, stone, soil, endurance, and the dead beneath. Many believe the earth literally is a sleeping giant, and that the great ruins of the islands are its dreaming.

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: Earth is the Aspect that does not answer, and its faithful count that a virtue. It holds up everything, takes back everyone, and has never once hurried. What the other Aspects do, they do on its back.

sections.title: Its names
paragraphs: Its primal names are Durn-Hakka, the Bone Below, and the Stone That Dreams. Its hearth-names are the Ground, the Old Back, and Mother Root.

sections.title: Rites and customs
list: **The standing-stone.** The Tarvan raise stones on the high moors, and say the Giant lies beneath them.
**The miner’s knock.** Three knocks on the rock before the first cut, to ask leave.
**The barefoot oath.** An oath sworn with bare feet on bare ground is sworn on the Giant’s back.
**Marsh and Magma.** Shamans call on its lesser children: Marsh with Water, Magma with Fire.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The giants of old are held to be its children, and the goliaths, who keep the giants’ god, honor it under the mountains. Miners of every people knock, whatever else they believe.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Tarvan on the Giant’s Table heard the Sleeping Giant turn over in its sleep. She went home and sold every horse she had.” (heard in the Northern Frontier)
“The ruins move. Not much. The Chartwrights re-measure the old ones every ten years and don’t publish the difference.” (a University surveyor)

facts: Durn-Hakka, the Bone Below, the Stone That Dreams
the Ground, the Old Back, Mother Root
mountains, stone, soil, endurance, the dead beneath, the giants of old
the native peoples, the Tarvan, miners, goliaths

epigraph.quote: The ground does not care what we think of it. That is why we can rest on it.
epigraph.by: A Tarvan herdsman on the high moor, at a standing-stone, to a lowland trader who asked for a better price

title: Sruth the Whisper-in-Coin
subtitle: The Whisper-in-Coin: secrets, betrayal, and blackmail
summary: Sruth is the god of the secret with a price and the friend who sells you out. Spymasters who feel no loyalty, informants, and blackmailers are Sruth’s.

sections.title: What Sruth keeps
paragraphs: Sruth keeps secrets, betrayal, and blackmail. Oda keeps what should not yet be said. Sruth keeps what can be sold. The creed has one line: trust is a thing you spend.

sections.title: Who turns to Sruth
paragraphs: Informants in every port, clerks who copy what they should not, and the kind of spymaster who serves a house only until a better offer comes. Honest spies, who exist, despise the faith and watch for it in their own people.

sections.title: Signs
list: **The coin to the lips.** A coin touched to the mouth before a secret is sold.
**The second copy.** The faithful never make one copy of anything.
**The price named first.** The secret is priced before it is described, so that the buyer has already agreed to want it.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Rose House’s spymaster keeps a shrine to him behind a panel. The Rose House would say that’s slander, and price it.” (a Heartland steward)
“The Chartwrights open no letters. They don’t have to. Somebody at each end has already sold the contents.” (a Goldwind advocate)

facts: a coin pressed to the lips
hidden shrines, in houses that employ spies

epigraph.quote: The secret costs a coin. The friend who keeps it costs more. The friend who sells it costs nothing, and that is why they are the most valuable of all.
epigraph.by: A spymaster of the Council's secret houses, to a young clerk who had just been paid to read a sealed letter

title: Stormcaller Vael
subtitle: The wild sea and the free wind
summary: Stormcaller Vael is the sea’s wild freedom: the storm you ride for the thrill, the wind that obeys no chart. Free captains, smugglers, and the Pirate Freeholds sail under Vael.

sections.title: What Vael keeps
paragraphs: Vael keeps the wild sea and the free wind. Where Lilim is the sea’s law and Okram its sustenance, Vael is the sea with no master. The faith has one virtue, nerve, and one sin, which is turning back.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: The free captains and the smugglers, and any sailor who has ever carried too much sail because it felt good. Vael has no priests. A captain who has ridden out a storm that should have killed the ship is listened to as one.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The torn sail.** A strip of canvas torn in a real storm, flown from the stern as a boast and a prayer.
**The late reef.** Sail is shortened a moment later than is wise, as an offering.
**The shout.** In the worst of the weather Vael’s sailors shout back at it. It is the only prayer they have.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Galven say Vael learned storms from their thunderbird. Vael’s captains say it was the other way round.” (a Galven storm-pilot)
“Three Armada captains keep a torn sail in a locker. The admirals know, and promote them anyway.” (an Armada purser)

facts: The wild sea, the free wind
a reef left unshaken a moment too long
free captains, smugglers, storm-riders, the Pirate Freeholds

epigraph.quote: Lilim gives you the sea you deserve. Vael gives you the one you dared.
epigraph.by: a free captain of the Freeholds

title: The Sword
subtitle: War, strength, wrath, and protection: war as a plain fact
summary: The Sword is the god of war as it is: neither a glory nor a sin, a plain fact of life that someone has to be good at. Mercenaries and defenders pray to it alike, often on opposite sides of the same field.

sections.title: What it keeps
paragraphs: The Sword keeps war, strength, wrath, and protection. It has no name and no stories. It takes no side, and it promises nothing but this: the one who is ready has a better day than the one who is not.

sections.title: The faithful
paragraphs: Soldiers of every house and banner honor it, and so do the swords for hire. It is the one god two armies can pray to before the same battle without either feeling cheated.

sections.title: Rites and signs
list: **The clean blade.** A weapon is cleaned before its bearer eats or sleeps.
**Point down.** A sword set point down in the ground means a truce to bury the dead.
**No thanks.** Nobody thanks the Sword for a victory. You thank it by being ready for the next one.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “It had a name once. The soldiers who knew it agreed to stop using it, and nobody remembers which war that was.” (a Bastion veteran)
“Brakkundr’s smiths say the Sword is their god’s unfinished work. The Sword’s soldiers say Brakkundr is their god’s blacksmith.” (a garrison sergeant)

facts: a weapon cleaned before you sleep
soldiers, mercenaries, garrison troops, anyone who stands a wall

epigraph.quote: War is not a sin, and it is not a gift. It is weather. Dress for it and get on with your life.
epigraph.by: A Bastion veteran, to a boy who had asked whether the wars would ever end

title: Tholmar, the Star-Wake
subtitle: The Star-Wake: navigation, safe passage, and the drowned
summary: Tholmar is the god who hangs the guiding stars and walks the deck of every ship that ever sailed. He is the art of crossing the sea alive, and he is the keeper of the drowned: the souls lost at sea pass through his hands, and he carries them to whatever waits.

sections.title: What he keeps
paragraphs: Tholmar keeps navigation, safe passage, and the drowned. Where Lilim is the sea’s law and Okram its sustenance, Tholmar is the navigator’s reckoning, the lighthouse flame, and the safe return. The same god guides the living across and carries the dead, and sailors find that fitting.

sections.title: The faithful
