The Arbiters hold an acknowledged public office. The Registrar, the alleged hunter of unlicensed casters in Goldwind’s fog, remains a figure whose existence the University and the Registry deny.

sections.title: The newly chosen Arbiters of 175 EC
paragraphs: Radan Sunmere, Amarise Vellune and Kettik of the Ninth Step are the three newly chosen Arbiters assigned to Goldwind for one full year, from the Charter Day draw of 175 EC until the next Charter Day.

Radan is an easygoing sorcerer used to odd jobs and extraordinary luck. Amarise owns a fashionable shop selling clothing and enchanted articles and enjoys a degree of local celebrity. Kettik brings the patient scrutiny of a warehouse assessor. Each exercises the office in their own way.

Radan and Amarise knew one another before the draw. She tried to change her posting, even offering two additional years of service to avoid being assigned with him. The assignment was absolute; the three will serve their original one-year term together in Goldwind.

facts: Registered casters, Third Circle or higher
One year, paid; near home when possible
Up to ten years in a lifetime
Personally woven Krysta-thread, attuned to its maker
Headwear and an embroidered eye, revealed or concealed at will
Resonance felt through the attuned regalia
source: Welcome to Kalvatar · Magic and the Arbiters · Kafeii’s setting text · 175 EC

epigraph.quote: You do not choose to become one; the year chooses you.

Each displays an embroidered eye.
illustration.caption: Radan Sunmere, Amarise Vellune and Kettik of the Ninth Step, newly chosen for the 175 EC term.

title: Radan Sunmere
subtitle: A little work, a little luck, and finally a salary
summary: A muscular, easygoing sorcerer who lives on odd jobs and improbable good fortune, newly chosen for a salaried year as one of Goldwind’s three Arbiters.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A handsome, deeply tanned human with a powerful muscular build, dark curls and a broad, easy grin. His enormous pointed hat bends beneath its own extravagance: turquoise, magenta and gold, with an embroidered eye. An open sleeveless vest leaves his arms bare; billowing trousers, sandals and a rich sash complete the outfit. Necklaces, rings, earrings and heavy cuffs catch the light whenever he moves.

sections.title: Before the thread
paragraphs: Radan has little money and makes his living taking whatever work comes along. A paid errand, a short contract or a job that needs a sorcerer keeps him moving until the next opportunity appears. His extravagant appearance is a poor guide to his finances.

His magic is innate, and he has a habit of improvising his way through situations that other people would prepare for. Astonishingly often, it works. The right person happens to be passing, a bad turn opens an unexpected door, or a plan invented halfway through the problem proves sufficient.
Being drawn as an Arbiter finally gives him a salary for a full year. He is pleased by the prospect of regular pay and appears entirely confident that the responsibilities will work themselves out.

sections.title: The newly chosen year
paragraphs: Newly chosen in the Charter Day draw for 175 EC, he serves a full one-year term, ending at the next Charter Day. His assignment is Goldwind.

His hat and woven regalia are attuned to him. He feels powerful magic through their resonance and can reveal or conceal the embroidered eye at will. He enjoys the public side of the office, though he is quite capable of hiding the eye when discretion serves him.

sections.title: Manner and judgment
paragraphs: Radan is sociable, physically confident and exceptionally laid-back. He tends to meet a new problem with the expectation that something useful will turn up. He listens, talks easily and adjusts his approach as events unfold. Long preparation rarely precedes the adjustment.

This ease can be reassuring to frightened witnesses and infuriating to a colleague who has already identified everything that might go wrong. His cheerful confidence survives setbacks, often just long enough for another stroke of luck to make him look justified.

sections.title: Amarise knew him before
paragraphs: Radan and Amarise knew one another before the Charter Day draw. She already knew his habit of winging it, and his apparent ability to get away with it. Sharing an assignment gives her a full year of close exposure to both.

Her complaints rarely disturb his composure. He can listen to a detailed account of his failings with the same relaxed attention he gives an interesting story. Their familiarity makes their exchanges immediately noticeable to anyone nearby.

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: He is an approachable official for a crew whose spellcasting has drawn attention. His method is conversational and improvised, and his lack of money gives regular employment a very practical appeal.
His good fortune should appear through circumstances and opportunities. Whether a power of luck actually favors him remains a rumor, and his relaxed attitude does not itself prove divine protection.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Some power of luck must have a soft spot for Radan Sunmere. Nobody gets that far on ‘it’ll probably be fine’ alone.” (a Goldwind regular)

facts: One full year, Charter Day to the next
Little money; Arbiter service provides a regular salary
Remarkable; a divine blessing is rumored

epigraph.quote: Tell me what you cast. Then tell me who was standing next to it.

source: Kafeii’s approved Arbiter illustration and NPC expansion · 175 EC

title: Amarise Vellune
subtitle: A very large hat and very little patience for the sun
summary: A pale, impeccably groomed owner of a fashionable enchanted-goods shop and a local celebrity, assigned to serve Goldwind alongside the maddeningly relaxed Radan Sunmere.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: An attractive pale human woman with long light hair and immaculate nails done in coral shellgloss. She dresses for the coast in a fine light blouse, a flowing tideskirt and delicate sandals. Her enormous sunhat casts a generous shadow over her face. An embroidered eye rests among its elegant gold-threaded patterns.
Her dislike of direct sun is immediately apparent. She adjusts a brim, seeks an awning or moves a conversation two steps sideways into the shade without interrupting what she is saying.

sections.title: Before the thread
paragraphs: Amarise owns Vellune: Finery & Enchantments, a Goldwind boutique selling fashion and enchanted articles. Her taste, presentation and recognizable style have made her something of a local celebrity. Fine clothes, careful grooming and discerning customers are familiar parts of her working life.

She is a practicing illusionist with a carefully kept spellbook. She expects things to be done properly and has little patience for the assumption that preparation can always wait until after a problem arrives.

sections.title: The spellbook
paragraphs: Amarise carries a substantial spellbook bound in ivory leather, with gilt geometric tooling, gilded page edges and an elegant clasp. Its careful spellwork sits comfortably beside the fashion and enchanted goods of her shop. She keeps it close at hand during her year as an Arbiter.

sections.title: The newly chosen year
paragraphs: Newly chosen in the Charter Day draw for 175 EC, Amarise serves a full one-year term, ending at the next Charter Day. Her assignment is Goldwind.

The Krysta-thread in her regalia is attuned to her. She feels its resonance beneath the broad brim, and can make the embroidered eye appear or disappear at will. With the mark hidden, her hat can pass as a particularly determined response to the climate.

sections.title: Manner and judgment
paragraphs: Amarise is composed, observant and dryly funny. She notices small inconsistencies in an account and dislikes an elaborate explanation that leaves the simple question unanswered. She often lets a person finish speaking before repeating their own words back to them.

Her manner can be cool, but she is attentive to embarrassment and privacy. A cooperative person may find her willing to conduct a difficult conversation quietly. An attempt to influence her through flattery usually earns a patient look and the original question again.

sections.title: An assignment she tried to change
paragraphs: Amarise and Radan knew each other before they were drawn. She detests his laid-back manner, his improvisation and the frequency with which things work out for him anyway. Finding his name beside hers on Goldwind’s assignment gave her every reason to expect a difficult year.

She tried to have the assignment changed. She even offered to serve two additional years as an Arbiter if the Registry would place her away from him. The assignment was absolute. The offer secured no change, and her actual term remains the original single year.
They will serve together in Goldwind alongside Kettik of the Ninth Step. Radan’s composure through her complaints has done very little to improve her opinion of the arrangement.

sections.title: Vellune, while she serves
paragraphs: Tessa Bellfold manages the boutique’s daily business while Oren Sedge keeps its cutting and repair work moving. Amarise returns for important fittings and commissioned spellwork during her one-year Arbiter term. The shop remains a familiar place to encounter her and, occasionally, the colleagues who interrupt her appointments.

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: Her shop and public profile give a crew reasons to know her before they see the embroidered eye. A customer seeking an enchanted article may discover that the woman behind the counter is also one of the city’s newly chosen Arbiters.

With Radan, let the irritation have a history: she knows the expression he wears when he has no plan, and he recognizes the tone that means she has noticed. Their familiarity can invite speculation without settling what either privately feels. Kettik remains their equally appointed colleague.

facts: Fashion and enchanted-goods shop owner; illusionist
One full year, Charter Day to the next
Ivory leather, gold tooling and clasp

epigraph.quote: We can discuss your Writ under that awning. The sun has contributed enough.

source: Kafeii’s approved Arbiter illustration and NPC expansion · 175 EC

title: Kettik of the Ninth Step
subtitle: Three feet tall, with every question written down
summary: An elderly kobold assessor newly chosen as an Arbiter for 175 EC, carrying a black turban, a small notebook and a lifetime’s habit of noticing what others overlook.

sections.title: Appearance
paragraphs: A wiry elderly kobold, about three feet tall, with weathered copper-brown scales, an angular reptilian snout, amber eyes and a short tail. His black turban bears a silver embroidered eye. Charcoal robes, subtle Krysta-thread seams, fitted leather shoes and a well-used satchel give him a restrained silhouette beside his flamboyant fellow Arbiters.
His notebook fits neatly in one hand. He looks up at taller people without seeming to grant them any particular advantage.

sections.title: Before the thread
paragraphs: Kettik belongs to the Ninth Step warren beneath Goldwind’s docks. He worked as a warehouse assessor and arcane examiner of cargo, tracing discrepancies between a manifest and the things that actually came ashore. Useful materials return to the warren, and he dislikes waste as much as an account that conceals it.

His familiarity with cramped storerooms and underdock passages is practical experience. He knows where a person can fit, where a crate could have been moved and how easily a supposedly sealed room can acquire another entrance.

sections.title: The newly chosen year
paragraphs: Newly chosen in the Charter Day draw for 175 EC, he serves a full one-year term, ending at the next Charter Day. His assignment is Goldwind.

The thread in his turban and robes is attuned to him and carries the resonance of powerful magic. He can hide or reveal the embroidered eye at will. With the mark concealed, he can return to the familiar work of asking warehouse questions without announcing his office.

sections.title: Manner and judgment
paragraphs: Kettik is patient, practical and quietly persistent. He favors short questions and records the answers before asking the next. He will hear an ordinary porter’s account as carefully as a captain’s. Being ignored while taller people discuss a problem often gives him time to inspect it.

He decides his own approach to each inquiry. Where Radan may begin with a conversation and Amarise with an inconsistency, Kettik often begins by asking who last handled the object, opened the door or changed the manifest.

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: He is a natural contact for cargo mysteries, concealed passages and magical incidents aboard merchant vessels. He appreciates a clear sketch, an intact object and witnesses who distinguish what they saw from what they assumed.
He finds Radan’s jewelry excessive but well maintained, an important qualification. Amarise’s care for fine materials earns his respect. He expects both to wait while he finishes writing.

facts: The Ninth Step, beneath Goldwind’s docks
Warehouse assessor and arcane cargo examiner
One full year, Charter Day to the next

title: Jewelfin
subtitle: The jewel that fights
summary: Beautiful, fiercely aggressive giant fish kept in private indoor pools by Jakupur’s wealthy households, now becoming fashionable among Heartland nobles.

sections.title: Beauty with a temper
paragraphs: A Jewelfin moves through the water beneath an extravagant spread of flowing fins. Its scales and fin membranes catch the light in rich shifting colors, turning a quiet pool into the center of a room. The beauty is accompanied by extreme aggression: a displaying fish can go from a slow, measured turn to a sudden rush at a rival.
The broad fins and flared gill covers that collectors admire are also part of its threatening display. A specimen spreading its colors across the water may be answering a challenge.

sections.title: The private pools of Jakupur
paragraphs: In Jakupur, wealthy households build indoor pools around a single Jewelfin. The pool may occupy the heart of a reception room, with guests seated around its tiled edge while the fish passes beneath them. Its water, space and upkeep are as much a declaration of wealth as the animal itself.

Collectors who want several maintain several separate pools. A row of rooms, each holding a different fish, can become a private gallery. The separation is necessary: these aggressive animals are not kept together as an ornamental school.

sections.title: Keeping a living jewel
paragraphs: Each fish needs a pool large enough to move freely and someone who understands its behavior. Owners admire color, the shape and condition of the fins, and the spectacle of a full display. Experienced keepers pay attention to the animal beneath the ornament.

A household pool is for the fish. People watch from the dry edge, and keepers treat feeding and maintenance as work around an aggressive beast. An expensive specimen remains a dangerous animal, however calmly it circles before dinner guests.

sections.title: The clandestine fights
paragraphs: Jakupur’s underground Jewelfin fights are lucrative events. Owners, handlers, organizers and bettors gather around contests where valuable fish and substantial wagers change the atmosphere of an otherwise private house. The same beauty that makes an animal desirable for display can make a fighting specimen recognizable.

The trade brings together two kinds of buyer: those who want a magnificent pool ornament and those interested in an aggressive contender. Behind a collector’s respectable introduction, a broker may be negotiating for either market.

sections.title: A fashion traveling north
paragraphs: Nobles and other wealthy people in the Central Heartland have begun importing Jewelfins for their own houses. The fashion carries Jakupur’s private pools into northern reception rooms, accompanied by the expense of bringing a large live fish across the sea and preparing its new home.

Visitors compare colors and fin shapes, hosts plan rooms around their acquisitions, and a second pool announces a collection. Southern keepers and dealers find new customers among people who have seen the beauty before they have learned the temperament.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “His lordship says the second pool is for a different color. The man who delivered the fish asked where the guests would place their wagers.” (a Heartland household servant)

facts: Nobles and wealthy households of the Central Heartland
source: Kafeii’s bestiary additions · Jewelfins and private pools · 175 EC

epigraph.quote: One jewel, one pool. If you want another jewel, build another pool.

illustration.alt: Seen from an upper gallery, a great turquoise-and-crimson Jewelfin swims fully submerged in a vast deep indoor pool in a wealthy Jakupur house, with ample open water around it and an adult owner at the far edge.
illustration.caption: A private pool in Jakupur. One jewel, one pool.

title: Vellune: Finery & Enchantments
subtitle: Good taste, by appointment
summary: Amarise Vellune’s shaded Goldwind boutique sells fine clothes, discreet enchantments and the pleasure of being recognized by its owner. During her Arbiter year, the staff keep the shop running.

sections.title: Finding the door
paragraphs: Vellune occupies a narrow-fronted shop on the rising streets above Goldwind’s harbor promenade, within an easy walk of the Turning. Its cream awning shades a blue-painted door and a window containing a single carefully chosen outfit. The name Vellune is picked out in small brass letters. People who copy its window display are rarely the people who can afford what is in it.

Inside, pale wood, linen curtains and brushed brass keep the room cool. A fitting alcove and ordinary full-length mirror occupy the rear. The proprietor’s closed ivory-and-gold spellbook has its place beside the ledger. Tea is offered while measurements are taken, and a customer can usually hear the street without being heard from it.

sections.title: What Amarise sells
paragraphs: The business rests on good cutting, well-chosen cloth and Amarise’s eye for what suits a person. Customers come for fittings, alterations, hats, accessories and bespoke outfits. Some arrive with an invitation and ask to be made ready for it. Others want one piece that will still be worth wearing after the season changes.

Enchanted articles are expensive, scarce work. A few finished pieces or demonstration samples may be displayed in the glazed counter; much of the real business is commissioned, repaired or sourced for a particular client. A matching sketch is no promise that the enchantment can be finished by tomorrow.

Each enchanted piece is described plainly: what changes, how the wearer controls it and what care it needs. Amarise’s shop keeps receipts and accounts for the Registry’s tenth on legal magical sales. The little household Ways used while sewing and cleaning are part of the workshop’s daily life.

sections.title: From the fitting book
paragraphs: These are examples of the shop’s work and recent commissions. Prices are starting quotations in Council coin; cloth, fit and the particular enchantment determine the final account. Completed magical pieces are not kept in unlimited stock.

rows: An unenchanted silk scarf, finished and dyed to Amarise’s standard.
A finely made broad sunhat, fitted to its wearer; unenchanted.
A bespoke unenchanted coat, with fittings and ordinary alterations.
Its wearer changes the silk among three chosen colors by smoothing its edge. The material and cut stay the same.
Keeps enclosed papers dry through rain or an accidental spill. Its clasp must be shut; it is not made for prolonged immersion.
Repeats one short phrase its owner deliberately records, in that owner’s voice, when fully opened. It retains only one phrase at a time.
table.caption: Examples from Vellune’s fitting book

sections.title: Tessa Bellfold, front of house
paragraphs: Tessa is a middle-aged halfling with chestnut hair, a practical plum waistcoat and a memory for measurements, appointments and unpaid balances. She manages the counter and fitting book. During Amarise’s public service, Tessa is the person most visitors meet first.

She is welcoming to someone who admits they need help and exquisitely polite to someone trying to impress her. She never mistakes an expensive outfit for a paid account. Her favorite answer to an impossible deadline is, “Certainly. Which of the other customers shall I disappoint for you?”

sections.title: Oren Sedge, needle and hem
paragraphs: Oren is a young human cutter and apprentice enchanter, usually found in the rear workroom with a pin cushion at his wrist. He is excellent at small repairs and too inclined to keep improving a piece after the agreed work is finished. He knows household Ways for untangling thread, lifting fresh ink spots and keeping a pinned hem in place.

He wants Amarise to trust him with a complete enchanted commission. Tessa wants him to finish the three ordinary garments already promised for collection. He is the most likely person to ask a visiting crew to fetch a missing parcel before either woman notices it has gone astray.

sections.title: People who keep coming back
paragraphs: Odelia Ferren, a prosperous salon hostess, orders restrained pieces and takes a close interest in what everyone else has ordered. She can turn a fitting into a survey of the next social gathering. Tessa discusses only Odelia’s own clothes, which Odelia treats as a challenge.

Pell Orris, a theatrical singer, brings beautiful sketches, uncertain money and very definite opening nights. His requests make excellent work for the window when they are actually finished. He sometimes pays a deposit with proceeds from the performance that made the commission possible.

The shop also receives people with one carefully saved sum and an occasion that matters to them. Amarise’s attention to such a fitting can be just as exacting as her treatment of a wealthy regular. That mix of customers helps explain why her name travels beyond the people who buy her enchanted work.

sections.title: A shopkeeper’s year of public service
paragraphs: Amarise remains the owner while she serves as one of Goldwind’s three newly chosen Arbiters for 175 EC. Tessa handles daily business and appointments; Oren keeps the workroom moving. Amarise returns for important fittings and commissioned spellwork when her duties allow.

Customers seeking an official decision are directed to arrange an official meeting. Amarise will not treat a purchase as payment for a favorable ruling. The shop’s standing makes that distinction visible, and its enemies would be delighted to see her blur it.

Radan knew the proprietor before either was drawn. His arrival can interrupt an orderly morning with the confidence of someone who thinks there is still plenty of time. Amarise recognizes that expression immediately. Kettik occasionally calls on either colleague; Tessa puts his tea within reach and waits for him to finish his question.

sections.title: Commissions that need outside help
paragraphs: The copied label. A visitor brings in a scarf bought elsewhere under Vellune’s name. Its advertised color change leaves dye on the wearer. Amarise wants to know where it was sold and who is using her label. The seller’s receipt, the cloth and the customer’s account give a crew three places to begin.

The missing fitting trunk. A completed outfit has been collected by a porter carrying the right claim slip, but the customer says nobody was sent. Tessa has a precise collection time; Oren remembers the porter’s coat; the customer wants the garment recovered before an evening appearance. Someone must establish how a valid slip changed hands.

The fan with the wrong last word. An owner returns a Last Word Fan that now repeats an unwelcome personal remark. The fan only preserves a phrase deliberately recorded by its current owner. Amarise asks for a discreet account of who owned it, borrowed it and gave it back. The commission may be a repair, a disagreement over ownership or a story the customer has not finished telling.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “He has a year’s salary now and still comes in just to ask what she thinks of his hat.” (a customer, on Radan Sunmere)
“If your fitting runs long, say nothing. You may leave with a better coat and the name of everyone attending the gala.” (heard near the Turning)

facts: Oren Sedge, cutter and apprentice enchanter
Fine clothes, alterations and commissioned enchanted articles
Staff run daily business through Amarise’s Arbiter term
source: Kafeii’s approved Goldwind development · Amarise’s shop expansion · 175 EC

epigraph.quote: Good. Now tell me where you intend to wear it.

illustration.alt: Inside Vellune, Amarise’s shaded Goldwind boutique, Tessa Bellfold writes in the fitting book beside a cream-and-gold coat, a blue gown and a glazed case of fine accessories.
illustration.caption: A fitting book, a few carefully chosen pieces, and a little shade above the harbor.

title: Gnoll Warbands
subtitle: Raiding bands of the Bonewilds
summary: Born in the drylands of the Bonewilds, gnoll warbands raid across Kalvatar. Their banners have recently been sighted in the Northern Frontier.

sections.title: From the drylands
paragraphs: The drylands around the Bonewilds hold the greatest concentration of gnoll warbands. Bands also raid the dry reaches of the Southern Wilds and cross the archipelago on captured ships or aboard smugglers’ boats. Reports from the Northern Frontier describe wired jawbones on banners seen on opposite sides of a strait.

New warbands still form, usually from splintered raiding parties or followers who walk away from a chief. Few last. The Sworn actively hunt these smaller bands, and many survivors have little choice but to join the Ironfang Warband, the Bonewatchers, the Ashmaws, or the Redjaws.
They do not cross the great white flats themselves. That is Shakarr's country, where nothing scavenges, and even the Sworn will not feed there.

sections.title: The Hunger
paragraphs: The Hunger is the first stage of demonic possession. One gnoll beginning to change during a raid can stir the same frenzy in others. The afflicted devour whatever they can, from provisions and livestock to captives. When there is nothing left, they turn on one another. Returning to their former selves is almost unheard of. Some sworn bands deliberately let the frenzy sweep through their ranks.

To the Sworn, gnoll flesh is the most delicious meat of all and the surest, quickest way to trigger The Hunger. They reserve a particular hatred for the Unsworn and attack them whenever they get the chance, eager to feast on their flesh. A feast that begins with fallen enemies can end with the Sworn devouring their own.

sections.title: The Flints
paragraphs: The rare survivors who emerge transformed are called Flints. Larger and stronger, they experience visions tied to the old pact. Among the sworn bands, a Flint often becomes a war leader or priest. Even when the frenzy passes, the possession has left its mark.

sections.title: Kharveth, the Hollow Maw
paragraphs: The daemon Kharveth receives the first bite of the raid from his sworn bands. His mark is a jaw with teeth turned inward. His priests call the visions of the Flints instructions, though two priests can hear the same account and send their bands to war against each other.

sections.title: The Unsworn
paragraphs: Some bands broke away from the worshippers of Kharveth so long ago that their singers count the separation in millennia. They still raid and ransom captives, and some chiefs keep bargains with settlements for years. They watch their own for signs of The Hunger and will drag an afflicted companion away from the others before the frenzy spreads.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Kharveth is older than the gnolls. He was one of the Orka's sixteen masks, and the old pact is theirs.” (a University scholar of the Orka)

illustration.alt: An Ironfang leader with a riveted iron jaw and oversized metal tusks leads a caravan raid beneath ancient titan ribs.
illustration.caption: An Ironfang raid in the Bonewilds.

title: Orc Tribes
subtitle: War banners and old rites
summary: Most orcs of the islands are dockers, drovers and townsfolk. The raiding tribes are kept scattered along the Frontier roads and the approaches to the Heartland, and are growing in strength in the Southern Wilds.

sections.title: Where the banners gather
paragraphs: Along the northern roads and approaches to the Central Heartland, garrisons and regular patrols keep most armed raiding parties scattered. In the Southern Wilds, some tribes have gained fighters, seized crossings and forced isolated settlements to pay tribute. Their strength varies with the season and with which chiefs can keep their followers together.

sections.title: Old rites
paragraphs: Among the tribes now drawing notice, the Embertusks carry coals from a shrine older than their oldest recorded ancestor, while the Reedskulls offer their first spoils to a presence they say lives beneath a drowned mound. The Telling survives among both, though each recites a different account of what the dead are owed.

title: Ironfang Warband
subtitle: The first bite belongs to Kharveth
summary: A sworn band that carries iron teeth and welcomes The Hunger in the midst of a raid.

sections.title: Iron in the mouth
paragraphs: Ironfang warriors wire iron caps over broken teeth. Their chiefs wear the caps of their predecessors on a cord and surrender them only to a successor who has survived The Hunger. Their standards show Kharveth’s teeth facing inward.

sections.title: The open pen
paragraphs: When a warrior begins to change, the priests cut the livestock loose and call the rest of the band to feed. The Ironfangs count every Flint who rises from such a raid as a new voice of Kharveth. They also remember the names of raids from which nobody returned.

title: Bonewatchers
subtitle: The watch at the edge of the white flats
summary: Unsworn raiders who guard their camps against The Hunger and sometimes keep terms with caravans.

sections.title: At the edge of the bones
paragraphs: The Bonewatchers camp along the rim of the Bonewilds, beyond the great white flats. A chief may take salt, livestock or a ransom and guarantee safe passage until the next well. Their sentries remember which caravans paid and which tried to ride around them.
What they watch, they say, is Shakarr's bones.

sections.title: Keep the night watch
paragraphs: Pairs of watchers sit apart from the feasting after a raid. At the first sign of a change, they draw the afflicted away from the fires and bar the trail behind them. Their singers name the ancestors who turned away from Kharveth, though they disagree about how long ago the break came.

facts: Paired bone stakes at the edge of camp

title: Ashmaws
subtitle: The jaws beneath the ash
summary: Kharveth’s wandering devotees mark their muzzles with ash and seek out raids foretold by their Flints.

sections.title: The trail of ash
paragraphs: The Ashmaws carry clay jars of ash from the fires of earlier raids. Before marching they rub it into their muzzles and press a jawprint into the dust behind them. A Flint chooses their destination from visions of places they have never seen.

sections.title: What the priests remember
paragraphs: They have crossed the dry country for a granary that offered little plunder, then passed within sight of a wealthy caravan without following it. Their priests claimed they had seen the granary door in a shared vision. The survivors of the raid remembered the Ashmaws calling for someone inside by name.

illustration.alt: An Ashmaw Flint leads ash-marked gnolls through a dry ravine at dusk.
illustration.caption: An Ashmaw Flint leads ash-marked gnolls through a dry ravine at dusk.

title: Redjaws
subtitle: Red jawbones on the sea roads
summary: The Redjaws are Unsworn raiders who learned to sail. Now an almost entirely maritime warband, they strike ferry landings and coastal stores as far north as the Northern Frontier.

sections.title: Life on the sea roads
paragraphs: The Redjaws learned to navigate between islands and now spend most of their time afloat. Their crews read tides, sound unfamiliar channels, and know which sheltered coves can hide a ship until a patrol passes. They still raid ashore, but they choose targets they can reach from the water and load their plunder aboard before the coast can muster a pursuit.

sections.title: The red jaw
paragraphs: The Redjaws dye their jawbone standards with red earth from the drylands. They raid isolated storehouses and ferry landings, then sell what they cannot carry. Their chief will return a captive once a ransom is paid. Settlements that refuse have found their ferryboats gone the following morning.

sections.title: A bargain in the north
paragraphs: Frontier watchmen tell of a Redjaw party that returned its captives under a truce and came back two nights later asking for shelter. The gnolls said they had left one of their own tied below deck after the first signs of The Hunger. By nightfall the ship was drifting back toward the landing.

facts: Maritime raiding along the sea roads

illustration.alt: Redjaw gnoll sailors navigate reef waters at dawn beneath a red jawbone banner.
illustration.caption: Redjaw gnoll sailors navigate reef waters at dawn beneath a red jawbone banner.

title: Embertusks
subtitle: The coals under the black ridge
summary: An orc tribe of the Southern Wilds that carries sacred coals into battle and raids the roads below its shrine.

sections.title: The buried hearth
paragraphs: The Embertusks say their shrine was burning when the first ancestor found it under a split ridge. They carry its coals in lidded clay pots. A war leader puts one down at the foot of a gate before demanding tribute, and the fighters wait for the answer while the pot smokes.

sections.title: The ridge road
paragraphs: They have drawn smaller bands into their ranks by offering access to the shrine and a share of the cattle driven up from the low roads. Some elders want the tribe to hold the ridge. Younger war leaders are pushing farther down the valleys, where a captured crossing can bring in more than a burned farm.

facts: Glowing coals in lidded clay pots

illustration.alt: An orc chief sets down a pot of sacred embers before a valley outpost.
illustration.caption: An orc chief sets down a pot of sacred embers before a valley outpost.

title: Reedskulls
subtitle: What sleeps under the drowned mound
summary: An orc tribe expanding through the wetlands of the Southern Wilds, where it claims the crossings and takes tribute in iron.

sections.title: The drowned mound
paragraphs: The Reedskulls bind reeds around animal skulls and hang them above channels they claim. At the lowest water they wade to a drowned mound and sink an iron offering. Their elders say something underneath learned the sound of their ancestors’ names and still answers when the water is low.

sections.title: The crossings
paragraphs: The tribe has taken more crossings as its numbers have grown. Reedskull parties cut ferry ropes and carry off boats from villages that refuse their demands. They prefer tribute in nails, tools and blades, and each haul renews the dispute over how much to forge and how much to give to the thing below.

illustration.alt: Reedskull orcs carry an iron offering through mist toward a drowned mound.
illustration.caption: Reedskull orcs carry an iron offering through mist toward a drowned mound.

title: Stormchanters
subtitle: Keepers of the Five Skies sanctuary
summary: Orc keepers of a shrine to the Five Skies in the Central Heartland. Once known for their quiet island life, they are preparing for war after Lord Mortimer Vanris laid claim to their shore.

sections.title: The shrine and the prison
paragraphs: Islanders say the five weathered stones on the ridge once marked a shrine to the Five Skies. In a later age the island became a prison for orcs. Below the shrine, families still call the old foundations the prison yard, though nobody agrees on when the last guards left.
The first prisoners were southern orcs, and they brought their sky-rite north with them. The stones still face south.

sections.title: Listening to the skies
paragraphs: Over generations, the orcs on the island developed a deep bond with the Five Skies. Their shamans keep vigil among the stones and teach children to sit through a change of wind before asking the skies for an answer. The tribe favors a quiet life of fishing, tending the shrine, and settling disputes around the hearth. Families have long formed ties with neighboring ports, and today the island is home to the largest concentration of half-orcs in Kalvatar.

sections.title: An old hatred
paragraphs: The other orc tribes despise the Stormchanters. Their war leaders say the people of the shrine have betrayed what it means to be an orc. The Stormchanters still recite their family lines through the Telling, including the names of the first prisoners. At the end of each recitation, they name the children born since the last one.

sections.title: Seventy years ago
paragraphs: In the Ascendant's War, the island's orcs went to war beside the other tribes in the first Grand Coalition. It is the only war they have fought, and they fought it for Kalvatar. Some islanders say the prison's last guards sailed for Goldwind that year and never came back.

sections.title: The port Vanris wanted
paragraphs: The Stormchanters lived peacefully until Lord Mortimer Vanris decided to build a port on their island. Islanders from nearby shores opposed the plan and asked him to build on a neighboring island or negotiate with the orcs. Mortimer took the appeal as an insult. At his urging the Nobles' seat brought the matter before the Council, which declared the Stormchanters “enemies of Kalvatar.”

sections.title: The storms they called
paragraphs: Ships of the First Fleet made the first attacks, joined by Hunters on Vanris's coin. In response, the Stormchanters called up storms powerful enough to sink ships. Their shamans and druids drew on primal powers to destroy any non-orc presence near the island. For the first time since the Ascendant's War, the Stormchanters are preparing for war.
Even the neighboring islanders who spoke in their defense now find themselves turned away. Vanris’s campaign taught the Stormchanters to distrust everyone outside the tribe.

The island sits astride important trade routes in the Central Heartland. The storms now force merchant captains to wait for clear weather or take longer passages. Mortimer wanted a port on a busy route. He now has to contend with a tribe of orcs who know those waters and have chosen to fight for them.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “For the first time in seventy years, the Stormchanters are talking about joining the other orc tribes in a war.” (heard in the Central Heartland)
“A thunderbird egg rests at the very top of the Stormchanters’ shrine. They say the tribe is keeping watch over it.” (heard in the Central Heartland)

facts: An island in the Central Heartland
Shamanic devotion to the Five Skies
Largest concentration of half-orcs in Kalvatar

illustration.alt: Stormchanter defenders gather at their island shrine as a storm bears down on ships offshore.
illustration.caption: The Stormchanters call a storm over the shipping lanes.

title: The Moot of Banners
subtitle: The peerage's year, decided in one hall
summary: Every Okram the whole peerage of Kalvatar meets at Goldwind, heads and heirs at the Long Horseshoe and bannerets in the Stands, to decide the year's pacts, routes, alliances, and how many soldiers each house sends to the war on the continent; and every fifth year, to choose who speaks for the nobles on the Council.

epigraph.quote: Ten Orsals a voice. For a banneret that is the price of a cow, and the view from the Stands is free.
epigraph.by: a Quillane banneret, from the top of the Stands

facts: every year, in the first Cycle of Okram
the Banner Hall, on Goldwind's river ring, since 56 EC; at Ironfort before that
the head or heir of every sworn house, often both; the bannerets in the Stands
the holder of the Nobles' seat, today Halsof Varselis
up to three for each of the Five, two for each other house of the Twenty, and one for each Warden, Holder, and banneret; every voice cast costs ten Orsals
seven, chosen on the last day, who see the Moot's word kept through the year; paid from the voice-money
every fifth Moot, in the years ending in 3 and 8; the next in 178 EC
about 4,100 soldiers, some sixteen warships, and the purses of the houses that send no men

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: The Moot of Banners is the peerage's own assembly. The Council of the Charted Isles governs the federation, and the noble houses have one seat on it. The Moot is where the houses decide among themselves what that seat will say, what they owe each other, and what they will send to the war.

Everything the peerage decides for the year is decided here: the pacts between houses, renewed or broken; the convoy routes and the passage of the strait; alliances, and the marriages House Veldane announces; the disputes the houses bring before the Hall of Scales' arbiters; and the Front Levy, the soldiers, ships, coin, and Krysta each house sends to the Alliance for the coming year.

sections.title: The Banner Hall
paragraphs: The Banner Hall stands on Goldwind's river ring, an old hall raised in 56 EC by the subscription of every house, when the Moot followed the Council south from Ironfort. Its floor is a long horseshoe of dark wood where the Twenty sit, with the benches of the Wardens and Holders inside it. Around the floor rise the Stands, tiers of plain benches climbing to the roof, where the bannerets sit by the age of their grants. The oldest bannerets sit nearest the floor. Quillane's newest sit at the top, under the rafters, where the acoustics are excellent and nobody can see them.
Every house's banner hangs from the roof beams, the Twenty's above the Horseshoe, and the bannerets' wherever House Veldane has found room. A banner that hangs crooked is a message.

sections.title: Who comes
paragraphs: Every sworn house sends its head or its heir. Most of the Twenty send both, and some send more than one heir, so that the Horseshoe is always crowded and the Stands are always full. A head who does not come and sends no heir is understood to have something to say by staying away.
Lady Elyria of Caelvaron comes once in ten years.
Lady Elara of Stormweaver has never come, and sends a different relative every year.
Lord Sten of Kaldmark sends his elder son.
Lord Johann Faust comes when he is in port, and when he is not, Gavriel sits in his chair.

sections.title: Who keeps it
list: **The chair:** the holder of the Nobles' seat presides. Today that is Halsof Varselis.
**The order:** Selvane bailiffs of House Varselis keep it, and have removed an Archlord once.
**The rolls:** Mardle clerks of House Holst keep them and count the votes, and no Mardle count has ever been challenged twice.
**The Stands:** House Veldane seats them, and the bannerets read their places the way the great houses read a wedding plan.
**The bargains:** the Rose House's Saphrels draw them up under Rose surety in a small room off the hall, and work through the last night.
**The ball:** Vol Kaern hosts the closing ball on the castle-heights, as it has since 56 EC.
**The year after:** the Board, which the Moot chooses on its last day.

sections.title: How it votes
paragraphs: Every voice cast costs ten Orsals, paid on the floor before the vote is counted. Each of the Five may cast up to three voices, each other house of the Twenty two, and each Warden, Holder, and banneret one. A house votes by its head, or by its heir in the head's absence, and a house whose head and heir disagree aloud on the floor has its voices counted as none and its money kept, which is the Moot's oldest joke and its least funny rule.

Ten Orsals is a great deal of money to a banneret, and most of them do not pay. They come to hear what the Horseshoe has decided and what will be asked of them, and they go home with their orders. They do vote on the lesser questions that touch their own shores, a road, a ferry, a quarrel between neighbors, where the Stands' voices decide the matter and the Horseshoe lets them. The Levy, the pacts, and the strait are the Horseshoe's.

sections.title: The Board
paragraphs: The voice-money does not go to any house. It goes to the Board, seven members chosen on the last day of each Moot, who sit through the year and see that what the Moot decided is done: that the pacts are kept, the routes kept open, and the Front Levy raised, paid, and shipped. The holder of the Nobles' seat chairs it. Five lords are chosen by the Horseshoe, and one banneret by the Stands. Its money, some fifteen thousand Orsals in a busy year, pays the Moot's clerks, bailiffs, and riders. A house that has not kept the Moot's word answers to the Board at the next Moot, in front of everyone.

The Board of 175 EC is Halsof Varselis in the chair; Gavriel Faust, Lady Vaela Vol Kaern, Lord Ignatius Emberheart, Lady Mirabel Veldane, and Lord Castor Pelagar; and for the Stands, Sir Rikard Crest, who is poor, honest, and the only member who has read every word of the Moot's rolls.

sections.title: The Choosing
paragraphs: Every fifth Moot, in the years ending in 3 and 8, the peerage chooses who holds the Nobles' seat on the Council of the Charted Isles. At the Choosing every sworn house may cast one voice, banneret or Archlord, at the same ten Orsals. That is why Quillane's seventy bannerets matter once every five years, why their voice-money is always paid, and why the house is courted that year as at no other time. A Varselis has held the seat for most of the federation's history. Halsof Varselis was chosen at the Moot of 173 EC, and the next Choosing is at the Moot of 178.

sections.title: The war of the houses
paragraphs: The Council of the Charted Isles is not at war with the Korvan Imperium. Its Armada keeps the strait and stops imperial warships and contraband, but it lets a diplomatic ship through under safe-conduct, and the peerage protests every time.

The noble houses are at war. The great houses fled the Sun-Throne, and most of them still hold their old oaths to the Alliance. They are the only part of Kalvatar truly at war with the continent, and they fight it with their own men, ships, coin, and Krysta, under their own banners.

sections.title: The Front Levy
paragraphs: The last great business of every Moot is the Front Levy: how many soldiers, ships, coin, and Krysta each house sends to the Alliance for the coming year. The companies sail at First-Sail in Ezra, on the Crown Route to Castia, with house warships for escort, and serve two-year turns at the Front under Alliance command and their own houses' banners.
The Levy of 175 EC sent about 4,100 soldiers from the Twenty and their bannermen.
list: **Faust:** about 2,000, the largest share, and four warships.
**Vanris:** about 400 marines and six warships.
**Vol Kaern, Emberheart, and Quillane:** about 300 each, Emberheart's with a battery of long guns.
**Varselis:** about 200.
**Caelvaron:** about 150 archers of the Elderwood.
**Sunforge, Holst, Solenne, and Kaldmark:** about 100 each: armorers, soldiers, healers, and huscarls.
**Stormweaver:** thirty storm-mages, whom the Alliance asks for by name.
**Alastor:** twelve Knights of the Pale Rose, and the largest purse.
**The rest:** coin, charts, information, Krysta, and, from House Veldane, a wedding gift for every company that sails.

sections.title: Customs of the Moot
list: **The reading.** The Moot opens with the names of every Kalvatari soldier who died at the Front that year, read by the presiding lord, house by house. Nobody sits during the reading, not even in the Stands.
**The first word and the last.** The Five speak in the order of their founding, except Vol Kaern, which never speaks first and always speaks last.
**The protest.** Every Moot since 171 EC has entered a formal protest against the Council's safe-conduct for the imperial Southern Survey. The Council receives it every year, with thanks.
**The gloves.** Quillane's bannerets wear muddy-gold gloves to the Moot, once.
**The ball.** The Moot ends on the castle-heights, masked, and the bargains that failed on the floor are often made again there.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: The Moot is the busiest week of Goldwind's year. Every inn on the river ring is taken, every great house's townhouse is open, and the salons run all night. On the floor, Halsof Varselis keeps the order with a gavel he rarely uses. In the Stands, the bannerets eat bread and cheese from their laps and argue about everything below them. Faust argues for a larger Levy, and the Heartland for a smaller one. The Rose House says very little and signs a great deal. Kastan Vol Kaern listens all week, speaks for five minutes on the last day, and the vote goes his way. Then everyone climbs to the heights and puts on a mask.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “At the Choosing of 173 EC the Quillane bloc voted for Halsof Varselis, and somebody paid for every vote.” (a Mardle vote-counter)
“The imperial envoy dined on the heights at last year's Moot ball, masked like everyone else, and Kastan seated him at his own right hand.” (a Saelwin footman)
“Faust asked for a Levy of three thousand this year and was given two. Gavriel Faust said something to the Heartland that the rolls do not record.” (a Selvane bailiff)
“The Selvane bailiffs removed an Archlord from the floor once. Nobody will say which house, and every house says it was another one.” (a Banner Hall porter)
“The Stands vote at the Choosing, and the Stands can be bought by the row, ten Orsals a seat.” (a Goldwind innkeeper)
“The Board's riders know the Front Levy's sailing dates before the captains do, and so does someone else.” (a Castia-bound sergeant)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A banneret needs someone to carry his house's banner to the Moot, because the last bearer did not arrive.
A house wants a pact broken at the Moot, quietly, before its rival can stand up and renew it.
The Choosing of 178 EC is coming, and someone is buying rows of the Stands.
A name has been left out of the reading of the dead, and the soldier's mother is in Goldwind.
The Front Levy needs escort for a company sailing at First-Sail, and the convoy has been promised a surprise on the Crown Route.

title: The Southern Survey
subtitle: Five imperial ships, under the Council's safe-conduct
summary: Since 171 EC, five dark imperial ships have lain in the Strangers' Roads off Ironfort under the Council's safe-conduct, sent, the Sun-Throne says, to chart the southern seas for its scholars. The peerage has protested every year. Nobody in the islands has ever seen them in a hurry.

epigraph.quote: They ask very polite questions, and they write down the answers before you have finished giving them.

facts: the Strangers' Roads off Ironfort, under the guns of Wakefort
five: the Clear Sight (flagship), the Measure, the Third Dawn, the Obedience, and the Steady Hand
the Iron Fleet's colors, by the Council's safe-conduct
every Moot of Banners since 171 EC

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: The Southern Survey of the Iron Fleet is the Korvan Imperium's only standing presence in the islands. The Council of the Charted Isles, which is not at war with the Imperium, granted it safe-conduct in 171 EC as a diplomatic and scholarly mission: to chart the southern seas and the ice for the Sun-Throne's scholars, and to carry an envoy who calls on the Council once a year.
The noble houses, who are at war with the Imperium, protested at the Moot of 171 EC and at every Moot since. The Council has thanked them every year and changed nothing.

sections.title: The ships
paragraphs: Five long, low, dark-hulled ships under sail, with tall masts and very little decoration, lying at anchor in the Strangers' Roads off Ironfort, where foreign ships wait for leave to enter. Their names are painted small, in the Common script and in Korvane.
**The *Clear Sight*,** the flagship, which carries the commander and the envoy.
**The *Measure*,** which goes south most often, and once lay off Everfall for three nights.
**The *Third Dawn*,** which carries most of the scholars.
**The *Obedience*,** whose crew never comes ashore.
**The *Steady Hand*,** the store-ship, which comes and goes from Ironfort's quays with crates.
Their crews keep to their ships. Their boats come and go at every hour. Nobody in the islands has ever seen a Survey ship race, fire a gun, or arrive anywhere in a hurry.

sections.title: Its people
list: **Than Val Corisse Tallaran,** the commander, a quiet, grey-eyed officer of the Iron Fleet who speaks Common without an accent and has never once been seen ashore without his gloves.

**Val Edrian Sarmeth,** the envoy, charming, curious, and well dressed, who calls on the Council once a year as an observer and dines wherever he is asked, which is more places than the peerage would like.
**The scholars,** who sketch coastlines, buy charts and books, measure tides, collect shells and stones, and ask very polite questions.

sections.title: Its terms
paragraphs: The Council's safe-conduct allows the Survey's ships to call at any Council port on notice, to take Council pilots, and to pay harbor dues like anyone else. It forbids them to carry arms ashore, to land on house ground without the house's leave, or to enter the Sealed Waters. The Survey has never been caught breaking a term.

sections.title: What the islands think
list: **The peerage:** that an imperial ship in Kalvatar's waters is an insult, and five are five insults.
**Faust:** watches the Survey from the Wakefort battery, and runs out the guns every morning.
**Vanris:** pilots the Survey's ships through the Serpent's Coil, at the full rate, and counts their masts.
**Holst:** inspects their papers at every port, and finds them perfect every time.
**The Council:** that a mission it can see is better than agents it cannot.
**The docks:** that the Survey pays in good Orsals, tips well, and never gets drunk.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The imperial survey ships take a Quellin pilot through the Coil like everyone else, and the pilots say those ships answer the helm faster than anything they have ever steered.” (a Pilot's Isle pilot)
“The Survey bought a Starborn chart through a Goldwind dealer, and sent it back a month later with a correction in the margin. It was right.” (an Aldmere apprentice)
“On still nights you can hear something humming under the Clear Sight's decks, like a hive.” (an Ironfort lighterman)
“The Survey's boats never come back the way they went.” (a Briarcrown carter)
“The envoy has dined at more great houses than the Council has, and some of them have never admitted it.” (a Goldwind cook)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A Survey scholar wants a guide to somewhere on the coast that is on no chart, and pays very well.
Faust wants to know what the *Steady Hand* unloads at Ironfort's quays at night.
The envoy has invited one of you to dine aboard the *Clear Sight*.
A Survey boat has come ashore on house ground without leave, and the house wants the Council to see it before the Survey can explain.
Someone in Ironfort is selling drawings that came off an imperial ship, and three houses want to buy them.

title: Jobs and Wages
subtitle: What a day's work is worth, from the docks to the Spire Floor
summary: Three Bits are a laborer's day, an Anchor his month, and an Orsal his year. Everything else in the islands is measured against that: a journeyman earns two Anchors a month, a master four to six, a physician ten, a magister forty, and a Fleetlord a hundred.

epigraph.quote: A string a Cycle, an Anchor a month, a sun a year, and a grave at the end of it. That is the whole of the laborer's catechism.

facts: by the month of thirty-six days; ten months and the five Still Days make the year
Coinsday, market day, every ten days
food and a bed (or a hammock) included in the pay
3 Bits a day; a string (30 Bits) a Cycle; 1 Anchor a month; about 1 Orsal a year
a University magister at 30 to 40 Anchors; a Grand Admiral at 200, and the first tot
1 Bit is a copper piece, 1 Tide a silver, 1 Anchor a gold, 1 Orsal ten gold

sections.title: The yardsticks
paragraphs: Every islander carries five numbers in their head, and every price in the islands makes sense against them.
**A Bit** buys a fishbread, a saltknot, a mug of small ale, or a cup of brightleaf.
**Three Bits** are a laborer's day.
**A string**, thirty Bits on a cord, is a laborer's Cycle of ten days.
**An Anchor** is a laborer's month.
**An Orsal** is a laborer's year.

So a lesser healing draught at fifty Anchors is five years of a field hand's life, a soldier's sword at fifteen is more than a year of it, and a proof-made rope at one Anchor is a month of it. Magic is not rare in Kalvatar because it is hidden. It is rare because it is expensive, and the same is true of good boots.

sections.title: The wage-book
paragraphs: What the islands pay by the month, in a common port. Goldwind pays a little more and charges a third more for everything.
**Field hand, laborer, net-mender:** 1 Anchor (3 Bits a day). About 1 Orsal a year.
**Servant in a good house:** 6 Tides, found. About 6 Anchors a year and keep.
**Longshore porter:** 4 to 5 Bits a day, about 1½ Anchors.
**Deckhand, a Hand:** 1 Anchor, found.
**Able seaman, an Able Blade in the Armada:** 1½ Anchors, found, and a share of prizes.
**Town watch:** 1½ Anchors.
**Journeyman craftsman:** 2 Anchors.
**Clerk, scribe, Reckoners' counter:** 3 Anchors.
**Sword for hire, an Ironfort company:** 3 Anchors; 6 in a war season.
**Master craftsman:** 4 to 6 Anchors.
**Merchant's factor:** 5 Anchors, and 2 to 5 in every 100 of what they buy.
**Registered caster of one or two rings,** on lantern-work and harbor wards: 8 to 12 Anchors.
**Physician in Goldwind:** 10 to 15 Anchors.
**Merchant captain:** 15 to 30 Anchors, and *privilege*: hold-space for their own cargo.
**University magister:** 30 to 40 Anchors.

The rest of the islands' trades, from the sailmaker to the governess, are in the entries that follow: Work at Sea, Harbor and Road, Crafts and Guilds, Learned Work, Service and the Great Houses, Swords and Hunters, and Field, Mine, and Herd.

sections.title: How the islands are paid
list: **On Coinsday.** Wages fall due every ten days, on Coinsday, which is also market day and the day debts are paid, so a laborer's string often passes from his employer's hand to his landlord's in the same hour.
**In strings.** Working people are paid in Bits on a cord and carry them at the belt, with a Tide or two sewn into a seam.

**Found.** A servant, a sailor, an apprentice, or a house soldier is paid less in coin and fed and housed besides. A found wage of 6 Tides is worth about as much as a laborer's Anchor, and is a great deal safer.
**In leaf-bricks.** Aboard ship, sailors are often paid partly in pressed bricks of brightleaf, by custom one brick, one Tide.
**In privilege.** A captain and crew carry their own small cargo free of freight, and many a sailor's real wage is the bale of coffee under the hammock.
**In prize money.** The Armada's true wage, when a prize is taken.

**In paper.** University scrip among Goldwind's scholars; Lodge chits for Hunters; and in the Charterhouse Company's towns, company brass, writ-tokens good only at the Company's own stores, which the workers call *collar-money*.
**In kind.** On the outer Frontier a night's lodging is *a nail a night*; in the deep Wilds a day's work is paid in cacao beans; on the ice in lamp-oil.

sections.title: What an Anchor buys
paragraphs: **A laborer's month,** in a common port, on about an Anchor:
A share of a room with two others: 1 Tide.
A loaf a day: 36 Bits.
Pickets, fishbread, or a bowl of chowder: about 25 Bits.
Small ale and brightleaf: about 15 Bits.
A pint of lamp-oil: 5 Bits.
Set aside for working clothes and boots: 2 Bits.
The Concord's tithe, one in twenty, freely given: 5 Bits.
Left at the end of the month: two or three Bits, if nobody fell ill.

A laborer's Anchor does not feed a family, and nobody expects it to. Everyone in the house works. The wife mends nets or takes in washing, the children run messages and sell saltknots, and the grandmother minds the stall.
list: **A journeyman's month,** on 2 Anchors: a room of his own for 3 Tides; food for two, about 11 Tides; guild dues and clothes set aside; a supper at the tavern on Restday; and a Tide and a half saved toward the day he makes his masterwork.

**A master's month,** on 5 Anchors: a craftsman's house and shop for 5 Tides; a servant at 6 Tides, found; food for a household of six, apprentices included, about 2 Anchors; guild dues of 5 Anchors a year set aside; good clothes for the guild feasts; the tithe; and an Anchor a month saved or lent, which is how a master's grandson becomes a merchant.

sections.title: Hiring by the day
paragraphs: What the islands charge for a day's work, for anyone hiring help on the road or at the docks. Most hiring is by the month, and a day costs a little more than its share.
**An unskilled hand:** 3 to 4 Bits, a porter 5, with a meal.
**A skilled hand,** a journeyman of any craft: 6 to 8 Bits.
**A master** who leaves his own shop for the day: 1½ to 2 Tides.
**A guide** who knows the country: 5 Bits to 1 Tide; double in the deep green or on the ice.
**A scribe:** 1 Bit a page.
**A pilot** through the Widow's Teeth: 1 Anchor, paid by the ship.
**A Bronze Hunter crew** riding along on a voyage: 5 to 10 Anchors a leg.
A stranger who offers a gold piece for a day's work, as the continent's adventurers do, has offered a month's wage, and will find the whole dock willing.

sections.title: The guild ladder
paragraphs: Almost every craft and trade in Council lands has a guild, and the guilds together are the Mercantile Congress.
list: **Apprentice.** Paid in keep: a bed, food, a coat a year, and a few Bits on Coinsday. The apprentice belongs to the master's house until the indenture ends.
**Journeyman.** Free to work for any master, at a journeyman's wage. Dues of 1 Anchor a year.
**Master.** By a masterwork, or by proof of business. Dues of 5 Anchors a year. A master's chain of office is worn like a crown, and unpaid dues cost the chain.
**The Ledger.** A name in the Reckoners' Ledger, three Coinsdays unpaid, can hold no master's chain in any guild.

sections.title: The top of the ladder
paragraphs: Wages stop somewhere around the magister's forty Anchors. Above that the islands speak of income, not pay.
**A banneret's holding:** 20 to 100 Orsals a year.
**A Warden's holding:** 200 to 1,000 Orsals.
**A Highlord's dominion:** 5,000 to 20,000 Orsals.
**One of the Five:** 30,000 to 80,000 Orsals.
**One of the Twelve Flags:** 20,000 to 100,000 Orsals of trade, and perhaps a tenth of that as profit.
A household soldier costs his house about two Orsals a year, keep included, which is why a thousand soldiers are two thousand Orsals, and why only the great houses keep them.

sections.title: Toil and its god
paragraphs: The working islands keep **Halvenir, the Reaper of Grain**, the god of harvest, seasons, plenty, and toil, who is too busy working for stories. His month is the month of salt and harvest. A laborer who dies at work is said to have *gone to Halvenir's table*, where the bread is always fresh and nobody is paid by the day.

sections.title: As the docks tell it
paragraphs: A Goldwind porter carries a hundredweight up from the Sentinel Docks for half a Bit and sings about it. A clerk in the Reckoners' Hall earns twice the porter's wage for sitting down, and the porter sings about that too. Every Coinsday the strings come out of the paymasters' chests, the landlords stand at the end of the line, and the taverns fill with people spending what the landlords missed.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The Longshore has priced a strike to the Bit. Morgha Wall-Holder knows what a day of a shut harbor costs every Flag on the Spire Floor.” (a Goldwind stevedore)

“Company brass changes at half its face behind the Company store, and somebody sells it back to the Company's own clerks at three-quarters. Nobody can prove the somebody is the Company.” (a Southhaven runaway)
“Prices are up a Bit on everything since spring, and wages are not.” (a Goldwind fishwife)

“There is a laborer in Easthold who found a perfect pearl in a mussel, sold it for three hundred Anchors, and has never worked a day since. He is the most miserable man on the coast.” (an Easthold net-mender)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A master needs a journeyman for a season and pays well, and nobody in town will take the work.
The Longshore is about to strike in a port where the party's cargo is waiting.
A Company town's workers want their brass changed for real coin, all at once, before the clerks hear of it.
A laborer has been paid in drowned Anchors for a month, and wants to know who his employer bought them from.
Someone is hiring every scribe in Goldwind for one night, at a Tide a page, and will not say what they are copying.

title: Work at Sea
subtitle: Hands, Able Blades, mates, whalers, and pilots, and what the sea pays them
summary: Half the islands live at sea for part of every year. A Hand earns an Anchor a month and his keep, an Able seaman half again, a merchant captain fifteen to thirty; but the sea's true wages are the ones nobody writes down: privilege in the hold, prize money, and the whaler's share of the oil.

epigraph.quote: The Council pays me an Anchor. The coffee under my hammock pays me three. The sea pays me in years, and takes them back.
epigraph.by: a Hand of the Corvane Line

facts: 1½ Anchors a month, found, and a share of prizes
15 to 30 Anchors a month, and privilege
about 100 to 120 Anchors a month in wages
a Grand Admiral at 200 Anchors a month, and the first tot
the Council takes a quarter; the rest is shared by rank, down to the last Hand
the Brine Brotherhood for fishers and whalers; the Shipwrights' Guild for the yards; the Free Sails for independent captains

sections.title: The merchant's pay-book
paragraphs: What a three-masted ocean merchantman of sixty hands pays in a month, about 100 Anchors with the captain's share:
**The captain:** 20 Anchors, and privilege.
**The first mate,** who keeps the log and the course: 6 Anchors. **The second mate:** 4.
**The bosun,** the carpenter, and the barber-surgeon: 3 Anchors each.
**The sailmaker:** 2½ Anchors.
**The cook:** 1½ Anchors, and every sailor's opinion.
**Fourteen Able seamen:** 1½ Anchors each.
**Thirty-six Hands:** 1 Anchor each.
**Two ship's boys:** half an Anchor each, and a beating from everyone.
All found: hammocks, biscuit, salt-fish, a lemon a day, and the noon tot. A long voyage south or to the ice pays a fifth more, and a captain who cannot find hands pays what the crimps ask.

sections.title: The Armada's pay
paragraphs: The Armada pays by the month, found, and pays on time, which is half the reason anyone joins.
list: **Hand:** 1 Anchor.
**Able Blade:** 1½ Anchors.
**Blade-Ensign:** 4 Anchors.
**Sword-Lieutenant:** 6 Anchors.
**First Blade:** 10 Anchors.
**Ship-Lord:** 20 Anchors.
**High Captain:** 35 Anchors.
**Fleetlord:** 100 Anchors, and table money.
**Grand Admiral:** 200 Anchors, and the first tot.

**Prize money** is the Armada's true wage. A captured ship or cargo is sold, the Council takes a quarter, and the rest is shared by rank down to the last Hand. A single good prize can pay a Hand more than ten years of wages, and every sailor in the islands can name the ship that made someone *anchored* overnight.

sections.title: Privilege
paragraphs: A captain and crew carry their own small cargo in the hold, free of freight. That is privilege, and it is the reason the islands never run short of sailors.
list: **A Hand's privilege** is what fits under his hammock: a bale, a cask, a sack.

**The arithmetic.** Twenty pounds of coffee bought in Southhaven at 4 Bits a pound cost 8 Tides, and sell in Goldwind at 2 Tides a pound for 4 Anchors. That is three months' wages for one voyage, and a Hand who does it twice a year lives nearly as well as a journeyman.
**A captain's privilege** is a corner of the hold, and on a good voyage it is worth more than the captain's wage.
**A bad captain** sells his crew's privilege-space to a factor, and has trouble finding a crew next season.

sections.title: The whalers
paragraphs: The **Brine Brotherhood's** whalers sail out of Frosthold for shares, not wages. The ship takes half the oil, and the crew divides the rest by the Brotherhood's old table.
list: **A green hand's share** is a barrel or two of oil, worth an Anchor apiece at the tryworks and three in Goldwind.
**A harpooner's share** is ten barrels, and a harpooner who has been south for twenty seasons owns a timber house, which on the ice is wealth.
**Ambergris** is shared apart. A lump the size of a fist, at 2 Anchors an ounce at the tryworks, is two years of a Hand's wages, and every whaler has dreamed of one.
**A bad season** pays nothing at all, and the Brotherhood keeps the widows.

sections.title: The fishers
paragraphs: The Brotherhood's fishers work every coast in the islands, humble and everywhere, and they can empty every fish-market in a week if crossed. A fishing smack costs 3 to 5 Orsals, more than most fishing families will ever hold, so most boats are owned by the share: a boat of four, and four families with a quarter each. A quarter-share clears about an Anchor a month in a fair season, and twice that in a good one. The catch is sold on the quay every morning, and the price of a barrel of salt-fish at Greyhaven, 4 Tides, is set before the boats are tied up.

sections.title: Pilots, and the ones who know the water
list: **The Widow's Teeth pilots** take a ship through for 1 Anchor, paid by the ship, and are worth it.
**Harbor pilots** in every great port take a Tide or two a ship, and know which captains do not tip.
**Coral tide-pilots,** the shore-lines of the deep courts, guide ships through pact-water, and are paid in sound as often as coin: a bell, a song, a music-box.
**Galven storm-pilots** run a ship into weather that would sink a sensible captain, and a Galven aboard is worth three Hands when the weather breaks. They are paid like mates, and fed like kings.
**Navigators** who can work an Aethyn star-table are paid like a first mate, and the Armada takes the best of them.

sections.title: The yards
paragraphs: The **Shipwrights' Guild** builds at Goldwind's Sentinel Docks, and the **Vanris yards** at Stormreach build the best storm-hulls in the islands and charge for it. A shipwright is a master craftsman at 5 or 6 Anchors a month, a journeyman of the yards 2, and a caulker who seals a hull with southern jungle-sap 1½. A refit after a hard storm costs about a tenth of the hull, and the yards pray for weather.

sections.title: Getting a berth
list: **The hiring-tide.** Crews are signed on Tideturn, sailing day, in the sailors' houses by the quay, with a mark on the ship's articles and a Tide in advance.
**The crimps.** In every great harbor the crimps sell bodies to short-handed captains at 2 Anchors a body. The body wakes at sea, and signs the articles or swims.
**The Driftborn** never come ashore at all. Their flotillas lash together every evening in the raft-up, a floating town for one night, and a sailor who wants work with no questions asks there.

sections.title: As the quays tell it
paragraphs: A Hand ashore with three months' pay and a bale of coffee is a rich man for exactly one Cycle. The sailors' houses charge a Bit a night for a hammock, the taverns a Bit a mug, and the Pocchin stalls whatever the Hand will pay for a jackdaw that counts. On Tideturn he signs on again, with a Tide in his boot for the voyage south and nothing else, and swears that next time he will save.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Hand off the Swift Return came home from one prize with forty Anchors and bought his mother a house. He was back aboard in a month. He said the house was too quiet.” (a Sentinel Docks crimp)
“The Brotherhood is short of oil this season, and the harpooners are being paid in promises.” (a Frosthold tryworks hand)
“A crimp in Ironfort sold a Hunter to a whaler by mistake. The whaler came home early.” (an Ironfort sailors'-house keeper)
“The best storm-pilot in the south is a Galven who has never been paid in coin. Every captain owes her a storm.” (a Southhaven harbor pilot)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A merchant captain will give the party privilege-space for one voyage if they sign as Hands.
A Hand's privilege bale has been stolen from the hold, and he swears it was more than coffee.
A Frosthold whaler needs a harpooner for the season and pays by the Brotherhood's table.
A crimp has pressed someone the party needs, and the ship sailed on the morning tide.
A prize is to be sold at Goldwind, and three crews claim a share of it.

title: Harbor and Road
subtitle: Porters, scale-men, ferrymen, couriers, and teamsters: the work that moves everything else
summary: Every cargo in the islands passes through a porter's hands, a scale-man's balance, and a clerk's seal before it reaches a buyer. The Longshore can shut a port with one whistle, the Corvane post carries a letter across a region for 3 Bits, and a saurian-cart and its driver can be hired in the south for 3 Bits a day.

epigraph.quote: The Flags own the ships. The Reckoners own the Flags. We own the gangplank, and nothing crosses it without us.
epigraph.by: Morgha Wall-Holder, boss of the Longshore at Goldwind

facts: 4 to 5 Bits a day, about 1½ Anchors a month
1 Bit across one island; 3 Bits to another port of the same region; 1 Tide across regions
3 Bits a day, in the south
the Longshore, porters and stevedores of every harbor

sections.title: The Longshore
paragraphs: The porters and stevedores of every harbor in Council lands belong to **the Longshore**, and the Longshore can shut a port with one whistle. A porter earns 4 or 5 Bits a day, more than a field hand and less than a journeyman, carrying bales, casks, and crates up from the holds and down to the warehouses. A gang of twelve unloads a merchantman in two days, and a gang-boss who can do it in one is paid like a master.

Goldwind's boss is **Morgha Wall-Holder**, an orc woman nobody has ever seen lose an argument or a tidecall match. The orcs and half-orcs of the islands are the backbone of the Longshore, the docks, and the droving-roads, and the Longshore's work-songs are sung in Gorrakh on every quay from Ironfort to Southhaven.
list: **The whistle.** A Longshore strike starts with one whistle on one quay and is heard in every harbor of the region by nightfall. It has happened four times in living memory, and the Flags settled every time inside a Cycle.
**The gangplank.** By old custom nobody but the Longshore carries cargo off a ship in a Council port. A crew that unloads its own hold finds its next cargo very slow to arrive.
**The Longshore's tithe.** A Bit in every string goes to the gang-box, which pays for the injured, the drowned, and the funerals.

sections.title: The scale-men and the clerks
list: **Scale-men** are licensed moneychangers with brass balances on every quay. They weigh coin for a Bit a weighing, change foreign metal for a fee, and test a doubtful Anchor on the ringing-stone. A busy scale-man takes a clerk's wage in a month of Bits. A merchant who does not trust a purse sends it to a scale-man, and a merchant who does not trust the scale-man brings his own weights.

**House Holst's customs-clerks** seal cargoes and collect the harbor dues, 5 Bits a tide for a coaster and 5 Tides a tide for a great ship, in every Council harbor. A Holst clerk earns about 3 Anchors a month, and an honest one is said to be the hardest thing in the islands to buy.
**Warehousemen** weigh, grade, and stamp every bale in the Congress warehouses, at a journeyman's wage, and the grade-stamp is where a poor bale becomes a good one, if someone pays.
**Tally-keepers** on the great quays count every cask aboard and ashore for 2 Anchors a month, and many of them are dwarves, because a dwarf's count is entered and never lapses.

sections.title: Light and water
list: **Lamplighters** walk the quays at dusk with a pole and a pint of Frosthold oil, for about a watchman's wage, 1½ Anchors a month. The great harbor-lights are the Lanternwrights' business, and a Lanternwright journeyman earns twice what a lamplighter does.
**Ferrymen** take a Bit a crossing on every harbor, river, and strait too narrow for a ship, and a ferryman with a good crossing earns more than a master craftsman.
**Water-carriers** sell fresh water by the bucket in the ports that have no wells, a Bit for two buckets, and the south's water-carriers are the first to know everything.
**Divers** go down for lost anchors, fouled cables, and dropped cargo, for a Tide a dive, and the Pearl Groove divers will not dive for anyone but the pearl-clans.

sections.title: Letters and couriers
paragraphs: The **Corvane Line**, *Every Tide, Every Port*, carries the islands' post and its fast packets.
**A letter across one island:** 1 Bit, carried by a town runner.
**A letter to another port in the same region:** 3 Bits, by Corvane post.
**A letter across regions:** 1 Tide.
**A sealed express by fast packet:** 1 Anchor.
**A scribe to write it:** 1 Bit a page, on any quay.

A town runner is paid by the letter, a few Bits a day, and the best of them are children who know every alley in the port. An out-of-town courier rides the Frontier's roads on a hired horse at 2 Bits a day, and is paid a journeyman's wage and his road-money. A Corvane post-captain is paid like a merchant captain and is trusted with every secret in the islands, which is why everyone tips him.

sections.title: The roads
paragraphs: The islands' great road is the sea, but every island has its carts.
list: **Teamsters and carters** drive the roads between the farms and the ports, at a laborer's wage or a little more, and own their own carts when they can.
**On the Frontier,** a horse is hired for 2 Bits a day, and the Northreach carters drive horse-teams; House Faust's war-wagons go behind domestic aurocs.
**In the south,** a saurian-cart and its driver are hired together for 3 Bits a day, because nobody but its driver can make a Loamback go anywhere.
**Drovers** walk the herds to market along the droving-roads, a Cycle or more at a time, at a laborer's wage and a share of the sale; most of them are orcs, and nobody steals from a drove twice.
**Guides** who know the country take 5 Bits to 1 Tide a day, and double in the deep green, on the ice, or anywhere near a thin place.
**Porters on the road,** for those who cannot afford a cart, carry a hundredweight on a frame for 4 Bits a day.

sections.title: Inns and the road-trade
paragraphs: The halflings own half the teahouses and inns in the islands, and an innkeeper is the first up and the last down.
list: **A hammock in a sailors' house:** 1 Bit a night. A bed in a shared room: 3 Bits.
**A potboy or a serving-girl:** 4 or 5 Tides a month, found, and the tips.
**An inn's cook:** 1 Anchor a month, found.
**An innkeeper** with a good house on a good quay clears a master's income and knows more than the harbor-master.
