paragraphs: “A bell has been ringing under the sea off Pearl Groove at midnight, and the Belmaris founders say it is not one of theirs.” (a Pearl Groove diver)
“The Whispering Current knows what was said on the Council's barge last month, and is asking a price nobody in Goldwind can pay.” (a Pelagar pact-warden)
“House Belmaris has been buying silver faster than it casts bells.” (a Goldwind jeweler)
“A Goldwind dealer sold a black pearl at the Coinsday market, and the buyer received an invitation the same night.” (a Goldwind salon-hostess)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A factor must carry a music-box down to the Glass Gardens, and the tune it plays has been sung before.
The Grey Fathoms have returned a drowned sailor's body, and want a song the family cannot sing.
A cargo of bare iron has been loaded onto a ship bound for Pearl Groove, and someone did it on purpose.
A pearl-factor needs proof that a rival's pearls are dyed.
The Whispering Current has a secret for sale, and the price is another one.

title: The Great Flows
subtitle: Where the cargo goes, what it costs to carry, and what the Council watches
summary: Each region of Kalvatar lives by what it has too much of and dies by what it lacks. The Frontier sends iron, salt, and horses south; the Heartland sends finished goods everywhere; the south sends coffee, sugar, cotton, and Krysta north; the ice sends oil to every lamp; and the Coral courts trade pearls for bells through Pearl Groove. Freight and duties add about a third to a cargo's cost for every region it crosses.

epigraph.quote: Salt goes south, oil goes north, coffee goes everywhere, and the Reckoners take a little of all of it.

facts: about a third added to a cargo's cost for every region it crosses; the ice doubles it
routinely sell for five or ten times their price at the source
a Tide a ton, paid to the Council for a place in an Armada convoy
from one in fifty on a coastal voyage to one in five to the ice
trades only through the Frontier's Gate
insurance triples, and the ports close for the Three Nights

sections.title: Who sends what
paragraphs: Read each region's line as what it sends to the others.
**The Frontier sends:**
to the Heartland: horses, salt-fish, iron, mast-pine, tartan, and furs;
to the south: salt-fish, horses, iron, and swords for hire;
to the ice: timber, salt, wool, and iron.
**The Heartland sends:**
to the Frontier: wine, glass, books, lamps, registered Krysta, and firearms;
to the south: tools, firearms, cloth, wine, books, and glass;
to the ice: grain, glass, medicine, brightleaf, and rope.
**The south sends:**
to the Frontier: coffee, sugar, citrus, and cotton;
to the Heartland: coffee, cacao, cotton, sugar, jade, gold, raw Krysta, ironwood, jungle-sap, and saurians;
to the ice: citrus, timber, grain, and coffee.
**The ice sends:**
to the Frontier: whale-oil and furs;
to the Heartland: whale-oil, ambergris, ivory, and icebrand;
to the south: whale-oil, ice, and frostcured fish.
list: **The Coral courts** trade almost wholly with the Heartland, through Pelagar and Belmaris. Up from the sea come pearls, kelp-silk, and reefpurple; down to the sea go bells, brass, silver, and glass.
**Assios** trades only through the Frontier's Gate. North go Krysta, horses, and salt-fish; south come steel, wine, books, firearms, aurocs, and silver.

sections.title: A price map
paragraphs: What the same thing costs in each region. The cheapest is where it is made; the dearest is where it is needed most.
list: **Salt, a sack:** Frontier 2 Bits; Heartland 5 Bits; south a Tide, at the Company's price; ice 4 Bits.
**Grain, a sack:** Frontier 4 Bits; Heartland 3 Bits; south 4 Bits; ice a Tide.
**Whale-oil, a pint:** Frontier 6 Bits; Heartland 5 Bits; south 4 Bits; ice a Bit.
**Timber, a beam:** Frontier 2 Tides; Heartland 5 Tides; south a Tide; ice 2 Anchors.
**Iron, a bar:** Frontier a Tide; Heartland 2 Tides; south 3 Tides; ice 4 Tides.
**Coffee, a pound:** Frontier 3 Tides; Heartland 2 Tides; south 4 Bits; ice 5 Tides.
**Sugar, a loaf:** Frontier a Tide; Heartland a Tide; south 3 Bits; ice 2 Tides.
**Brightleaf, a brick:** Frontier 1½ Tides; Heartland 6 Bits to a Tide; south 1½ Tides; ice 2 Tides.
**Sunhold wine, a table bottle:** Frontier 5 Bits; Heartland 3 Bits; south 6 Bits; ice a Tide.
**Kellum, a tot:** Frontier a Bit; Heartland 3 Bits; south 2 Bits; ice 2 Bits, as icebrand.
**A lemon:** Frontier a Bit; Heartland a Bit; south five for a Bit; ice 3 Bits.
**Cotton cloth, a bolt:** Frontier an Anchor; Heartland 8 Tides; south 4 Tides; ice 2 Anchors.
**A mug of ale:** Frontier a Bit; Heartland a Bit; south 2 Bits; ice 2 Bits.
**A night's private room:** Frontier a Tide; Heartland 2 Tides; south a Tide; ice a Tide, and 6 in Fairweather.

sections.title: Freight
paragraphs: What it costs to carry a ton, by convoy or fast and alone.
list: **Ironfort to Goldwind:** an Anchor by convoy; 2 fast.
**Goldwind to Southhaven:** 2 Anchors by convoy; 4 fast.
**Southhaven to Jakupur:** an Anchor by convoy; 2 fast.
**Southhaven to Varan Port:** 4 Anchors by convoy; 8 fast, and pray.
**Goldwind to Varan Port:** 6 Anchors by convoy; 12 fast.
**The rules of thumb:**
**A third a region.** Freight and duties add about a third to a cargo's cost for every region it crosses, and the ice doubles it.

**The rest of the gap** between the price at home and the price in Goldwind is the factor's margin, the warehouse, the shopkeeper, and the risk. Luxuries routinely sell for five or ten times their price at the source.
**Convoy or alone.** A convoy is cheaper and slower, a third longer on the water. A fast hull is a third quicker and costs double.
**Convoy money.** The Armada's Rear Admirals charge a Tide a ton for a place in a convoy, paid to the Council.
**Hunter escorts.** A Bronze crew rides along for 5 to 10 Anchors a leg; a Silver crew for 30 to 60.
**Privilege.** A captain and crew carry their own small cargo free of freight.

sections.title: The life of a cargo
paragraphs: How a bale of Southhaven coffee becomes a cup in Goldwind, and where every step can be bent.
**The grower** sells to a factor, often a half-elf, sometimes a Pocchin family. Here the price is set.
**A Congress warehouse** weighs, grades, and stamps it. Here the grade is forged.
**The Reckoners' Hall** writes a bottomry bond, a sea-loan forgiven if the ship sinks, and the captain pays the premium. Here a convenient sinking becomes profitable.
**House Holst's customs-clerks** seal it and collect the harbor dues. Here the seal is copied.
**The voyage,** in convoy, under a Hunter escort, or alone and fast and praying. Here it is lost, taken, or *lost*.
**The destination market,** a Congress hall, a coffee-house cellar, a Pocchin stall. Here it is cut, watered, or relabeled.
*Every step has a stamp. Every stamp has a forger.*

sections.title: Insurance
paragraphs: The Reckoners' bottomry premium, for one voyage:
**Coastal, within one region:** one in fifty.
**Between the Frontier and the Heartland:** one in twenty-five.
**To the south:** one in ten.
**To the ice:** one in five.
**In a King Tide year:** three times the above.
**Into the Sealed Waters:** none. The Hall will not write it at any price.
The bond is forgiven if the ship is lost, which is why, every year, a few ships are lost very conveniently, and why the Reckoners employ people whose whole work is finding out which.

sections.title: What the Council watches
list: **Krysta.** Registered, taxed, and licensed for the Gate. Every stone has papers, or it is dark glass.
**Firearms and cannon.** Made in Aurelion and Everfall, imported from the Free Cities, governed by the Council's arms-laws and broken by everyone.
**Ironwood and mast-pine.** Keels and masts. The Armada buys first; everyone else buys what is left.
**Jungle-sap.** It seals every hull in the Armada, and nothing else does it as well. The Armada would sink in ten years without the south.
**Whale-oil.** Every lamp, every lighthouse, the Goldwind lanterns. A bad whaling year puts the capital in the dark.
**Salt.** It preserves the fish that feeds the fleets. The Company now holds the southern salt, and the Council is only beginning to understand what it gave away.
**Grain.** The ice starves without it, and the Frontier one year in four.
**Horses and war-saurians.** The Council permits private cavalry and fears private saurian armies.
**Silver.** The islands have never mined enough, and most of it comes south through the Gate, which means the continent could squeeze the islands' silver any year it chose.
**Charts.** A chart without a Chartwrights' stamp is illegal for navigation. A chart with one is a weapon.

sections.title: The King Tide of 177 EC
paragraphs: The next King Tide is due in 177 EC, and the Reckoners are already pricing it. In a King Tide year insurance triples and the ports close for the Three Nights, when the deep climbs with the tide and the Veil thins. Coastal warehouses are emptied a season early, and every Flag on the Spire Floor is buying high ground.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Somebody has been buying coastal warehouses cheap all year, against the King Tide.” (a Goldwind factor)
“The convoys are slower this year, and the Rear Admirals have doubled the escorts without doubling the money.” (a Corvane post-captain)
“A ship sank off Southhaven last month in a flat calm, fully insured, and her cargo was sold in Hollowkey the week before.” (a Reckoners' wreck-clerk)
“The Company wants to call the board-price, and when it does, every price in the islands will change.” (a Spire Floor runner)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A cargo must cross two regions and arrive before the price falls, and a convoy is too slow.
The Reckoners want someone aboard a ship whose owner has insured her for twice her worth.
A Rear Admiral's convoy is short an escort, and the party's ship is armed.
A factor needs proof of where a cargo was really graded.
A Flag wants high ground on an island before the King Tide, and the island's owner will not sell.

title: Luxuries of the Isles
subtitle: What the rich buy to be seen buying, and where it comes from
summary: A luxury in Kalvatar is anything that sells for five or ten times its price at the source, and the islands have dozens: reefpurple and kelp-silk from the deep courts, pearls, sapphires, ambergris and scent, great vintages and aged kellum, jade, heartcedar, scrimshaw, champion Swiftcrests, and the great-aurocs that come south through the Gate.

epigraph.quote: A pearl is a pearl. A pearl that everyone saw you buy is a career.

facts: reefpurple, 30 Anchors a vial for one sash; kelp-silk, 20 Anchors a bolt
a black pearl, 1,000 Anchors and up
a Swiftcrest of champion blood, 5,000 Anchors
a great Sunhold vintage, 1 to 10 Anchors
a kin-knit sweater, a Vorthani four-handed heirloom, a named work, a companion that chose you
luxuries sell for five or ten times their price at the source

sections.title: The great luxuries
paragraphs: Where each comes from, what it costs, and who buys it.
list: **Reefpurple,** a vial for one sash. From the Coral courts, by Pelagar and Belmaris. 30 Anchors. Council seats and high clergy wear it by custom; anyone else risks the room going quiet.
**Kelp-silk,** a bolt. From the Glass Gardens. 20 Anchors. Heartland nobles and the Rose House.
**A perfect pearl.** From Pearl Groove and the Glass Gardens. 10 to 500 Anchors. Everyone with a neck.
**A black pearl.** From the deep courts. 1,000 Anchors and up. Collectors, and the Quiet Auction.
**A sapphire.** From the Sapphire Isle. 20 to 2,000 Anchors. The Jewelers' Guild sets the price, and everyone else pays it.
**Ambergris,** an ounce. From the ice. 10 Anchors. Every perfumer in the islands.
**Silverport scent,** a vial. From House Saffrane. 5 to 50 Anchors. The Heartland's salons.
**True Pocchin perfume,** a vial. From the Pocchin caravans. 20 to 200 Anchors. Noble boudoirs that do not ask where it came from.
**Greymoor coffee,** a pound. From Southhaven. 3 Tides in Goldwind. Anyone who wants to be seen keeping the boycott.
**Drinking-chocolate,** a cup. From southern cacao. A Tide in a Goldwind coffee-house. The fashionable, this season.
**A great Sunhold vintage.** From Sunhold. 1 to 10 Anchors a bottle. Weddings, treaties, and apologies.
**Goldcask kellum, aged twenty years.** From the Heartland stillhouses. 5 Anchors a bottle. Captains on the day they retire.
**Icebrand, the clear reserve.** From Kaldmark. 2 Anchors a bottle in Goldwind. People who want to talk about the ice without going.
**Jade, carved.** From the Confederacies. 5 to 500 Anchors. Heartland collectors, to the south's lasting disgust.
**A heartcedar chest.** From the south. 30 Anchors. Every bride with a dowry.
**Scrimshaw and ivory.** From the ice. 1 to 50 Anchors. Sailors, collectors, and nostalgic Fleetlords.
**Frosthold ice,** a block. From the ice. A Tide in Southhaven. Planters, to cool burnmouth in the still-heat.
**Stormglass.** From Stormreach's beaches, by the Galven. 5 to 50 Anchors. Lantern-makers and collectors.
**A Swiftcrest of champion blood.** From Jakupur. 5,000 Anchors. Gamblers who cannot afford to lose it.
**A great-auroc.** From Balmor and Amalor, through the Gate. 500 Anchors and up. Northern houses with a point to make.
**An Aurelion fine-work pistol.** From Aurelion. 200 Anchors and up. Captains, duelists, and House Faust's younger sons.
**A Highspire spyglass.** From Highspire. 100 Anchors. Every captain who has one, and every one who wants one.
**A Vorthani four-handed heirloom.** From the monasteries. Almost never sold at any price. Nobody, which is the point.

sections.title: What the rich buy, region by region
list: **On the Frontier:** Aurelion war-gear, great-aurocs, Free City pistols, Heartland wine, glazed windows, a Highspire spyglass, and a good seat at the Bastion tourney.

**In the Heartland:** reefpurple where custom allows, kelp-silk gowns, ambergris scents, a tamed saurian on a silver chain, a Swiftcrest in the Sunspine Run, a box at the Charter Match, a share in a coffee-house, Krysta charms, auroc-drawn carriages, and a great vintage opened in front of witnesses.
**In the south:** northern wine and cloth, Free City pistols, a Sukuun war-mount, books with the pages still uncut, Frosthold ice in a glass of burnmouth, and gold worn openly on the body.
**On the ice:** a timber house with glazed windows, southern coffee, Heartland wine, Aurelion harpoon-steel, fine wool, and a stove that does not smoke.

sections.title: What is never sold
list: **A kin-knit sweater.** To offer to buy one is an insult.
**A companion that chose you.** To offer to buy one is an insult.
**A lodge hound.** The Lodge assigns one.
**A Chartback Tortoise,** outside its three trades.
**A grommoth.** A Pocchin will sell you anything but this.
**A named work.** Wars are fought over them.
**A memory-pearl,** except as a court's gift. Any other memory-pearl is stolen.

sections.title: The false luxuries
paragraphs: Every luxury has its forgery, and the islands know them all.
list: **Dyed pearls,** sold as true.
**Horn,** sold as ivory.
**Cindren glass,** sold as sapphire.
**False Greymoor:** any coffee, stamped with the boycott's mark and sold at its premium.
**Watered kellum,** and goldcask that is two years old and not twenty.
**Pocchin perfume,** which is sometimes Silverport scent with a Pocchin label, and sometimes the other way round.

sections.title: As the salons tell it
paragraphs: In Goldwind's upper rings a luxury is a sentence in a language everyone speaks. A reefpurple sash says *I sit on the Council*, or *I would like you to think so*. A kelp-silk gown says *the Rose House sends me its dressmaker*. A black pearl says nothing at all, very loudly, and the people who know what it means leave early. A great Sunhold vintage opened in front of witnesses says *this is an apology*, and the witnesses are there to make sure it is accepted.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A Silverport scent and a Pocchin perfume were poured side by side at a salon last month, and nobody could tell them apart. The Perfumers left in a body.” (a Goldwind salon-hostess)
“A great-auroc came south through the Gate last spring with a Balmor brand and an imperial saddle.” (an Ironfort stable-hand)
“There are more black pearls in Goldwind this year than the deep courts have given up in a century.” (a Pearl Groove pearl-factor)
“The Jewelers' Guild has quietly raised the price of silver-work three times since spring.” (a Goldwind jeweler's apprentice)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A great vintage must be carried unbroken to a treaty-supper in Goldwind, and someone wants it broken.
A collector will pay anything for a carved jade that the Confederacy it came from wants back.
A black pearl has been delivered to the party by mistake, with an invitation.
A Swiftcrest of champion blood must be shipped from Jakupur to Goldwind alive and calm.
A perfumer needs a lump of ambergris before the Artisans' Faire, and the ice is a season short.

title: The Kalashtar
subtitle: The dreamers: humans who sleep with the door open
summary: No one is born a kalashtar. Every kalashtar was born human, and one night began to dream a place that was not theirs: the far shore, a country behind sleep that is not the Faewild, though the fae walk it freely. The dreams come back every night after that, and they leave a touch that does not wash off.

epigraph.quote: My mother asked the priest when it would pass. He said, the way the tide passes.

facts: the first true dream, most often between childhood and the first grown years
a faint light in the dark, and the color of the season they dream
less than other people, and dreaming every hour of it
Skaia, the Dreaming Sky, beside the faith they were raised in; they fear Naxithe the Dream-Eater above all
few; most islanders have met one, and fewer know it
born human, and some of them begin to dream

sections.title: The Opening
paragraphs: The first true dream is called **the Opening**, and every kalashtar remembers the night of it. It comes most often between childhood and the first grown years, sometimes later, rarely before seven or after thirty. It comes most often to those born or raised near a **thin place**, where the Veil wears through, and in a King Tide year more than in any other. A child who wakes from it weeping, or laughing, or speaking Lisseth she never learned, has opened, and the family knows it by morning.
It runs in some families more than chance allows. The children of a kalashtar are born human, like everyone else, and some of them begin to dream.

sections.title: The touch
paragraphs: What the far shore leaves behind.
list: **The eyes.** A kalashtar's eyes keep a faint light in the dark, and over the first year they take the color of the season the kalashtar dreams: green for the First Bloom, gold for the Burning Crown, red for the Red Harvest, white for the Long Silence. Most dream one season all their lives, and the color stays.

**The sleep.** They sleep less than other people, and dream every hour of it. A kalashtar kept from dreaming, by fever, by a sleeping-draught, or by a jailer who knows what he is doing, grows grey, then strange, then dangerous.

**The voice without ears.** Most can lay a thought in a mind nearby, as plain as a whisper and heard by no one else. The islands are not comfortable with it, and a kalashtar who does it uninvited at a lord's table will not be asked back.
**The Veil.** They feel a thin place the way a sailor feels a draft below decks. At the King Tide and the Still Days their dreams grow loud.
**The cold stone.** Krysta does nothing across the Veil, and a kalashtar finds it quiet and cold. On the nights they want to rest, some sleep with a stone in their hand, because it dulls the dreams.

sections.title: On the far shore
paragraphs: Kalashtar do not agree on what they dream. Some dream a court and its endless feast, some a forest that knows their name, some a sea that runs uphill. They say they meet one another there, and know one another on waking, and more than one kalashtar has married someone met first on the far shore.

The far shore is not the Faewild, whatever the old books say. Dreamers call it **the Roam**: open country behind sleep, with no lord and no fence, crossed by roads that run to everywhere a mind has ever been. It has the four seasons of the Courts, each in its own country, and a dreamer opens in one of them. The fae step into the Roam as easily as off a porch, and most of the folk a dreamer meets out there are fae a long way from home. No Court's law holds. There are way-houses, road-agents, staked claims, and whatever law the nearest person can enforce.

The fae notice their dreamers. A bargain struck in a dream is kept in the waking world, so every kalashtar learns the fae's rules early: never a true name, never a thank-you, every bargain counted three times. They have more reason than anyone.

sections.title: Faith and the islands
list: **Faith.** Most keep the faith they were raised in, and add **Skaia, the Dreaming Sky**, whose dream-readers in Greyhaven have counseled dreamers for as long as there have been dreamers. Above every other power they fear **Naxithe the Dream-Eater**, who rots the dreams Skaia keeps.

**The Concord.** A new kalashtar is blessed at a door in the name of **Varneth**, the Threshold Warden who watches the line, and his priests keep a roll of the dreamers in every Council port, by custom and not by law.
**The Registry.** The Arcane Registry has argued for forty years whether a dream is a working. It registers no kalashtar for dreaming, and registers every kalashtar who casts.
**Sailors** are split. Some say a kalashtar aboard dreams the wreck before it happens, and so the ship never meets it. Others will not sail with one at all.
**The south** knows them best, because the south has the most thin places. The chant-keepers say a kalashtar *sleeps with the door open*.

sections.title: Names, dress, and family
paragraphs: Kalashtar keep their human names, their human families, and their human lives; a Faust who begins to dream is still a Faust. Many are also given a name on the far shore. They give it only to other kalashtar, because a name given on the far shore is a true name.

Many wear something of their season: a green thread, a gold ring, a red scarf, a white stone. Smoked lenses at night hide the light in their eyes, and are the surest sign that someone has something to hide.

sections.title: Playing a kalashtar
paragraphs: A kalashtar is a human with something more. Ask yourself:
What season is in your eyes, and has anyone in the Courts noticed it?
Have you made a promise in a dream that someone in the waking world is now holding you to?
Did your family hope the dreams would pass?
Is there a dreamer you have met only on the far shore?
What do you see when you sleep beside a thin place?

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There is a dreamer in Goldwind whose eyes have no color at all, and the other kalashtar cross the street when she passes.” (a priest of Varneth)
“A kalashtar in Southhaven dreamed a ship's name three nights running. The ship came in on the fourth day, and nobody aboard had ever heard of her.” (a Southhaven harbor pilot)
“The Registry keeps a second roll of the dreamers, and it is not the priests' roll.” (a Goldwind clerk)
“Never let a kalashtar sleep in your house on the Still Days. Whatever comes for the dream comes through the door.” (a Greyhaven grandmother)

sections.title: At the table
paragraphs: A child has opened, and the family wants a dream-reader from Greyhaven before the neighbors notice.
A kalashtar has made a bargain in a dream, and a stranger has come to collect it.
Someone is drugging kalashtar to keep them from dreaming, and two of them have already gone strange.
A ship's captain will pay for a kalashtar to sleep aboard through the Widow's Teeth.
Two kalashtar who met only on the far shore want to find each other in the waking world.

title: Kalvatar in Ten Minutes
subtitle: Everything a new player needs before the first session
summary: A sea of more than five thousand islands, south of an empire nobody wants to go back to. Monsters own the wild places, magic is rare and watched, and the people who hunt the monsters carry a badge. This page is the short version; every part of it has a longer entry.

epigraph.quote: You don’t need the whole chart to leave harbor. You need the next three days of it.

facts: 1 Anchor is a laborer’s month, and a gold piece at the table
the King Tide, every three years; the next is 177 EC
the wild belongs to the Savage Lords

sections.title: 1. Where you are
paragraphs: Kalvatar is an archipelago on the world of Argentus, running south from the continent of Assios to the polar ice. The last census counted more than 5,800 islands, and nobody believes the count. The Council of the Charted Isles governs about one island in six. The rest is frontier, wild water, and rumor.

sections.title: 2. Why people came
paragraphs: About 190 years ago the houses that would not bow to the Imperium fled the continent and crossed south. The islands count their years from that Landing: this is 175 EC. The war on the continent has never ended, and the Imperium has never forgotten the islands.

sections.title: 3. The five regions
list: **Northern Frontier:** fortress-islands, horses, iron, and old feuds, nearest the continent.
**Central Heartland:** the rich middle, with Goldwind, the Council, the banks, and the University.
**Southern Wilds:** jungle, saurians, old tribes, and most of the map nobody has drawn.
**Icy Expanse:** whalers, sealers, and the deep holds under the ice.
**The Coral Kingdoms:** the courts under the water, which trade with the surface on their own terms.

sections.title: 4. The sea is big
paragraphs: Everything takes weeks. A voyage from the far Frontier to the ice takes five or six months without misadventure, and news is months old when it lands. A promise to be somewhere by a date is a serious promise.

sections.title: 5. The wild has owners
paragraphs: The great beasts of the islands are called the Savage Lords, and each rules a country of its own. People do not kill them. People learn their moods, stay off their ground, and pay for the mistake when they forget.

sections.title: 6. The Hunters
paragraphs: The Hunters are the guild that takes contracts on monsters, lost ships, and anything else too dangerous for a town watch. Most adventurers carry their badge. They rank by metal, Bronze to Platinum, and their Lodges stand in the great ports.

sections.title: 7. Magic is rare
paragraphs: Most islanders never see a true spell. Small magic, the Small Ways, is everywhere in daily life. Anything of the Third Circle or above is watched: in Council lands a caster is registered, ringed, and needs a Writ. Krysta, the crystal that holds magic, is the most wanted thing in the islands.

sections.title: 8. Money and time
paragraphs: Ten Bits make a Tide, ten Tides an Anchor, ten Anchors an Orsal. A laborer earns three Bits a day, about an Anchor a month. The year has ten months of thirty-six days, and five Still Days that belong to no month.

sections.title: 9. The King Tide
paragraphs: Every three years the sea rises for Three Nights, and things come up with it. The last King Tide was in 174 EC. The next is due in 177 EC, and every islander knows how far off it is.

sections.title: 10. Who you can be
paragraphs: Humans are the most numerous people, and far from the only one: the winged Aethyn, the Cindren, the Galven, the Tarvan, the Pocchin, the Sporrn, the coral peoples, and many more share the ports. Nearly everyone keeps a companion, a small animal with a job. Pick a people, pick a trade, and decide what you left behind to go to sea.

sections.title: Where to go next
paragraphs: The Start here tour reads the ten longer entries behind this page, in order. After that, read your own region and your own people.

title: The Warforged
subtitle: Made, not born, and nobody alive knows how
summary: A warforged is a made person: a body of metal, stone, and wood, older than any people of the islands. Nobody can build one now. Every warforged in Kalvatar was found asleep and woken, woke on its own, or has been awake for longer than anyone can check.

epigraph.quote: I asked it how old it was. It asked me how old the harbor was. Then it waited.

facts: very few; most islanders have never seen one
some lie still for ages and wake without warning
patience, long memory, and keeping their word

sections.title: At a glance
paragraphs: A warforged is built like armor with someone inside it: plates of metal and stone over a frame of dark wood, with a face that moves less than a person’s and eyes that give a little light. They eat nothing, tire slowly, and do not age in any way a physician can measure. The islands call them warforged because the first ones found were plainly built for war.

sections.title: How one wakes
list: **Found and woken.** Dug out of a ruin, hauled up in a net, or found standing in a sealed hall under the jungle, and woken by someone who did not know what they were doing.
**Woke on its own.** One day, for reasons it cannot give, it opened its eyes.
**Never slept.** A few say they have been awake all along. They are very old, and they remember more than they tell.

sections.title: What they carry
paragraphs: Most warforged remember nothing of their making. Some keep pieces: a voice that gave them their work, a sky that looked different, a war fought overhead.

A handful of people in the world can open a warforged and change what it was told to be. The islands call it **rewriting**. It is rare, costly, and dangerous, and to a warforged it is the one thing worse than being broken.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Most islanders have never seen a warforged, and a port that has one tends to remember its name.

Hunter crews value them: a warforged stands a night watch without complaint and walks into water that would drown a diver. Priests are less sure what to do with them. Some warforged pray, and say nothing answers.

sections.title: Known in 175 EC
paragraphs: **Crys** is a paladin of the oath of the ancients and a Hunter of some name in the south.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Whoever made them is gone, and the University won’t say who it was. I think the University knows.” (a Goldwind bookbinder)
“There are more of them asleep under the Wilds than awake above it. Whole halls, standing in rows.” (a Jakupur guide)
“They weren’t all made in the shape of people. A crew out of the south swears it saw a dragon of gilded metal that stood like a statue until it moved.” (a Hunter of the southern Board)

title: The Shifters
subtitle: Born with a beast in the blood
summary: A shifter is born, not bitten. Somewhere back in the family a beast got into the blood, and it shows: a tail, fangs, claws, eyes that catch the lamplight. Every shifter can let the beast rise for a short while, and then has to bring it back down.

epigraph.quote: My grandmother had the ears. My mother had nothing. I have the tail, and my mother still hasn’t forgiven either of us.

facts: to shifter families, and sometimes to families that thought the beast was gone
one or two each; no two shifters carry the same
the beast rises for a short while, then goes back down
everywhere, and most in the Southern Wilds
keen senses, quick tempers, and long family arguments

sections.title: At a glance
paragraphs: No two shifters carry the same marks, and most carry one or two: a tail, fangs, claws, a ridge of pelt along the spine, ears that turn on their own. The children of a shifter are often shifters and sometimes not, and sometimes the beast skips a generation and turns up in a grandchild nobody expected.

sections.title: The rising
paragraphs: Every shifter can let the beast up for a short while. The islands call it **shifting**. The marks grow and the body follows, with tougher hide, longer teeth, quicker feet, or a hunter’s senses. Then it goes back down, and the shifter is tired, hungry, and themself again. Most learn it as children. A shifter who cannot bring it back down is the thing every shifter family fears.

sections.title: What the beast gave
paragraphs: The islands sort shifters by what the beast gave them, not by which beast it was.
list: **Tooth:** fangs and jaw, a wolf’s, a shark’s, or a great cat’s.
**Stride:** legs and tail, a monkey’s, a goat’s, or a hare’s.
**Hide:** pelt and hide, a bear’s or a boar’s.
**Sense:** eyes, ears, and nose, a hound’s or an owl’s.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: The ports are used to shifters; inland villages less so. A tail is easy to hide under a coat and hard to hide in a bathhouse.
Hunter crews take shifters gladly: a nose, teeth, and night eyes are worth a share. Many shifters keep a quiet respect for the Savage Lords, the way a sailor respects a storm.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The beast in the blood is a Savage Lord’s. Live long enough in a Lord’s country and it gets into you, the same as it gets into the trees.” (a chant-keeper of the Southern Wilds)
“You can tell which Lord by the marks, if you know the old countries. I wouldn’t say it to a shifter’s face.” (a Hunter Scout)
“A shifter born a thousand leagues from any Lord has a grandparent who wasn’t.” (a Goldwind midwife)

title: The Cat-kin
subtitle: Nine lives, and counting down
summary: Quick, curious cat-folk of the southern ports and the jungle behind them. Every cat-kin is born owing nine lives to a luck spirit, and wears the count as a name.

epigraph.quote: Six left. Don’t ask about the other three unless you’re buying.

facts: every southern port, and the jungle behind it
balance, curiosity, and leaving by the window

sections.title: At a glance
paragraphs: The cat-kin are one of the old peoples of the south: furred, tailed, sharp-eared, and very hard to keep indoors. They come in two builds, and both turn up in the same litter. The small roof-folk of the ports stand no taller than a halfling. The long-limbed hunters of the jungle stand as tall as anyone.

sections.title: The count
paragraphs: A cat-kin is born owing nine lives to **Mishri the Nine-Lived**, a trickster spirit of luck, and pays one back each time death is cheated. The count is worn openly as a byname: Eight-Left, Six-Left, Three-Left. A low count is a boast and a warning at once. Nobody has met a cat-kin who admits to One-Left twice.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Ships hire cat-kin for the rigging and regret it only on payday. In the ports they keep to the rooftops and the night markets. In the jungle they live by tribe like their neighbors, and a cat-kin of the tribes names a homeland before anything else.
They pray to Fortura the way a gambler does: often, and with conditions.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Short and purring: Sashi, Nimsha, Jhirra, Kesh. After the name comes the count, a luck-name such as Twice-Landed, or the tribe.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “They don’t have nine lives. They have one, and the nerve of nine.” (a Southhaven bosun)
“Mishri keeps the count, not the cat. Ask one how many are left and watch them look at the sky first.” (a night-market cook)

title: The Pride-kin
subtitle: The loud law of the grass
summary: Tall, maned lion-folk of the southern savannas. A pride hunts, eats, and judges together, and settles its quarrels before the next meal.

epigraph.quote: We argue in front of everyone. It saves time, and it saves knives.

facts: the savannas, and the grass at the edge of the Bonewilds
the pride: a few families under one fire

sections.title: At a glance
paragraphs: The pride-kin stand a head above most folk, maned or sleek, golden to dust-brown, with a voice built for open country. They are a people of the grass and do not love walls, though plenty take a Hunter’s share or a caravan’s pay and see the ports for themselves.

sections.title: The pride
paragraphs: A pride is a few families that share one fire, one hunt, and one judgment. A quarrel inside the pride is settled before the next meal, aloud, in front of everyone. A quarrel with an outsider belongs to the whole pride, which is why travelers are careful how they bargain on the grass.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Prides trade hides, horn, and guard-work to the caravans that cross the savannas. Along the edge of the Bonewilds they keep to the grass and leave the white flats to those who have business there.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Open and rolling: Raoru, Harrun, Gaharra. The pride comes after the name, as in Raoru of the Long-Grass Pride, or the tribe if the pride runs with one.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A pride-kin alone in a port left the pride or lost it. Don’t ask which.” (a caravan master)
“They say the first roar on the grass was an answer to something out on the white flats, and the prides have been answering it since.” (a chant-keeper)

title: The Ivory-kin
subtitle: The south’s long memory
summary: Huge, grey, tusked folk who walk long circuits between the wells of the south. Each one carries a single memory for the whole herd, and keeps it as a name.

epigraph.quote: You write it down so you can forget it. We don’t have that luxury.

facts: the long roads of the savannas, from the Bonewilds to Mirrormere
the herd, and the circuit it walks
patience, memory, and never being hurried

sections.title: At a glance
paragraphs: The ivory-kin are the largest folk most islanders will ever share a road with: grey-skinned, tusked, long-nosed, and slow to anger. A herd walks the same circuit of wells and markets year after year, and the south sets its calendar by their passing.

sections.title: The remembering
paragraphs: At coming of age an ivory-kin is given one thing to remember for the herd: a drought, a debt, a road, a name. It is carried for life and worn as a name, as in Ombalo who Remembers the Dry Year. When one of them dies, the memory is handed on before the body is cold. A herd is a library that walks.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Caravans pay well to walk behind a herd, since nothing on the grass troubles one twice. Courts and trading houses send for an ivory-kin when two parties remember a bargain differently. The answer is slow, exact, and final.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Long and low: Ombalo, Tumbuu, Lombaru. The memory comes after the name, or the tribe for those who walk with one.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “They visit the titan bones on the white flats the way you’d visit a grave. I never heard one say whose.” (a Bonewilds guide)
“Somewhere there’s a herd that remembers the day the Orka fell. They’ve never been asked politely enough.” (a Southhaven archivist)

title: The Centaurs
subtitle: Wealth is distance covered
summary: Four-legged folk of the open grass. A herd owns no ground, remembers every well, and counts its wealth in the distance it has run.

epigraph.quote: You call it wandering. We call it checking on everything.

facts: the southern savannas, and a few herds in Northreach
endurance, archery, and strong opinions about fences

sections.title: At a glance
paragraphs: The centaurs are horse-bodied folk of the open country. A herd keeps no town and no field. It keeps a run: a great loop of grass, wells, and meeting-grounds that it covers in a year, and knows the way a farmer knows a furrow.

sections.title: The run
paragraphs: Wealth among centaurs is distance. A foal’s first full run is its coming of age, and the old are honored by how far they have gone. Nobody rides a centaur. The few folk who have been carried were carried once, as the payment of a debt, and do not joke about it.

sections.title: In the islands
paragraphs: Most herds run the southern savannas beside the pride-kin and the ivory-kin. A few crossed north long ago and run the gorse and heather of Northreach, where the stud-farms hire them as horse-masters. Neither side is quite sure who works for whom.

sections.title: Names
paragraphs: Striding names: Hathren, Stravan, Galleth. The herd comes after, as in Hathren of the Tall-Grass Herd, or the tribe the herd runs with.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “A herd that stops running has seen something on the road ahead. Ask them what before you go that way.” (a caravan scout)
“The Northreach herds came north by ship, standing up the whole crossing. They still haven’t forgiven the sea.” (a Bastion ostler)

title: The Slowwater
subtitle: The marsh that breathes
summary: A flooded plain in the western interior of the Wilds: knee-deep water for leagues, sawgrass taller than a person, and islands of trees. Its water rises and falls twice a day, and no tide reaches it.

epigraph.quote: When the water laughs, you’ve left. Until then, mind where you sit.

facts: Southern Wilds, between the jungle and the Nine Mouths
the Bogborn, lizardfolk, and the Reedskulls at the crossings
the Breath, slowfire, and islands that are not on yesterday’s count

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: The Slowwater lies between the jungle and the delta of the Nine Mouths. The water stands knee-deep for leagues and barely moves. Sawgrass grows taller than a person and cuts like its name, and the only high ground is the tree islands. The lizardfolk named it first, for the water, the way they name their own tribes.

sections.title: The Breath
paragraphs: Twice a day the water rises a hand’s width and falls again, though the sea is far off and no tide reaches the marsh. The locals call it the Breath and set their day by it. Ask whose breath, and they will tell you to mind your own.

sections.title: Seeing it
paragraphs: Travelers go by flat reed boat, poled or pulled by a murkstrider, and they go with a guide. The channels move. So, the guides say, do some of the islands.
The marsh ends where the water starts to run and make noise. That is the delta, and the delta belongs to the Laughing Flood.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “Count the islands when you camp and count them again at dawn. If there’s one more, don’t ask it anything. Go.” (a Bogborn guide)
“The Breath is the Mud That Breathes, doing what the name says. The whole marsh sits on its chest.” (a lizardfolk trader)

title: The Bogborn
subtitle: The Kin of the Slowwater
summary: Marsh families of the Slowwater, descended from settlers who went upriver to dodge the tax-collectors and never came out. They talk slowly, wrestle razorfins, and answer to no law but the family.

epigraph.quote: We ain’t slow. We’re just not goin’ anywhere you are.

facts: mostly human, with halflings and goblins mixed in
the Slowwater, in roosts up in the tree islands
slowfire, razorfin wrestling, and the reed collar

sections.title: At a glance
paragraphs: Outsiders call them the Bogborn. They call themselves the Kin. Every one of them wears a collar of braided reed, soaked in a bitter root that keeps the blood-flies off. The braid tells which family you belong to, and a Bogborn reads it before your face.
Their people came upriver in the first decades after the Landing, to keep their coin from the tax-collectors and their children from the levies. They liked it and stayed.

sections.title: The Slow Talk
paragraphs: The Bogborn speak slowly and take their time answering. Outsiders call it the Slow Talk and take them for fools. The Bogborn have never corrected anyone, and they have sold a great deal of slowfire that way.
The south argues between the chant-keepers’ law and the colonial courts. The Bogborn recognize neither. A matter is settled between families, on somebody’s deck.

sections.title: How they live
list: **Roosts:** stilt-houses up in the trees, with a deck at the front where everything important happens.
**Slowfire:** their marsh-cane liquor, illegal in every port and sold in every port.
**Razorfin wrestling:** the local sport. A champion is known by the fingers he is missing.
**Hand-fishing:** an arm goes into a hole in the mud and comes out with whatever bites.
**Murkstriders:** ridden, and used to pull the flat reed boats.
**Music:** gourd fiddle, jug, and the rib-board, a board of razorfin ribs scraped with a bone.
**The Morning Reckon:** each family counts the islands of its water at dawn. One too many, and the family moves that same day.
**The Big Sit:** once a year all the families gather for music, wrestling, and weddings, and every feud is on hold until it ends.

sections.title: Neighbors
paragraphs: The lizardfolk have been their partners for generations, and the Bogborn are the only warm-blooded folk who learned to bargain with them word for word. The Oruma of the delta buy their slowfire and hides and ask no questions.
The Reedskulls are another matter. The villages that refuse the orcs’ tribute are Bogborn villages, and the quarrel is over iron.

sections.title: Three of the Kin
list: **Maw Hobbin:** matriarch of the largest roost. She makes the best slowfire and settles the feuds between families.
**Dob Cray:** razorfin-wrestling champion, with seven fingers and proud of each one.
**Juny Oke:** the best guide in the marsh, fourteen years old. Hunters hire her and never ask her age twice.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “The old families can stay under longer than a body should, and their hands are cold when you shake on a deal.” (an Oruma boatman)
“A tax-collector went up the Slowwater in my grandfather’s day. He lives there now. Has grandchildren.” (a Southhaven clerk)

title: The Savannas
subtitle: The long grass of the south
summary: The open grass between the jungle’s edge and the white flats of the Bonewilds: herd country, crossed by long roads from well to well.

epigraph.quote: In the jungle you hear trouble first. Out here you see it a day off, and it sees you.

facts: bellowback herds, the long roads, and a sky with nothing in the way

sections.title: The place
paragraphs: Where the jungle thins, the grass begins, and it runs to the dead trees at the rim of the Bonewilds. There are flat-topped trees, red earth, dry riverbeds that fill in an hour when the rains come, and wells that are worth more than towns.
The savannas are the south’s pasture. Bellowbacks graze here in their thousands, and aurocs carry the herders who mind them.

sections.title: Who lives there
paragraphs: Three old peoples share the grass with the herding tribes. The **pride-kin** hunt it and guard what crosses it. The **ivory-kin** walk it in great slow circuits, and the south sets its calendar by their passing. The **centaurs** run it in herds that own no ground and remember every well.
A well belongs to whoever dug it and is open to whoever arrives thirsty. Fouling one is the worst crime the grass knows.

sections.title: The long roads
paragraphs: The roads of the savannas are not built. They are worn: by herds, by caravans, and by the ivory-kin, who have walked the same line for longer than anyone has kept count. They run from the Bonewilds to the Mirrormere, and caravans pay well to walk behind a herd.

sections.title: If you come from here
list: You can judge distance, weather, and the mood of a herd at a glance.
You know which wells are sweet, which are seasonal, and whose they are.
You have sat a night watch against something that never came into the firelight.
Walls make you restless, and the jungle makes you feel watched.

sections.title: Rumors
paragraphs: “There’s a well out past the last thorn-trees that fills on its own in the dry season. The centaurs go around it.” (a caravan scout)
“Before the rains, the whole grass goes quiet for one night. The herders say that’s the night the Shadow leaves the flats to drink.” (a bellowback herder)
